From roughing it to Arctic luxury: Two sisters and three countries in two weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

Greenland, Iceland and Norway offer some of the most cinematic landscapes on Earth. But travelling through them reveals three very different relationships with tourism – one thrust into the geopolitical spotlight, to tourism-savvy Iceland and the breathtaking beauty of Norway.
There are probably more glamourous ways to begin a luxurious Nordic adventure than boarding a crammed Ryanair flight at London Stansted, but that’s exactly how this adventure started – a once in a lifetime tour for two weeks.
My sister Nyeema and I were fairly certain they had squeezed a few more seats onto the aircraft since either of us last flew with them. But there we were, two British sisters embarking on a girls-only holiday that would take us through Greenland, Iceland and Norway – from the decidedly and deliberately non-luxurious to the seriously expensive, with an extraordinary amount packed in between.
By the end, we decided we could describe each destination in just three words.
For Nyeema, Nuuk was “remote, dystopian and mesmerising”. Mine were “sci-fi, raw and out-of-this-world”.
Reykjavík? She chose “charming, colourful and vibrant”. I went for “fresh-fishy, stunning and commercial”.
And Norway?
“Picturesque, historic and rainy,” according to my sister.
For me: “Luxurious, fairytale and quality.”
Those words turned out to say rather more about our journey than we realised.
Greenland: Raw, beautiful and suddenly everyone is talking about it
After a quick stopover in Copenhagen, we headed for Nuuk, Greenland’s capital, arriving to a spectacular bright daytime sky after midnight and a landscape that immediately felt unlike anywhere else.
There is undoubtedly something almost otherworldly about Greenland.
The scale, silence, water and mountains, punctuated by tiny splashes of colourful buildings, can make you feel as though you have landed on a film set... or the moon.
Filmmakers have already discovered it. Borgen: Power & Glory, starring Sidse Babett Knudsen put Greenland at the heart of a story about resources, Denmark and competing global interests in the Arctic.
Watching the real Greenland, those themes suddenly don’t seem particularly fictional.
Because one man seemed to be everywhere we went.
Donald Trump.
We had travelled to Greenland expecting to talk about landscapes, ice, culture and Arctic tourism. Instead, the US President’s name followed us around Nuuk.
Restaurants. Shops. Museums. Conversations with people we met and everybody seemed to have an opinion.
Some people we spoke to believed Trump’s repeated interest in taking control of Greenland had inadvertently done the country a favour. Whatever they thought of his politics, they liked the attention he had brought – and some thought it could ultimately benefit tourism.
A few were surprisingly relaxed, even telling us they didn’t particularly care if America took over. Most of the people we encountered, however, hated the idea.
What fascinated me was that a US president thousands of kilometres away had somehow become part of the everyday experience or travelling through Greenland.
We met Alice Burton, a former Head of Press Section at the US Embassy in Vienna, in our shared accommodation, who would become our partial travel companion, who had been hearing similar things from the locals.
“Nuuk is the most quiet capital I’ve ever visited,” she told me.
There are for sure few cars, little honking, hardly any sirens and remarkably few people on the streets.
“A world in itself,” Alice reflected.
Yet politically, Greenland now feels anything but isolated.
Official tourism research estimated that just over 149,000 international tourists visited Greenland in 2024, with almost two-thirds arriving by cruise ship. Nuuk’s international airport is meanwhile transforming access to the capital.
For a destination with a population of fewer than 60,000 people, those numbers really matter.
What tourists don’t necessarily see in Greenland
It was how strongly I sensed a “them and us” relationship between Greenlanders and the Danes.
Along with Donald Trump, the divide surfaced in conversations with people we met unprompted, and in the way some Greenlanders spoke about Denmark, language, history and identity.
These individuals are not a measure of wider public opinion, but the sense of separation was striking – especially in the museums we visited.
Rather than presenting visitors with a sanitised Arctic idyll, Nuuk’s cultural institutions openly explore Greenland’s complicated relationship with Denmark.
Alice, Nyeema and I were all particularly struck by Nuna, an exhibition at Nuuk Art Museum examining land, identity and Greenland’s relationship with outside powers. At its entrance was a message requiring little explanation.
'Greenland is not for sale'
Talk to people and another Greenland begins to emerge – a society having its own conversation about identity, autonomy and Denmark while simultaneously confronting extraordinary new interest from the outside world.
Climate change, military security, natural resources, Indigenous identity, tourism and the interests of global powers increasingly collide here.
And yet everyday life carries on around the geopolitical noise.
On the water, however, there are bright blue mini-icebergs, mountains rising directly from the waves, rocks, sky and sea stretching into the distance and an undeniable silence, exactly the Greenland one imagines.
Perhaps “out of this world” wasn’t such an exaggeration after all.
Iceland: When tourism becomes a well-oiled machine
Arriving in Reykjavík after Greenland felt like jumping several stages forward in the evolution of a tourism industry.
If Greenland feels like a destination being on the cusp of something, Iceland has had years to work out what international visitors want.
And it shows.
The statistics underline just how important tourism has become. Statistics Iceland recorded an estimated 10.16 million overnight stays in registered accommodation in 2025, up 9.1% in a year.
Tourism directly accounted for 8.8% of Iceland’s GDP in 2025, while tourism consumption by domestic and international visitors reached almost ISK 914 billion, which equates to over 6.5 billion euros.
Those are substantial numbers for a small island nation and as a traveller, you can see the sophisticated industry that has grown around them.
Reykjavik is charming and colourful but also extremely tourism-savvy.
Excursions are offered everywhere and so are restaurants, shops selling Icelandic designs, outdoor clothing galore, Viking paraphernalia and row upon row of traditional woollen jumpers.
The latter look as they are going to itch and after my sister and I tried on a very wide variety of designs, we realised that they didn’t.
They do, however, shed hair like a loveable dog.
And then there was the food.
Fish was a highlight: extraordinarily fresh cod, tasting unlike any cod that you will be served in the UK, despite it being renowned for fish and chips.
There’s also smoked salmon, shrimp and warming soup served inside a bread bowl.
For the more adventurous, menus can venture into horse, whale steak and slithers of smoked puffin.
Iceland has become extremely good at turning what makes it distinctive into an experience visitors can easily access, but there is, however, one unavoidable issue.
It is very expensive.
But again, as in Greenland, there is no ignoring the disappearing glaciers, pollution of the oceans and land and the doom of climate change and for a country so dependent on both tourism and fishing, these aspects are difficult to ignore.
And perhaps at that is the contradiction at the heart of Iceland’s success. It has become supremely good at selling the experience of Iceland. But the thing that everybody has fundamentally travelled there for is something nobody has created.
Nature.
Our own excursion beyond Reykjavik may have had us packed together liked sardines, but once the city disappeared behind us it became increasingly difficult for us to complain.
Iceland straddles the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. Fissures cut through the landscape, geothermal activity bubbles beneath it and volcanoes, waterfalls and vast expanses of open land make it feel as though the planet is showing.
Hollywood clearly agrees.
Game of Thrones turned Icelandic landscapes into territory north of “the Wall”, while Christopher Nolan transformed parts of the country into another planet for Interstellar starring Matthew McConaughey and Anne Hathaway. The Star Wars universe has also found a home within Iceland’s otherworldly scenery.
Norway: When expensive starts to feel worth it
Bergen greeted us with torrential rain, which cleared the following morning.
We wanted to travel from Bergen through Myrdal to Flam, but there was one problem, and that was the direct trains we wanted were all sold out, but we found an alternative router from Bergen towards Myrdal via Voss, before joining the famous Flam Railway.
Mountains stretched beyond what the eye – or an iPhone camera – could properly absorb.
Water cascading from waterfalls and wild rivers, tiny settlements beneath enormous peaks.
The Flam Railway runs for around 20 kilometres through spectacularly dramatic mountain scenery towards the fjord below and has become one of Norway’s best-known rail experiences.
Hollywood has also exploited this country with good reason. Tom Cruise has repeatedly returned with the Mission Impossible franchise. Mission Impossible: Fallout features the spectacular clifftop finale at Preikestolen with Cruise and Henry Caville and in Dead Reckoning, Cruise launched a motorcycle from Helsetkopen. Daniel Craig’s final James Bond film, No Time to Die, also used Norwegian locations, as did the hit series Succession, featuring Brian Cox and Jeremy Strong.
The price of luxury
Norway is also expensive, but tourist don't appear to be staying away.
Norwegian commercial accommodation recorded 40.6 million guest nights in 2025 up 5.2% in a year.
International visitors accounted for a record 14.2 million guest nights – an increase of 14% – and around three quarters of foreign guest nights came from European markets.
Germany was the largest overseas market, followed by Sweden, the Netherlands, the UK and Denmark.
Bergen itself is flourishing, with the wider region recording around three million commercial guest nights in 2024, 13.5% higher than in 2019.
Eirik Gjøvåg Berge, Chief Communications Officer at Visit Bergen, told Euronews that it is important to distinguish between Norway’s reputation for high prices and what visitors are actually doing.
He points out that the evidence, does not suggest high costs are driving international travellers away.
“In fact, favourable exchange rates for many international visitors, combined with Norway's strong appeal as a nature and experience destination, have helped drive continued growth,” he says.
Does quality justify the price?
Hilde Berentsen, General Manager of Home Hotel Havnekontoret, seems to think so. “If you pay for a service then you can have a higher quality,” she told me. “If you always go for the cheapest thing, then you don’t have quality around you.”
Berentsen has watched Bergen’s tourism industry develop since the hotel opened in 2006.
One of its first celebrity guests was football legend Diego Maradona, who stayed with his team and the hotel has subsequently attracted considerable publicity for its luxury suite, which became known as Bergen’s most expensive hotel room. More famous guests have since followed suit.
“Everything cannot be for everybody,” she said, pointing to camping, caravans and cheaper accommodation as alternative ways of experiencing the country.
According to Visit Bergen, tourism supports around 13000 jobs and generates approximately more than 617 million euros (NOK 6.7 billion) in annual value creation.
Three countries, three very different versions of northern tourism.
By the time my sister and I had reached the end of our journey, that decidedly non-luxurious flight out of Stansted seemed a very long way away.
We had travelled through three countries united by extraordinary natural beauty but offering remarkably different experiences.
There were no Mediterranean beaches, no sun loungers and frankly, not a great deal of sun on this holiday.
Instead, there were fjords, mountains, volcanoes, waterfalls, tectonic plates, Viking jumpers, fresh fish, packed trains, unexpected friendships and Donald Trump.
Two sisters beginning this journey with no expectations, but the end allowing three words to describe each location, but probably, they were nearly not enough.

How the ECB rate hike will affect mortgage borrowers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:00:20 UTC
14:00:20 KST

The ECB’s decision was largely priced in before it was announced, but mortgage rates could rise further across the eurozone’s biggest economies as banks respond to persistent inflation and elevated market rates.
Mortgage rates have continued to climb across the eurozone’s four biggest economies since August, although the effect of the European Central Bank’s latest interest-rate increase varies significantly between countries.
Quoted fixed rates now range from around 2.2% in Spain to an average of 4.46% in Germany, although the figures cover different mortgage terms and are therefore not directly comparable.
The ECB’s latest increase was largely priced into mortgage offers before it was announced, brokers said. Banks in France, Italy and Spain had already anticipated the decision, while German mortgage rates continued to follow 10-year government bond yields more closely.
The increases follow a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields examined by Euronews Business in August. Higher government borrowing costs have already fed into mortgage offers in Germany and, indirectly, Italy, while French and Spanish rates remain more closely linked to ECB expectations.
French mortgage rates could approach 4%
French mortgage rates rose by 10 basis points in early September, taking the average rate on a new 20-year fixed mortgage from 3.44% in August to around 3.54%, according to Pierre Chapon, co-founder of mortgage broker Pretto.
Chapon said banks had already priced in the ECB’s decision but could raise rates again before the central bank’s next meeting.
“We expect the same range of increase next month as the inflation trend continues,” he said, referring to a possible rise of another 10–20 basis points.
France is an overwhelmingly fixed-rate mortgage market, with such products accounting for 99.6% of new housing loans in the latest available Banque de France data.
Pretto said the average rate on a 20-year fixed mortgage could reach 3.8%–4% by the end of the year if inflation does not ease.
A rise from the current 3.54% to 3.9% would add about €37 to the monthly repayment on a new €200,000 mortgage over 20 years. It would also increase the total interest bill by approximately €8,930.
French banks are not tightening their lending conditions, according to Pretto. It said strong balance sheets, relatively cheap deposits and fierce competition in a subdued mortgage market were helping to protect borrowers.
Italian variable-rate borrowers face a quicker impact
In Italy, the ECB increase is expected to have a more immediate effect on variable-rate mortgages.
“Following today’s decision, we expect the average nominal interest rate, or TAN, on new 20- and 30-year variable-rate mortgages to rise from approximately 2.80%, recorded during the first weeks of September, to around 3.05% over the coming weeks,” Nicoletta Papucci, marketing director at MutuiOnline.it, told Euronews Business.
A 25-basis-point increase would add approximately €25 to the monthly repayment on a €200,000 variable-rate mortgage with 20 years remaining, assuming it is passed through in full. That is equivalent to just under €6,000 in additional interest over the period.
Fixed-rate mortgages, which accounted for 92.2% of Italian mortgage applications in 2026, respond more closely to long-term euro interest-rate swaps than to individual ECB decisions.
Nevertheless, MutuiOnline expects the average rate on new 20- and 30-year fixed mortgages to rise from 3.46% in August to about 3.75% by the end of 2026. On a new €200,000 mortgage over 20 years, that would add around €30 to the monthly repayment and approximately €7,200 to the total interest bill.
Italian mortgage pricing had already been affected by rising government bond yields and, more directly, by higher long-term swap rates. Banks raised rates on different fixed-rate products by between 10 and 40 basis points during August and early September.
The increases also affected green mortgages, “which had previously been among the most competitively priced products”, Papucci said.
A significant part of the repricing had therefore taken place before the ECB’s decision. However, MutuiOnline has not observed widespread increases in deposit requirements or significant restrictions on credit.
Spanish mortgage rates could rise further
Fixed mortgage rates in Spain remain below 3%, but brokers expect some lenders to increase their offers following the ECB decision.
A significant part of the latest rise had already been priced into fixed-rate offers because Euribor, the benchmark used for many Spanish mortgages, had anticipated the ECB’s move several weeks earlier.
Since the previous ECB increase in June, rates on popular 30-year fixed mortgages have risen from around 2%–2.5% to approximately 2.2%–2.8%, according to Spanish mortgage broker iAhorro.
Initial rates on mixed mortgages — which are fixed for a certain period before becoming variable — have increased from around 1.85% to approximately 2%–2.1%.
Spokesperson Laura Martinez told Euronews Business that “several lenders will likely revise their mortgage products upward in the coming weeks”.
She expects increases of up to 0.5 percentage points at some banks, although others may raise rates by a more moderate 0.2 percentage points or hold them steady to attract customers and meet year-end sales targets.
For a €200,000 mortgage over 30 years, iAhorro calculated that the rise in Euribor from 2.172% in September 2025 to a provisional 3.101% in September 2026 would increase repayments by €98.92 a month, or €1,187.03 a year.
That calculation reflects the full year-on-year rise in Euribor, rather than the effect of the ECB’s latest 25-basis-point increase alone.
Borrowers with Euribor-linked mortgages due for review in September will feel the increase first. Those reviewed between October and December could follow, with repayments rising by around €100 a month if Euribor remains above 3.1%.
Competition between Spanish banks nevertheless remains strong. At iAhorro, mixed-rate products accounted for 52% of completed mortgages in August, with almost all the remainder on fixed rates and variable-rate products representing a negligible share.
German mortgages continue to follow Bund yields
German fixed mortgage rates continue to be driven more by government bond yields and other long-term market rates than by individual ECB decisions.
“The markets had already priced in the second rate hike this year, so it had no impact on government bond yields and, consequently, on mortgage rates,” Michael Neumann, chief executive of Dr Klein Privatkunden, told Euronews Business.
Dr Klein said its best available rate for a 20-year mortgage had risen from 3.99% to 4.24% over the previous month. For a €200,000 mortgage, this would add about €42 to the monthly repayment.
Neumann nevertheless expects mortgage rates to stabilise and move broadly sideways over the rest of the year.
Another brokerage in Germany, Interhyp, said its average rate for a 20-year fixed mortgage had risen from 4.32% in mid-August to 4.46%. “Since the outbreak of the Iran conflict at the end of February, rates for 20-year fixed-rate mortgages have increased by around 0.5 percentage points, from approximately 3.9% to around 4.4%."
Interhyp attributed the increase to inflation concerns, elevated energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty, which have pushed up long-term bond yields and lenders’ funding costs.
It said the outlook remained highly uncertain: its panel of experts was almost evenly divided between those expecting German mortgage rates to rise, remain stable or decline by the end of the year.
Despite the higher cost of borrowing, both German brokers said demand for home ownership remained strong. However, rising rates and high transaction costs were making purchases increasingly difficult to afford.

Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz following the launch of the latest bout of unprovoked American-Israeli aggression against the country on February 28.
The Islamic Republic and the United States agreed on a 60-day reopening period as part of a Pakistan-mediated memorandum of understanding in June.
Iran took measures to ensure safe and legal transit through the chokepoint in keeping with the understanding, but American violations forced the country to reestablish the closure.

“Under these circumstances, we are entitled to take measures to protect the country’s security,” he stated.
The waterway became “somewhat safer” following the Islamabad MoU, the spokesman noted, adding that Iran honored its commitments after the understanding, while the United States violated its own commitment 23 days later.
“Their (the Americans’) pretexts [for committing the violations] had no basis,” Baghaei said.

Corruption probe rocks Bolsonaro son’s presidential campaign weeks before Brazil vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:58:20 UTC
13:58:20 KST

Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro is facing an investigation into alleged corruption and money laundering, shaking the right-wing campaign just weeks before the country’s October election.
A newly released court document shows police have been investigating the 45-year-old senator since July over possible crimes linked to financing the production of a forthcoming film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Police carried out dozens of raids Thursday as part of a broader investigation into the alleged embezzlement of public funds by the company producing the film, Dark Horse, which stars US actor Jim Caviezel as Jair Bolsonaro.
“I have nothing to hide. The film is completely legal,” Flavio Bolsonaro said at a campaign event Friday.
Film financing under scrutiny
According to court documents, investigators believe Flavio Bolsonaro met several times with Daniel Vorcaro, the fraud-accused head of the collapsed Banco Master, to discuss financing for the film.
Investigators are also examining the transfer of $12.3 million from a company indirectly linked to Vorcaro to another company connected to an attorney for Flavio’s younger brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro.
Police said Thursday’s raids targeted, among others, Karina Gama, head of the company producing the film, and pro-Bolsonaro congressman Mario Frias, who is listed as its executive producer. Both have been barred from leaving Brazil while the investigation continues. Frias has denied wrongdoing and called the probe a “smoke screen.”
Police officials said the money under investigation came from parliamentary funds available to lawmakers for special projects, often in their electoral strongholds.
Bolsonaro and Lula remain neck-and-neck
The investigation comes as Flavio Bolsonaro and leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva remain closely matched ahead of the Oct. 4 first-round vote.
Flavio entered the presidential race after his father was jailed for attempting a coup following the 2022 election. He has presented himself as a more moderate version of Jair Bolsonaro while campaigning on crime, corruption, food prices and public debt under the slogan of “God, country, family and freedom.”
Lula, meanwhile, has made tackling organised crime a central campaign issue, while Flavio accuses the incumbent of failing to take violence seriously enough.
Political scientist Mayra Goulart of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro said corruption scandals could hurt Lula more broadly, but new evidence involving Flavio could affect voters whose preferences remain undecided.
An investigation does not prevent Flavio Bolsonaro from running for president. If neither candidate wins an outright majority on October 4, Brazil will hold a runoff on October 25.

Johnson is planning a vote next week on legislation addressing data-center energy costs but has not indicated plans for broader AI regulation before Nov. 3, the day of highly anticipated US midterm elections, with hundreds of Senate and House seats hanging in the balance.

Addressing religious scholars, intellectuals and businesspeople in India on Friday, President Pezeshkian argued that history shows that bullies, oppressors and those who rely on force eventually face defeat or destruction. He said individuals, families and rulers would be accountable for how they treated other people and whether they helped those in need.
The president said Iran’s resistance to the United States and the Israeli regime is rooted in its opposition to bullying and its support for oppressed people. He rejected the idea that a powerful government should be entitled to impose its will on other nations or compel them to follow its decisions.
He also said the United States is seeking to prevent nations from becoming independent, saying pressure, conflict and efforts to create divisions in Iran had increased since the victory of the Islamic Revolution in 1979. He stressed that nations and individuals have equal rights and should be able to live together through justice and fairness.
President Pezeshkian said the teachings of prophets across different communities have centered on establishing justice and preventing oppression. He referred to Quranic teachings that every community had a messenger and that prophets were sent to help establish truth and justice among people.
The president said all people were originally one community and that guidance was intended to resolve disputes fairly, prevent conflict and ensure that justice prevailed in society. In his interpretation, differences emerged when people allowed selfishness and personal interests to replace truth, leading to division, oppression and the abuse of power.
President Pezeshkian said the essence of the straight path is to act justly, avoid wrongdoing, respect the rights of others and serve people. He emphasized that these principles should apply to everyone regardless of religion, belief, ethnicity, gender or nationality.
He also explained the concept of piety, saying that a pious person is one who moves toward a goal without wrongdoing or deviation. From this perspective, he said, people are judged by their conduct and commitment to justice rather than by their identity or background.
Referring to the Quran’s teachings about social responsibility, President Pezeshkian highlighted the importance of helping orphans, supporting the poor and standing beside those who suffer injustice. He said religious practice cannot be separated from service to people and protection of vulnerable members of society.
Moreover, President Pezeshkian called on Iranian and Indian manufacturers and traders to expand healthy economic relations, saying stronger interaction can contribute to growth, development and public welfare. He expressed hope that cooperation would help create societies free from oppression, exploitation and colonial domination.

Death toll from Philippines ferry fire rises to 35, as officials warn toll will grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:53:10 UTC
13:53:10 KST

The bodies of passengers killed in a ferry fire off the Philippines arrived at a port near the resort town of Coron, Palawan, on Saturday morning, as the country’s coast guard warned the death toll of 35 would grow.
Tents were being set up to receive 30 bodies brought from the M/V June Aster, which ran aground near the tourist hotspot after a fire erupted on Wednesday evening and tore through the vessel “in seconds”.
Coast guard spokesperson Noemie Cayabyab told a Saturday press conference the remains would be turned over to police forensic investigators for “proper disposition and identification” before allowing local authorities to inform family members.
“Currently, we are focused on the retrieval, and after that we will proceed with the investigation,” she said, confirming the bodies had been found in the ship’s economy accommodation area.
Police investigators were seen arriving at the port shortly after the press conference ended.
Asked how many bodies remained aboard the ship, she said authorities would provide an update later in the day.
Cayabyab told AFP on Friday evening that the first transfer had been capped at 30 bodies because of the capacity of the patrol vessel transporting them and that additional cadavers remained on the ferry.
Five others had been confirmed dead in the immediate wake of the fire.
Photos released by the coast guard showed rows of body bags being placed into a small ship alongside men in hazmat suits. Thirty passengers and 13 crew have so far been rescued, while 54 people remain unaccounted for.
On Friday, Cayabyab had told a radio station the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.
“From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly,” she said of survivors’ accounts.
“Everything happened in seconds,” she said, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on lifejackets.
Myra Cabilan said she had flown to Coron to find her missing brother, 40-year-old Rammel Gonzaga, who had taken the ferry from Manila on a business trip with his brother-in-law.
“His wife had just given birth a month ago. He was so happy he was given a daughter,” Cabilan said, fighting back tears.
“At dawn, I still believed he survived. But he’s still missing. I have lost hope.”
Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.
The ferry’s manifest listed 134 crew and passengers, but two had not boarded, according to the coast guard. The ferry was also carrying goods, an electric vehicle, a pickup truck, and motorcycles.
The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas.
Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country’s more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.
On Thursday, the company that owns the M/V June Aster, Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc, said it was fully cooperating with the investigation.

Russia deploys highest number of nuclear warheads in nine years – SIPRI
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
07:47:00 EEST
13:47:00 KST

Russia deploys highest number of nuclear warheads in nine years – SIPRI
Russia has increased the number of nuclear warheads deployed on launchers and ready for use for the fourth consecutive year. The figure has reached its highest level since 2017 amid increasingly frequent nuclear threats by Russian officials against European countries.
Source: The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI)'s 2026 annual report, World Nuclear Forces
Details: According to SIPRI analysts, as of January 2026, Russia's nuclear arsenal consisted of 5,420 warheads. Of these, 2,604 were held in central storage, 1,020 were considered retired and 1,796 warheads were deployed on launchers.
The number of warheads deployed on launchers in Russia has steadily increased since the beginning of the full-scale war against Ukraine. There were 1,588 in 2022, 1,674 in 2023, 1,710 in 2024 and 1,718 in 2025.
Compared with 2020, the Kremlin has increased the number of deployed nuclear warheads by 14%, the highest figure since 2017, when there were 1,950.
By comparison, the US, which has a similarly sized arsenal, has not changed the number of its deployed warheads. The figure remains at 1,770.
France and the UK have also kept their figures unchanged, with 280 and 120 deployed warheads respectively.
China, meanwhile, increased the number of its deployed warheads from 24 to 34, out of a total arsenal of 620.
In 2025, India deployed 12 nuclear warheads on nuclear-powered submarines for the first time. Analysts estimate that New Delhi's total nuclear arsenal stands at 190 warheads.
SIPRI experts noted in its analysis of Russia's nuclear triad that Russia's land-based forces can carry up to 1,092 warheads. At present, around 892 warheads are deployed on intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The Russian Navy has 13 strategic submarines with a combined capacity of 928 warheads. As two submarines are undergoing major refits, the actual number of deployed warheads available to the fleet is 704.
Another 586 warheads are deployed on Russia's strategic bombers. SIPRI analysts noted that in 2025, the Russian Aerospace Forces suffered operational losses following attacks by Ukraine's defence forces on Russian air bases.
This forced the Russian military command to disperse a significant number of Tu-160/M and Tu-95MS aircraft to the remote Belaya air base in Irkutsk Oblast, Dyagilevo air base in Ryazan Oblast and Olenya air base in Murmansk Oblast.
The institute's experts point out that Russia's nuclear modernisation programme is facing significant delays due to Western sanctions, industrial inefficiency and the prioritisation of conventional weapons production for the war in Ukraine. Despite this, Moscow continues to deploy new systems, such as Oreshnik missile systems, including in Belarus.
The report also recorded growing secrecy surrounding nuclear arsenals around the world. This has been influenced by the expiry in February 2026 of the Russian-US Treaty on Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms (New START), which was not extended.
Quote: "While the global total inventory of nuclear warheads continues to fall as retired weapons are gradually dismantled, year-on-year increases can be seen in the number of operational (stockpiled) nuclear warheads. This trend seems likely to continue and will probably accelerate in the coming years."
Background:
- In November 2024, Russia updated its nuclear doctrine, expanding the list of scenarios in which the use of weapons of mass destruction could be considered.
- In February 2026, the New START Treaty expired. The agreement was not replaced by a new treaty, depriving the international community of an important source of transparency.
- In addition, Russian and Belarusian leaders have repeatedly claimed that tactical nuclear weapons, Iskander systems and Oreshnik missiles have been deployed in Belarus.

‘The family paid the price’: India’s deadly online gambling crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:46:56 UTC
13:46:56 KST

‘The family paid the price’: India’s deadly online gambling crisis
Debts and deaths are mounting, as a soaring online gambling industry adapts to evade an Indian government ban.
Nizamabad, India – When Harish began betting online, his family did not imagine that a smartphone would eventually consume their savings, land and, ultimately, their lives.
The 22-year-old from Yedapally village in the Nizamabad district of India’s southern Telangana state started betting online during the COVID-19 pandemic. What began with small wagers gradually turned into heavy losses and borrowing.
Police say Harish eventually spent about 1.8 million rupees (more than $21,000 in 2024) on betting and borrowed money from at least 12 people in his village.
His parents tried to rescue him from the growing debt. His father, Ranganaveni Suresh, 53, was a farmer who also ran a grocery shop. His mother, Hemalatha, 45, worked alongside him. The family sold a plot of land to repay some of what Harish owed. It was not enough. As the debts mounted, Harish and his mother began working for a caterer to raise money. But the pressure continued to grow.
On October 3, 2024, Harish and his parents died by suicide at their home. “We did not know how much money he had borrowed until people started coming to our house asking for their money back. By then, the situation was already out of control,” said Mukesh Kumar, a cousin of Harish.
It is a refrain that is increasingly echoing across India, as the country grapples with the growing and fast-adapting challenge of an online gambling addiction crisis. The country had about 591 million gamers in 2024, according to an industry report. India’s online gaming sector generated about $3.7bn that year — a figure that was then projected to more than double to $9.1bn by 2029. Gaming involving money accounted for about 86 percent of the industry’s revenue in 2024.
In 2025, the Indian Parliament passed a law banning all online gaming involving money, trying to plug regulatory gaps that platforms pushing internet betting were exploiting. However, smartphones, global connectivity and a black market ecosystem have allowed online gambling to shapeshift and survive.
How online gambling works
The deaths in Yedapally offered India a glimpse of the risks surrounding its expanding online betting economy, where the promise of quick money can draw young users into repeated wagers, losses and debt.
Betting no longer requires a bookmaker, a cash transaction or a visit to a betting shop. It can happen on a smartphone, often while a cricket match is playing and advertisements promising winnings appear on the same screen.
For some users, a few hundred rupees lost becomes another wager to recover it. That wager can become a loan, and the loan can become a debt that reaches far beyond the person who placed the bet.
The first encounter with online betting does not always look like gambling. For a young cricket fan, it can begin with fantasy sports or a prediction game. The language is about knowledge, competition and skill. Advertisements are bright and polished, and often appear alongside the sport itself. India’s enormous smartphone and gaming market has provided fertile ground for the business.
Behind the legitimate gaming economy is a much harder-to-track illegal market. A 2025 report by public-policy organisation CUTS International estimated that the 15 largest unauthorised online betting platforms received more than 5.4 billion visits from India during the 2024-25 financial year. It estimated annual deposits on illegal gambling platforms at about $100bn and documented the use of phone banking, mule bank accounts and mobile applications to move money. The figure is an estimate rather than an official measurement of India’s gambling market, but it illustrates the scale of demand facing regulators.
The money is generated through several layers of the online betting economy. Operators earn from amounts users stake or lose, while legal gaming platforms have built businesses around entry fees and commissions. Advertising, celebrity endorsements, affiliate networks and user acquisition add further commercial incentives.
Just one such gambling app, Mahadev Online, is estimated to have generated about 430 billion rupees (about $5bn) over seven years, according to prosecution documents filed by India’s financial crimes agency, the Enforcement Directorate. But while at one end are enormous sums flowing through betting networks, at the other are families struggling to understand where their money went.
When winning and losing become an obsession
In Hyderabad, the capital of Telangana, Selam Manoj, a 20-year-old aeronautical engineering student, died by suicide in February 2024 after reportedly becoming addicted to online games and betting. His father told police that Manoj had borrowed 300,000 rupees (about $3,600) from friends.
The family repaid the debt, but Manoj died by suicide. In another Telangana case, 27-year-old cattle-feed trader Balagoni Pavan Kumar accumulated hundreds of thousands of rupees in betting losses. Police said his father had previously cleared his debts and warned him to stop. However, the betting continued. Pavan Kumar later died by suicide.
“The betting did not affect only him. The whole family paid the price. We lost our peace, our savings and the future we had planned,” said Kalpana, his sister.
These cases cannot establish that gambling alone caused the deaths, say experts and police officials. Suicide is complex and can involve multiple factors. But they show how financial losses, addiction, shame and pressure can collide.
Research has also examined the relationship between gambling disorder and suicide. A 2026 meta-analysis of 14 observational studies found significant associations between gambling disorder and suicidal ideation, suicide attempts and suicide mortality, although the strength of those associations varied across studies and regions.
For families, however, the crisis often begins with a simpler question: Where did the money go?
The chase
Gambling addictions have a particularly destructive financial logic.
So, if a person loses 5,000 rupees ($53) and decides to win it back, the next wager is likely to be 10,000 rupees ($106). Another loss follows. A loan makes another bet possible. The gambler may no longer be trying to make money. They are trying to recover money that has already disappeared.
That pattern can be difficult for families to recognise. Parents may pay off a debt believing the crisis has ended, only to discover that the betting has continued, say experts.
That dynamic appeared repeatedly in Telangana’s reported cases. Harish’s parents sold land. Manoj’s father repaid his son’s debt. Pavan Kumar’s father also cleared earlier debts. The financial burden moves outward from the gambler to the family. Savings disappear. Jewellery is sold. Loans are taken from relatives and neighbours.
Manoj Kumar Sharma, professor of clinical psychology at the Bengaluru-based National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), India’s top mental health facility, said it is easy for people to move from casual gaming to money games and eventually to higher-stakes gambling.
“Wins can produce a strong sense of reward, while losses can create guilt and regret alongside the belief that the money can still be recovered,” Sharma said. “That expectation can keep people gambling even as their losses increase, creating a cycle that becomes increasingly difficult to break.”
In rural communities, where land can represent generations of security, gambling debt can threaten more than a household’s monthly income. It can threaten the family’s future.
India draws a new legal line
For years, India’s gambling laws were fragmented. Betting and gambling are primarily regulated by the states, with various state laws taking different approaches.
State laws determined what forms of offline betting and gambling were permitted or prohibited, while courts historically examined whether particular activities were games of chance or involved sufficient skill. That distinction became central to the growth of online fantasy sports and real-money gaming, with companies arguing that their products involved skill rather than gambling — and so should be allowed.
But the smartphone created a parallel challenge for regulators. A player could be sitting in one state, using an application operated elsewhere, while payments moved electronically and the operator could be based outside India. The Mahavir app, for instance, was run by a businessman based in the United Arab Emirates.
The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 changed all that, prohibiting online money games, including those based on chance, skill or a combination of the two. It also prohibits their advertising, promotion and facilitation. Banks and payment systems are barred from facilitating transactions connected to prohibited online money games, while authorities have powers to block unlawful services. The law came into force on May 1, 2026.
But tougher laws have not eliminated the appetite for betting.
The offshore problem
As India has tightened restrictions, illegal and offshore operators have increasingly become a focus for enforcement agencies.
A website can disappear and return under another domain. A social media account can be removed and replaced. Users can be redirected into private messaging groups. Affiliate networks can also promote betting services without appearing to operate the betting platform themselves.
That makes enforcement harder than closing a physical betting shop.
Advertising has become another battleground. In June 2026, India’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting warned celebrities and influencers against endorsing or promoting offshore online betting and gambling platforms, including through surrogate advertising. The Advertising Standards Council of India has documented the scale of the problem.
Its 2025-26 annual report said it identified and escalated 7,927 offshore betting advertisements in 2025. Offshore betting accounted for 72 percent of advertisements found to be in violation in its monitoring. The ASCI also identified 854 influencers involved in offshore betting promotions between April and December 2025.
Selling the dream
Celebrity influence has helped make online money gaming familiar to millions of Indians.
Cricketers, actors and social media personalities have appeared in advertisements for gaming and fantasy-sports brands, helping turn digital money games into an apparently ordinary part of sporting culture.
For companies, the attraction is obvious. A famous face can lend legitimacy to a product that might otherwise appear unfamiliar or risky. The viewer sees a celebrity they recognise, rather than an offshore company operating behind a screen. The message becomes less about gambling and more about entertainment.
In 2025, former Indian cricketer Suresh Raina was questioned by the Enforcement Directorate as part of an investigation into illegal betting-app promotions. Reports said the investigation also examined other celebrities associated with platforms under scrutiny.
But it is already too late for several families. For the companies and networks that profit from betting, India’s 1.4 billion people represent a sizeable digital market.
For families such as Harish’s, though, online betting has meant something completely different. In Yedapally, the story began with a young man trying to make money through his phone. It ended with three deaths.

China’s Xi lands in India for BRICS summit overshadowed by wars
Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, are expected to dominate the summit.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has landed in New Delhi to attend a BRICS summit, alongside leaders from India, Russia and Iran, as wars, trade and energy test the divided grouping.
Xi departed on Saturday for the 18th BRICS summit at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua reported. His entourage includes Foreign Minister Wang Yi and high-ranking Chinese Communist Party official Cai Qi.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4China’s Xi visits Egypt’s el-Sisi: Why it matters
- list 2 of 4Multipolarity gives middle powers more choices, but fewer guarantees
- list 3 of 4Next BRICS summit can get an Iran ceasefire
- list 4 of 4Putin, Pezeshkian in India for BRICS summit clouded by Iran and Ukraine war
The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, are expected to dominate the two-day meeting of the 11-nation bloc.
Xi’s visit, his first to India since 2019, will also be closely watched as the biggest step yet in the cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
The trip comes six years after a deadly 2020 military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border along Tibet.
Beijing said on Friday that it was “ready to work with India … by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences”.
Xi is due to hold face-to-face talks with Modi later on Saturday, according to India’s Ministry of External Affairs.
“They are looking for ‘early and substantial harvest’ when it comes to the border issue,” Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne, said, as reported by the AFP news agency. “You cannot have a buildup of your forces on the border … but at the same time say ‘we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships.'”
Deep mistrust remains, however, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Dozens of Tibetans living in exile, like their spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, protested in New Delhi on Friday, waving placards against Xi’s visit.
The Russian and Iranian presidents arrived in the Indian capital on Friday for the summit.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin held talks with Modi on Friday and agreed to further strengthen the “special” relationship between their countries.
During a meeting with Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, Modi underscored the need to protect freedom of navigation and commerce, as well as the safety and wellbeing of ships’ crews.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the United States-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

Hundreds of migrants vanish after UK returns them to France – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:24:50 UTC

Hundreds of migrants vanish after UK returns them to France – media
Hundreds of illegal migrants, including more than 40 “age-disputed” children, who were returned from the UK to France under the ‘one in, one out’ deal have disappeared, The Guardian reports, citing human rights organizations.
The migrant exchange scheme was brokered by Paris and London last summer and hailed as a groundbreaking achievement at the time. Under the deal, the UK can return illegal migrants who cross the Channel to France while accepting asylum seekers with legitimate claims who had not previously attempted to enter Britain illegally.
The scheme has proven to have a very limited impact, with around 1,400 migrants returned since it was signed in September last year, compared with around 32,000 illegal arrivals. Moreover, hundreds of migrants sent back to France under the scheme have disappeared, The Guardian reported, citing figures provided by NGO representatives working on the ground.
Among them were at least 41 “age-disputed” people – individuals claiming to be unaccompanied minors – according to Maddie Harris, the director of the Humans for Rights Network. Holding unaccompanied minors in adult immigration detention centers is illegal, and they are excluded from the ‘one in, one out’ deal.
The Home Office has strongly denied the allegations, insisting that all those returned were adults. “This is categorically untrue. Nobody has been returned to France, where their age is in dispute,” it told the newspaper.
The fate of the deal remains unclear, with the agreement set to expire in October and neither side confirming or denying whether it will be extended. According to British media reports, Paris wants to scrap the current arrangement and replace it with an EU-wide deal with the UK.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has reportedly conveyed this intention to his British counterpart, Shabana Mahmood, and told her that Paris will not prolong the scheme. Under the French proposal, London would be obliged to receive migrants from all 27 EU member states in exchange for those returned to the bloc.
“For our part, we want to move away from this bilateral relationship with the UK. We consider that France should not have to carry it alone and that it would be better to integrate it into an agreement between the EU and UK,” Nunez reportedly told a French parliamentary inquiry.

Ratio of Japanese singles seeking marriage drops below 80 pct for 1st time: gov't survey

TOKYO, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- The percentage of young single people in Japan who said they intend to marry one day has fallen below 80 percent for the first time for both men and women, according to a government survey.
According to the survey released Friday by the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research, among unmarried respondents aged between 18 and 34, 75.1 percent of men said they intend to marry eventually, down from 81.4 percent in the previous survey in 2021, while the figure for women dropped from 84.3 percent to 77.8 percent.
The institute has conducted surveys on birth and marriage trends almost every five years since 1940. The latest survey was conducted as of June 2025, with more than 11,000 single people and married couples responding.
Interest in having children continued its downward trend. Among married couples surveyed, the ideal number of children averaged 2.18, down from 2.25 in the previous survey. The average number they actually plan to have fell below 2 for the first time on record, slipping to 1.95.
Meanwhile, more than 30 percent of unmarried respondents said they do not wish to have children, the highest percentage since comparable data became available in 2002.
Among men, 33.0 percent said they do not want any children, up 9.8 percentage points from the previous survey, while the figure for women rose 8.8 points to 32.4 percent, the survey said. ■

RCEP drives 21 pct surge in Cambodia's regional trade in Jan.-Aug.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12

13:24:07 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's trade volume with Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) member states saw a year-on-year surge of 21 percent in the first eight months of 2026, driven by tariff preferences and trade facilitation under the mega-regional pact, official data showed on Saturday.
The Southeast Asian country recorded 31.93 billion U.S. dollars in trade with RCEP countries during the January-August period this year, up from 26.35 billion dollars in the same period last year, according to a report from the Ministry of Commerce.
Cambodia's exports to RCEP members grew 8.9 percent to 7.22 billion dollars, while imports climbed 25 percent to reach 24.71 billion dollars, the report noted.
The free trade pact remains Cambodia's largest market, accounting for 61.2 percent of the country's 52.1-billion-dollar total global trade volume during the eight-month period.
China, Vietnam, Singapore, Japan, and Thailand stand as Cambodia's top five trading partners within the bloc.
Penn Sovicheat, a secretary of state and spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce, said the RCEP continues to drive robust trade growth.
He emphasized that it serves as a primary catalyst for Cambodia's long-term export expansion and a powerful incentive for foreign direct investment.
"The regional trade pact will help us graduate from the Least Developed Country (LDC) status in 2029, transition into an upper-middle-income country by 2030, and fast-track our goal of becoming a high-income country by 2050," he told Xinhua.
Entering into force in 2022, the RCEP comprises 15 Asia-Pacific nations.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, attributed the rising trade volume to Cambodia's deepening integration into regional economic networks.
"RCEP's unified rules of origin are lowering trade barriers, boosting market access for Cambodian agricultural and manufactured products, and positioning the kingdom as an increasingly attractive destination for light manufacturing, foreign direct investment, and regional supply chains," he told Xinhua. ■

London tourist tax on accommodation will be capped at 5pc, mayor says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:12:16 UTC
13:12:16 KST

London tourist tax on accommodation will be capped at 5pc, mayor says
A new tax on overnight stays in London will be capped at 5 per cent of the cost of accommodation, the BBC has reported.
Under the legislation, local authorities will be able to charge a flat fee or a percentage of the cost of an overnight stay for domestic and international guests in London accommodations.
London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan told BBC London that he welcomed plans by the government and promised it would not be above 5 per cent per night.
The exact amount has not yet been determined.
"I fully support the government's decision, after years of lobbying, to give us the same powers that other cities, from New York to Los Angeles, from Chicago to Paris … have, which is the ability to raise a levy on those who come to our great city," he said.
"We've got to invest in making sure that [our] city continues to be attractive."
There are concerns the costs could put visitors off heading to London, an extremely popular destination for Australians heading abroad.
How will the tax work?
Between November of last year and February of 2026, the UK government consulted on the design of a new power for English councils to introduce overnight visitor levies or a "tourist tax".
The legal framework to do so will be introduced in the Overnight Visitor Levy bill, which has not yet been tabled in parliament.
A visitor levy set by English mayors would apply to hotels, guesthouses, bed and breakfasts, hostels, campsites, self-catering properties, and short-term lets, and university and religious accommodation when let commercially.
The levy would be set as a percentage of the price of the accommodation.
Mayors would be able to set local exemptions.
They would also be able to choose to set a visitor levy in some of their local authority areas but not others.
Members of the combined authority would be able to reject a levy by a two-thirds majority.
It will bring England in line with Scotland and Wales, which have already introduced powers for local authorities to raise a visitor levy.
Why is it being implemented?
The bill proposes that English mayors can spend revenue from the levy for "broader initiatives which have a positive impact on the region's economic health."
"Mayors will be empowered to deliver more long-term, locally led investment in transport, regeneration and cultural assets that can unlock growth and make places more attractive for residents, businesses and visitors," the bill said.
"The government will not compel any mayor to introduce this levy, nor will central government reduce funding for mayors if they decide to do so."
The levy could raise up to £240 million ($450 million) annually, according to Central London Forward, which represents 12 London local authorities and is based on a 3 per cent levy on the cost of a room.
Where else has it been applied?
Similar schemes have been implemented around the world.
In Europe, a city tax is the norm for many popular locations, including Venice, Rome, Amsterdam, Barcelona and Berlin and is used to fund local infrastructure and manage over-tourism.
In Paris, travellers pay from $2 to $15 per night depending on how the hotel is rated.
In New York, several taxes are applied to an overnight stay, which total about 14 per cent per night.
Japan also charges an overnight stay tax for foreign visitors per night.
How has Australia responded?
According to the most recent data from Visit Britain, 1.2 million Australians travelled to the UK in 2024.
During the travellers' visits, their total expenditure was a record £1.7 billion, with an average spend of £1,358 ($2,561) per visit.
Australians have criticised the proposed changes amid the growing expenses of overseas travel.
Australian Travel Industry Association chief executive Dean Long previously told the ABC the decision to tax travellers would add to an already expensive long-haul destination at the top of many Aussies' bucket lists.
"We're entering a new era where governments are increasingly targeting travellers with taxes," he said.
"It's a never-ending battle that ultimately means less money spent in the economy and less revenue for the small businesses employing the people who deliver the experiences."

OpenAI confirms AI agents disrupted software service during testing: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:06:04 UTC
13:06:04 KST

Darren Lyn
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
OpenAI confirmed Friday that artificial intelligence agents it was testing were involved in an incident that disrupted the RubyGems software service, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The financial daily reported that OpenAI agents created accounts and uploaded hundreds of files to RubyGems in May, overwhelming its systems and prompting the platform to suspend new account registrations for four days.
OpenAI said the activity was not malicious.
“Based on our review, our agents used the RubyGems platform to access the internet to carry out benign tasks and retrieve public information,” said an OpenAI spokesperson. “We’ll continue to investigate as part of our broader review of agent activity during training and evaluation.”
The agents had been assigned tasks such as filling out spreadsheets and creating reports, according to the Journal. OpenAI said the agents apparently used RubyGems to access publicly available information in a training environment where they lacked full internet access.
“It was a major attack in terms of what we see in volume,” Marty Haught, director of open source at Ruby Central, the nonprofit that operates RubyGems, told the Journal.
The incident, dubbed “GemStuffer,” began May 11, with new accounts created every two to three minutes and large numbers of files uploaded to the platform, according to the report.
Joseph Edwards, a threat researcher at cybersecurity firm Socket, said researchers initially suspected the activity had been generated by AI “due to the speed of it and due to the names.”
OpenAI agents had also been involved earlier in a separate incident affecting software company Hugging Face.
AI safety research organization METR reported in July that as many as 1,200 agents coordinated through a makeshift message board they created during testing without OpenAI’s knowledge.
The incidents have added to concerns about how increasingly autonomous AI agents behave during training and evaluation and whether existing safeguards are sufficient to prevent unintended activity.
OpenAI previously called for stronger industry standards for reporting “misalignment incidents,” in which AI systems act beyond their intended behavior.

Nearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthis advance along Red Sea coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:00:24 UTC
13:00:24 KST

Nearly 50,000 people have fled a sudden advance by Houthi forces in western Yemen, with entire villages emptied and families trapped near frontline fighting with depleting food supplies, according to aid workers.
Civilians in the Middle East’s poorest country have found themselves victims of a global struggle for control over one of the most important shipping routes in the world, which threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war.
In a lightning advance this week, the Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized a string of towns along the Red Sea coast from forces aligned with the US- and Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Many fear a return to the full-scale civil war that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.
The UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday that 46,000 people had been displaced across the governates of Taiz and Hodeidah, where steep verdant mountain ridges give way to arid coastal plains. For many families, this was their second or even third time they had been forced out of their homes.
A significant number of people were observed to be leaving the city with their belongings. Fighting has cut key roads, while phone lines are down in some areas. “The scale of displacement is increasing rapidly,” said Joe Lowry, IOM’s Middle East and north Africa spokesperson in Cairo.
The most urgent needs were emergency shelters, cash assistance, food, drinking water, household items, healthcare and protection services. “Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,” Lowry said.
“Many of those fleeing have arrived with very few belongings after leaving suddenly, due to shelling and frontline advances.”
Lowry said aid workers were having to constantly reassess access, and adapt movements, as the situation changed. “It’s a highly fluid and uncertain situation marked by rapid territorial changes, population movements and growing concern among communities about further escalation,” he said.
The Houthi advance has come unexpectedly and fast, particularly the fall of the strategic port city of Mocha – widely regarded as the birthplace of the global coffee trade and the eponym for chocolate-flavoured coffee.
Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told Agence France-Presse there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the city. Another man, Mujahid Tahami, who set off for the southern government-held city of Aden, said some families had fallen victim to “looting by gangs as they tried to flee”.
Others reported that they had managed to flee in time, some on motorbikes, but other family members were not so lucky and were stuck.
Yemen analysts have long criticised the US and its allies for taking a security-focused approach to the country that undervalues diplomacy and development. Washington launched a campaign of drone attacks against Sunni al-Qaida militants for much of the 21st century, but did not pay significant attention to the hardline Shia Houthi insurgency until its forces claimed the capital in 2014.
By taking control of key areas this week, including islands off the coast, the anti-west Houthis hope to gain a direct presence near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a 20-mile stretch of water and vital trade and energy route that connects Asia with Europe. 
The strait’s name is roughly translated as “the gate of tears” or “the gate of grief”, and its strong currents and winds made the passage between the Arabian peninsula and Africa’s east coast hazardous for centuries. Modern-day cargo ships have no physical issue passing through.
But if the Houthis were to close the natural chokepoint, the impact on the global economy could be disastrous. Ships would have to reroute around the southern tip of Africa, adding thousands of extra nautical miles. The fighting has already contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.
The fighting in Yemen, as well as Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, is the most significant violence in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022.
The UN special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, told an emergency security council meeting on Thursday that the country faced “a new and more dangerous phase of war”.
“This renewed war should alarm us all,” Grundberg said. “It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the UN-brokered truce. It not only threatens to plunge Yemen into a prolonged and expanding war, but also risks yet again dragging the country into the wider and unresolved regional confrontation, with global repercussions.”
Instability in Yemen has been exploited by regional powers such as Saudi Arabia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates to fight proxy battles, and the failure to end the violence has led to the growth of powerful militias. The US-Israeli war on Iran has only heightened the tensions, with regional animosity at an all-time high.
This has compounded one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The most recent UN humanitarian report, released last month, warned that the country of 40 million was facing a deepening malnutrition crisis, with roughly half the population facing acute food insecurity nationwide.
“Years of conflict, economic deterioration, displacement, climate-related shocks and regional tensions have steadily weakened livelihoods and household resilience,” the report warned. “At the same time, declining humanitarian funding and operational constraints are limiting the ability of aid organisations to provide assistance at the scale required.”
On the Red Sea coast, those who escaped the latest wave of fighting had their lives, but were left in shock.
“It’s a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing,” said Mohammed Khudairi, who fled the fighting to a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near the areas of Khokha. “We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there.”

Firewall compromised: has Friedrich Merz blown ‘democracy’s last shot’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:00:23 UTC
13:00:23 KST

A cataclysm. A 9.0 earthquake. A five-alarm fire. A bitter rejection of Germany’s joyous reunification three decades ago, and a threat to the democratic postwar order.
Sizing up the repercussions of last weekend’s win for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, German commentators expressed a sense of doom, panic and helplessness in the political establishment.
With nearly 44% of the vote, the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its media savvy chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is racing to find enough support from the other parties to prop up what would be the first rightwing extremist state government since the Nazi period.
It is still anyone’s guess whether he will succeed, leaving a corrosive uncertainty at the heart of Europe’s top economic power. Hanging in the balance is the fate of Friedrich Merz’s centre-right government, once called “democracy’s last shot” to prevent an extremist takeover in Germany.
The result in Saxony-Anhalt has put the conservative chancellor on the ropes, with further punishment for his Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) expected in two more state polls later this month.
“This is the worst defeat for the CDU in years – decades – and something has changed, not just in Saxony-Anhalt but in all of Germany,” he said on Monday.
Whether or not he survives politically until the next general election, due in 2029, will have dramatic repercussions for Germany and its European allies trying to beat back anti-democratic forces. Pivotal elections are due next year in countries including France, Spain, Italy and Poland.
Merz’s many critics say the 70-year-old former BlackRock executive is the wrong man at such a consequential crossroads, calling him a ham-fisted and empathetically challenged leader who is erratic in his messaging.
Only in office 16 months, the chancellor often seemed incapable of one of the basic tasks of leadership: making the case to voters that accepting bitter pills now could lead to a brighter future, said the political scientist Thomas Biebricher of Frankfurt’s Goethe University.
“The prevailing impression at the moment is that, in terms of communication, he is unable to explain the many reforms – and the sacrifices they entail – to the public, and thereby win their acceptance,” Biebricher said, referring to planned cuts to the statutory pension and healthcare schemes.
The former chancellor Angela Merkel, Merz’s longtime rival within the CDU, has criticised him publicly for his hardline rhetoric on migration and integration but said she took no pleasure in the debacle given the stakes.
“This is a turning point – a real turning point – in the history of the federal republic of Germany,” said Merkel, who left office of her own accord in 2021 after 16 years in power. “As a CDU member it breaks my heart.”
Speaking at a digital affairs conference on Tuesday, she advised Merz to rethink his messaging in a changing political ecosystem in which emotions counted more than facts.
Merkel, 72, noted that the CDU had pointed to data during the Saxony-Anhalt campaign showing that joblessness had fallen and household wealth had risen in the small, relatively poor state. “And then [Siegmund] says: ‘That may be so, but that’s not how it feels.’”
The AfD formed in 2013, during Merkel’s tenure, as a Eurosceptic outfit opposed to bailouts for debt-mired countries. It grew increasingly radical during the 2015-2016 refugee influx, when she left the borders open to more than a million asylum seekers fleeing war and hardship.
Merz took office last year saying he would put the country back on track after the implosion of the previous government under Olaf Scholz. He promised a return to economic growth, a restoration of defence capabilities and urgent repairs to the creaking social welfare system.
His recipe for confronting the far right – one of his key pledges – was competence in governing and solutions for Germans’ most urgent problems.
Merz also promised a rejection of Merkel’s open-border policy in an attempt to rob the AfD of its signature issue. He had infamously accepted support from the far-right party for a tough draft law on migration just before the February 2025 general election, before back-pedalling in the face of protests.
As “irregular” arrivals of migrants have fallen sharply since Merz took office, the AfD has successfully pivoted to a broader range of concerns about deindustrialisation, regional identity, affordability and crime to gain ground far beyond its eastern heartland.
The AfD, widely seen as more radical than comparable European parties, had been relegated to permanent opposition in Germany by the “firewall” strategy of shunning by the mainstream parties. But this policy is now widely seen to have failed, allowing the AfD to snipe from the sidelines about the slow pace of any positive change.
Biebricher said that for all Merz’s weaknesses, replacing him would not be a magic bullet for the mountain of challenges facing German security and prosperity.
As well as the threat from Russia, he cited decrepit infrastructure, the demographic crunch on social welfare benefits, competition from China in once mighty industries such as car manufacturing, and geopolitical upheaval weighing on supply chains and energy imports.
“None of that simply goes away the moment you have someone who communicates better,” Biebricher told public radio.
Merz’s centre-right CDU-CSU bloc, divided between conservatives and moderates, is nevertheless known for its internal discipline in times of crisis – if only out of fear of even graver consequences from drastic changes.
The situation is seen as so grim that it has triggered paralysis, with neither the popular North Rhine-Westphalia state premier, Hendrik Wüst, or Bavaria’s ambitious leader, Markus Söder, keen at this stage to snatch the poisoned chalice.
“Merz has now reached a stage where the crisis – which he himself constantly exacerbates – is stabilising him,” said the veteran political journalist Bernd Ulrich of Die Zeit newspaper.
“The CDU and the government (in coalition with the Social Democrats) as a whole are in such a dire state that, as far as anyone can tell, no one wants to take over his post.”
Wüst, 51, leads a coalition with the Greens in Germany’s most populous state and faces a re-election battle next April. If he wins, the calls for Merz to make way for him may grow louder.
Söder, who represents the bloc’s conservative wing, shares Merz’s view that it needs to echo the AfD’s harsh rhetoric on migration in order to win back support – a strategy political scientists have long disparaged as counterproductive.
Yet the dangers of keeping a revolt at bay by betting on a status quo voters so clearly reject are apparent.
Much will depend on how bad the news is from the regional elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on 20 September. The AfD is polling well in both states, with clear momentum after Saxony-Anhalt, putting pressure on the CDU in particular.
During a fiery clash with the AfD in parliament this week in which he laid out the threat it poses to German democracy, Merz was reflective about how to steer the country – and himself – out of the current straits.
He quoted from a letter he received from the rector of a theological university arguing how many opportunities still lay ahead for Germany and advising him not to give in to despair.
Merz said he intended to take this to heart and stay on as chancellor using a new roadmap: “Admit mistakes, forgive, get back on your feet, shape the future.”

When Indonesia burns, these women run towards the fire
Meet the all-female volunteer brigade risking their lungs and lives to fight Indonesia’s devastating wildfires
Irma smells the fire before she sees it: a column of thick, yellow-tinged smoke rising above the tree line near her small wooden home.
She pulls on heavy rubber boots, checks her equipment and drives straight into the impenetrable smog emanating from wildfires devouring the peatland and ancient forests of Borneo.
“I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous,” the 39-year-old mother told This Week in Asia, moments before disappearing into the murk that has settled over the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan.
Irma, who like many Indonesians only goes by one name, is one of roughly 150 Muslim women who make up Power of Mama, an all-female volunteer firefighting unit that heads out every day during the dry season to battle blazes smouldering deep beneath the island’s peatlands.
They fight fires lit, deliberately or otherwise, by the agricultural burning of poor farming communities clearing land the cheapest way they know how. This year, those fires arrived earlier and burned harder than most can remember, fuelled climate anomalies and drought conditions.
“We are the ones who feel its effects most,” said Irma, who is the group’s coordinator, explaining that it was women who were left to care for housebound children through increasingly long stretches of the year.
