How the body adapts to extreme heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

How the body adapts to extreme heat
New methods could help vulnerable people acclimate to higher temperatures
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
“I can’t do this,” the woman in her 60s said as she lowered herself into the 40° Celsius water that filled a big silver tub at the end of a dimly lit room in the University of Ottawa’s Human and Environmental Physiology Research Unit. It was only after the temperature dropped a degree that she immersed herself, shoulder-deep, for the next two hours. Then she did it again — and again and again — every day for a week. “I’m going to be straight up: People hated doing this,” says Caroline Li-Maloney, a Ph.D. candidate at the university who studies how the human body adapts to extreme heat.
Li-Maloney is trying to figure out whether women in their 60s, 70s and 80s, a group particularly at risk of death during heat waves, could train themselves to cope better with hotter temperatures. If they could, it would be a convincing demonstration of heat acclimation in older individuals — and it could pave the way for protecting vulnerable groups in heat waves.
Extreme heat can kill. When a person’s core body temperature rises above 37° for prolonged periods, heat exhaustion often sets in; hotter temperatures can eventually lead to delirium, seizures, organ failure and death. But repeated exposure to high temperatures in young, healthy individuals has been shown to trigger a host of protective physical changes that help cool the body, including modifications to sweat responses and blood vessels. Now, researchers are trying to work out whether these changes hold for the rest of us — and whether we can train ourselves to better handle the heat that is becoming increasingly severe with climate change.
As heat wave–related deaths mount globally — more than 10,000 Europeans are estimated to have died during a heat wave in June alone — harnessing the body’s natural responses could be one way to survive in an increasingly hot world.
“With more frequent periods of extreme heat … can we actually acclimate older populations, especially those with chronic diseases?” asks heat physiologist Daniel Gagnon of the Montreal Heart Institute and the Université de Montréal. He’s hoping that the answer is “yes.”
How the body prepares for extreme heat
Studies, primarily in athletes, soldiers and outdoor workers, have long shown that repeated exposures to heat trigger physiological responses that help the body better cope with subsequent bouts of heat. Sweating, which uses moisture to wick away heat, starts earlier and is more intense in people who have recently been exposed to hot temperatures, compared with naïve individuals. Tiny vessels in the skin also dilate more quickly in heat-exposed individuals, allowing more blood to move from the body’s toasty interior to its surface, where heat can radiate outward. These changes initially force the heart to beat faster to keep blood pressure steady; over time, the body adapts by expanding blood volume, reducing the heart rate.
How the body copes with heat
Controlled exposures to heat can induce protective changes across the body — from the brain to the heart and even within individual cells — that help it better handle subsequent hot spells, studies suggest. While scientists are still working out the details, they’re finding that intentionally inducing these changes could increase the odds of surviving heat waves.
The hypothalamus, a brain region that acts like a thermostat, becomes more sensitive to temperature and acts more quickly to trigger sweating and blood-vessel widening.
Sweating, which cools the body when the fluid evaporates, starts sooner upon heat exposure and is more intense.
Cells in the blood (and probably elsewhere in the body) produce more heat shock proteins, which help protect cells from heat-related damage.
The heart initially has to beat faster to accommodate the redistribution of fluid, but then blood volume expands, reducing the heart rate.
Small blood vessels in the skin enlarge, drawing more blood from the body interior to the surface where heat can dissipate.
Studies in mice suggest that some of these responses are regulated by a thermostat-like brain structure called the hypothalamus. During successive heat exposures, nerve cells there become more sensitive to body temperature and are quicker to send out signals directing sweat glands to enlarge and vessels to expand, Gagnon explains.
Adaptation may also be happening at the cellular level. Integrative physiologist Jeremy McCormick, also of the University of Ottawa, and colleagues had a small group of healthy men in their 60s and 70s participate in a weeklong hot water immersion protocol similar to the one used by Li-Maloney’s team.
Analyzing the immune cells in participants’ blood at the end of the experiment showed a rise in concentrations of heat shock proteins, McCormick’s team reported in August in the Journal of Sport and Health Science. These molecules — found in most organisms, including plants and bacteria — stabilize and repair other cellular proteins damaged by heat and other physiological stressors. Alongside other molecular changes that the team observed, the increase “seemed to alleviate some of the cellular stress,” McCormick says.
Some like it hot
While researchers are still figuring out precisely how these physiological adaptations work, some scientists believe they are at least partly behind why people in climates that are hot year-round tend to suffer less from heat.
Residents of countries including Kuwait, India and Thailand, for example, show signs of being well-adapted to relatively high average daily temperatures.
Every population has a minimum mortality temperature, where the risk of death from natural causes is the lowest. Many scientists interpret this to be an optimal temperature to which a population is adapted. In cooler places such as the United Kingdom, this hovers in the high teens or low twenties. But in hot countries, “it sits far higher,” says critical care physician Abderrezak Bouchama of Saudi Arabia’s King Abdullah International Medical Research Center, who studies heat physiology.
To compare the heat tolerance of people from different places, Bouchama and colleagues calculated the minimum mortality temperature for two groups: the residents of Mecca, Saudi Arabia, and the hundreds of thousands of international visitors who traveled to the city for the annual Islamic pilgrimage known as the Hajj from 2006 to 2014. Looking at patterns of natural deaths for both populations during the five-day period revealed a minimum mortality temperature of 26° for Meccans and 23.5° for pilgrims, the scientists reported in 2023 in Environmental Health Perspectives. But even the residents of Mecca have physiological limits, the team found in another study: Their mortality numbers started skyrocketing above 38°.
In general, such differences at the population level could be due to many factors, Bouchama says, including access to air conditioning, outdoor conditions and possibly even genetic factors. But physiological acclimation probably also plays a role, he says.
In regions with distinct warm and cold seasons, there’s some evidence that young adults can acclimate over summer, exhibiting slightly higher sweat rates and lower skin temperatures at the end of the season versus the beginning.
But the reverse can also happen, molecular biologist Elaine Lee of the University of Connecticut in Storrs and colleagues have found. The team’s unpublished study of several dozen athletes suggests that it takes them longer to acclimate in the late winter compared with early winter, hinting that they lose their summer adaptations over the cold season.
Some scientists have posited that acclimation is why early summer heat waves are often deadlier than ones later in the summer. Because people undergoing heat acclimation protocols typically lose their adaptations within weeks, Gagnon suspects they would similarly lose any acclimation benefits in the cooler periods between heat waves.
“We know for sure that the body can acclimate, but we have to be exposed to heat on a regular basis,” Gagnon says. “It has to be a pretty considerable dose.”
Finding the right dose
The science of heat adaptation in young, healthy people is well-established. But what about older individuals or those with chronic health conditions? Scientists have long known, for example, that the ability to effectively sweat and vasodilate declines with age.
New research suggests that intentional heat acclimation can boost these responses just as effectively in older adults as in younger people. Gagnon and colleagues asked 15 adults in their 20s and 30s and 16 adults in their 60s and 70s to immerse themselves in 40° water for an hour and then spend the next hour alternating between shoulder-high and waist-high water levels to ensure their body temperature stayed at or above 38.5°.
After repeating this process for seven days, both groups started to sweat and vasodilate earlier upon heat exposure. They also experienced a 0.4° lower body temperature, on average, than they did at the beginning of the experiment. The scientists also observed a five-beats-per-minute lower heart rate, on average, in both groups by the end of the protocol, they reported in May in the Journal of Physiology.
The upshot of the study, Gagnon says, “is that even if we’re older, our body still has the ability to adapt to heat.”
That idea led some of the women in Li-Maloney’s study to take part, hoping the experience would brace them for summer heat waves. “They love the idea that a study like this might make them at least feel better when summer starts,” she says.
To find out, Li-Maloney’s team had the women endure an artificial heat wave before and after the experiment. Volunteers spent an hour sitting in a room set to 36° and 45 percent humidity. “It sucks, I’m not going to lie,” Li-Maloney says.
The team saw a significant difference in participants’ physiology during the second artificial heat wave. After the acclimation period, the women maintained a 0.2° lower core temperature and a several beats-per-minute lower heart rate than before the acclimation period, the researchers reported in April at the American Physiology Summit in Minneapolis. The team was particularly struck by how long the women avoided hitting the peak body temperatures they had reached during the first heat wave.
What’s still unclear is whether this translates to meaningful reductions in heat-related illness. Scientists will have to deeply consider the safety of such protocols, especially for people with heart disease, mobility issues or cognitive impairment. “If they were ever left to do it by themselves outside of a laboratory environment, are they potentially at risk?” asks physiologist Jessica Mee of the University of Worcester in England.
But with further study, hot water immersion could one day be a viable strategy to prepare vulnerable populations for the extreme heat of summer months — and a safer alternative to other proven acclimation methods like hot yoga or walking or running at hot temperatures, Li-Maloney says. “By the time the first heat wave hits, you should be more protected.” Some participants in the study are already convinced. One woman traveled to Thailand, exploring its sweltering capital in heat often in excess of 30°. “‘Everyone [else in] my tour group was suffering,’” Li-Maloney recalls the woman telling her, “‘and I felt great.’”

‘They’re lifesavers’: the Birmingham clinic giving hope to traumatised asylum seekers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:57:03 UTC
01:57:03 KST

Azad*, an asylum seeker from Iran, recounts his story in a gentle and mild manner, seated in the stillness of a therapy room at a trauma clinic in Birmingham.
The centre, which opened its doors in July last year to address the “unmet mental healthcare needs of those seeking sanctuary”, is run by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders. It provides specialised trauma-focused psychological care for refugees and asylum seekers in the city and surrounding areas.
It has so far received more than 350 referrals from the NHS and refugee organisations, and held 521 consultations for patients – many of whom have survived conflict, persecution, torture and other forms of violence and exploitation in their home countries or on their migration journey.
Data MSF shared with the Guardian by MSF shows that of 150 case files reviewed by MSF, 88% documented experiences of violence and one in three detailed suicidal thoughts at the moment they came to MSF.
Azad, who arrived in the UK on a small boat , was approached by MSF at the hotel he was being accommodated in Birmingham. He had known for a long time that he needed help, he said, but had nowhere to turn. “It was the only person who didn’t see me as a number, listened like I’m a human,” he said.
Azad’s journey to the UK had begun several years earlier, when the Iranian authorities cracked down on protests that had swept across the country in late 2022 against the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in police custody. She had been arrested for allegedly violating rules requiring women to wear the headscarf.
Azad, a Kurdish-Iranian civil engineer, took part in the demonstrations and said he had witnessed people being shot and others blinded. After authorities spotted him spraying graffiti, his father urged him to flee the country, fearing for his safety. The authorities later ransacked his family home, he said.
Azad travelled to Germany, where he applied for asylum but was rejected – a decision he said was driven by a “racist” interviewer and delays that prevented an appeal hearing. The decision left him feeling hopeless. “There were times that I was feeling I have nothing to live for,” he said as he recalled an attempt to take his own life.
The UK was his last and only option, he said. When he arrived, he alleged border officials had sworn at him. MSF staff said the mental health struggles of their patients had been further compounded by the rise in “hostility and anti-migrant sentiment in the UK”.
Some of their clients had to be moved from hotels far-right protesters routinely targeted. Others described being physically assaulted.
A clinical psychologist at the clinic, who did not want to be named, said: “What they are routinely sharing with us is a lot of fear around the environment in the UK. Attitudes towards migrants becoming more and feeling more hostile.
“And that’s a combination of policy but also the general kind of narrative and rhetoric within the UK.”
The charity said it was important for MSF to provide such intensive psychological treatment in the countries where refugees and asylum seekers hoped to settle.
“If you open a wound and you cannot heal it, the wound will get worse,” said Fouzia Bara, head of MSF’s migration taskforce. “Birmingham is the safe place where we can start the healing process. This is why we are providing highly intensive care because unfortunately the journey of migration, it’s a journey of violence.”
Azad, who has been diagnosed with complex post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and is nearing the end of his treatment, described the transformative impact the support has had on his life.
“They are lifesavers. I had nothing, there was no life in me. But they showed me, no, you can have a life,” he said.
*Name has been changed
In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

Ukraine Codifies “Steppe Wind” Strike Drone With 90+ km Range and Optical Guidance

Ukraine Codifies “Steppe Wind” Strike Drone With 90+ km Range and Optical Guidance
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has codified the domestically developed Steppe Wind strike unmanned aerial system, clearing the way for its procurement and delivery to units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
The medium-range drone was developed by Ukrainian company Unwave in cooperation with Sky Composite Engineering, according to information the company provided to Militarnyi on September 11.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The system is designed to strike stationary targets, armored vehicles, and personnel. Its official codification allows the Ukrainian state to procure the drones and supply them to Defense Forces units.
The Steppe Wind has a tactical operating radius of up to 70 kilometers, while its maximum route length exceeds 90 kilometers. The drone can remain airborne for up to 65 minutes.
The UAV can carry a payload of up to 5 kilograms and is equipped with an optical terminal guidance system designed to improve targeting during the final stage of flight.
The drone is launched from a dedicated platform without the use of a catapult and can be deployed within 20 minutes. The system supports automatic, semi-automatic, and manual control modes.
The Steppe Wind is among several Ukrainian strike drone systems currently advancing toward wider battlefield deployment. Ukrainian defense manufacturer GrimTech is also completing development of the Grim LA-80, a fixed-wing strike UAV capable of carrying payloads of up to 5 kilograms and operating at ranges of up to 80 kilometers.
A company representative presented details of the Grim LA-80 at the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland. While the system shares structural similarities with Russia’s Molniya-type drones, its developers are focusing on combining extended range and payload capacity with relatively low production costs.

“Land of Angels” wins Grand Prix at Kazan International Film Festival
TEHRAN- Iranian filmmaker Babak Khajehpasha’s “Land of Angels” received the Grand Prix for Best Feature Film at the 22nd Altyn Minbar Kazan International Film Festival, during the closing ceremony of the event in Kazan, the capital of Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan on Thursday.
The film, which focuses on the plight of children in Gaza amid the ongoing war, was also recognized in two other major categories at the festival, IRNA reported.
Syrian actress Sulaf Fawakherji won the award for Best Actress for her performance in the movie, while Iranian cinematographer Alireza Barazandeh received the award for Best Cinematography for a feature fiction film, the report added.
The awards were presented during the closing ceremony of the festival at the Galiaskar Kamal Theater in Kazan.
Khajehpasha received the festival’s top prize from renowned Iranian filmmaker Majid Majidi, who headed the jury of the main competition.
In a brief speech after receiving the award, Khajehpasha referred to the children who have lost their lives in Palestine and said that if he were to stand before God one day and be asked what he had done for the Palestinian children, he could present the film as the least thing he could have done for them.
The film tells the story of the suffering of children in Gaza and portrays the human consequences of war through the experiences of a woman who struggles to survive while protecting a group of innocent children from the horrors of conflict.
“Land of Angels” was written and directed by Khajehpasha and produced by Manouchehr Mohammadi. The production was jointly undertaken by the Tasvir-e Shahr Institute and the Soureh Cinema Center.
The film features Arab actors and centers on the lives, dreams and struggles of children against the backdrop of the war in Palestine. Rather than presenting the conflict solely through political or military events, the film approaches it from the perspective of civilians, particularly children whose lives have been profoundly affected by the violence.
The production was filmed in Tehran over a period of one and a half years. The film’s international screenings began with its participation in the Kazan festival, following its successful national festival run in Iran.
Prior to its appearance in Kazan, “Land of Angels” was the most decorated film at Iran’s 44th Fajr International Film Festival, where it received five Crystal Simorgh awards and eight honorary diplomas in February.
Among its Fajr honors, Khajehpasha received the jury’s special prize for directing, while Fawakherji was honored for her performance. The film also received awards for set design, visual effects and other categories, establishing it as one of the major productions of the festival’s 44th edition.
The 22nd Altyn Minbar Kazan International Film Festival was held from September 4 to 8 in Kazan. The festival received a record 1,030 submissions from 66 countries, with 146 films selected for its competition and non-competition programs.
The event is one of Russia’s established film festivals focusing on human, cultural, social and spiritual themes and has been held since 2005. This year’s edition was particularly significant as Kazan has been designated the Cultural Capital of the Islamic World, making the festival one of the major cultural events associated with the designation.
The festival’s main competition brought together films from different parts of the world, with the jury headed by Majidi. In addition to “Land of Angels”, the jury recognized films and filmmakers from countries including Sri Lanka, Uzbekistan and India.
The Kazan festival also introduced a new “Spirituality in Cinema” award this year, following a proposal by Sheikh Rawil Gaynetdin, Grand Mufti of Russia. The inaugural award went to the Russian-Uzbek film “The Teacher”, which portrays the life of Shihabuddin Marjani, a prominent Tatar scholar who lived during the Russian Empire.

Hilaj Theater to show legal drama filmed theater “Inter Alia”

Hilaj Theater to show legal drama filmed theater “Inter Alia”
TEHRAN – The filmed theater “Inter Alia” directed by Justin Martin will be shown at the Hilaj Theater in Tehran on Sunday.
“Inter Alia” is a legal drama play written by Australian playwright Suzie Miller. It had its world premiere at the National Theatre in London in 2025, starring Rosamund Pike as Crown Court Judge Jessica Parks.
The play centers on Jessica Parks, an eminent and pioneering London Crown Court Judge. Her career exists inter alia (among other things). She is a compassionate and sharp legal mind, often challenging the system from within, particularly in cases of sexual violence. However, her life is a constant juggling act between her high-powered career and her roles as a wife and mother. She handles the majority of the domestic and emotional labor, from planning dinner parties to having crucial conversations with her teenage son, Harry, while her husband, Michael, a less professionally successful barrister, often remains a passive figure in her domestic world.
The central conflict of the play arises when an event from her personal life collides with her professional principles. Her son, Harry, is accused of rape by a classmate after a party. Jessica, a proud feminist who has presided over countless sexual assault cases, suddenly finds her professional and moral convictions put to the ultimate test. The play delves into the ethical and emotional turmoil she faces as she must reconcile her unwavering commitment to justice with her instinct to protect her son.
Miller's work explores the ambiguities of consent, the challenges of raising boys in the digital age, and the difficult moral territory a parent must navigate when their child is accused of a crime.
The production uses elements like live music, shifting sets, and flashbacks to blur the lines between the courtroom and Jessica's home life, showcasing the psychological and emotional pressure she endures.
Susan "Suzie" Miller, 62, is an Australian playwright, librettist, screenwriter, and lawyer. She has written over 40 plays. Her best-known play is “Prima Facie,” which was staged in a West End theater in London starring Jodie Comer in 2022, directed by fellow Australian Justin Martin. The production won two Olivier Awards, three years after a highly successful run in Sydney in 2019. It was also broadcast live to cinemas around the UK through NT Live, and later around the world.
The National Theater, officially the Royal National Theater since 1988 and sometimes referred to as the National Theater of Great Britain, is a performing arts venue and associated theater company located in London, England, adjacent to the Southbank Center. The theater was founded by Laurence Olivier in 1963, and many well-known actors have since performed with it.
In June 2009, the theater began National Theater (NT) Live, a program of simulcasts of live productions to cinemas, first in the United Kingdom and then internationally. NT Live productions have since been broadcast to over 2,500 venues in 60 countries around the world.
In November 2020, National Theater at Home, a video-on-demand streaming service specifically created for National Theater Live recordings, was introduced. Videos of plays are added every month and can be rented for temporary viewing, or unlimited recordings can be watched through a monthly or yearly subscription program.
“Inter Alia” will be shown at 7:30 pm on Sunday at the Hilaj Theater, located at No. 22, Samandarian (Mohajer) Alley, Iranshahr St., Karimkhan Ave.

Akbar Zanjanpour to stage Athol Fugard’s “The Island” at Tehran’s City Theater
TEHRAN – Iranian actor and theater director Akbar Zanjanpour will stage the play “The Island,” written by South African playwright Athol Fugard, at the Tehran’s City Theater from September 16.
The play has been translated by Mohammad Hefazi; Zanjanpour will also perform in the 75-minute performance alongside Saeed Dakh.
The apartheid-era drama, inspired by a true story, is set in an unnamed prison clearly based on South Africa's notorious Robben Island prison, where Nelson Mandela was held for twenty-seven years. The Island focuses on two cellmates, one whose successful appeal means that his release draws near and one who must remain in prison for many years to come. They spend their days performing futile physical labor and nights rehearsing in their cell for a performance of Sophocles' “Antigone” in front of the other prisoners. One takes the part of Antigone, who defies the laws of the state to bury her brother, and the other takes the part of her uncle Creon, who sentences her to die for her crime of conscience.
The play draws parallels between Antigone's situation and the situation of black political prisoners. Tensions arise as the performance approaches, especially when one of the prisoners learns that he has won an early release and the men's friendship is tested.
The play was first performed in Cape Town, at a theatre called The Space, in July 1973. In order to evade the draconian censorship in South Africa at the time (plays dealing with prison conditions, etc., were prohibited), the play premiered under the title, “Die Hodoshe Span”. It was next staged at the Royal Court Theater in London and then made its way to Broadway in 1974.
Athol Fugard (1932 – 2025) was a South African playwright, novelist, actor, and director. Widely regarded as South Africa's greatest playwright and acclaimed as "the greatest active playwright in the English-speaking world" by Time magazine in 1985, he published more than 30 plays.
He is best known for his political and penetrating plays opposing the system of apartheid, some of which have been adapted to film. His novel “Tsotsi” was adapted as a film of the same name, which won an Academy Award in 2005. Three plays he wrote, and two plays he co-authored, were nominated for the Tony Award for Best Play.
SS/SAB

Belarus will bolster its military combat readiness and could even announce “mobilization” to test it, President Alexander Lukashenko has said.

During his visit, Lukashenko met top military officials and inspected communications and control systems. The president said that he was set to continue vetting the country’s forces, revealing that an artillery brigade and signal troops are currently undergoing extensive inspections.

We understand that attacking anyone – say, one of our neighbors – would be tantamount to suicide. We cannot win a conflict against the ‘monsters’ – the states situated along our borders,” he said.
While it was not immediately clear which countries exactly Lukashenko described as “monsters,” most of the Belarusian neighbors’ militaries greatly surpass its capabilities. Other neighbors of Belarus, Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia are NATO member states. While the two Baltic nations have tiny militaries, Warsaw has been actively building up its force recently. Numbers-wise, the country’s military has become the third-largest within the NATO bloc, surpassed only by the US and Türkiye.

UK lawmakers urge Burnham to back ban on superintelligent AI after chilling warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:54:35 UTC
01:54:35 KST

More than 70 MPs and peers have urged Andy Burnham to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology after a week of warnings from experts of a 10% chance it could kill all humans.
Fifteen former government ministers, along with the former head of the civil service Robin Butler, senior Labour MPs including John McDonnell and leading Conservatives, Liberal Democrat and Scottish National party MPs have written to the prime minister. They urged him to throw the government’s weight behind a bill, tabled in the Commons on Tuesday, that would prohibit ASI – an as-yet-nonexistent AI that would outcompete human capabilities in most domains.
They have escalated their campaign to Downing Street after concerning statements from current and former AI insiders. Evan Hubinger, a senior employee at Anthropic, said he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity, and Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at Anthropic, who previously worked at OpenAI, quit on Tuesday with a warning that went viral, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”, they were “gambling with our lives” and were locked in a race for AI supremacy.
Alex Sobel, the Labour MP behind the bill, said he and other signatories – ranging from the children’s TV presenter Floella Benjamin to the former Conservative environment minister Zac Goldsmith and former Northern Ireland first minister Arlene Foster – want Burnham to foster “a clear framework where superintelligent AI cannot be created”. He added: “AI companies have made it clear that they will develop agents without constraint. They’re trying to develop superintelligence, while openly admitting there is a significant risk of human extinction.”
The bill mirrors legislation banning ASI promoted in Washington DC by Bernie Sanders, who this week said: “You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down.” It is backed by the Nobel prize-winning nuclear proliferation campaigner Beatrice Fihn and the leading Berkeley AI professor Stuart Russell, as well as Control AI, a transatlantic lobby group funded by the billionaire Skype co-founder and self-described “anti-extinctionist” Jaan Tallinn.
A ban on ASI in the UK, but not in the US or China where the frontier models are being created, risks having little impact. But the parliamentarians’ bill aims to pave the way to an international agreement. They call on Burnham to use next year’s UK presidency of the G20 to create “a coalition of the willing to tackle this national and international security threat”.
A government spokesperson said: “While we do not consider the measures proposed in the bill to be the right approach, we are exploring whether additional targeted interventions may be needed in future to address the most significant AI-related national security risks.”
Others have played down the risk, saying that ASI remains only theoretical and that guardrails could work to prevent the worst outcomes. Experts warn that these could include catastrophic cyber-attacks, novel biohazards and AIs in control of autonomous weaponry. This week’s wave of concern follows a spate of more minor but still worrying incidents involving unexpected misbehaviour by AI agents under training by OpenAI and Anthropic in which they broke out of training environments, secretly conspired and hacked into other systems.
Elon Musk, who runs xAI as part of his SpaceX empire, suggested without evidence that this week’s warnings of catastrophic risk were part of a “psyop” that “has been prepared for a long time”. The world’s richest man gave a different read on the state of AI, claiming: “AI+robots will more than double the global economy in less than 10 years.”
Anthropic revealed another incident of a rogue AI this week and said criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists had attempted to use its AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents. At its main rival, OpenAI, Paul Christiano, an AI adviser to the US government, joined the lab’s non-profit foundation and immediately warned the company was not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level.

They never saw 9/11. But they grew up living with its consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:52:13 UTC
01:52:13 KST

Washington, DC — Emily Carter was born nine days before two planes struck the World Trade Centre on September 11, 2001. Her mother told her that once, in passing, the way you might tell a child where they were born. For years it meant nothing more than a coincidence of timing.
"I was born right before it happened," Carter, who turned 25 recently, told TRT World. "I didn't really know what that meant. I just knew people talked about it every year around my birthday."
That is close to the whole of her relationship to September 11: a story told to her, not a memory she carries. Twenty-five years on, that distance defines an entire generation. 
They inherited the wars, the airport lines, and the vocabulary of a conflict they never witnessed. 
The scale of that gap is now measurable.
A Pew Research Centre survey conducted in late August 2026 found that one in ten American adults were born after the attacks, learning about that cataclysmic morning only through what others told them.
Among Americans aged 18 to 24, six in ten say they first encountered 9/11 in a classroom rather than at a kitchen table or in front of a television, and 4,025,933 children were born in the United States in 2001 alone, according to the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention: an entire cohort that grew up inside a country already reshaped by that morning.
A single morning, four different childhoods
Farid Ahmad was born in Kabul the same year Carter was born in New Jersey. Years later, his father told him something had happened in America. Then his father told him something else.
"He said America came to Afghanistan," Ahmad, 25, says.
Ahmad grew up inside the consequence rather than the event, and a quarter-century later he is unconvinced the story is finished.
"People say it's over," he says. "But I don't know. Everybody knows somebody who was affected."
For Carter, the same phrase arrives secondhand, off a screen. "It was just this thing America was doing after 9/11," she says. "I never really thought about what the phrase actually meant."
Ahmad belongs to an even younger country than Carter's.
Afghanistan's population, estimated at roughly 38 million, has a median age of about 19, and by United Nations Population Fund estimates, close to two-thirds of Afghans are under 25.
Almost the entire country has lived its whole life inside the war that followed September 11, a fact of demography as much as of history.
A question that follows
Asina Rahman was six months old on September 11, 2001, growing up Pakistani American in Chicago. Her father tried to inoculate her early against a conclusion he knew she'd otherwise be handed by others.
"He said, 'They're not doing it because they're religious,'" Rahman, 24, told TRT World. "He wanted me to understand that."
She has needed the reminder more than once. A stranger once asked her, laughing, whether she knew any terrorists. "I laughed too, which I don't know why I did," she says. "I was just uncomfortable."
Omar Hassan, 20, born in Michigan five years after the attacks on 9/11, has fielded a version of the same question. "Someone asked me once what I make of September 11," he says. "I was like, 'I wasn't even alive.' I didn't really know what else to say."
Carter has never faced that question, and she knows exactly why.
"I think that's probably different for me," she says.
Rahman and Hassan belong to a US Muslim population that Pew Research Centre put at 3.45 million people in 2017, about 1 percent of the country, younger on average than the general population.
Explaining it to someone younger
Ask each of them how they'd explain September 11 to a child, and the answers don't quite match, even when they are circling the same ground.
Carter starts confident and then hedges. "Some terrorists flew planes into buildings, and a lot of people died," she says. "I'd probably have to explain the rest because that's a lot for a kid."
Ahmad has one addition he treats as essential. "I'd say some people attacked America and a lot of people died. Then America went to war," he says.
Rahman's version carries a warning her own father gave her years earlier. "I'd tell them what happened. The planes, the buildings, the people who died," she says.
"And I'd tell them that religion in general had nothing to do with it. I think that's very important."
Hassan's answer lands close to Rahman's, almost word for word, though the two don’t know each other.
"I'd say terrorists attacked the US and a lot of people died," he says. "And I'd probably tell them Muslims didn't, like, all do it or anything. It was some bad people."
No fixed address
None of the four young people who spoke to TRT World in the weeks before the 25th anniversary of 9/11 was old enough to remember the day that would shape their lives.
What they hold instead are secondhand images, family caution, checkpoints and a phrase that means something different depending on which side of the war it landed on.
For Carter, it is history, if inconvenient enough to still explain each September. For Ahmad, it is a story about Afghanistan, his homeland. For Rahman and Hassan, it is inseparable from growing up in America and being asked to answer for something they were too young to understand.
Twenty-five years later, the towers are a photograph to all four of them.
Says Rahman, “I don’t remember that day. I think my generation has mostly grown up trying to understand what happened, and hopefully we can move forward from it.”

Ansar Allah Now Commands Bab al-Mandab Strait
Yemeni forces secure 5,400 km²; Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree confirms ban on Saudi vessels remains active
TEHRAN – The Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF) have seized control of the country’s western coast, further consolidating their hold over the vital Bab al-Mandab Strait after capturing more than 5,400 square kilometers of territory from Saudi Arabia.
In a sweeping ground campaign along Yemen’s western coast, the YAF entered Dhubab, a town located directly on the Bab al-Mandab Strait opposite Perim Island.

Footage released by YAF members shows the scale of weapons abandoned by Saudi-backed forces. It includes U.S.-made Oshkosh M-ATV mine-resistant vehicles, pickup trucks mounted with heavy weapons (technicals), armored vehicles, artillery pieces, and large quantities of ammunition and small arms.
The capture of the Red Sea coast marks a major catastrophe for the United States and Saudi Arabia. Full control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait will strengthen Ansar Allah’s position over the vital maritime chokepoint. For Saudi Arabia, it undermines Riyadh’s influence and military objectives in Yemen.
The Saudis will also find it increasingly difficult to export oil, with Ansar Allah controlling Bab al-Mandab and Iran controlling the Strait of Hormuz. Together, these two strategic chokepoints constrain the Kingdom’s ability to move its oil to global markets, tightening supplies and putting upward pressure on prices. The disruption to Saudi oil exports is already being reflected in the rising cost of oil on global markets.
This is while the United States faces greater risks to shipping and protecting Israeli interests. The regime’s media outlets continued to follow developments. Israeli Channel 14 said that Ansar Allah’s control of Mokha port on the Red Sea coast “constitutes a strategic event that could have far-reaching consequences.”
During the military front in support of and in solidarity with Gaza amid the U.S.-backed genocide in the Strip, the YAF’s threat in Bab al-Mandab had been directed only at Israeli and Israeli-affiliated ships. This was followed by American ships that attempted and failed to break the YAF’s Red Sea blockade on the regime’s vessels.
Saudi Arabia has been carrying out heavy airstrikes against several provinces in an effort to reinforce its military buildup on the ground.
Throughout the rapid YAF military advance, Ansar Allah’s political bureau affirmed that the western coastal areas are Yemeni territory and that Yemenis have the right to reclaim them from Saudi Arabia. Ansar Allah has noted that the entry of the YAF into these areas was widely welcomed by residents.

Ukrainian drone strikes degrade Russian oil refining industry – IEA
That is according to the International Energy Agency, Ukrinform reports, citing Bloomberg.
"It now appears likely that the persistent drone strikes and the patchwork nature of repairs are having a cumulative negative effect and degrading the [Russian] refining system," the agency said in its monthly oil market report published on Friday.
Ukraine has been attacking Russia's energy infrastructure to reduce the nation's ability to process and export crude and curtail the Kremlin's revenues used to finance the full-scale invasion. In August, the Russian oil refineries were hit at least 22 times, the highest monthly total since the start of the war, according to a Bloomberg tally based on public statements from both nations.
The IEA revised down its baseline outlook for Russian oil processing over the next 18 months to around 4 million barrels a day, down 30% from levels before the invasion of Ukraine, it said.
"Risks remain that even this more cautious assessment may yet understate the problems that Russia's refining complex faces," according to the report. "Longer lead-times to source replacement parts and the approach of colder weather could compound the stress placed on the Russian system."
Ukraine's military capabilities have been improving, including the efficacy of its strikes on Russian refineries, according to the IEA.
"Ukrainian forces are using multiple drone waves against single sites, overwhelming protective netting and air defenses," the report said. "The targeting also appears more precise."
Drones are now hitting secondary-processing units at Russia's refineries, which may require six to eight months to replace, according to the IEA estimates. International sanctions against the Russian energy industry are limiting its access to replacement equipment, further complicating the repairs.
The IEA has also lowered its 2026 forecast for Russia's crude supply forecast by 125,000 barrels per day to 8.7 million barrels per day amid lower refinery runs, it said.

Russia sends sanctioned ships to Mediterranean as NATO tracks 'Syrian Express' convoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:47:32 UTC
01:47:32 KST

Four Russian ships, including sanctioned cargo and tanker vessels escorted by a destroyer, entered the Mediterranean via Gibraltar on 27 August, ending the first interruption of Russia's naval presence there since 2013.
Russia's navy has returned to the Mediterranean for the first time in two months, ending what military sources described as the first interruption to its Mediterranean presence since 2013 — with ships reportedly detected switching off their tracking transponders before passing through the Strait of Gibraltar.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, a senior European military source said the "Syrian Express" ships had arrived at the Syrian port of Tartus on Monday.
The informal name "Syrian Express" refers to Moscow's maritime logistics network that transfers military supplies, weapons, and equipment between Russian ports and Tartus.
It has been running intermittently since Russia's military intervention in Syria in 2015, frequently involving sanctioned vessels that have also been associated with Russia's broader shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to circumvent Western sanctions.
The latest Russian convoy included the sanctioned cargo vessel Sparta, the sanctioned tanker General Skobelev, and the replenishment ship Akademik Pashin, all escorted by the destroyer Admiral Levchenko.
Tight European surveillance
Despite its return to the Mediterranean, Russia's navy remains under tight European surveillance.
The ships in question were closely tracked by the Italian Carabinieri frigate as they sailed through the central Mediterranean after they were spotted at Gibraltar.
Euronews obtained exclusive photos of the Italian frigate alongside the Russian ships.
Tracking data from the specialised website MarineTraffic indicates that the vessels switched off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders — which automatically broadcast ships' identity, position, speed, and course — before passing through the Strait of Gibraltar.
Britain deployed three ships — HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn — to monitor the convoy as it sailed through the English Channel.
The military source told Euronews that in recent months, Syrian express ships have begun cutting off AIS transponders even "more frequently" than in the past, with this practice almost becoming "systematic".
Russia retains post-al-Assad presence in Syria
Tartus is Russia's only naval base outside the former Soviet Union and its sole resupply and maintenance point in the Mediterranean.
The Soviet Union established the facility in 1971 under a lease agreement with Damascus, using it to sustain its Mediterranean fleet during the Cold War.
Russia intervened militarily in Syria in September 2015, entering the country's civil war on the side of Bashar al-Assad at a moment when his forces were losing ground to opposition groups.
Moscow initially said its strikes were targeting the so-called Islamic State terrorist group, but international organisations documented that the majority of Russian air strikes hit opposition-held civilian areas, with the Airwars monitoring group assessing that those strikes resulted in the deaths of more than 14,000 Syrian civilians.
The nine-year campaign in Syria was the Kremlin's most significant military participation in a war outside the former Soviet Union before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
When the al-Assad regime finally collapsed in December 2024, Russian warships evacuated from Tartus within days — a precautionary move to avoid being seized or denied departure.
In August, Damascus announced it had reached a deal with Moscow to retain Russia's future presence in the two military bases it has in the country.
On 9 August, Syria’s state news agency SANA quoted the Foreign Ministry as saying the Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval base would become “joint training and capacity-building centres” under new arrangements aimed at preserving "mutual interests".
The senior European military source outlined several factors which are hindering Moscow's ability to maintain its presence in the Mediterranean including Russia's ageing navy, European sanctions against its shadow fleet, as well as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones targeting its Black Sea fleet.
European and Ukrainian pressure on the shadow fleet is also pushing Russia to deploy military escorts for its oil tankers.

While official spokespersons in Seoul were quick to stress that no final decision had been made regarding any deployment, South Korea had previously acknowledged that it was actively considering “contributions” to US security efforts along the vital maritime corridor, provided that its own military readiness was not compromised.
Under South Korean constitutional law, should Seoul decide to deploy armed forces to the strait, the executive branch cannot act unilaterally; it would require formal parliamentary approval by a majority vote in the National Assembly—a hurdle that grows increasingly steep as public opposition intensifies.
Public outrage and street protests in Seoul
Dozens of South Korean anti-war activists, civil society leaders, and ordinary citizens gathered across from the massive United States embassy compound in Seoul on Wednesday to demand that their government unequivocally reject Washington’s pressure to deploy troops to the strategic Strait of Hormuz, fiercely slamming the ongoing campaign as an “illegal war”. The protesters unfurled banners and waved signs bearing powerful messages such as “Do not join a war of aggression”. They voiced their collective indignation as South Korean political and military leaders continue to weigh a potential “contribution” to the waterway’s security at the behest of the White House.
With passions running high against foreign military entanglements, the crowd echoed a resounding plea directly toward the presidential office: “We cannot send our young people into a sea of death!” Speaking outside the embassy, Jung Kyung-jik of People’s Solidarity for Participatory Democracy affirmed that Iranian concerns are grounded in legal reality: “As Iran has said, the deployment of our troops to the region would amount to direct participation in an illegal war”.
Choi Young-ok from Korean Peace Solidarity for Sovereignty and Reunification added, “Sending our troops to an illegal war waged by the United States is unacceptable... There is no reason for us to send troops when no other country has done so or said it would.”
The prospect of South Korea's potential military involvement in the Persian Gulf has drawn strong warnings from authorities in Iran, who have made it clear that any foreign intervention alongside hostile American forces will not go unanswered. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei has emphasized that such involvement would amount to “direct” support for the United States and would inevitably lead to serious consequences.

Baqaei: IAEA risks becoming instrument for justifying aggression against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11

Baqaei: IAEA risks becoming instrument for justifying aggression against Iran
TEHRAN- Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei has sharply criticized the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and its Director General, Rafael Grossi, accusing them of undermining the agency’s independence and turning its technical assessments into a basis for political pressure and justification for military action against Iran.
In a post on X, Baqaei said the IAEA Director General had transformed an institution whose authority was founded on “technical expertise, impartiality, and independence” into a link in a chain connecting technical reporting to political justification and, ultimately, war.
His remarks came shortly after the IAEA Board of Governors voted to refer Iran’s nuclear file to the United Nations Security Council over alleged non-compliance with its safeguards' obligations.
The resolution, introduced by the United States, Britain, France and Germany, was adopted on September 9 by 23 votes in favor, three against and eight abstentions. Russia, China and Niger voted against the measure.
Baqaei argued that the development illustrated the growing politicization of an institution that is supposed to operate as an impartial technical body.
“When IAEA reports become raw material for threat narratives and for the construction of a political and legal case against a country,” he wrote, “the line between technical oversight and laying the groundwork for military aggression becomes dangerously blurred.”
The Iranian spokesman said the issue went beyond reputational damage to the agency or its director general, warning that the IAEA’s most valuable asset—its credibility as an impartial and independent authority—was being squandered.
“Once that credibility is subordinated to political agendas,” Baqaei said, “the Agency risks becoming an instrument for rationalizing and facilitating aggression.”
He described such a development as a “profound institutional failure,” arguing that the agency had effectively become involved in the political preparation of an unlawful war.
Baqaei further accused the IAEA of contributing to a political process serving the interests and ambitions of a “genocidal regime,” a reference to Israel, which Iran has repeatedly accused of obstructing efforts to establish a West Asia free of weapons of mass destruction.
“An institution entrusted with contributing to international peace and security should never become part of the machinery used to manufacture a pretext for war,” he said.
The Iranian spokesman also rejected the notion that responsibility for aggression and war crimes should be confined solely to those who order or physically carry out military attacks. In his view, accountability must also encompass actors whose actions knowingly contribute to the political, legal or evidentiary foundations used to justify military action.
He warned that those who present disputed assessments as authoritative grounds for coercive measures cannot simply distance themselves from the consequences of such actions.
Baqaei’s comments came amid a sharp escalation in the dispute between Iran and the IAEA following the Board of Governors’ latest resolution. Iran has rejected the resolution as politically motivated and without a sound legal basis, while maintaining that its nuclear program is peaceful.
Western governments, meanwhile, claim that Iran has failed to provide the agency with sufficient access and information concerning its nuclear activities.
The latest vote has added a new layer to an already deeply strained relationship between Tehran and the UN nuclear watchdog, with Iran warning that the politicization of the IAEA could ultimately undermine confidence in the international nuclear safeguards system itself.

BRICS: The gears of change keep grinding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:46:01 UTC
01:46:01 KST

BRICS: The gears of change keep grinding
BRICS leaders are meeting in New Delhi this weekend for the group’s 18th annual summit.
India took over the rotating chair of the group in January and has adopted a different tone. Rhetoric about de-dollarization and overhauling the current financial system has taken a back seat to more practical considerations of economic connectivity.
The summit comes against a mixed backdrop. On the one hand, Chinese President Xi Jinping will be in attendance in what will be his first visit to India in seven years. This underscores the importance Beijing attaches to BRICS. Also traveling to Delhi is Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On the other hand, recently joined BRICS members UAE and Iran have found themselves on opposite sides of the hostilities in the Middle East. A two-day meeting of BRICS foreign ministers in New Delhi in May concluded without a joint statement due to divergent views on the Middle East, and this weekend’s summit will be taking place in the shadow of this tension.
Nevertheless, as trade ties among key BRICS countries keep growing, the methodical work of creating new financial channels and architecture continues apace. BRICS is slowly but surely building an entire institutional ecosystem for trade, investment, and settlement. It is a process often unfolding without loud pronouncements and far from news cycles.
RT takes a look at what’s going on in BRICS these days.
Progress on payments
Perhaps the most important tangible proposals on the agenda for this year’s summit are ones to link the payment systems of BRICS countries.
There are two tracks for this.
The first is the BRICS Pay project. This is an effort to create an interoperable payment system across BRICS countries that would connect national and commercial payment systems with the aim of supporting settlements in national currencies. BRICS Pay exists at the pilot level but has not yet been rolled out commercially across the bloc.
When implemented, it will make sending money between BRICS countries more like making a domestic electronic payment rather than sending money through a chain of banks and currencies. Currently, for example, if an Indian company buys something from a Brazilian company, the cross-border payment can involve such hassles as correspondent banks and currency conversions – not to mention additional costs.
According to Kremlin aide Kirill Dmitriev, an agreement on BRICS Pay is forthcoming at the summit, where a specific emphasis will be placed on financial questions.
“We are focusing specifically on the financial track. We lead the group responsible for cooperation on financial issues, and payments are a very important part of this,” he said.
This does not necessarily mean, however, that the entire BRICS Pay architecture is about to become operational, but it does mean that the project might receive a large push.
The second track is the proposed linking of members’ central-bank digital currencies (CBDC) for cross-border payments, which India has reportedly included on the agenda of the event.
Linking up the CBDCs of BRICS countries would make the central-bank-issued digital money interoperable across countries. This initiative represents a deeper level in the financial plumbing than BRICS Pay. It would allow cross-border transactions to be settled more directly and with fewer intermediaries and steps. It would also represent an additional settlement route outside the Western-centered architecture.
Importantly, however, this is explicitly not being framed as the creation of a BRICS currency, an initiative that has at times been the subject of speculation.
The CBDC link-up project remains at the discussion stage.
BRICS trade
Trade within the group continues to grow. Intra-BRICS exports totaled about $1.2 trillion in 2025. India’s trade with the other BRICS members, for example, reached around $416 billion in 2025, growing at nearly 10% annually from 2021–25.
Up for endorsement by leaders at the summit is the BRICS Economic Partnership Strategy 2030, which is an extension of an existing BRICS economic strategy document that, among other things, focuses on trade and investment, the digital economy, and financial cooperation.
A major aim of the initiative is to facilitate a broad reduction in institutional friction for economic activity within the group. It also emphasizes supply-chain resilience and support for small and medium-sized businesses, among other areas.
It is this type of unglamorous nitty-gritty work that can provide the foundation for BRICS economic infrastructure to eventually match the size and scale of the group’s economies.
Meanwhile, the New Development Bank, established by BRICS in 2015, has now approved roughly $43 billion in lending. While still relatively small in scale, the bank is an example of a BRICS institution that is now up and running.
Energy ties
The crucial energy trade continues to expand as well, notwithstanding Western attempts to suppress Russian exports of oil and gas.
India’s imports of Russian crude reached 2.47 million barrels per day in July 2026, a record 50.8% of India’s total crude imports and 62.4% above the figure from the year prior. For April–July 2026, Russia supplied 43.25% of India’s crude imports, up from 37% a year earlier. Russia remains China’s largest crude oil supplier and the two countries continue to develop energy ties.
Meanwhile, Russia’s recently launched greenfield Vostok Oil, a massive cluster of fields deep in the Arctic, is expected to greatly expand Russia’s energy trade with Asia via the Northern Sea Route, although it will be years before volumes are expected to reach capacity. Nevertheless, this represents a strategically important route that bypasses the fraught Middle East.
Nuclear cooperation has also been a prominent part of the broader BRICS energy and technology agenda. China, India, and Russia are all major powers in civilian nuclear energy and have sought to boost cooperation in recent years.
The bigger context
BRICS has sometimes moved more slowly than proponents would like and has at times been derided, especially in Western policy circles, for a perceived lack of concrete action.
Some expectations placed on the group may have been unrealistic. Financial architecture certainly has enormous inertia, and incumbent systems with decades of accumulated infrastructure and well-established channels are not displaced quickly, even when the need for alternative mechanisms becomes apparent.
Meanwhile, the crisis in the Middle East, in which BRICS members Iran and the UAE are at odds, is being portrayed as a challenge for unified action.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov acknowledged that the differences between Iran and the UAE had a “negative impact” on efforts to prepare a joint declaration, although he expressed optimism that diplomatic efforts could bridge the gap.
However, behind the scenes and at a remove from the vicissitudes of politics, work continues to create the infrastructure that will provide nations representing half of the world’s population and 40% of GDP greater economic autonomy. Developing this infrastructure is also at the heart of efforts to create alternatives to Western-dominated systems.
The on-ramp may be long, but once this infrastructure is in place at scale, global financial channels could start looking very different.
This weekend's summit is another step in this direction.

Nearly 2,400 Yemeni families displaced in a day amid fighting in Taiz, Lahj

Omer Asur Cuhadar and Mohammad Sio
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
Yemeni authorities said Friday that 2,398 more families were displaced in a single day amid the latest military escalation, including 823 families in Taiz province and 1,575 in Lahj.
The figures were published by the Executive Unit for the Management of Displacement Camps and carried by the official Saba news agency.
The unit said the new displacement was recorded on Sept. 10, bringing the total number of documented displaced families to 9,746, up from 7,348 a day earlier.
It said the main areas of origin were locations affected by fighting in Taiz, Al-Hudaydah and along Yemen’s western coast, particularly the districts of Jabal Habashi, Al-Ma’afer, Maqbanah, Al-Wazi’iyah, Mawza, Mocha, Hays and Al-Khawkhah, as well as other areas.
Field teams are continuing to register displaced families, verify their data and places of arrival, assess needs and coordinate humanitarian assistance, the unit said.
It added that several schools in Al-Mudaraba district in Lahj had been opened to shelter displaced families, while local residents had also taken in some families in private homes.
The unit also held a coordination meeting Friday with the UN refugee agency to discuss assistance and the growing humanitarian needs, while maintaining contact with international and humanitarian organizations to expand the response.
Urgent needs include shelter, food, life-saving assistance, dignity kits, hygiene supplies, drinking water and water and sanitation services as families continue to arrive in reception areas.
Earlier Friday, the International Organization for Migration said at least 46,000 people had been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week, warning that the number was rising “at an alarming rate.”
The organization did not specify the areas from which they had fled.
Yemen’s battlefield map has shifted in recent days as fighting between government forces and the Houthis intensified after clashes resumed in early July following years of relative calm.
The Houthis say they now control all of Al-Hudaydah province and have advanced in western Taiz, taking Mocha city and its Red Sea port and reaching areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime routes.
Government forces, meanwhile, have made gains in the northern province of Al-Jawf near the Saudi border and moved closer to Al-Hazm, the provincial capital, while fighting continues on fronts in Marib, Al-Bayda and Al-Dhalea.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

AfD files criminal complaint against Merz
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has filed a criminal complaint against German Chancellor Friedrich Merz after he claimed that the right-wing party is calling for ethnic cleansing. Merz made the remark in a heated parliamentary debate following the AfD’s resounding victory in the regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt.
The AfD is the most popular party in Germany, according to multiple polls, enjoying the support of 28% of respondents nationally. The right-wing opposition Eurosceptic party advocates tougher immigration controls and is also highly critical of the German government’s support for Ukraine, as well as sanctions against Russia.
In a statement on Thursday, the AfD parliamentary group – the largest opposition faction in the German parliament – accused Merz of defamation that goes beyond constitutionally protected free speech in parliament.
Speaking in the Bundestag on Wednesday, the chancellor claimed that in promoting ‘remigration’ the AfD is essentially advocating “ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin color.”
Stephan Brandner, the secretary and legal counsel for the AfD parliamentary group, stated that with “his baseless and repugnant remarks” directed not only at the party itself, but also at millions of German citizens, Merz has “crossed a line… in a way that carries criminal implications.”
The concept of ‘remigration', which has been gaining traction among right-wing circles in Europe in recent years, is usually understood to mean the return of criminal and ‘non-assimilated’ immigrants and, more broadly, residents with a migrant background to their countries of origin.
Merz made the remark days after the AfD won Sunday’s regional elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt with 43.8% of the vote.
The chancellor’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party finished a distant second, securing just over 17.2%.
Speaking at a press conference, Merz acknowledged that the Christian Democrats, who had for years dominated Saxony-Anhalt’s political landscape, had suffered the “most serious electoral defeat in decades.”
However, the chancellor refused to change course and vowed to “strengthen our political order and our firm anchoring in Europe,” while blaming the CDU’s dismal results on poor communication with the voters.
An INSA poll published by Bild in late August indicated that support for the governing Christian Democratic CDU/CSU bloc had dipped to 20% nationwide, with 78% of respondents dissatisfied with Merz’s coalition government.
Meanwhile, Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said on Thursday that the party does not “categorically demonize the production of defense equipment, because we will naturally need the appropriate tools for the subsequent remigration and deportation drive.”
“This is also in the interest of internal security, our own stability, and state defense,” the politician stated in response to a journalist’s question that referenced recent media reports of negotiations between Israel’s Elbit Systems and regional authorities. The arms manufacturer is reportedly seeking to set up a plant in the town of Sangerhausen.
In recent months, multiple establishment political figures have called for the opposition AfD to be banned for presumably posing a threat to Germany’s constitutional order and democracy.
In late August, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Wurttemberg Governor Cem Ozdemir said that the AfD should be outlawed as it supposedly calls into question the “inviolability of human dignity” enshrined in the German constitution. The politicians who represent the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the Green Party, respectively, cited the right-wing party’s tough-on-immigration stance.
The AfD has already been placed under surveillance by the German federal authorities, which classify the party as a ‘suspected right-wing extremist’ entity. In several regions, local AfD chapters have been subjected to even wider monitoring.

From Bishkek to New Delhi, Xi advocates Global South cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

From Bishkek to New Delhi, Xi advocates Global South cooperation
Chinese President Xi Jinping is heading to New Delhi for this year's BRICS gathering just over a week after he took part in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek.
The two back-to-back multilateral engagements converge on a single, defining theme: galvanizing solidarity and cooperation across the Global South.
EXPANDING FAMILY
The SCO "takes root in the Global South, its heart beats with the Global South, and it is an important pillar of South-South cooperation," Xi said at the Bishkek summit on Tuesday last week, calling on the SCO to "promote the development and rise of the Global South through the SCO Wisdom."
The Chinese leader is expected to put forward further proposals on Global South cooperation at the upcoming BRICS summit, as he has noted that the BRICS is "standing at the forefront of the Global South."
This year marks the 25th founding anniversary of the SCO and the 20th anniversary of the BRICS cooperation mechanism, both milestone occasions.
Chinese President Xi Jinping chairs the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" Meeting in Tianjin, north China, Sept. 1, 2025. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)
 
 
 Riding the wave of the collective rise of the Global South, BRICS and the SCO have over the years expanded their membership and broadened their networks of developing partners. Their members jointly account for more than half of the world's population and about 30 percent of the global economy. This illustrates the fact that the two groupings have evolved into major platforms for Global South cooperation.
Xi has not only joined other leaders of member countries in pushing for their respective expansions, but also put forward new ideas and initiatives like the "BRICS Plus" cooperation approach and the building of an SCO community with a shared future, opening up new vistas for win-win cooperation among Global South countries.
"China has consistently provided a clear vision and momentum for BRICS and the SCO, both conceptually and practically," said Humprey Arnaldo Russel, head of the ASEAN-China Research Center at the University of Indonesia.
Photo taken on Aug. 24, 2017 shows a flowerbed at the Xiamen International Conference and Exhibition Center in Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province. (Xinhua/Jiang Kehong)
"It transformed BRICS from a relatively exclusive grouping into a broader platform for cooperation among developing countries and the wider Global South," he added.
DEVELOPMENT FIRST
At the SCO summit last week, Xi called on countries to "stay committed to putting development first, and open up the prospects for shared prosperity."
Amid a turbulent and rapidly changing international landscape, development still faces severe challenges, and the road to prosperity for the Global South will not be straight.
Chinese expert Li Guiqiang (L) gives instructions on vegetable cultivation at the China-Ethiopia Addis Ababa Agricultural Technology Demonstration and Training Center in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Aug. 20, 2025. (Xinhua/Han Xu)
 
 "The Global South emerges for development and prospers through development. We should make ourselves the main driving force for common development," Xi said during the 2024 BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia.
For Xi, development has always been a priority. He sees it as "the master key to solving all problems," and has consistently called for countries worldwide to jointly pursue development and prosperity.
Xi has stressed repeatedly that no one should be left behind in the fight against poverty in China, and has led a formidable campaign that ended extreme poverty nationwide, which was hailed as "the greatest anti-poverty achievement in history."
His "leaving-no-one-behind" conviction also extends to his efforts to support poverty reduction and spur development across the Global South. "On the path to modernization, no one, and no country, should be left behind," Xi said.
Last week in Bishkek, Xi called for consolidating cooperation in both traditional and emerging fields, from trade, investment, connectivity and energy to artificial intelligence (AI), the digital economy and green industries.
Responding to the Global South's aspirations for common development and modernization, Xi has proposed the Global Development Initiative (GDI), which marks its fifth anniversary this year.
In the last five years, the GDI has mobilized more than 23 billion U.S. dollars, provided support for over 1,800 "small and beautiful" livelihood projects, and sponsored training programs for more than 200,000 people in different professions.
Serik Korzhumbayev, editor-in-chief of the Delovoy Kazakhstan newspaper, said: "Under Xi's leadership, the concept of development has acquired a new international dimension and become part of a broader vision for humanity's shared future."
GREATER VOICE
As the Global South rises, it deserves a bigger say in global affairs.
Last year's SCO Tianjin summit witnessed Xi's proposal of the Global Governance Initiative, a major proposition of China to advance a more just and equitable global governance system.
At the heart of this vision is the conviction that every country has a place and an equal role to play in global governance.
Xi has long argued that international affairs should not be dictated by those with more muscles. "World affairs should be discussed by all, and international norms should be set by all," he said in Bishkek last week. "The domination of international affairs by a few is an injustice left over from history, and global governance dictated by one, a few or a bloc of countries is not true multilateralism."
"As an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs," Xi said.
Robotic arms work in an energy storage production workshop at the Sigenergy Nantong Smart Energy Center in Nantong, east China's Jiangsu Province, July 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Yehua)
 
 
 Over the years, the SCO and BRICS have grown into vital venues for Global South countries to articulate their interests, coordinate their positions and strengthen their collective influence.
Their growing role can be seen in political coordination. The two groupings have issued statements on international and regional hotspot issues. In March this year, for example, SCO member states issued a statement expressing grave concern over developments in the Middle East and the strikes on Iran.
Xi has also pushed for improving global economic and financial governance. In 2014, Xi and other BRICS leaders formally signed an agreement establishing the New Development Bank, creating a new channel for financing infrastructure and sustainable development in emerging markets and developing countries.
At the SCO Bishkek summit, the members reaffirmed the importance of establishing the SCO Development Bank.
Now the push for a greater say is extending into emerging areas that will shape the future. In July this year, Xi announced the creation of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, and called for joint efforts to build a just and equitable system of global AI governance.
"We must carry out extensive international cooperation and help Global South countries with capacity building to bridge the AI and digital divides, promote sustainable development, and prevent creating new historical injustice in AI," Xi said.
An aerial photo taken on Oct. 22, 2025 shows wind turbines of De Aar Wind Power Project in De Aar, Northern Cape, South Africa. (Xinhua/Han Xu)
 
 
 Beyond the SCO and BRICS, China has also promoted cooperation and greater representation for the Global South through frameworks such as the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation and the China-ASEAN summit.
Xi has said on many occasions that China has always been a member of the Global South and will always belong to the developing world.
"No matter how the international landscape evolves, we in China will always keep the Global South in our heart, and maintain our roots in the Global South," he once said.

British man encouraged group chat members to abuse partners, exchange images
LONDON - A British man pleaded guilty in court on Sept 11 to encouraging other men in an online group chat to sexually abuse their unconscious partners and exchange images of the abuse.
It is the latest in a string of UK criminal cases involving men accused of abusing their partners while asleep or sedated and often going on to share images of their offences.
Darren Conway, 52, pleaded guilty to multiple charges including voyeurism, possessing an extreme pornographic image and assisting or encouraging sexual assault and the sharing of intimate images.
He admitted to messaging a man in 2025, asking the man to assault his wife while she was asleep and share images of the crime.
He also solicited images of sleeping women online at least 10 times between 2023 and 2026.
Conway was charged following an investigation by Britain’s National Crime Agency (NCA) into an online forum linked to multiple, international cases of men encouraging or committing this type of offence, known as drug-facilitated sexual abuse.
Global awareness of the crime has grown following the high-profile conviction in France of Dominique Pelicot, who drugged and raped his then-wife Gisele for nearly a decade alongside strangers.
The judge in the north London court dealing with Conway’s case said he would be sentenced on Oct 30.
“Messages found on his devices showed Conway encouraging other group chat members to engage in drug-facilitated sexual offending, alongside images and videos of a sexual nature,” London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
“Conway’s actions were shocking,” Met police commander Andy Day said.
“By encouraging others to engage in sexual offending against victims who were unconscious, asleep, or otherwise stupefied, he has put women at a serious risk of harm in their own homes – all for his own sexual gratification.”
Police said while “much of the offending” on Conway’s group chat is believed to have taken place in the UK, “it is also possible that some victims are based overseas”.
In a separate case, a man in central England pleaded guilty in July to 32 sexual offences against his girlfriend while she was allegedly drugged or asleep.
In Manchester in north-west England, the husband of a woman who was allegedly drugged and sexually assaulted is set to stand trial this month alongside 12 other men accused of taking part in the abuse. AFP
