Democrats are in a ‘death match’ with the Left over Israel. How will it impact the midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:31:52 UTC
01:31:52 KST

The Trump administration’s approval rating has reached a record low. What does that mean for the midterms, and what should we be keeping a close eye on as the Democrats attempt to take back Congress?
Mondoweiss U.S. correspondent Michael Arria spoke with political consultant Peter Feld about the primary results, AIPAC’s role in the elections, the centrist obsession with Hasan Piker, and what to expect in November.
Let’s start with the primaries, where we saw some big progressive wins across the country in races where Israel and AIPAC became flashpoint issues.
Before we started recording, you said you thought the primaries were a mixed bag for progressives: there were some big wins, but centrists held their ground in many places. Can you talk about that?
Well, sure, it was really exhilarating, the primary season that we just had, for those of us who support Palestine and are looking to see some kind of change in policy and particularly within the Democratic Party. We had three major wins in New York with Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier, and Brad Lander. In Colorado, we had Milat Kiros, Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Dr. Adam Hamawi in New Jersey.
We did very well, but we also fell short, in areas that fall under the category of unforced errors. And we also had some bare scrapes, like Abdul El-Sayed, who was supposed to be winning by 12 or 15 points, scraping by by less than one. Of course a win is a win, and he goes on to the general election.
But I think the primary season left the establishment holding cards that they think they can deal with. They can push back on us and have been pushing back very hard, including the demonization of Piker as part of it. They understand, right now, that they’re in a death match with us.
And they won some important races. They just won the Senate nomination in New Hampshire with Chris Pappas. Progressives were somewhat hopeful that our candidate Karishma Manzur was cresting, but obviously not enough. And maybe if there’d been more investment we would have won that one. Several of the real villains, like Richie Torres, Jared Moskowitz, Greg Stanton, all skated by.
And then we have this new retrenchment by Hakeem Jeffries and the Democratic establishment to double down on their rejection of Medicare for All, double down on their support for Israel, put key people on Middle Eastern foreign policy committees who are the worst supporters of Israel that we have. They’re looking to elect Hakeem Jeffries as Speaker after what a lot of people expect will be a big Democratic win in the midterms. And when they do that, our position may not be as strong as we would like.
Let’s talk about the midterms. I think there’s an expectation that the Democrats will do well based on Trump’s low approval ratings, a bad economy, and an unpopular war. What are you looking at closely here, in terms of the Democratic Party, and do you expect them to take back Congress?
We really don’t know, and it’s going to be one of the most interesting things that we see. Right now it looks like Trump is really on the ropes. The war in Iran is a big part of it. The convention he just held seems like a flop. And the Republicans are demoralized.
What usually happens in a midterm is that very few swing voters take part. People often assume that persuasion drives these swings from Republican to Democrat or Democrat to Republican. But what’s really happening is differential turnout. The enthusiasm gap drives that. So you could say, all right, Republicans are demoralized, they may be likely to stay home. The Democrats may be energized, and they may turn out. And that’s why I think some of the very established and sober analysts are moving their forecasts and making it look like this could be a big Democratic sweep.
The other scenario is that some of this Democratic infighting catches up with the party. That the pro-Palestine base continues to be disenchanted, and that the enthusiasm gap comes back down to earth sometime between now and November. Maybe Trump pulls a rabbit out of the hat in Iran — I mean, he probably should because they’re kicking his butt. There is a scenario where things snap back. If you want to go back, we saw that in 2022 when Republicans were expecting a big blowout midterm because Biden was weak. And then Democratic chances mostly returned to normal, and Democrats had a better-than-expected night. You could go all the way back to 1982, which is before probably a lot of people watching were born. Reagan was supposed to have a really terrible midterm. He ended up pulling a lot of rabbits out of the hat, and the Democrats did well indeed, but not nearly as well as they had been expected to do.
An interesting situation for progressives is that there are bright spots under both scenarios. If the Democrats have a blowout year, I think a lot of our progressives who might be in difficult districts, like Bill Lawrence in Michigan 7, or Angie Nixon and her statewide race in Florida for the Senate — a rising tide could lift those boats. And we could end up seeing a lot of our champions going to Congress, along with a lot of Democrats who are more mainstream and establishment.
But in the other scenario, if the Democrats have a weak night, to some extent I think that’s going to be blamed on Jeffries. Because the leader of the party in Congress usually takes that blame. And you get, maybe, a narrow Democratic majority in the House that is smaller than the progressive contingent, old and new — so you have the Squad with AOC and Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan, etc., and then you have all these new people coming in, some of whom are very radical.
And if that bloc is bigger than the Democratic majority, they have the kind of leverage over Jeffries that The Freedom Caucus had several years on the Republican side. And they can use that leverage to force different things if they want to. If they’re strategic enough.
We don’t know what’s going to happen. It’s certainly going to be an interesting seven weeks.
I’d like to talk about the Israel Lobby, specifically AIPAC, which has spent big in the primaries as usual and is expected to spend even more in the midterms.
Recently, Axios reported that Mike Rogers, the GOP nominee for Senate in Michigan, was wary about AIPAC’s name being all over his ads, presumably because the organization has become deeply unpopular with the American people.
What do you make of AIPAC’s current situation, and how do you expect them to adapt to that political reality?
AIPAC certainly had some very, very spectacular failures this cycle, and I think that’s where this all comes to a head, particularly in Michigan, which Mike Rogers is looking at because $60 million was spent on Haley Stevens’s behalf. I think the largest chunk of that came from AIPAC. And she lost.
Now, she only lost by one point instead of the double digits. It could have been a win. So we can’t say they had no power, and if they had won the election by one percent instead of losing it by one percent they would have been out there the next day saying, “See? Supporting Israel as good policy and good politics” like they always do. So we have to recognize that, on the one hand, they failed; on the other hand, it’s a near miss.
There’s been tremendous work, including by Track AIPAC to really make AIPAC toxic. And they are. I did a lot of polling for Corbin Trent’s PAC, A Fight Worth Having, this cycle, where we over and over again showed that AIPAC was incredibly unpopular with Democratic voters — even in districts that were in the process of re-electing more mainstream, pro-Israel incumbents. Even in Richie Torres’ district. His renomination was taken as a sign that, well, people don’t care so much about Israel up in the Bronx. It’s not true. We found in our message testing that it wasn’t true. It’s just that they weren’t really aware of his background [on Israel]. But AIPAC itself was hugely unpopular, and we saw that in Missouri 1 where Cori Bush ended up unfortunately losing to Wesley Bell, but AIPAC was still radioactive and hugely unpopular. We saw this in Arizona 4, where Greg Stanton beat a progressive challenger, Kai Newkirk. But AIPAC was 65% unfavorable. And a lot of the rest are people who are just unsure and haven’t heard of them.
So has it disabled them? I don’t think so. They certainly spent big in the California special election against Aisha Wahab, and they lost. They have to be taking a step back and realizing that Israel is just incredibly unpopular, especially in Democratic primaries, and as I think we’re going to see, among independents and Republicans in the general election. Will that stop them? No, they have a huge amount of money to spend, and they are gifted at shape-shifting and setting up ancillary organizations with money that’s hard to trace.
And I think we also have to say that AIPAC is pretty effective in their messaging. In some ways, more so than the progressive left when it comes to paid messaging. Because they know how to stay away from Israel. They know how to attack people on other issues, like they didn’t support Kamala Harris or they voted against Biden’s infrastructure bill and other things that we’ve seen.
I just come back to this point: AIPAC and Jeffries and all these people understand that they’re in a death match right now. And this is the reason they’re leaning into the infighting: because they feel like they can’t afford to lose. So I don’t think that AIPAC is going to shrivel up. But I do think that they’ve been damaged, and they’re going to have fewer options for how they intervene in some of these contexts.
I’m going to ask you a cynical and direct question here: Does any of this AIPAC backlash ultimately matter?
Obviously, they don’t represent the entire lobby. There are other ways for people like Jeffrey Yass, or whoever, to spend big money on electoral races, but also wondering whether the rejection of AIPAC means anything in terms of the U.S./Israel relationship. We see lawmakers talk about AIPAC money like that’s the problem, as opposed to the wider issue of U.S. military support for the country, or Zionism more broadly. It sometimes reminds me of lawmakers, like Bernie Sanders, talking about “Netanyahu’s Israel” as if there’s some sort of distinction to be made there.
Do you think this runs the risk of becoming a situation lawmakers can reject AIPAC rhetorically and draw in voters that way, but continue to back Israel? We saw similar things happen during the BLM protests, where politicians were voicing their support for change and then continuing to back the same policies, so one would understand why activists would be wary.
I agree that there is a danger in having too much of it hung onto AIPAC. You and Mondoweiss have been warning about this because it’s not just AIPAC. But on the other side of the equation, we know that the ratings for Israel are also poor, and they’re falling across the board among Democrats. And not just younger but also older Democrats. That they’re falling among independents, that they’re falling among Republicans. We’ve seen races where AIPAC itself wasn’t really the factor, like Mamdani’s race last year in New York, where they tried to use Israel talking points against him, and they just didn’t work. People are smart, and they know that the issue is with Israel, not just AIPAC, and not just Netanyahu. We’ll see what happens with the Israeli elections next month.
I would also say that other pro-Israel groups have also been falling short. Democratic Majority for Israel’s candidate Maura Sullivan lost a congressional primary to Stefany Shaheen, Jeanne Shaheen’s daughter, in the New Hampshire primary two nights ago.
The Israel arguments don’t work, and they’re really not going to work. with the voters. The problem is really accountability. Can the Israel lobby and the AIPAC establishment and the politicians who support them get away with it?
There were a couple of posts a couple of days ago by Adam Johnson, very gloomy posts considering all the great news that we’ve seen in the primary, saying that the Zionist establishment is reasserting its control through Jeffries, the fake antisemitism smear of Hasan Piker is working, and Palestine has been driven off the agenda.
What they’re trying to do is they’re trying to make us radioactive. They’re trying to make Abdul radioactive and call him an antisemite because of his connection to Piker. They’re trying to make Mamdani radioactive, hyping this idea that he should not go to the 9/11 25th memorial commemoration in New York City. They’re doing everything they can.
Hakeem Jeffries’s moves in the last few weeks are part of this. He went on television and doubled down on aid to Israel and no Medicare for All. Then it turns out that he’s met with Jared Kushner. And then the next day, instead of trying to do damage control over the Kushner story, which was so damaging that even centrists like James Carville attacked Jeffries and said, “What are you doing?” — the very next day, they announced Moskowitz and Wasserman Schultz in key positions on the Foreign Affairs Committee. If they were trying to mollify the base, they wouldn’t do that. Instead, they’re picking a very intentional fight with the base because they need to win this, and they need to win this fight more than they need gains in the midterm.
I heard you and Yumna last week asking, why are they doing this? They’re doing this because it’s existential for them. And we’re seeing it in other ways. In the ban on federal aid to universities who “boycott Israel” that they passed, with 33 Democrats breaking off, and voting to condemn socialism, and other Israel votes.
What they’re saying is this: This is what it’s going to be. Get used to it. We’re being tone policed on criticizing Jeffries. But to me, the meeting with Jared Kushner is everything. We have to realize that the differences between Jeffries and Kushner over Israel are microscopic. I’m not aware of any difference of opinion that either of them has ever had with each other.
For all purposes regarding Israel, Hakeem Jeffries becoming Speaker might as well be Speaker Jared Kushner. That’s what we’re going to have next year. And they’re telling us that in the immediate wake of all of our victories.
Jeffries is there in the first place because of Israel. He is there in the first place because he won the 2018 contest against Barbara Lee for number two to Pelosi in the House leadership after AOC had defeated Crowley in the primaries that year. And Barbara Lee, though she’s not the most progressive Democrat we’ve ever seen, was notable for being the only one who voted against the authorization for the use of military force in Afghanistan right after 9/11. So she was considered unacceptable, and they put Jeffries in there, and they protected him all along. And now he’s poised to become Speaker as a result. And it all traces back to Israel.
So I think we have to look at our strategy and say, how are we going to fight back against this? It may not be enough to send our champions to Washington as a contingent of 10 or 20. What is the strategy going to be? Many of [the incoming progressives] have preemptively endorsed Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker. Certainly Brad Lander has, and a number of the others. Mamdani and AOC did a tremendous amount of work to clear obstacles from Hakeem Jeffries’ path. And to me this is a horrible thing because, apart from anything that we could say about Israel, he’s a terrible leader and communicator. And he did a terrible job of holding his caucus in line to prevent two Democrats from defecting and giving Republicans a procedural win.
If Hakeem Jeffries becomes Speaker, it will be a generational catastrophe. I don’t see a way to dislodge him without a Democratic wipeout, which I don’t think any of us wants to see. He’s going to be the first Black speaker, and anybody who attacks him is going to be attacking “the first Black speaker.” So to get back to your original question, this is how AIPAC is going to deploy its power, through these people — through Moskowitz and Wasserman Schultz and Greg Meeks, and other strongly pro-Israel supporters who are going to be in key positions. They’re saying they don’t care about public opinion, and don’t care what the Democratic base wants. And they think they can take their electability theories and bully progressives into getting behind whoever they push through the 2028 primaries. And so I think that you know Adam Johnson and others are right to sound the alarm. And it’s right to make it not just be about AIPAC, it’s about this whole constellation.
Let’s talk about Hasan Piker. I don’t know that there’s much to say that hasn’t already been said, but he’s become this Bogeyman on the right, and he’s also been attacked by a number of prominent Democrats, including people like Governor Gavin Newsom and Senator Jon Ossoff, who probably have presidential aspirations.
Another issue we haven’t addressed yet is the 2028 presidential campaign, and I’m wondering if you think these two things are connected. Are Democrats trying to pave the way for a centrist nominee by punching left on figures like Piker?
Well, I think they’re more than just connected. I think that’s what the attacks are all about. And Vox just ran an article saying Democratic moderates have one goal right now: not winning the midterms by the biggest possible margin, but making Piker a liability for 2028.
So the Democratic establishment and the Republicans were putting Piker up on the Jumbotron last night, they’re actually very closely allied in their way. Or at least they’re working in tandem. The Neera Tandens of the world, the head of the Center for American Progress, who’s very, very aggressive in fighting progressives, will take this thing on the Republican Jumbotron and say, See, if we stick with Piker, we’re going to be opening ourselves up to these kinds of criticisms. And of course, that was never said about Democrats associating with Charlie Kirk or Mike Savage, or any of the ones that Gavin Newsom was talking to. And it does show the hypocrisy, but they don’t really care about it. What they really care about is bullying us.
So, to your question: do these [2028 presidential] candidates think they’re helping themselves by attacking Piker? I think they’re soldiers in the fight. I think that Gavin Newsom and John Ossoff potentially feel threatened by a candidate who does have support from Piker. Say if Piker decides to support AOC, who herself has been a little bit muddled in how she’s addressed all of this. But they want to remove a progressive asset.
And you’ll remember that from 2024 and earlier, the Democratic establishment was shaking their heads and moaning about “how are we going to get a Joe Rogan of the left?” Well, they got Joe Rogan of the left, and all they want to do is suppress him and ostracize him and make him unfit to take part in any campaign. They’re saying, “Why don’t you stay away from Abdul’s race? Don’t you know any better? Just be quiet.”
Well, the thing is, what he’s saying is very, very popular, and I don’t think he is going to shut up. I think Newsom and Ossoff are really making themselves unacceptable to the progressive left.
This is all what it’s about. They want to win this fight more than they want to win a big margin in the 2026 midterms. And that’s why they’re focusing on it now.
And they would love to see the progressives lose and all these moderate, “central casting” candidates that the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has come up with — all the ones that are like, “I served six tours of duty in Iraq and Afghanistan” — they want those people to win. And their theory of electability is to be proven in these midterms.
And the progressive theory of electability holds that El-Sayed, Bill Lawrence, and Angie Nixon could win, and a few of the others, Amish Shah in Arizona, and a few Bernie Sanders is supporting in some swing districts — Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin and Sam Forstag in Montana.
So in the ideal scenario for the establishment, they would win the midterms without any of these progressives coming through. Then they can say, see. We’ve got to pull together and focus on electability. And of course they want Piker to be completely disarmed and disabled during this whole process. And that’s what we’re seeing right now.
How much does Israel factor into the concerns about Piker? He’s a very public anti-Zionist. Is that where the establishment’s anxiety comes from?
I think almost all of it comes from that, with the remaining small percentage coming from private health insurance. Avoiding Medicare for All, which they’re also desperate to do.
Basically, Jeffries and Schumer and the Democratic leadership answer only to the donor class. And Israel is not the only part of the donor class, but it overlaps with other parts, like real estate and private health insurance, the Democratic side of the tech world and the gig economy. Of course, we saw that after Obama left office, his top aides went to work for places like Uber and DoorDash. All of those are very few degrees of separation from Israel anyway — I mean, the Silicon Valley tech world is very aligned with Israel. And so sometimes it’s hard to know where one of these ends and the next one picks up.
But I think Israel is the 800-pound gorilla. It’s why they want to beat El-Sayed. It’s why they wanted to beat Mamdani. It’s why they wanted to beat Darializa and Claire Valdez. We won’t ever see the end of it.
But the Iran war is a big challenge for them. And I think that we’ve just got to gather our momentum. Frankly, I think what we have to do in response to all this is lean into Hasan Piker. “Piker now more than ever!” We have to not give in to them, and not accept the bullying, and push back. And if we don’t, we’re going to be on our heels.
So, when voters go to the polls during midterms, what do you think will be the central issues they’re basing their choices on?
David Hogg made a really interesting point about what’s going on. We basically have three levels of issues that have really energized the progressive Democratic base. At the local level, it’s the cameras and surveillance that people can see in their communities.
At the state levels, it’s data centers, and of course, data centers have really transformed a lot of these contests in the primaries and, I think, still in the general election.
At the global level, it’s blocking aid to Israel. It’s the genocide in Gaza. It’s the Iran war. It’s everything that goes along with that.
So I think we have to be sober about the setbacks that we’ve had in several places, but I think we also have to lean into our strengths. And find these alliances and commonalities. And I think the progressives can and should still win.
I don’t want to be gloomy and negativistic. But I think we can’t claim bigger victories than we’ve had. This is just a step along the way. The Empire always strikes back.
And the Empire knows they’re in a death match with us, and they want to win it more than they want to win a big victory for Democrats in the midterms.

Iran urges BRICS to expand use of national currencies in trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:31:40 UTC
01:31:40 KST

Iran urges BRICS to expand use of national currencies in trade
TEHRAN— Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian called on BRICS members on Friday to expand the use of national currencies in trade, strengthen financial cooperation, and build more resilient economic ties among member states, warning that economic security can no longer be separated from national and regional security.
Addressing the BRICS Business Forum in New Delhi, Pezeshkian said the grouping's true strength would emerge only when the economic capacities of its members are transformed into practical networks of trade, investment, and financing — a transition, he stressed, "from potential cooperation to operational cooperation."
"Economic resilience is not possible without diversification of trade partners, financing sources, and payment mechanisms," Pezeshkian told the forum, noting that Iran has faced extensive sanctions over the years, pressures that he said entered a "very difficult and dangerous phase" in recent months with US and Israeli military aggression against the Islamic Republic.
That aggression, he added, alongside its human and material costs, once again laid bare a fundamental reality: "Economic security is not separate from national and regional security. Whenever a country's trade, energy, infrastructure, or financial system comes under political-military pressure, its effects transcend that country's borders and impact the region and even the global economy."
The Iranian president said the growing use of economic tools for political pressure, along with geopolitical uncertainty and disruptions to supply chains, have made the global economic environment more complicated. He urged BRICS to develop mechanisms that would prevent any country from disrupting legitimate trade by monopolizing financial or technological instruments.
From fragmented cooperation to integrated trade infrastructure
Pezeshkian called for a shift "from fragmented cooperation to the gradual integration of trade infrastructure" within BRICS, proposing greater digitalization and integration of customs procedures, the removal of regulatory and administrative barriers, expansion of cross-border markets, and facilitation of joint private-sector investment.
He also called for stronger cooperation on standardization so that BRICS could move beyond raw-material trade toward integrated value chains and joint industrial production.
Describing food and energy security as "two fundamental pillars of economic security," Pezeshkian said Iran, given its major energy reserves and strategic geographic position, is ready to serve as a strategic partner in BRICS energy, food, and transportation supply chains.
National currencies and a reinforced 'New Development Bank'
Pezeshkian identified expanding the use of national currencies in intra-BRICS trade as one of the most important steps, saying it should be accompanied by mechanisms for managing currency risks, "because the current financial system, due to its concentration on a limited number of currencies, is vulnerable to political shocks."
To turn trade cooperation into real investment, he proposed that the New Development Bank become a major source of financing for infrastructure and energy projects through special credit lines, local-currency financing, and guarantees to attract private investment.
$10 billion joint reinsurance company
In one of his most concrete proposals, Pezeshkian called for the establishment of a joint BRICS reinsurance company with initial capital of $10 billion to cover risks associated with major infrastructure and energy projects and to increase private-sector confidence.
AI and digital economy
Turning to emerging technologies, Pezeshkian said BRICS "should not merely be a consumer of technology" but should contribute to knowledge production and the development of digital-economy standards, while also strengthening cybersecurity for critical infrastructure amid 'a fundamental transformation of the global economy driven by artificial intelligence.'
From dialogue forum to executive engine
He called on the BRICS Business Council to move from being a forum for dialogue to an executive engine of economic cooperation, with its working groups setting concrete and measurable projects based on indicators such as intra-BRICS trade growth, the share of national currencies in trade, and the volume of private investment.
Pezeshkian concluded by expressing Iran's readiness to serve as an important economic link within BRICS due to its strategic geography and energy resources, and to work with all members toward a more open, resilient, and equitable global economy.
"We believe BRICS will become a real force in the global economy when our cooperation is visible in contracts, factories, ports, and the economic life of the people of member states," he said.
BRICS, a key platform to counter unilateralism and expand economic cooperation
Speaking before departing for New Delhi to attend the 18th BRICS Summit, Pezeshkian described the grouping as a vital platform for dialogue with major countries and for expanding economic, trade, industrial, and scientific cooperation among member states. He emphasized that BRICS serves as an important mechanism for strengthening multilateralism in international relations, with the participation of China, Russia, Brazil, India, and other regional countries offering valuable opportunities for bilateral and multilateral consultations.
Pezeshkian noted that BRICS currently comprises 21 members—11 full members and 10 official partners known as BRICS Plus—accounting for more than 45 percent of the world's population and approximately 35 percent of global territory. He identified countering unilateralism and enabling countries to preserve their independence while expanding commercial relations as one of the bloc's principal objectives, adding that this year's summit centers on solidarity, sustainability, resilience, and innovation.

Self-driving cars should be taxed to offset job losses, thinktank urges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:31:07 UTC
01:31:07 KST

Taxes on self-driving cars should be introduced now in the UK to offset the rise in congestion and threats to jobs they pose, a thinktank has urged.
The first robotaxis on London’s streets only started this month, but government projections are that up to 40% of cars sold could have self-driving capability by the middle of the next decade.
The report says widespread autonomous vehicle (AV) adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk, while individual ownership is likely to increase car usage at the expense of public transport, and increase congestion.
Introducing charges now on self-driving vehicles could ease the transition and provide a future revenue stream to replace dwindling fuel duty, according to the report from Centre for British Progress, a non-partisan thinktank focused on economic growth.
Wayve, a British tech firm pioneering autonomous cars, said it would “penalise the UK’s most promising innovators”.
About £27bn a year is brought in by fuel duty, which is projected to disappear with the transition to electric vehicles.
While the report acknowledges potential benefits in safety and different skilled jobs in the sector, it said ministers should act early to mitigate the effects on England’s 417,000 taxi and private hire drivers, (121,000 in London), as “self-driving vehicles will eventually make much of this work obsolete”.
It notes that almost half of the mileage covered by Waymo’s robotaxis in California occurs with no passenger on board, that the costs of an empty vehicle are minimal without a driver to pay – and that driving around is potentially cheaper than parking.
According to the Department for Transport forecasts, highly automated driving will bring a 24% rise in road miles by 2050, with significant effects on congestion and road speeds.
Taxes should be implemented now before AVs become commonplace, the report urges. It states: “There is not yet a substantial constituency of AV owners who will resist a charge; once there is, taxing them becomes far harder.”
The thinktank calculates that by 2050, an AV charge set to match the social cost of congestion – about 88p per mile – would raise £47bn per year.
David Lawrence, one of the authors of the report, said that the experience of fuel duty, introduced in 1909 before mass car adoption, showed it was best to build up before “a political fight later on – our view is that now is the time to do it”.
He added: “In terms of the way that bond markets behave, even if tax revenue doesn’t peak until 2050, that’s still going to affect your 30-year bond yields today, which obviously is something the government is having to deal with. It can have an immediate impact on fiscal headroom, even if the actual revenue doesn’t come until much further down the line.”
Ministers have backed the introduction of AVs as a “transformative opportunity” for UK, heralding the start of robotaxi services in London this year as bringing “cutting-edge technology to British roads, creating thousands of jobs and unlocking billions for the economy by 2035”.
Uber, partnering with Wayve, has started limited AV services in the capital, with Google’s Waymo and the Chinese firm Baidu vying to join. Robotaxis already operate in the US, China and the UAE, and Europe’s first fully driverless taxi trials started in Zagreb, Croatia, this week.
Sarah Gates, VP global affairs and assurance at Wayve, said AVs were “a major growth opportunity for the UK – an industry in which we hold a genuine competitive advantage” and would bring high-value jobs and corporation tax revenues from a share of a £700bn global market.
She added: “A sector-specific tax at this early stage would undermine the government’s growth agenda and send precisely the wrong signal: that the UK will penalise its most promising innovators, rather than give them the conditions to scale and succeed.”
The GMB union, which represents taxi and private hire drivers, said a tax on AVs would not go far enough. Simon Rush, president of the GMB London region drivers branch, said: “Driverless cars threaten the livelihoods of private hire drivers and the businesses that depend on them. GMB has asked the government, TfL (Transport for London), and operators for a plan to reskill and redeploy drivers, but to date our questions have gone unanswered.
“An AV charge could go some way to mitigating the economic disruption caused by the rollout of these vehicles, but we need more.”
Uber declined to comment.

US diplomacy under fire as Russia escalates attacks on Ukrainian officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:30:48 UTC
01:30:48 KST

US diplomacy under fire as Russia escalates attacks on Ukrainian officials
The Witkoff-Kushner visit to Moscow was immediately followed by Russian attacks on Kyiv.
United States envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been seen as embarrassing and amateurish after their latest attempt to secure a ceasefire in Russia’s war in Ukraine, suggesting that European patience with the US administration of Donald Trump is running out.
“Jared Kushner’s incompetence was on full display this weekend,” wrote Slate magazine. “The Witkoff-Kushner circus act is an embarrassment,” said the Daily Telegraph, while the Financial Times titled its story, “Kushner and Witkoff’s blind amateurism.”
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Russian strike hits shopping centre in central Ukraine
- list 2 of 4Amnesty accuses Russia of trafficking foreigners to fight in Ukraine
- list 3 of 4Putin, Pezeshkian in India for BRICS summit clouded by Iran and Ukraine war
- list 4 of 4Russian strikes kill two in Kyiv as Moscow targets capital’s fuel stations
Washington has pursued negotiations without its European allies since US President Donald Trump cut off military aid to Ukraine and agreed to meet with Putin last year.
Witkoff caused outrage after he openly flattered Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“When we retire, we’ll have all these incredible stories and incredible memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all,” he told Putin.
Ukraine stopped firing missiles and drones at Moscow between September 5 and 7 to enable the US envoys aircraft to fly safely between the capitals.
Russia also paused attacks as they visited Kyiv.
“Please come more often, so that our people have the chance to live normally,” Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy joked at a media conference with them.
But as soon as Witkoff and Kushner left, Russia showered drones and missiles on Kyiv killing at least four civilians on September 8 and 9.
Russia has shown little sign that it is ready for a deal. Putin’s diplomatic aide, Valery Ushakov, told the US envoys that Moscow was committed to achieving all its goals in Ukraine.
“Russia intends to achieve the goals of the special military operation,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov asserted on September 8.
“Of course, we’re all interested in ending the conflict as quickly as possible. Moreover, it must end on our terms, in order to prevent the possibility of it recurring in the future or spreading into a global conflict,” former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev told Vedomosti newspaper two days later. “Nuclear weapons can be used in certain circumstances. This isn’t a scare tactic,” he warned.
Zelenskyy has insisted that only leverage on the battlefield will force Moscow to negotiate.
“Without a strong position on the ground, there will only be ultimatums,” Zelenskyy said this week.
Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Kyiv on the fourth anniversary of Ukraine’s Kharkiv offensive, which reclaimed 11,500sq km (4,440 square miles) of northern Ukrainian territory from Russian occupation, including more than 500 settlements.
Shortly after that, Russian forces withdrew from roughly 8,000sq km (3,100 square miles) of territory it had occupied on the right bank of the Dnipro River in the southern region of Kherson, deeming it to be indefensible.
Both actions, along with Russia previously lifting sieges on Kyiv, Sumy and Chernihiv, reduced the Russian occupation from more than a quarter of Ukrainian territory to less than a fifth.
Since then, Russia has made only marginal gains for mounting losses.
Ukraine’s military leadership said that since the beginning of the war, Russia has suffered 1.5m losses of personnel – both soldiers killed or incapacitated.
This year, Russia has again suffered setbacks, notably during the Oleksandrivka counteroffensive, which reclaimed 745sq km (290 square miles) in the eastern and southern Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
Russian targets
Russia has appeared to have escalated its targeting of Ukrainian officials in recent days.
On September 4, a drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s internal security service, the SBU. “The drone was deliberately directed at the office of the Head of the Security Service of Ukraine, Oleksandr Poklad,” said the SBU.
Ukrainian defence adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said it was a jet-powered Geran-4 Russian drone – one of two launched from the occupied eastern Donetsk region and sent in tandem towards Kyiv.
One of the SBU’s main tasks is to arrest Russian agents guiding enemy artillery and drone strikes on Ukrainian soil. Beskrestnov believed an agent within 5km (3 miles) of SBU headquarters directed the drone intended for Poklad in its final stages.
“I instructed Poklad to respond appropriately, significantly and, if possible, in kind,” said Zelenskyy, later adding that “the geographical areas for the response have been determined”.
On September 8, Russia also came close to blowing up Zelenskyy’s plane as it waited on the tarmac the Moldovan capital, Chisinau.
The plane was carrying Zelenskyy, his wife Olena and Moldovan premier Maia Sandu to Oslo for the funeral of King Harald V.
Norwegian premier Jonas Gahr Store said the plane came close to being hit.
Both incidents came after Zelenskyy warned airlines on September 1 that “Russian airspace is becoming completely dangerous” and was “in effect closing” due to Ukrainian long-range drone operations.
Ukraine’s long-range strikes
Ukraine continued its long-range operations during the past week, targeting Russian oil and military infrastructure.
Between September 4 and 10, Ukraine struck at least seven refineries and gas condensate processing plants, two of them at an unprecedented 3,000km (1,860 miles) range from its border – the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky gas condensate plants, are beyond the Ural Mountains in the Siberian Arctic region of Yamalia.
Closer to home, Ukraine also struck the military airfield at Rostov-on-Don and the Russian port of Makhachkala on the Caspian Sea.
The Ukrainian military said they were “used to supply military personnel in both directions: components and attack UAVs of the Shahed type from Iran to the Russian Federation, [and] explosives, components for drones and ammunition from the Russian Federation to Iran”.
Ukraine sees the attacks as effective, since Russia’s finance ministry reported a $67.9bn deficit for the first eight months of the war. That is one-and-a-half times its deficit during the same period last year and far beyond the $44.5bn deficit budgeted for in all of 2026.
The ministry cited rising expenditures and falling revenues from oil and gas.
Those revenues were 16 percent lower than the first eight months of 2025, at just under $58bn, said Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service.
The expenditures are almost certainly military. The Intelligence Service assessed that Russia spent a record $126.7bn on defence in the first half of this year. That is 30 percent higher than in the same period of last year, 65 percent higher than in the first half of 2024 and 145 percent higher than in the corresponding period of 2023.

Mail on Sunday ends up funding state school scholarship via payout to MP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:30:31 UTC
01:30:31 KST

A new scholarship supporting state-educated students will be inadvertently funded by the Mail on Sunday (MoS), using a payout it made after being threatened with legal action by the Labour MP Catherine Atkinson.
The Derby North MP says she will use the proceeds of about £5,000 from the newspaper to fund scholarships for local law students at the University of Derby who – like her – attended state schools.
In early July the MoS said Atkinson attended a private school and accused her of concealing it from her biographical entry in Who’s Who.
Despite Atkinson correcting the journalists who contacted her, the MoS published an article making the false claim, accompanied by a large photograph of the MP. The newspaper later apologised and paid damages and legal costs after the former lawyer responded firmly that she had attended state schools.
“I am grateful for the state-school education that helped me build a 17-year career as a barrister,” said Atkinson, who attended Sacred Heart high school, a Catholic comprehensive in Hammersmith, west London.
“The claim that I had concealed a private education from my constituents was false. I am using the money from this settlement to support students from Derby’s state schools in beginning their own careers in law.
“Strengthening our justice system means taking seriously who gets the opportunity to work in it. When financial barriers keep capable people out of the profession, the public loses the benefit of their talent.
“The legal profession has a shared responsibility to help remove those barriers. We should be looking for future lawyers in every school and supporting those who need help to get started.
“There are students in Derby today who could spend their careers defending the rights of others. They deserve the opportunity to build that future.”
Atkinson was elected at the 2024 general election as MP for Derby North, where the University of Derby’s law school is situated.
At least £5,000 from the settlement after expenses will go towards the Catherine Atkinson future lawyers award, providing a £500 award each year for at least 10 years. The award will be open to first-year law students who were educated at a state school within the city of Derby.
Prof Kathryn Mitchell, the university’s vice-chancellor, said she welcomed Atkinson’s support.
Mitchell said: “At the University of Derby we firmly believe in the transformative nature of education and, as a champion of social mobility and inclusion, aim to create opportunities for all across our region and beyond, regardless of age, background or location.
“We want talented students from Derby’s state comprehensive schools to have every opportunity to pursue a career in law.
“The Catherine Atkinson future lawyers award will provide financial support as recipients begin their degrees. We welcome Catherine’s commitment to social mobility and her investment in local students over the next 10 years.”
DMG Media, which owns Associated Newspapers and the MoS, was contacted for comment.

China, Russia reject pressure on Iran as nuclear dispute returns to UNSC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:27:41 UTC
01:27:41 KST

China, Russia reject pressure on Iran as nuclear dispute returns to UNSC
TEHRAN- China and Russia have jointly rejected renewed Western pressure on Iran over its nuclear program, challenging the legal and political basis of efforts to revive sanctions and bring the Iranian nuclear issue back under the scrutiny of the United Nations Security Council.
The positions were voiced during a Security Council meeting on Iran’s nuclear program on September 10, a day after the IAEA Board of Governors adopted a resolution introduced by the United States, Britain, France and Germany that referred Iran’s nuclear file to the Security Council over 'alleged non-compliance' with its safeguards' obligations.
The Security Council agreed to place the Iranian nuclear issue on its agenda by a vote of 11 in favor, with China and Russia voting against and two members abstaining. China and Russia, however, used the meeting to reaffirm their opposition to the reimposition of sanctions against Iran and to the so-called snapback mechanism.
China and Russia reject snapback
According to Al Jazeera, China’s representative at the meeting warned that insisting on restoring sanctions against Iran could endanger international peace and security.
The Chinese envoy said Beijing supported Russia’s statement and maintained that the snapback mechanism had expired.
“We believe that the snapback has come to an end, and we are witnessing the sunset of the JCPOA,” he said, expressing regret that some Security Council members continued to insist on the issue.
He warned that such measures could not only complicate relations among UN members and within the Security Council but could also undermine international peace and security.
Russia’s representative likewise reiterated Moscow’s opposition to resolutions targeting Iran and said the snapback mechanism had expired.
The Russian envoy said Moscow supported China’s position on the issue, again stressing that the mechanism had reached its end and that the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, or JCPOA, was entering its “sunset.”
The coordinated positions of Beijing and Moscow place them at odds with the United States and the three European parties to the JCPOA — Britain, France and Germany — which have sought to intensify international pressure on Iran over its peaceful nuclear activities.
Iran challenges Security Council proceedings
Iran, for its part, has rejected the renewed proceedings as legally and politically unfounded.
Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and chargé d’affaires to the United Nations, said the Security Council meeting on Iran’s nuclear file constituted an abuse of the Council’s procedures and authority.
In a letter circulated to the Council president Darzi said Iran categorically rejected “unfounded allegations and distortions” concerning its peaceful nuclear program.
He argued that UN Security Council Resolution 2231 expired on October 18, 2025, and that all nuclear-related provisions, measures and restrictions associated with the resolution were therefore terminated.
Darzi also disputed the legal basis for the European powers’ attempt to invoke the snapback mechanism, arguing that the E3 had failed to meet their own obligations under both the JCPOA and Resolution 2231 and therefore lacked the legal standing to activate the mechanism.
Iran’s envoy further attributed the current nuclear dispute to 'unlawful US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful and safeguarded nuclear facilities.'
He argued that attacks against safeguarded nuclear sites had seriously undermined confidence in the international safeguards system and the broader nuclear non-proliferation regime.
Darzi maintained that the renewed allegations against Iran were political rather than technical, pointing to Iran’s membership in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty since 1970 and its long-standing engagement with the International Atomic Energy Agency.
He said Iran had been subject to extensive IAEA monitoring for nearly 25 years and stressed that the agency had reported no diversion of nuclear material in Iran.
The Iranian envoy called on the IAEA to remain impartial, professional, independent and non-political, arguing that political pressure could not replace an objective assessment of safeguards obligations.
Iran denounces IAEA resolution
Darzi also sharply criticized the IAEA Board of Governors’ resolution adopted on September 9, describing it as a politically driven measure backed by the United States and the E3.
The resolution was adopted by 23 votes in favor, three against and eight abstentions. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
The measure was introduced by the United States, Britain, France and Germany and referred Iran’s nuclear file to the United Nations Security Council over alleged non-compliance with its safeguards obligations.
Iran has rejected the resolution, arguing that it fails to meet the requirements of objectivity and impartiality and does not address the attacks on its safeguarded nuclear facilities.
Darzi said the IAEA Board’s latest action, like previous resolutions, was silent on 'unlawful attacks' by the United States and Israel against its nuclear installations.
He warned that Security Council procedures should not be used to advance politically motivated or unsubstantiated allegations against UN member states or to provide political cover for 'unlawful acts.'
Iran has therefore called on the Security Council to adhere strictly to the UN Charter and international law and to reject attempts to politicize its procedures and mechanisms.
The dispute now moves into a more consequential diplomatic phase, with Iran rejecting the legal basis of the renewed Security Council proceedings, China and Russia opposing the restoration of sanctions and the snapback mechanism, and the United States and the E3 pressing ahead with efforts to place Iran’s nuclear activities back at the center of the Council’s agenda.

Suspects accused of swindling American women out of $6 million in romance scam extradited to U.S. from South Africa
Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6 million through online romance scams will be extradited to the United States on Friday, South African police said.
The men, who were arrested in the South African city of Cape Town in 2021, are set to be handed over to officials from the Federal Bureau of Investigation on Friday and taken to the U.S. to face wire fraud and money laundering charges.
They are accused of belonging to a criminal network known as the Black Axe, which Interpol describes as being part of criminal groups responsible for a significant share of the world's cyber-enabled financial fraud, typically through romance scams, cryptocurrency and investment scams.
The move comes less than two years after a prominent leader of the Black Axe was extradited to the U.S. for conspiring to engage in internet scams and money laundering.
According to South African police, the men are alleged to have targeted more than 100 women in the U.S., defrauding them of more than $6 million through online romance or love scams.
Among the alleged victims were pensioners and businesspeople who were reportedly targeted through sophisticated online relationships, police said in a statement.
"Through the coordination of Interpol South Africa, the six will today be transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town to Cape Town International Airport, where they will be handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service, who arrived in South Africa this morning," said police spokesperson Katlego Mogale.
A recent operation by Interpol targeting West African organized crime groups led to the arrest of 58 people and the identification of 263 suspects linked to various criminal networks involved in similar crimes, the multinational police body said last month.
The operation aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets and support arrests and prosecution.
In South Africa, authorities raided seven locations in the city of Johannesburg linked to a syndicate that ran romance and investment scams targeting retirees in English-speaking countries.
In that operation in South Africa, police arrested 39 people, seized $2.67 million and froze more than 250 bank accounts, Interpol said.
More than 64,000 Americans were taken for over $1 billion in romance scams in 2023— double the $500 million just four years earlier, according to the Federal Trade Commission.
In 2024, a CBS News investigation uncovered a large-scale romance scam operation in Ghana.
"I fish everywhere in the world," a syndicate boss in Ghana who called himself Voodu told CBS News. But he said of the easiest victims to catch, "They are Americans."

A drone beside a Ukrainian cargo plane is costing Russia its last consulate in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:23:58 UTC
01:23:58 KST

More than 150 Russian mission staff and their family members must leave Germany after Berlin ordered Russia's last consulate in the country to close, The Moscow Times reported, citing the Russian embassy. The German government published no figure of its own and expelled nobody by name. What it did was close institutions, a step ZDF judges the hardest-hitting of the German diplomatic measures. Berlin ordered the earlier closures for a different reason: Russia had restricted German missions first.
The response Berlin chose, and the one it did not
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced the measures on 1 September with Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, after Berlin blamed Russian services for an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle airport. The Bonn consulate closes on 18 September, and the agreement covering the Russian House of Science and Culture, Moscow's state-run cultural center in Berlin, is rescinded. Germany will also propose more Russians for EU sanctions lists, tighten entry checks, and press harder on the shadow fleet of tankers moving sanctioned Russian oil, he said.
Measured against what was on the table, the package is restrained. Berlin declined to expel individual diplomats, rejected a blanket entry ban for Russian citizens, refused to designate Russia a terrorist state, and kept Moscow's ambassador in Berlin. Wadephul called the closure a serious restriction of Russian capabilities in Germany, and said he had thought it through.
Germany suspects Russian intelligence behind arson attack as hybrid warfare threat grows across Europe
Where the figure of 150 comes from
The embassy's statement is where the number originates, and it counts families alongside staff. It described the Leipzig find as a broken drone of unclear origin that harmed nobody, and said hundreds of thousands of German citizens and Russians living in Germany lose access to consular services because of it.
German officials had put the scope differently, describing a double-digit number of affected staff. Every registered consulate employee must go, along with every Russian House worker seconded from Russia, and Berlin refused to let consulate staff transfer to the embassy.
Why the Bonn consulate
The target was not chosen at random. Citing internal information from Brussels circles, Bild reported that EU diplomats regarded it as a support point for hybrid operations against the Benelux countries, EU institutions, and NATO headquarters in Belgium. Citing security circles, the paper put 15 to 20 intelligence officers at the consulate under diplomatic cover. Germany withdrew the operating permits of four other Russian consulates in May 2023, which leaves Moscow with its embassy alone. The Bonn site stays in Russian ownership after the staff leave.
Moscow's answer
Russia's foreign ministry withdrew consent for Germany's consulate general in St Petersburg on 7 September, matching the deadline Berlin had set for Bonn. The Goethe-Institut branches in Russia close as well—Germany's state cultural institute, the counterpart to Moscow's Russian House—and their seconded staff must leave by 13 September.
Germany will close Russia’s Bonn consulate after attributing Leipzig Airport drone attack to Moscow
Five weeks from a drone near a runway to two consulates ordered shut
- On the night of 4 August and into 5 August, a drone carrying explosives turned up beside a Ukrainian An-124 at Leipzig/Halle, where it lay unnoticed for hours.
- Four weeks later, on 1 September, Berlin blamed Moscow and set out its measures.
- The next day German officials gave their own order of magnitude at a government briefing, and it was a double-digit number rather than three figures.
- On 4 September the closure order and its 18 September deadline were public, with the Russian embassy confirming them.

Russia Launches First Commercial 5G Networks For First Time Since Nearly a Decade of Delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:21:10 UTC
01:21:10 KST

Russian mobile phone operators launched their first commercial 5G networks following nearly a decade of delays caused by Western sanctions and regulatory disputes.
Russia’s Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media Ministry announced the decision on Friday, Sept. 11, noting that it was carried out on the instructions of Russian President Vladimir Putin himself. According to the Ministry, company executives marked the launch at events organized in Tver, Samara, Yekaterinburg and Novosibirsk.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Fast mobile internet today is needed for absolutely everything, always and everywhere,” Maksut Shadayev, Russia’s minister of digital development, communications and mass media said, according to TASS.
“The fourth-generation mobile networks already cover 90% of the total inhabited territory of our country, 95% of mobile subscribers use LTE [‘Long Term Evolution,’ an advanced version of 3G] services every day,” he continued.
Coverage across the country
All four of Russia’s major carriers – MegaFon, Beeline, T2 and MTS – launched the 5G simultaneously in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg.
Elsewhere, coverage varies by operator. For example, MegaFon and MTS will cover Novosibirsk and Kazan, Beeline and MegaFon Samara, and MegaFon alone will cover Veliky Novgorod, Krasnodar, Nizhny Novgorod and Tver.
In Volgograd, Krasnoyarsk, Perm and Chelyabinsk, T2 is responsible for launching the service. Additionally, MTS is operating by itself in Ufa and Beeline in Yaroslavl.
Lukashenko Floats Mobilization, Says Attacking Neighbors Would Be ‘Tantamount to Death’
“Mobile internet traffic volume has grown more than threefold over six years,” the Ministry said, adding that “the rollout of 5G is especially important for large cities, where network load is highest.”
By the end of 2026, the Ministry plans to extend 5G coverage to 50 more cities.
Iphone compatibility remains uncertain
The Ministry said Android users will gain access to the service “in the near future,” without providing a specific timeline, while iPhone compatibility remains uncertain.
Russian mobile operators were allocated the 4.63-4.99 GHz frequency band rather than the 3.4-3.8 GHz range used internationally for 5G, since the military and security services have kept exclusive control of that spectrum.
Because iPhones operate at a lower frequency, they won’t connect to Russian 5G networks unless Apple Corporation decides to make direct changes on its end.
“In the first stage, we use the existing infrastructure, which allows us to increase the speed of data transmission by 20-25%,” Dmitry Grigorenko, Russian Deputy Prime Minister said, according to TASS.
“Next, we will go to new frequencies that have already been provided to telecom operators. At the same time, we will consistently increase the share of domestic equipment. Our task is to bring the share of Russian 5G base stations to 100%,” he continued.
A rollout nearly a decade in the making
Russia first discussed launching 5G in 2017, with test zones appearing in Moscow the following year, IntelliNews reported on Aug. 21, 2024.
However, the project stalled repeatedly, missing launch dates in 2020, 2022 and 2023, largely due to a lack of domestically produced base stations and financial strain on operators.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, several telecom equipment giants closed their business activities in Russia.
According to Reuters on Aug. 29, 2022, Ericsson began gradually exiting the market that August, while Nokia said it would leave the country entirely by the end of the year.
The exit pushed carriers like MTS and Tele2 toward Chinese suppliers such as Huawei, prompting Moscow to lean on Beijing to sustain its telecom buildout – one small part of a much broader dependency.
Since the beginning of the invasion, China has emerged as one of Russia’s most important allies, despite officially portraying itself as a neutral party in the war.
More than 550 Chinese soldiers took part in internships at Russian military institutions under bilateral training programs, according to Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) on July 8. The intelligence agency also said that more than 180 Russian troops underwent similar programs in China during November 2025 alone.
Beyond military training, the alliance extends to weapons hardware. Russia has been expanding its use of jet-powered drones fitted with Chinese-made engines, which can reach speeds of up to 400-600 kilometers per hour (around 249-373 miles per hour) – up to three times the speed of previous Shahed versions provided by Iran – making them significantly harder to intercept.
Earlier on Friday, Russian jet-powered Shahed drones struck a building belonging to Ukraine’s largest telecom company and deliberately targeted gas stations across Kyiv, killing two and injuring at least nine people.
The strikes come as President Zelensky said Thursday, Sept. 10 that Moscow intensifies attacks whenever diplomatic efforts gain momentum.
Following the departure of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who traveled to Kyiv and Moscow throughout the weekend in an effort to broker an end to the war, Russia increased its strikes on Ukraine nationwide, killing seven people and injuring more than 120 through Thursday.

EU Fails to Extend Russia Sanctions For Second Time
Russia used Oreshnik twice
Oreshnik is a Russian nuclear-capable intermediate-range ballistic missile reportedly capable of traveling at hypersonic speeds and carrying multiple warheads.
Russia first used the missile against the Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Nov. 21, 2024. Russian leader Vladimir Putin presented the launch as a warning to Ukraine and its Western partners.
Moscow used Oreshnik for a second time on Jan. 9, 2026, striking near Lviv, close to Ukraine’s border with Poland. Ukrainian officials said the missile carried inert warheads that rely on kinetic energy that caused limited damage to a state-owned facility.
The latter launch was part of a wide-ranging Russian attack involving 242 drones and 36 missiles. Four people were killed in Kyiv during the barrage, while more than 500,000 households temporarily lost electricity.
European and Ukrainian officials condemned the second Oreshnik launch as a dangerous escalation involving a weapon capable of carrying a nuclear payload.

Iranian president urges BRICS to prevent obstruction of legitimate trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:16:43 UTC
01:16:43 KST

Ahmet Dursun, Sami Sohta and Lina Altawell
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
- BRICS strength will become clearer when it moves from ‘potential cooperation to operational cooperation,’ says Iranian president
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday that BRICS must create an environment that prevents any country from obstructing the legitimate trade of others, saying Iran has entered a “far more dangerous” phase of economic pressure following the war with the US and Israel.
Pezeshkian made the remarks during a speech at the 18th BRICS leaders’ summit in the Indian capital New Delhi.
BRICS is a global economic bloc founded in 2006. It includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, while Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Ethiopia and Iran later joined. Indonesia’s accession was announced in early 2025.
Pezeshkian said the world is going through one of its “most complex periods,” warning that the increasing use of economic tools to exert pressure has endangered the legitimate trade of other countries. "What is BRICS’ response to these problems?” he said.
He added that BRICS’ strength would become clearer when the group moves from “potential cooperation to operational cooperation.”
“Iran has faced comprehensive sanctions in recent years, and these pressures entered a far more dangerous phase following the US-Israeli aggression,” Pezeshkian said.
He said the aggression once again revealed an important reality alongside human and material losses: that economic security cannot be separated from national and regional security.
“When a country’s trade, energy, infrastructure or financial system is subjected to political and military pressure, the effects go beyond that country’s borders and affect regional stability and the global economy,” he said.
Pezeshkian stressed the need to create an environment that prevents any country from obstructing the legitimate trade of others.
He also emphasized the importance of expanding the use of national currencies in trade among BRICS countries.
The Iranian president expressed his country’s readiness to serve as a “strategic partner” in the group’s energy and transport supply chains.
“Iran is ready to work with BRICS members to build a more open and just economy,” he said.

====================================================================================================

3D printing, AI and reused objects form a bathing prototype for year 2050
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:15:57 UTC
01:15:57 KST

3D Printing turns Discarded Objects into 2050 Bathing Prototype
What happens when an abandoned industrial jam vat, a mis-measured window, and architectural-scale 3D printing are brought together around one of the oldest domestic rituals: bathing? Sustainable Decadence v2.0 by Ross Stevens explores how AI, digital manufacturing, and discarded objects can combine to create a new bathing environment with reduced environmental impact. Developed as both an experiment and a prototype for architecture looking toward 2050, the project examines the role of large-scale 3D printing in connecting existing objects with new architectural components. The approach builds on Stevens’ interest in giving discarded industrial materials new uses, while addressing the challenge of bringing unrelated found elements into a coherent architectural system.
AI, 3D printing, and the reuse of discarded objects in daily rituals
As part of his exploration of what a contemporary equivalent of mid-century modernism might look like in 2050, designer Ross Stevens considers how emerging technologies could establish new relationships between existing materials, manufacturing processes, and everyday rituals. The project continues an investigation that began with Sustainable Decadence v1.0 in 2011. Stevens, an industrial designer, has focused on finding new applications for discarded industrial waste, but combining an eclectic collection of existing objects into a unified design presents a particular challenge. Architectural-scale 3D printing provides a means of resolving this relationship. Components can be designed around the dimensions and characteristics of existing objects, filling the gaps between them with digitally manufactured elements. In this sense, the 3D printer acts as a connecting system between found materials and newly produced architecture.
AI is also considered as a potential collaborator within this process. Its possible roles include identifying opportunities for reuse, translating design ideas into physical forms, generating CAD files for 3D printing, and monitoring printing processes by observing and adjusting production as required. At the center of the project is the role of bathing as an everyday ritual and a source of personal pleasure. Sustainable Decadence considers how such experiences can be incorporated into contemporary design while limiting the environmental resources required to produce them.
the exposed layers are retained as an acknowledgement of its tectonic process
REUSED INDUSTRIAL OBJECTS SHAPE FLEXIBLE 3D PRINTED BATHING SPACE
Several discarded and surplus components form the basis of the project, including a stainless-steel industrial jam cooking vat, a ventilation pipe, an incorrectly measured double-glazing window, and a leftover section of balustrade glass. The reused stainless-steel vat becomes the central element around which the new architectural components are organized. Large-scale 3D printing mediates between these existing objects, producing stairs, balustrades, roof components, and enclosures that respond to their individual forms. This approach allows irregular and unrelated components to remain part of the design while establishing a coordinated spatial system around them.
A large 3D printed pivoting roof provides protection and insulation when the pool is not in use while allowing the bathing space to shift between indoor and outdoor conditions. The roof pivots around an extended tubular point that distributes structural stress across its surface, allowing it to open fully in fine weather. When rain arrives, the roof can be partially closed to create a sheltered position from which to observe the surrounding weather. When completely closed, the roof separates the bathing space from the exterior environment and changes its acoustics. The sound of water ripples becomes more pronounced, while a double-glazed skylight maintains a connection with the sky and introduces natural light into the enclosed space.
the complex roof form is driven by the shapes of the pivoting tube, rectangular skylight, and circular tub
CUSTOM 3D PRINTED ELEMENTS ADAPT TO EXISTING INDUSTRIAL FORMS
The stairs and balustrade are 3D printed to follow the shape of the reused stainless-steel vat. Their curved geometry demonstrates how digital fabrication can mediate between existing industrial components and newly designed architectural elements. The balustrade is printed in PETG and reinforced with two continuous 16 mm nylon ropes encased in epoxy resin. A hand recess runs continuously beneath the balustrade, providing a more secure grip while integrating the functional requirement into the geometry. The combination of digital modeling and large-scale printing allows these components to be customized to the existing structure, avoiding the need to standardize the reused object around a predetermined architectural system.
The hot and wet conditions of an exterior bath provide a demanding environment for architectural-scale 3D printing. The project therefore tests the performance of printed components across several architectural and technical applications. The roof, skylight, stairs, balustrade, electrical enclosures, and plumbing enclosures all form part of the experiment, requiring the printed architecture to demonstrate structural functionality and durability under demanding environmental conditions. By combining reused industrial objects with digitally designed and fabricated components, Sustainable Decadence v2.0 investigates how large-scale 3D printing can support a more adaptable approach to architectural reuse. The project also points toward further research into fully 3D printed architecture and the potential role of digital fabrication and AI in future building systems.
the pivoting roof gives bathers the option to shelter if the weather changes
a large 3D printed roof pivots between enclosed and open conditions
the precision of the polymer (PLA) printing process allows for easy installation of the skylight
the roof’s double-glazed skylight gives protection and connection to the outside
the roof and stairs fan out from the center of the tub
a continuous hand recess is integrated beneath the 3D printed balustrade
the 3D printed stairs step up around the circular tub
the curvaceous 3D printed balustrade connects to existing structures
a continuous recess on the underside of the balustrade offers a fluid and firm grip

Air Force BMT Puts Finishing Touches on 1st Airbase Training Range—and Plans for More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:15:45 UTC
01:15:45 KST

JOINT BASE SAN ANTONIO-LACKLAND, Texas—Under a late summer sun, Air Force basic trainees practice safely rearming a retired F-16 Fighting Falcon here with mock AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles. Nearby, a bulldozer levels the ground where the rest of this first new airbase training range will sit.
If all goes well, two retired C-130 Hercules aircraft that arrived on base in late August will join the F-16 on the mock airbase’s completed tarmac as early as December, Col. Kellie Courtland, commander of the 37th Training Wing that oversees Basic Military Training, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a Sept. 2 interview.
“The goal is to have it ready by December-ish timeframe or early 2027,” Courtland said. “But we’re within months of all of that happening.”
Officials from the 2nd Air Force first revealed plans this past January to inject more realism into Basic Military Training by building mock airbases where future Airmen can get hands-on training with real aircraft. The long-term plan is to have four similar areas each with one F-16 and two C-130s, plus another, more expeditionary training range with dirt airstrips.
The project is part of a sweeping effort in BMT to instill “airmindedness” in new Airmen—making sure they understand the basics of generating airpower, especially if their base falls under attack.
“We want Airmen that are going to rise to the occasion. … What we don’t want is an Airman to say, ‘OK, he’s out of the game, she’s out of the game, and he’s out of the game, therefore the game’s done and we’re not going to do the mission,’” Courtland said. “No, what we want is you to say, ‘She’s out. I may not do her job, but that maintainer that’s over there working, I can hand him the wrenches, or that Airmen that’s got to go out there and fuel that plane now, I can help him pull that hose out and make sure that jet is grounded.’”
Training started on this first F-16 in April. Trainees are tasked with a mission to rearm the fighter, organize into small groups, develop a plan, brief the plan to Military Training Instructors, and complete the mission.
They work out of two containerized training stations on the site that contain training materials: videos and mock AIM-9 missiles and smaller 2.75-inch rockets for the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System.
The mock munitions are much lighter than live ordnance, but MTIs take care to ensure trainees understand it takes three Airmen to carry an AIM-9 and two to carry a 2.75-inch rocket.
“These are training rounds; they’re not weighted … but we highly emphasize the fact that ‘hey, you will do a three-person lift’ just some sense of realism because in reality those missiles weigh about 400 pounds,” said Tech Sgt. Johnny Ngo, an MTI with the 322nd Training Squadron.
Tech. Sgt. Brandon Cruz, an MTI with the 331st Training Squadron, said watching trainees train on a real F-16 brought back the excitement he felt when he went through his technical training to become a loader.
He remembers walking into the hanger, “and there’s these four aircraft out there, and it’s almost a surreal moment; like you feel it in your chest, and I was like, wow, I’m in a Transformers movie or something,” Cruz said. “These trainees are getting that experience in BMT within the first five weeks of actually being here. They’re getting that surreal reality check.”
Tech Sgt. Jeremy Hudson said he remembers how different BMT was when he went through in 2014. “It was the basics—drill, dormitory, and discipline,” the MTI from 322nd said. “It was folding shirts. It was making sure your dormitory and your living area was clean, and then it was drill.”
Trainees coming into BMT now are getting much more realistic training, Hudson said. “Five weeks ago, six weeks ago, they were civilians, and now they get to see an F-16 firsthand,” he said.
Overall, the effort is progressing well, but Courtland, the 37th Training Wing commander, acknowledged there are always logistical hiccups when sorting through multiple changes simultaneously.
“You’re trying to build a new curriculum at the same time, you’re trying to do the construction at the same time, and you’re trying to train the MTIs so that they can train the trainees,” she said. “So, you’re always going to have those little clunky pieces in there, but overall, I think it’s going good, and I think it’s got the support [from the Air Force] it needs to thrust it through.”
When completed, this mock airbase training range will have 16 containerized training stations that trains eight key tasks:
- Arming fighter aircraft
- Refueling
- Casualty transfer and evacuation
- Cargo loading
- Post-attack and repair
- Aircraft marshaling
- Aircraft familiarization
- Airbase entry control
There is also a much broader plan to grow the airbase into a four-quadrant training range—each with duplicate set-up consisting of two C-130s and an F-16—by 2031, Courtland said.
BMT officials also plan to build a forward airbase training range with a more expeditionary flavor for PACER FORGE, the final field training exercise of BMT that stresses trainees’ agile combat employment skills.
There will be two dirt air strips that intersect and a towable aircraft fuselage, 37th Training Wing Command Chief Master Sgt. Caleb Vaden said, adding that the plan also involves having an F-16 and one C-130. Currently, the simulated airbase at PACER FORGE consists of some hard structures that allow Airmen to practice skills such as perimeter defense.
The forward airbase training range is also scheduled to be completed by 2031, Vaden said.
“It’s going to have a hangar in the middle, so some of those same types of things they’ll be training on here, like well, it’ll split your team up, and hey, some of you are going to be supporting airfield ops. Some of you are going to be supporting a repair team, should there be damage that you have to go out and assess, and those types of things,” Vaden said. “So, it’s just going to be what you have here, forward with reduced resources like we’ve had in real life, and just a lot of chaos going on to really kind of stress them out.”
