SCO Summit Produces Surprising Winners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:43:00 UTC
23:43:00 KST

The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan August 31-September 1 marked a quarter century since the organization’s founding. Its anniversary motto, “Together for Sustainable Peace, Development and Prosperity,” hinted at ambitions considerably grander than the institution’s record. The SCO now encompasses ten member states, including China, India, Russia, Iran, Pakistan, and four Central Asian republics – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – representing nearly half of humanity and a substantial share of global economic activity.
Yet headlines emerging from Bishkek often highlighted the organization’s internal dynamics and differing national priorities. Unlike last year’s summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi did not hold a formal bilateral meeting, although their brief interaction during the summit quickly became a meme template among Indian netizens. Modi and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif traded predictable barbs. Most stunningly, Modi directly urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine “for humanity’s sake.” This comes shortly after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that China delivered an ultimatum to Russia not to use nuclear weapons in Ukraine, something China has not denied.
This focus on discord is not merely dramatic headline chasing; it reflects a genuine and consistently noted problem with the SCO. The organization brings together several geopolitical rivals. It is therefore difficult to imagine the institution ever evolving into a mirror of NATO. The SCO lacks the degree of institutionalization necessary to impose coherent policy on its members, while its principal powers lack sufficient leverage over one another to establish a common strategic direction.
But these features should not lead observers to dismiss the organization’s practical value for its members, especially the smaller ones.
Institutionalization is a slow process, particularly among states with divergent political systems and strategic interests. The SCO already possesses permanent structures, including its Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) in Tashkent, while members continue to debate additional mechanisms for economic and security cooperation.
The summit featured credible proposals for institutional development, including Xi proposing AI hubs, Uzbekistan proposing an industrial cooperation mechanism, Kyrgyzstan pushing its Tamchy Special Financial Investment Territory for joint SCO projects and advocating for Bishkek as the headquarters of a joint development bank, and Tajikistan pushing for a regional digital agro-ecological platform.
Other developments emerged from the forum, especially multilateral initiatives in which the SCO serves not as an institutional organizer but as an exhibition hall for projects that individual governments want to pursue.
This has created an unusual dynamic within the organization. While SCO’s largest powers are often stalemated by competing interests, institution-building initiatives that make the greatest practical progress frequently emerge because smaller member states want them to.
SCO summits have increasingly become venues where host governments promote their own economic and diplomatic priorities. The pattern was particularly visible after the 2017 meeting in Astana. The massive Astana Expo opened the following day, underscoring how the summit could function as a platform for the host country’s broader international ambitions rather than simply as a meeting of an increasingly institutionalized organization.
Kyrgyzstan continued that tradition in Bishkek this year. As the outgoing chair and summit host, Bishkek had an obvious incentive to use the gathering to advance national priorities. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway received prominent attention. The project, a flagship Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) corridor running from Kashgar through Kyrgyzstan into Uzbekistan, has the potential to reshape the country’s position within Eurasian transportation networks. Kyrgyzstan also successfully promoted emerging trade routes connecting with India and Pakistan via China and the China Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and inked a deal to drastically increase trade with Pakistan.
Kyrgyzstan, like many smaller SCO members, appears interested in maximizing the benefits of participation without presenting itself as uncritically aligned with the organization’s largest powers. While Bishkek has been open about its close economic relationship with Beijing, it retains an interest in attracting capital from outside the SCO’s economic orbit. Western capital remains valuable precisely because it provides an alternative source of financing, expertise, and commercial relationships. The establishment of the Tamchy Special Financial and Investment Territory in 2025, a special economic zone which serves as an outpost of Western regulatory codes and law in the region, illustrates this broader effort to create a more attractive investment environment.
This behavior should not be interpreted as contradictory or even unique. For smaller SCO states, strategic ambiguity is an asset. Kyrgyzstan has no interest in choosing between China, Russia, India, and Western investors when it can instead extract advantages from all of them. The same logic explains why Central Asian governments routinely embrace Chinese infrastructure while simultaneously seeking European, American, Turkish, Gulf, Japanese, and South Korean investment. Their objective and chief concern is maintaining their own agency.
That agency may be one of the SCO’s most fascinating unintended characteristics. Multilateral institutions often develop institutional behaviors their founders did not explicitly design. The European Union, NATO, and ASEAN all have political cultures and operating assumptions that went beyond the intentions of their architects. The SCO appears to be developing something different: an environment in which its smaller members possess greater freedom of economic maneuver than the organization’s nominal power structure would suggest.
China, India, and Russia each have substantial reasons to use the SCO for their own strategic purposes. That divergence limits any one major power’s ability to turn the SCO into an instrument of strategic alignment.
China has the largest economy in the organization and increasingly supplies the infrastructure connecting its members. Russia retains military influence and longstanding political relationships. India possesses substantial economic and demographic weight while maintaining relationships with both Russia and the West. Yet, none can herd the others into an arrangement that systematically disadvantages the others or Western involvement.
The result is particularly visible in Central Asia. Governments there have little incentive to surrender their ability to balance among external powers. Chinese railways and investment can expand economic opportunity, while American or European capital can provide diversification. Turkish, Gulf, Indian, Japanese, and Korean partnerships provide additional options. For governments sitting between much larger powers, dependency on any single patron is inherently dangerous.
The SCO therefore produces a paradox. Its smaller members often determine whether any institutionalization actually moves forward. The major powers may act as veto-players or set strategic priorities, but implementation often depends on whether smaller governments see a direct benefit. It seems that the SCO’s largest members increasingly result to multilateral arrangements bypassing the SCO when convenient.
This is why Bishkek may ultimately prove more revealing than dramatic images of Modi, Xi, and Putin standing together. The central question is not whether the three largest powers can appear united, nor is it whether they can identify areas of common interest. The more important question is whether they can convert that shared interest into an institutional structure capable of constraining the strategic choices of the organization’s other members.
The answer so far: no.
The organization’s most surprising winners are the states that were never expected to exercise much influence over it. Kyrgyzstan successfully used the summit and its 2025-2026 chairmanship to promote its economic priorities. Other small SCO states in Central Asia have long done the same, using the organization to attract capital, build connections, and preserve strategic options.
This is a very different outcome from the emergence of a unified Eurasian bloc or some grand anti-Western alliance some have predicted. For Washington, that distinction should matter. The SCO should not be dismissed as an ineffectual talking shop, but neither should it be treated as an embryonic anti-Western alliance with the activities of Beijing or Moscow ascribed to all of its members. Washington too would be better served by watching the multilateral announcements on the sidelines of the organization rather than taking grand declarations at face value.
So long as Beijing, New Delhi, and Moscow remain at loggerheads, they will be unable to impose a common strategic direction, and the organization’s smaller states will retain outsized influence and room to maneuver – particularly in the economic domain.
In Bishkek, that room was on display. The summit produced declarations, initiatives, infrastructure commitments, and political theater. More importantly, it showed that the organization’s smaller members can use a China-India-Russia-dominated forum without becoming subordinate to any single major power. The SCO may eventually become a more coherent institution. Until then, its greatest surprise is that the tail continues to wag the dog, and its smallest states, by converting membership into tangible development gains, are the biggest winners.

EXPLAINER - What is Bab el-Mandeb and why it matters?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:42:00 UTC
23:42:00 KST

A narrow stretch of water between Yemen and the Horn of Africa has become a new focal point in the widening regional crisis.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints, linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean.
The waterway has gained renewed significance after Yemen's Houthi group advanced along the country's Red Sea coast, raising concerns about the security of one of the main routes connecting Asian and European markets.
On Friday, a Yemeni government military source told Anadolu that Houthi fighters had seized Perim Island, also known as Mayyun, which sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The takeover means the group has completed its control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the source added.
The Houthis were also reported to have taken the coastal town of Dhubab, which faces the island, and the Hanish Islands farther north.
A day earlier, the group seized the historic port city of Mokha, about 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The internationally recognized Yemeni government has signaled that it intends to respond.
Yemen's UN envoy Abdullah al-Saadi told an emergency Security Council session that the Houthis were continuing their military escalation and seeking to impose a “new reality” in the Red Sea.
So what exactly is Bab el-Mandeb, and why does it matter?
Bab el-Mandeb, whose Arabic name means the “Gate of Tears,” separates Yemen from Djibouti and Eritrea in the Horn of Africa.
It connects the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea with the Red Sea. At the northern end of the Red Sea is Egypt's Suez Canal, one of the world's most important shortcuts between Asia and Europe.
That makes Bab el-Mandeb the southern gateway to the Suez corridor.
A ship traveling between Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal must first pass through Bab el-Mandeb.
The strait is about 18 miles (29 kilometers) wide at its narrowest point, with shipping traffic divided between two channels.
Perim Island divides the passage, with a channel between the island and mainland Yemen and a wider passage toward the African side.
Its location gives whoever controls the island an important vantage point over vessels approaching or leaving the Red Sea.
The Hanish Islands, farther north along Yemen's western coast, also sit close to important maritime approaches.
Control of these positions, together with Mokha and Dhubab, could give the Houthis a significantly stronger military presence around the shipping route.
Bab el-Mandeb is not only an oil route.
The strait forms part of a wider maritime corridor carrying manufactured goods, agricultural commodities, grain, fertilizers, vehicle parts, electronics and other products between Asian and European markets.
Before the latest cycle of Red Sea disruption, the Suez Canal handled an estimated 12% to 15% of global trade and about 22% of worldwide seaborne container trade in 2023, according to UN Trade and Development.
Bab el-Mandeb is indispensable to that route. If ships cannot safely enter the Red Sea from the south, much of the commercial value of the Suez Canal as an Asia-Europe shortcut is lost.
Vessels must instead sail around South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope. For an oil tanker traveling from the Arabian Sea to Europe, the diversion can add approximately 15 days, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
The longer journey consumes more fuel, ties up ships and crews for additional time, reduces the number of vessels available elsewhere and raises freight and insurance costs. Those expenses can eventually filter through to the prices paid by manufacturers and consumers.
The consequences have already been demonstrated. After the Houthis began attacking commercial shipping in late 2023, oil flows through Bab el-Mandeb fell from 9.3 million barrels per day in 2023 to 4.1 million in 2024 as operators diverted vessels around Africa.
By May 2025, tonnage passing through the Suez Canal remained 70% below its 2023 level, according to UN Trade and Development.
The latest crisis has given the strait another layer of importance: the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz.
Hormuz, between Iran and Oman, is the main maritime outlet for much of the oil and liquefied natural gas produced in the Persian Gulf.
The ongoing conflict involving Iran and the US has sharply reduced traffic through the waterway.
US Energy Information Administration data show that oil flows through Hormuz fell from 21.6 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 4.9 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026.
Saudi Arabia responded by moving more crude through its East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing the kingdom to bypass Hormuz.
As a result, oil and petroleum-product flows through Bab el-Mandeb climbed from 5.4 million barrels per day in the final quarter of 2025 to 8.1 million per day in the second quarter of this year.
This has turned the Red Sea route into a crucial relief valve for an energy market already coping with restricted Gulf exports.
Yet Yanbu’s location creates a geographical divide. Saudi oil destined for Europe can travel north through the Suez Canal or Egypt’s Suez-Mediterranean, or SUMED, pipeline without crossing Bab el-Mandeb.
Cargoes heading from Yanbu to major Asian customers, however, normally sail south through Bab el-Mandeb. If that route becomes unusable, those ships would have to travel north through Suez and then circle Africa, a substantially longer and more expensive journey.
Territorial control on the Yemeni side would significantly improve the Houthis’ ability to threaten shipping, but it would not give the group uncontested command of the full waterway.
The strait is bordered on the western side by Djibouti and Eritrea, and the principal international shipping passage extends toward the African coast.
International law also protects navigation through straits connecting two parts of the high seas or exclusive economic zones. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, ships and aircraft enjoy a right of transit passage that should not be impeded.
The International Maritime Organization reaffirmed in July that transit through international straits must not be threatened, denied, hampered or suspended.

Libyan parliament, High Council of State heads agree to revive 6+6 election committee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:41:55 UTC
23:41:55 KST

Muetaz Wannes and Lina Altawell
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
Libya’s House of Representatives Speaker Aguila Saleh and High Council of State President Mohamed Takala agreed to reactivate the joint 6+6 committee tasked with drafting election laws and hold a meeting of the body in Türkiye.
The agreement came during a meeting between Saleh and Takala in the Turkish capital of Ankara on Thursday, according to a joint statement.
“The meeting resulted in several understandings aimed at strengthening national consensus, supporting political and institutional stability in Libya, and affirming continued coordination between the two councils on national obligations,” the statement said.
The joint 6+6 committee, formed by Libya’s House of Representatives and the High Council of State, was established on June 6, 2023, following talks in the Moroccan city of Bouznika to draft laws for the expected elections. However, some of its provisions faced opposition from Libyan parties, preventing the laws from being enacted.
 
The two sides stressed that Libya’s political process must remain within the framework of the constitutional declaration, the legal framework and the political agreement regulating the work of both councils, while respecting the powers assigned to each council.
They also praised “the efforts of the sisterly Republic of Türkiye” and its readiness to host the 6+6 committee in the coming days, enabling it to complete its work on election laws and paving the way for the long-awaited electoral process.
Efforts to end division
During the Ankara meeting, the two councils also stressed the need to unify sovereign positions and the executive authority, and end institutional division in a way that strengthens the unity of state institutions and leads to a unified executive authority ahead of the elections demanded by the Libyan people.
“Takala handed Saleh a letter regarding the board of the High National Election Commission,” the statement said, adding that the letter would be presented to the House of Representatives to take the measures it deems appropriate according to its procedures and powers.
In January 2021, a 13+13 committee formed by the House of Representatives and the High Council of State met in Bouznika, Morocco, to discuss appointments to Libya’s sovereign posts.
The positions discussed by Libyan parties included the head of the Supreme Judicial Council, the attorney general, the governor of the Central Bank, the head of the National Oil Corporation, the head of General Intelligence and the head of the Election Commission.
Separately, security sources said Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met with Saleh and Takala in Ankara on Thursday.
The meeting discussed developments in Libya and the region, possible steps to deepen cooperation between Libya and Türkiye, efforts to achieve political and military unity and maintain stability in Libya, as well as ways to make lasting progress on outstanding issues and reach broad consensus among Libyan parties.
The participants stressed the leading role of both councils in promoting stability and moving the political process forward, agreeing on the goals of achieving political unity and unifying institutions.
Libya has long been the subject of discussions over holding presidential and parliamentary elections, ending disputes over the executive authority, and achieving full military and political integration, without a resolution being reached despite various initiatives.
The Ankara talks are significant as the first meeting between the heads of the two institutions held under Turkish sponsorship and hosted in Türkiye to discuss these issues and make tangible progress on stalled tracks.
Libya remains divided between two rival governments: the Government of National Unity, headed by Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh and based in Tripoli, which governs western Libya, and the government of Osama Hammad, which was appointed by the House of Representatives in early 2022 and based in Benghazi, governing the east and most southern cities.
The UN mission in Libya has been pursuing efforts to lead the country toward elections that could resolve the crisis.

Gambia bans protests without permits after unrest over power cuts

Gambia bans protests without permits after unrest over power cuts
BANJUL, Sept 11 - Gambia's police chief has announced that no further protests will be allowed in the West African nation without permits, after authorities used tear gas earlier in the week to disperse crowds that had formed to denounce prolonged power cuts during the hottest months of the year.
The protests over multiple nights highlighted frustration with President Adama Barrow ahead of elections in December.
"From this very moment, nobody is allowed to protest without an approved permit," Seedy Mukhtar Touray, Gambia's inspector general of police, said in a statement late Thursday.
"Nobody is allowed to converge, cause havoc, distort the peace and tranquility of the nation, especially during the night. Any violation to this will be met with necessary force."
During the unrest earlier this week, a police post was vandalised and "detainees were unlawfully released from custody", Touray said, while the national utility, National Water and Electricity Company Ltd (NAWEC), said it had closed three branches after attacks severely damaged buildings, infrastructure and office equipment.
Authorities have arrested 11 people in connection with vandalism during the unrest, Touray said.
'YOUTHS ARE FRUSTRATED', OPPOSITION CANDIDATE SAYS
In an interview with Reuters, Talib Ahmed Bensouda, mayor of Kanifing Municipality, said he understood why protesters were upset.
"If you can't sit in your house because of the heat. If you don't have [a generator] to do basic business or even to carry out informal activities… you're forced to take the matter to the streets," said Bensouda, who plans to challenge Barrow in the December election. "That's not something we support, but we understand the matter."
NAWEC said in a statement on August 15 that it was experiencing "an unforeseen surge in electricity demand during the peak period," which it attributed to high temperatures.
Barrow visited NAWEC facilities on Tuesday morning and promised that Gambia would receive new generators this week and restore electricity by the end of October.
He said the government was in the final stage of installing an additional 24-megawatt generation machine and that it awarded a contract for a 50-MW solar power plant.
But Bensouda faulted Barrow for relying too much on energy imports, leaving Gambia exposed to global supply disruptions.
"Youths are frustrated, and I think not just about energy, they're frustrated about a lot of things," Bensouda said. "There's a lack of opportunity and this is what's driving irregular migration to Europe." REUTERS

Nigeria parliament boycotts South Africa events over anti-migrant attacks
ABUJA, Sept 11 - Nigeria's parliament has suspended official visits to South Africa and ordered lawmakers to boycott South African-hosted legislative activities, citing reports of attacks on Nigerians and other African migrants there.
The decision reflects growing concern in Nigeria over the safety of its citizens in South Africa and signals rising frustration over a problem that has periodically strained relations between the continent's two largest economies.

US declares end of largest recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:41:06 UTC
23:41:06 KST

US declares end of largest recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak
The US health authorities on Sept 11 declared the end of the nation’s largest recorded multi-state cyclosporiasis outbreak, after thousands fell ill from consuming contaminated iceberg lettuce.
The outbreak sickened 12,883 people across 21 states, resulting in 570 hospitalisations and two deaths, according to the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and Prevention.
The CDC said the contaminated lettuce, which federal investigators linked to produce from Taylor Farms, is no longer available in stores or served at restaurants and recent infections associated with the outbreak have declined significantly.
Cyclosporiasis can be contracted by consuming food – typically raw fruits and vegetables – or water contaminated with feces.
The CDC said on Sept 11 that there is currently no risk of people contracting cyclosporiasis from lettuce. The agency also noted that all products tied to the outbreak are past their expiry dates and no longer available in stores or restaurants.
The lettuce-linked outbreak accounted for more than half of the 19,595 laboratory-confirmed US cyclosporiasis cases reported since May 1, according to CDC data, making 2026 by far the worst year on record for the parasite-borne illness.
Michigan was among the states hardest hit by the outbreak with over 14,000 cases and two deaths linked to the parasite, according to federal and state health officials. Ohio and Missouri also saw thousands of infections tied to contaminated lettuce from Taylor Farms. REUTERS

BRICS achievements and West’s attempts to regain leadership: Putin’s statements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:40:42 UTC
23:40:42 KST

NEW DELHI, September 11. /TASS/. The West is attempting to regain its lost leadership by any means, including unsavory methods, Russian President Vladimir Putin said while speaking at the BRICS Business Forum.
He also noted that strong and reliable business ties within BRICS form the basis of international relations, making them more resilient.
TASS has summed up the Russian president’s key statement.
BRICS achievements
Strong business ties within BRICS form the foundation of international relations and make them more resilient: "Evidently, a robust economic partnership and reliable business ties largely form the foundation of international relations, making them more resilient and stable, and enabling us to overcome the crises facing today’s world."
Dynamic domestic markets in BRICS countries underpin the group’s success: "BRICS countries, home to about half the world’s population, have vast, dynamic domestic markets. Cities in our countries are developing rapidly and growing, urbanization is proceeding swiftly, and national companies are increasingly making their mark as global players."
Russia hopes that its initiative regarding the establishment of a BRICS new investment platform will be supported by other members of the association: "We hope this idea will be supported by members of our association."
BRICS nations have generated more than 40% of global GDP over the past five years, whereas the contribution of the Group of Seven (G7) stood at just 29%: "Over the past five years, more than 40% of global GDP was generated by the BRICS states, while the contribution of the Group of Seven – the so-called Big Seven, though I don’t understand why it’s called 'Big' – amounted to just 29%."
BRICS nations have accounted for nearly half of global economic growth over the past five years: "If we look at global economic growth over that same period [the last five years - TASS note], nearly half of that growth was driven by the countries of our association. Meanwhile, the G7 contributed only 18%."
The BRICS’ economic rules are not imposed by the "global one percent": "Through the joint efforts of government bodies, the business community, and expert circles, BRICS is forging a new, sustainable platform for global growth. It is very important that its key elements, the rules regulating the operations of companies and organizations are not imposed from outside, are not imposed on us by the so-called global one percent."
BRICS member states have proven that they know how to work hard and cooperate as equals and they are prepared to respond to any challenges: "Our rules are based on innovative business approaches and breakthrough technological solutions, while prioritizing the national interests of countries, the interests of our people. It is indeed about difficult and painstaking work, but BRICS nations have proven that they know how to work hard and honestly, cooperate as equals, see the big picture and mutually beneficial prospects. They can respond to any challenges, which means that our endeavors will be successful."
The Western attempts to regain leadership
New "engines of growth" have come to replace the old leaders of the global economy today: "It [the world] is currently undergoing a phase of profound structural transformation. This is driven by the fact that new engines of growth are replacing the old leaders – or, let’s say, the old leaders who were at the forefront of economic growth in the second half of the last century."
The West is attempting to regain its lost leadership by any means, including unsavory methods: "But, unfortunately, our Western competitors are currently trying to regain their former leadership by any means possible. Today, this competition is sometimes taking on unsavory forms - something a colleague from Iran also just mentioned here. Moreover, these unsavory forms are manifesting at the state level."
The West seeks to aggressively impact logistics, destroy infrastructure and seize ships in a bid to maintain its leadership: "The tools that are used even include measures of direct impact on or destruction of industrial and logistics facilities, pipelines and so on. Attempts are made to block international transport corridors, seize seagoing vessels, and illegal restrictions are also employed, together with threats of the so-called secondary sanctions on those who are unwilling to act in someone else’s interests but protect their own national interests."
The decline in industrial production in the leading eurozone economies has reached 8% over the past few years: "This is a big figure for them."
Sanctions
The countries that initiated the sanctions are facing an economic downturn and are no longer able to pursue an innovative policy similar to that of Russia: "In the countries that initiated the sanctions, which are facing the full-blown problem of budget deficits, growing public debts and industrial decline, it is not possible to pursue such an [innovative] policy."
Some 30,000 sanctions have been imposed against Russia, twice as many as against all other countries of the world combined: "But more than 30,000 sanctions have been imposed against Russia. This is almost twice as many as against all countries of the world combined. That is the statistic."
Russia has strengthened its national sovereignty and is now expanding cooperation with reliable, predictable partners: "We have strengthened our national sovereignty and are developing ties with reliable, predictable partners. In just four years, the geography of our foreign trade has changed dramatically."
The economic problems facing the European countries that initiated sanctions against Russia are a fact of life: "These are not mere speculations; these are figures from their own statistics. I mentioned budget deficits, rising national debt, and the industrial downturn - these are all facts of life."
Russia’s economy
Russia's economic growth rate over the past three years has exceeded the global average, with the country's GDP growing by 10.3% between 2023 and 2025.

Trump Loses the Other Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:40:15 UTC
23:40:15 KST

Trump Loses the Other Strait
The Houthi advance is bad news for the U.S., and even worse news for Saudi Arabia.
As recently as last week, the Iran war appeared to be turning slightly in America’s favor. The Houthis—the Yemen-based militia that is Iran’s most formidable remaining ally in the Middle East—were under pressure from their local rivals, and the Saudi air force was pounding them with air strikes. The president of Yemen’s internationally recognized government issued a triumphant statement declaring that the Houthis’ miscalculations “will open the door to their complete collapse.” With their Houthi partners wounded, Iran’s leaders would have one more reason to back down and agree to Donald Trump’s terms.
Yesterday morning, those delusions drifted away like smoke as Houthi forces broke through their enemies’ defenses and seized the towns and islands around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the most important maritime choke points in the world.
That loss leaves Trump, who had been hoping to win back control of the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, with a bitter surprise. His enemies now control both of the two important straits in the Middle East, through which a combined total of about a third of the world’s oil shipments pass every day.
It also underscores a stubborn fact: For all the setbacks suffered by Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” over the past year or two, its forces retain an ideological fervor and an esprit de corps that is sorely lacking on the other side. The Gulf states’ failure to work together against the Houthis has been catastrophic, and it echoes Trump’s own failure to devise a plausible or coordinated strategy against Iran.
Although the Houthis already had the ability to threaten shipping in the Red Sea, the capture of the Bab el-Mandeb “means you can literally sit on the coast and fire at passing ships,” April Longley Alley, a Yemen expert at the Washington Institute on Near East Policy and the former political adviser to the United Nations special envoy for Yemen, told me. “It makes it easier and cheaper, and it solidifies, from a military and political point of view, that they have a stranglehold on the strait.”
The United States might not be able to do much about this, even if the Pentagon launches a new round of air strikes on the Houthis. (The Saudi leader, Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman, called Trump twice yesterday urging him to strike the Houthis, Axios reported.) Bombs and missiles would achieve little without a ground force to take advantage of them, and America’s Yemeni allies are now battered and divided. The Trump administration waged a seven-week war against the group last year, and although it succeeded in killing some Houthi commanders, it did not dislodge the group or alter its ability to wage war, as Trump had promised.
The Houthi advance is even worse news for Saudi Arabia. For many years, the Saudis have been struggling to tamp down the Houthi threat on its border. Now the Houthis have inherited a great deal of Saudi and Emirati supplies left behind by the official Yemeni government’s retreating forces. A video circulated yesterday of Mohammad Ali al-Houthi, one of the group’s top commanders and a cousin of its supreme leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, riding though Mokha in an Emirati armored vehicle.
The mess that Saudi Arabia faces in Yemen is partly of its own making. The Houthis were born three decades ago in reaction to Saudi meddling in Yemen’s religious and political sphere. In December, tensions between the Saudi and Emirati leadership led Riyadh to demand that the Emiratis—their nominal allies—withdraw from Yemen, leaving the Saudis in charge of a patchwork of militias with divided loyalties. The various Yemeni factions continued to squabble among themselves even as their Houthi enemies were at the gates.
“There was no coordination between commanders, between the intelligence and the drones, between the coast guard and the army—nothing,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at the think tank Chatham House, told me.
The Houthis have clearly benefited from the Gulf’s disunity. “Last time the Houthis made a breakthrough at Marib in 2022, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia were able to jointly support a devastatingly effective Yemeni-government counterattack,” Michael Knights, the head of research at the consultancy Horizon Engage, told me.
The Houthis, meanwhile, were disciplined and focused. “They sacrificed hundreds if not thousands of fighters,” a member of Yemen’s officially recognized government, who asked not to be identified for fear of repercussions, told me. “Our bullshit activists were putting out fake news about victories, while the Houthis were working in silence.”
With the momentum on their side, the Houthis could now go on to seize more terrain in other parts of Yemen, including Marib province, where much of Yemen’s oil is located. They could also extend their power bloodlessly, by cutting deals with tribal and regional leaders in the south and east. All of this would further consolidate their power and strengthen their Iranian patrons.
The Houthi victories have already put into doubt the value of the Mecca Alliance, the mutual-defense pact formed in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey. Islamabad and Ankara have shown no inclination to help the Saudis, despite a rash of recent Houthi strikes on targets in southern Saudi Arabia.
Iran’s vaunted Axis of Resistance is not a bulletproof covenant either. The Houthis were absent earlier this year when the United States and Israel started bombing Iran.
But unlike their enemies, the Houthis and the Iranians have a deep ideological bond, one that their soldiers willingly die for. And the Houthis do not need to win every battle. As long as they can sink an occasional oil tanker, they will hold a whip hand over their Saudi neighbors, and over the rest of the world too.

UK lawmakers reject bill to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales

UK lawmakers reject bill to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales
The bill had proposed allowing adults with fewer than six months to live to apply for an assisted death, subject to approval
UK lawmakers on Friday voted down legislation to allow terminally ill adults in England and Wales to choose to end their lives.
The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was opposed by 286 members of parliament, while 270 voted for it.
The vote brings an end to a two-year debate in parliament about assisted dying.
On two previous occasions in 2024 and 2025, the elected House of Commons had backed the bill, but it did not become law because it was effectively filibustered by unelected lawmakers in the revising House of Lords chamber.
The bill had proposed allowing adults in England and Wales, with fewer than six months to live, to apply for an assisted death subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.
The government took a neutral stance, saying it was a matter of conscience.
The new UK leader, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, did not vote because he said he did not want to “unduly influence the debate”.

US abused post-9/11 global solidarity – Lavrov
Unknown

US abused post-9/11 global solidarity – Lavrov
The US exploited the wave of international sympathy and solidarity in the wake of the 9/11 attacks to expand its global influence, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said. He also argued that Washington’s conduct during the invasion of Afghanistan served as a pattern for further conflicts in Iraq, Libya, and other countries.
In an interview with RBK on Friday, which coincided with the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks, Lavrov reflected on their global aftermath. He recalled that Russia – like many other countries – had thrown its weight behind the US response, sharing intelligence and providing other support for operations against Al-Qaeda and the Taliban.
Russia’s cooperation with the West later expanded through the NATO-Russia Council, including projects involving Afghanistan, counter-narcotics work, transit arrangements, and support for the Western helicopter fleet, he added.
However, Lavrov noted that Washington used both the international coalition assembled after the attacks and the political mandate it received for its selfish goals. “The United States exploited this international solidarity… not so much to combat terrorism as to pursue its own geopolitical objectives and to broaden its presence and sway,” he said.
He pointed to the 2003 invasion of Iraq, noting that the subsequent dismantling of Ba’ath Party and the country’s military helped produce forces that became the backbone of the Islamic State. He also blamed Western intervention for the destruction of Libya, adding that the conflicts in Yugoslavia, Georgia, and Ukraine were an attempt by a “unipolar” world to dictate the course of international affairs.
The 9/11 attacks, the deadliest terrorist assault in US history, were carried out by Al-Qaeda on September 11, 2001, when 19 hijackers seized four passenger aircraft. Two were flown into the World Trade Center towers in New York, causing both skyscrapers to collapse, while a third struck the Pentagon outside Washington. The fourth aircraft crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers and crew fought back against the hijackers. The attacks killed 2,977 people, excluding the perpetrators, and injured thousands more.
Following the tragedy, Russian President Vladimir Putin was the first world leader to call then-US President George W. Bush, offering both condolences and assistance.

Dutch Government Advocates for EU-Wide Minimum Age for Social Media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:35:30 UTC
23:35:30 KST

Strict rules are needed to ensure the safety of digital services like social media. However, until these services meet adequate safety standards, the Dutch government advocates for the introduction of a European minimum age. To develop a reliable, safe, and effective measure in collaboration with all Member States, minister Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty) has submitted proposals to the European Commission on behalf of the government, outlining the requirements for implementing such a minimum age. The Netherlands and Spain are jointly submitting the proposals to the European Commission.
Social media offer numerous benefits but also pose significant risks, such as addictive algorithms and harmful content. These risks must be addressed. Until these services are sufficiently safe, the Dutch government supports a European minimum age for social media. Introducing a minimum age involves age restrictions and verification processes that may impact freedom of expression, privacy, and the protection of personal data in some cases. This is precisely why the Netherlands and Spain are calling for privacy-preserving verification methods and for the European Commission to thoroughly assess in advance whether the proposed measures are necessary and proportionate.
Minister Aerdts (Digital Economy and Sovereignty): “We would not accept unsafe products for children in the physical world. The same stand should apply online. As long as social media platforms fail to adequately protect children from addictive design and harmful content, we need a minimum age. This should be regulated at the European level, so that children across Europe benefit from the same protection.”
Platforms Must Demonstrate That Their Services Are Safe for Children
Extending an age restriction beyond social media to other digital services would need to be carefully designed and clearly scoped, taking into account children's access to the internet and the practical impact of additional verification requirements. The Dutch and Spanish governments therefore propose a European framework for independently assessing whether social media platforms — and, where relevant, other digital services — are safe enough for children. Providers must demonstrate that their services meet safety standards. Platforms that can prove their services are safe may be exempted from the age restriction. The Dutch-designed Children’s Rights Impact Assessment (KIA) and the rules under the Digital Services Act (DSA) could serve as the foundation for such a European assessment framework.
Uniform Rules Across the European Union
The Dutch and Spanish governments advocates for a single set of rules applicable across the entire European Union. Digital services like social media are not bound by national borders. Introducing EU-wide rules creates certainty for regulators, businesses, and - most importantly - parents and children. The government therefore supports embedding the minimum age in an EU regulation, and limiting introducing national derogations as much as possible, with enforcement organised at the European level.
Age Verification with Respect for Privacy and Proportionality
To enforce a minimum age, it must be possible to verify a user’s age. Various methods exist for this purpose: through age verification, where users must prove they meet the minimum age requirement; through age estimation based on physical characteristics; or by relying on self-declared information. The guiding principle is that any method must be both effective and privacy friendly. For this reason, it currently considers age verification the most suitable approach for enforcing a European minimum age. To protect individuals’ privacy as much as possible, verification should only confirm whether a user has reached the age threshold, without processing any additional personal data.
Europe Must Develop Its Own Child-Safe Digital Services
The goal of the Dutch and Spanish governments are not to restrict access to digital services but to make them safe for everyone. Therefore, a minimum age should be part of a broader package, including European efforts to develop safe alternative digital services for children. Once these are available, enforcing a minimum age will become easier. Additionally, the government calls on the European Commission to prioritize the protection of minors in international discussions and collaborations with non-EU countries, ensuring that digital services are designed with global safety in mind and that age restrictions can be effectively enforced.

STOCKHOLM — With two days to go before Sweden’s knife-edge general election, Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has a warning for Europe: Don’t trust the left on defense.
His country has been almost totally united in its support for Ukraine and in backing the decision — after decades of neutrality — to join NATO two years ago. But speaking to POLITICO in the capital Stockholm, the center-right Moderate party leader argued that Europe should wake up to the security risks of the rival left-wing bloc taking power — which polls suggest may happen.
Asked what's at stake for Europe in Sunday’s vote, Kristersson said: “I would say security policy. If the left side would win, two out of three, or two out of four parties voted against the Swedish NATO membership. I mean, that is a real, real thing.”
Advertisement
He continued: “That means a government that will not be able to make the domestic decisions needed to fulfill our NATO obligations, for example — like spending, like all the missions.”
Sweden became NATO’s newest member in 2024, the national mood having shifted in favor of taking sides in the face of Vladimir Putin’s territorial aggression in Europe. That decision was “a big thing” for the country of 10.6 million people, which was neutral during both world wars and throughout the Cold War, Kristersson said.
“But after becoming a member, we have made a NATO-related decision every month in government,” the prime minister added. “And if government is not united, they simply cannot make the decisions.”
Kristersson speaks to reporters on Sept. 11, 2026 in Stockholm. | Tim Ross/POLITICO
Since becoming a member of the alliance, Sweden has sent hundreds of troops to join a NATO force in Latvia, pledged warships for patrolling the Baltic Sea and deployed Gripen fighter jets to police the skies in the region.
Asked if he believed support for Ukraine would be in doubt too, Kristersson said: “I hope, really not, because we have been united on Ukraine — with one single exception. The Left Party voted against the very first support package to Ukraine. From that [point] on, eight parties out of eight have been united.”
Kristersson’s comments follow a pointed intervention from Social Democrat opposition leader Magdalena Andersson, who demanded the PM come clean about his allies’ links to Russia in a POLITICO interview published this week.
Advertisement
Until recently, Sunday’s upcoming vote seemed like it would be a comfortable victory for Andersson’s Social Democrats and their political allies in smaller parties on the left. But their poll lead shrank dramatically in the past two weeks to as low as 2.6%, within the statistical margin of error.
Far-right friends
Kristersson’s center-right coalition has been governing for the past four years with the support of the far-right Sweden Democrats. He defended his decision to cooperate with a party opponents claim is too extreme despite its internal efforts to clean up its past neo-Nazi links.
“I have full respect for the fact that there are eight parties in the Swedish parliament,” said Kristersson. “None of these parties are even close to a majority of their own. If you cannot unite parties on specific topics and ambitions, then you will simply not get anything done at all.”
Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson, the first woman to serve as Swedish PM, leads the polls. | Tim Ross/POLITICO
Under leader Jimmie Åkesson, the Sweden Democrats are in second place behind Andersson’s Social Democrats in the polls. Åkesson has said he’s eyeing up the chance of becoming prime minister at the next vote, due in 2030.
If Kristersson returns as prime minister after Sunday’s election, he has said he’s ready to give Sweden Democrat politicians roles as ministers in his government for the first time. It would be a major change for Sweden — and the left-wing bloc has campaigned against it.
Kristersson suggested that being part of a team would limit the opportunities for any individual ministers to go rogue with extremist policies.
“In Sweden, we have a collective decision-making process in government,” he said. “I would never say that one minister is not important, but every minister is part of a team that jointly makes all the decisions — so there is very little room for people to play in a role of their own.
“And since I will be the person that is forming that government, and the person that will appoint every one of them, I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government.”

Lebanon pupils record sharp decline in reading and maths: OECD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:35:18 UTC
23:35:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon pupils record sharp decline in reading and maths amid war, unrest
Lebanon has recorded weak results in reading, mathematics and science among 15-year-old students, according to the latest OECD education assessment cited by Beirut-based newspaper Al-Modon.
Results from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2025 placed Lebanon among the lower-performing education systems covered by the study.
Lebanese students scored an average of 331 points in reading, 372 in science and 377 in mathematics.
Compared with 2015, the national averages were 20 points lower in mathematics, 19 points lower in reading and 15 points lower in science.
However, the OECD cautioned that this apparent decline should not be read simply as evidence that learning outcomes have worsened across the board.
The share of Lebanon's 15-year-old population represented in PISA has risen significantly over the past decade, meaning more students from groups that were previously underrepresented in secondary education are now included in the assessment.
The OECD said this change in coverage could explain much of the fall in national average scores.
Among the more advantaged group of students who were already represented in the assessment in 2015, science performance actually improved over the decade, while reading and mathematics remained broadly stable.
The reading results nevertheless point to serious problems with basic proficiency.
PISA does not test reading simply as a language skill, but assesses whether students can understand, evaluate and interpret information and apply it in real-life situations.
Only 22% of students in Lebanon reached at least Level 2 in reading, the level the OECD considers the minimum proficiency threshold, compared with an OECD average of 69%.
At this level, students should be able to identify the main idea in a moderately long text, locate information using explicit criteria and reflect on the purpose and form of a text when directed to do so.
Lebanon's average reading score of 331 therefore points to widespread difficulties in reaching basic reading proficiency, rather than an inability among students to read.
The mathematics results were also weak, with Lebanon recording an average score of 377.
Science performance stood at 372 points.
The OECD also cautions that national averages can conceal large differences between the strongest and weakest-performing students.
PISA tests the ability of 15-year-olds to apply knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science to real-world problems rather than simply recalling information learned in class.
The assessment also divides students into proficiency levels to show what they are able to do in practical terms.
The Lebanon results do not, however, cover the entire country.
Students in the south were excluded from the assessment because of the war, meaning the published figures apply only to the population covered by the test rather than to all Lebanese 15-year-olds.
The exclusion is significant given the scale of education disruption in southern Lebanon, where schools have repeatedly closed or been converted into shelters during the conflict.
Overall, 7,382 students at 270 schools took part in Lebanon, representing an estimated 56,700 15-year-olds, or about 90% of the country's total population in that age group.
The exclusion of parts of the country is significant because some of the students whose education was most severely disrupted in recent years may not have been included in the sample.
Lebanon’s education system had already been under severe pressure before the latest war, with the country’s economic crisis disrupting schooling and contributing to repeated teacher strikes, closures and students dropping out.
Children have also faced repeated interruptions to learning from overlapping crises, including the financial collapse, the Covid-19 pandemic, the Beirut port explosion and successive rounds of conflict.
During the latest war, hundreds of thousands of children faced further disruption as schools closed, classes were reduced and public buildings were used to house displaced families.
The situation has been particularly acute in the south, where more than 100 schools have been damaged during the conflict.
Even before the latest escalation, UN data had warned that Lebanon’s overlapping crises were pushing growing numbers of children out of education and increasing pressure on families struggling to afford schooling.

Hate speech against Rohingya refugees on the rise in Malaysia

Hostile social media content, disinformation campaigns, and a petition calling for their expulsion: in Malaysia, a wave of hate speech has been targeting Rohingya refugees, a Muslim minority driven out of Myanmar. The rising hostility has already led to the eviction of more than 100 people from a village and forced the temporary closure of schools serving refugee children.
For a long time, Malaysia was considered a safe country for Rohingya Muslims fleeing persecution in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar.
But the situation began to change in 2020, at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, with the emergence of hate speech online. Recently, anti-Rohingya rhetoric has taken several forms: disinformation, a petition calling on the Malaysian prime minister to expel them that got more than 400,000 signatures before it was taken down, and the spread of slogans like “Save Malaysia from the Rohingya”.
The FRANCE 24 Observers team spoke with a representative of the NGO Article 19. She preferred to remain anonymous for security reasons:
 "The recent wave of hate speech against the Rohingya refugees has been one of the most intense on the volume of it, on the scale of it, and it lasted longer than previous times.
For example, they put out narratives like, 'Oh, these people are flying from Myanmar. They're looking for jobs.' And 'Oh, they are here to take away our land,' and stuff like that.
But they’re not telling the truth, because the thing is they're running away from ongoing genocide 16’22 and the violence against them in Myanmar."
Hostile slogans appeared this summer in the village of Kuala Muda, in the state of Penang, where Rohingya families have lived for years. More than a hundred of them fled the village at the end of July, seeking refuge in the capital, Kuala Lumpur.
Malaysia’s government announced plans in July to send 5,000 of the Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar. Human rights groups warned they could face serious danger, and the government backtracked, saying the refugees would not be deported if they faced persecution.

One giant step: first known T rex footprints found in North Dakota
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:34:07 UTC
23:34:07 KST

The first known series of footprints from an adult Tyrannosaurus rex has been found in North Dakota by a team of scientists.
The 23ft-long trackway – consisting of four three-toed footprints, two left and two right – was first identified in the south-west of the state, in the dinosaur fossil area known as Hell Creek Formation, last year by researchers from the Denver Museum of Nature and Science in Colorado and Liverpool John Moores University in the UK.
The findings, which have now been published in a scientific journal, date from 66.5m years ago and are the first of their kind to be found and identified. While isolated footprints and juvenile, or related species, tracks have been found before, this is the first known series of footprints left by a wandering T rex.
“Bones tell us an enormous amount about these animals, but footprints capture a moment of behavior,” said Tyler Lyson, senior curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Denver museum.
“With a trackway, we can actually follow an animal as it moved across the landscape. That is incredibly rare for T rex.”
Each of the footprints is about 3ft (0.91m) long, with a stride of about 13ft (3.96m). The research team used high-resolution 3D surface scanning to document each footprint and create physical 3D reproductions. From this work, researchers were able to make a rough estimate that the animal was walking about 3.5-4.5mph – about the same as a brisk human walking pace.
The T rex, the most famous of all dinosaurs, lived about 66-68m years ago during the Cretaceous period, according to the known fossil record. The creatures, which stood 12-13ft tall, were among the last non-avian dinosaurs to walk the Earth before a mass extinction event wiped them out.
Three of the discovered footprints are set to be recovered by helicopter later this year and transported to the museum in Denver. The findings are a particular joy for the Colorado schoolteacher who stumbled upon the site.
“As a teacher, I’m always telling my students that science starts with curiosity, passion and careful observation,” said Kent Hups, who is a longtime museum volunteer and also co-authored the paper. “I never imagined that could lead me to a discovery like this.”

Ebola case detected in seventh DR Congo province
Case found in northwestern province of South-Ubangi bordering the Central African Republic and Congo-Brazzaville.
The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached a seventh province bordering the Central African Republic and Congo-Brazzaville, according to local authorities.
The acting governor of the northwestern province of South-Ubangi, Jean-Rene Galekwa Vundawe, issued a statement on Friday saying Ebola was detected following laboratory analysis of a suspected case in the province.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Ebola spreads to two new zones in DRC; 60 areas now affected
- list 2 of 4Over 6,000 Ebola cases confirmed in DRC as death toll nears 3,000
- list 3 of 4DRC: Ebola fears grow as children return to school
- list 4 of 4WHO chief warns Ebola response must ramp up to stem DRC outbreak
Jean-Jacques Muyembe, head of DRC’s National Institute for Biomedical Research in Kinshasa, confirmed that a man had tested positive for Ebola.
Until now, the Bundibugyo virus, the rare kind of Ebola that caused the current outbreak, had been in six provinces in the country’s east and northeast. Local transmission has not yet been confirmed in South-Ubangi, meaning it has not been added to the list of provinces officially affected by the epidemic.
The outbreak, DRC’s 17th, is already the deadliest and the biggest in the country’s history in terms of case numbers – a milestone reached in late July.
As of Wednesday, 6,942 cases and 3,349 deaths have been reported, according to the latest government figures, well above the 2,299 deaths recorded in DRC’s 2018-2020 outbreak of the Zaire Ebola virus, previously the country’s worst on record.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has said the current outbreak remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak across West Africa, which killed more than 11,325 people, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Friday’s statement by the South-Ubangi governor’s office said a sample from a patient in the Bulu health district was tested by DRC’s national research institute, and laboratory results found the presence of the Bundibugyo virus.
The patient who died in South-Ubangi had developed symptoms in the capital of Tshopo province, Kisangani, where Ebola cases have been reported, after travelling through Rwanda, Uganda and Ituri province in northeastern DRC, Galekwa said. The patient then travelled by boat on the Congo River.
“The route taken both by the patient and by the boat exposes the populations” of the provinces of North-Ubangi, Tshopo and Mongala, Galekwa said.
“Thirty-eight people have been identified as having been in contact with the patient and have been placed in quarantine,” he said.
In recent weeks, new cases and deaths have declined in Ituri province, the outbreak’s epicentre, but risen sharply in neighbouring North Kivu and Upper-Uele.
The Bundibugyo variant of Ebola currently has no approved vaccines or treatments.
However, several treatments and vaccines are being tested.
The outbreak has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15, as weak health infrastructure, the region’s remoteness, and ongoing conflict near DRC’s borders with South Sudan, Uganda and Rwanda have hindered efforts to respond to cases.

"We are dealing with these circumstances with all the strength we have, despite the Israeli measures and the army's restrictions on us, which prevent us from moving around."

"One month into the ongoing siege of families in Qusra, the horrific reality for Palestinians remains the same," Talbot said, adding "the situation in Qusra demonstrates why the UK's latest commitments to upholding and enforcing international law must be implemented rapidly and comprehensively."
Even if the settlers are permanently removed from the area and the army leaves, Aisha said that it will take time for the residents of Qusra to feel safe again.
“It is true that I am optimistic that life will return to normal, but sometimes, when I see the current circumstances, I feel that things could get worse because of the presence of the settlers," she told The New Arab, adding "At other times, I tell myself that perhaps our lives will return to normal."

Why a Divided BRICS Poses No Challenge to America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

When the leaders of BRICS, the bloc of emerging economies, gather in New Delhi on Saturday for their 18th summit, they will have plenty to talk about. The group began with Brazil, Russia, India and China, then added South Africa in 2010. It has since expanded to include 11 countries.
The leaders and diplomats of BRICS member states are meeting in New Delhi to consider how their combined political and economic muscle might be used to build an alternative to the American-led global order. In some ways, President Donald Trump’s refusal to allow America play its traditional postwar leadership role has created new opportunities for the bloc. Yet its ambitions remain constrained by an inconvenient fact: India, China, Russia and Brazil do not align particularly well.
Here are the dynamics to watch this weekend. India, the host, wants the summit to accomplish as much as possible without antagonizing the United States. India continues to value the stability of its relationship with Washington, particularly as a counterbalance to China’s expanding influence in Asia and beyond. India, along with Brazil, has also resisted Russian and Chinese calls for a common BRICS currency and new lending to sanctions-hit Russia.
For its part, China is seeking to extend its global influence. For President Xi Jinping, this summit is another stage in an international roadshow that has included a leading role at this year’s Shanghai Cooperation Organization gathering in Kyrgyzstan, a visit to Egypt to help mediate the ongoing war in the Middle East and, later this month, a state visit to the White House.
In Delhi, Xi hopes to present China as a stable, predictable alternative to American influence. He will also seek to erode the dollar’s continuing dominance as the world’s principal reserve currency by promoting more channels for nondollar lending, the wider use of the renminbi to settle trade, and progress toward linking digital payment systems, an effort India has long resisted.
Given the sometimes violent border clashes between China and India in recent years, observers will also be watching Xi’s and Modi’s body language closely. Despite their differences on key agenda items, they are likely to be all smiles. Neither has an interest in airing grievances. India, as host, wants a smooth show. China, which will host next year’s summit, also wants a positive atmosphere. And Xi’s overriding goal is to present his country as a mature and constructive global leader.
Russia, of course, wants whatever diplomatic, political, and economic support it can get for its stalemated war with Ukraine. Brazil, meanwhile, hopes to forge new economic linkages and reaffirm its commitment to being a full BRICS partner, even as some fear that a Flavio Bolsonaro victory in next month’s presidential election could undermine the country’s commitment to the bloc.
The founders will not be the only delegations in attendance. Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, all new members, will be there, introducing fresh tensions into the agenda and some awkward photo calls. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the UAE’s leader Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, however, are expected to dispatch lesser officials in their place.
The central question is how the summit’s final communiqué will address the war. The recent Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit produced a final document that included implicit criticism of the United States and Israel. We will see whether the UAE delegation allows for similar language from Delhi.
Whatever emerges from the gathering, BRICS is unlikely to become an anti-American or anti-Western power bloc anytime soon. Its clout is already limited by the rivalry between China and India. The four founding members also have divergent interests whenever a conflict carries major consequences for energy markets: Russia and Brazil are major exporters who want higher energy prices while China and India, as major importers, prefer lower ones.
Equally important, the bloc now includes American treaty allies or longstanding partners, among them the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia. Their presence will impose another check on BRICS’s ambitions. All of them want to hedge against dependence on an increasingly unpredictable America. Most of them also want to preserve a stable relationship with the global superpower.

In Gaza, we’ve seen horror unfold with global powers’ support. Is that a blueprint for horror elsewhere? | Ahdaf Soueif
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:29:23 UTC
23:29:23 KST

Last week, Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s minister of national security, put out an AI-generated video that showed a conveyor belt of overweight Palestinian prisoners – dreaming of food and education – entering one of his prisons; he pops the dream bubbles above their heads and they come out emaciated and crying. Ben-Gvir is building an execution site for Palestinian prisoners with spectator booths, and he recently showed up at Damon prison in northern Israel and taunted female prisoners who complained about the poor conditions. He is digging a moat around a new high-security jail and planning to introduce crocodiles to patrol it. In all this, he has the approval of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, while the law that he championed mandating the death penalty for Palestinians deemed terrorists by military courts and convicted for lethal attacks is built on public support.
Sometime around 2017, many Palestinians and their supporters in the global media felt a change. Articles about Palestine no longer drew the hate mail we’d been accustomed to and events in support of Palestinian rights were hardly heckled. It seemed that people were less and less convinced by the image long cultivated by Israel and its supporters – the bearer of “western values” in the Middle East, the home to the “most moral army in the world”, a country acting only in self-defence – while it regularly assaulted Gaza and continued to expand its illegal settlements in the West Bank.
It had been a widely held tenet that if enough people in the democratic western world knew the reality of what Israel was doing to the Palestinians, they would pressure their governments, and Israel would be made to observe the norms of international law. Eventually, a reality would be born in which Jews, Muslims and Christians would live as equals within some political system that would be as good – and as flawed – as others. South Africa was always cited as the example, where rising international pressure over the decades was decisive.
But what looked like the winning of the moral, rational argument was offset by an acceleration of the processes of occupation, an increase in the frequency and blatancy of settler attacks in the West Bank, and of Israel Defense Forces (IDF) attacks on Gaza. The past three years have been the logical development of this. In the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 attacks, Israel escalated its killing, maiming and displacement of the Palestinians to the level of certifiable genocide. The defence minister, Israel Katz, says he is committed to the ethnic cleansing of Gaza, while a West Bank settler proudly tells the BBC that one Jewish life is worth 10 million Palestinian lives. Social media is awash with Israelis – from pundits on TV news debates to IDF soldiers – stating and performing the outrages necessary to achieve the objective of a Palestinian-free Palestine.
And while people across the world now know the truth of what is happening in Palestine and repeatedly and full-heartedly reject it, many democracies across the west continue to send arms and provide intelligence to Israel – even in a time of genocide. The US president’s Board of Peace makes a mockery of Palestinians, while hundreds of Israeli trucks clear the rubble from Gaza – and, with it, evidence of war crimes. The US attacks international institutions, such as the international criminal court, that seek to offer some semblance of justice for Palestinians. And to repress the constant protests of hundreds of thousands of their citizens, western democracies compromise their justice systems, attack their educational institutions and undermine their own democratic freedoms. Some have belatedly announced sanctions limited to Israeli settlements – illegal settlements that have should have been sanctioned years ago.
In 2014, I served on the jury of the Russell Tribunal on Palestine. In the preface to the report, which came after Israel’s third war on Gaza in six years, I wrote: “If not genocide, then genocide is not far behind.” Today I wonder if the genocide is not also a trailer for something more to come.
If the genocide was not a surprise, neither is the fact that the old colonial masters have no particular aversion to it. In a line of continuity with their own history, western countries have for decades partnered with Israel on weapons production and intelligence and surveillance technology. The west has sought Israeli advice and training in counter-terrorism, interrogation and civilian population-control techniques. A selling point for Israeli weapons has always been that they have been tried and tested.
And now, as Israel’s genocide is livestreamed, the establishment watches, enables, protects and helps tidy up. We may be watching a research and development exercise, a blueprint, a template, an example being created. We are already in a world where – it has been argued – some populations are surplus to requirements. Some of them live in areas that are a property developer’s dream.
This war is not only about Palestinians and Israelis, but about ideologies of supremacy and domination that threaten the people of the world, its civil societies and what is left of its international organisations. For the moment, it is the Palestinians who are on the frontline, the Palestinians who are being killed and maimed and tortured and displaced. But the Palestinians are also standing between all of us and a world remade in Israel’s image.

====================================================================================================

The Atlantic hurricane season just quietly broke a new weather record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
14:28:59 UTC
23:28:59 KST

The Atlantic hurricane season just set a new record. While it’s not unusual for the Atlantic hurricane season to take a while to get going—the typical peak in storm activity is late August through September—it is unusual not to see a single hurricane form by September 11. But that’s exactly what has happened this year for the very first time since reliable records began.
And with no likely contenders set to turn into a hurricane for at least the next seven days, that record will extend. In fact, the 2026 season is easily set to have the latest-forming hurricane whenever one does spin up, meteorologist Michael Lowry wrote on his blog. That’s assuming that one spins up at all.
There has been some meager storm activity this year, with five tropical storms so far. These have included Tropical Storm Dolly, which coincidentally formed only days after singer Dolly Parton died.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The reason the Atlantic has been so quiet this year is the same reason the eastern Pacific—and particularly Hawaii—has seen a bonanza of storms: El Niño. The cyclical climate phenomenon features an eastward shift in a pool of warm water in the tropical Pacific that changes where heat enters the atmosphere. That shift causes a domino effect in the atmosphere, altering major wind patterns around the world.
Over the Atlantic, El Niño tends to create more of what is called wind shear, or winds that travel in different directions and speeds at various levels of the atmosphere, which cuts off the convection that fuels tropical cyclones. As a result, any seeds of storms may have ample warm ocean water to feed on, but wind shear cuts them down before they can really develop.
On the flip side, wind shear decreases over the eastern Pacific during an El Niño, leaving more room for storms to spin up into destructive beasts. And shear has been particularly low around Hawaii, leaving it uncharacteristically vulnerable to storms.
This El Niño is a doozy, already at record strength for this time of the year and expected to be among the strongest events in living memory. Its effects on the world’s weather will be more pronounced than in the past. And there is more recent evidence that climate change may be driving more of these “Super El Niños.”
Lowry noted that “it’s still more likely than not we’ll see a hurricane or two on the back side of the season” because there hasn’t been a season in the reliable records (going back to about 1950) without a single hurricane. There are no recorded hurricanes for the 1907 and 1914 seasons, but those happened before we had satellites to spot storms that remained out at sea, he explained. But if there were to be a year without a single Atlantic hurricane, “this would probably be the year,” Lowry said.
