Same Appeasement, Same Mistakes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:54:00 UTC
22:54:00 KST

This past weekend, Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner (who negotiates on behalf of the US with no official government role) traveled to Russia and Ukraine to restart peace negotiations for Europe’s largest war.
According to reporting, proposals floated by Russian negotiators were focused on the “root causes” of the conflict and included the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from parts of Donetsk and Ukraine’s abandonment of future NATO membership, In total, the proposal differs little from those advanced a year ago.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
We’ve seen this all before: representatives of the second Trump administration visit Russia in search of a potential peace process, Putin delivers a maximalist vision as a starting point to his American audience, and Trump’s emissaries take this at face value and report this ploy for conquest and subjugation as a breakthrough in the peace process. When Ukraine questions the proposal and tries to rationalize compromises, President Volodymyr Zelensky will be framed as a spoiler. Rinse and repeat. See you six months from now.
At least this time Kushner and Witkoff managed to visit both Moscow and Kyiv, rather than just focusing on Russia and Putin’s circle of advisers. Nevertheless, Trump’s envoys still managed to carry Putin’s water, pushing a deal that makes less sense today than it did even a year ago when Russia’s military prospects seemed brighter.
‘Russia Will Feel It Firsthand’: Budanov Warns of Deeper Ukrainian Strikes
Kushner, once again showing both naivete and willful ignorance, referenced a potential “win-win” resolution to the war. Trump and his representatives are still approaching this war like a transaction and a real-estate deal without any comprehension of the geopolitical stakes embodied in this clash between democracies and authoritarian regimes.
The bizarre reference to all the “incredible memories” the American side would have from their negotiations with Putin further underscores that Kushner and Witkoff are completely out of their depth.
There is nothing we will learn from this round of diplomacy that we didn’t already know, and the failure of this round of talks was prescribed before the envoys left the United States. That being said, there are two elements that observers should focus on when viewing this exchange in the context of the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and the parade of Trump’s foreign policy failures.
The first is that, under Trump, the United States’ aura of indispensability has been absolutely shattered. The Russians know it. The Chinese know it. The Iranians know it. And America’s allies know it.
Trump has rendered the US irrelevant and much of the world view this moment an era to be suffered through. Trump’s closest allies can be played like a fiddle, and by this point the Ukrainians have no expectations for any serious American-led efforts to end the war. In 2022 and 2023 our decisions shaped the direction and outcome of the conflict. Now, we’re a sideshow that can be safely ignored by Kyiv and Moscow, as well as by other great and middle powers.
The second crucial element of this visit that observers should consider is how this display of doomed diplomacy fits in with the recent visit by CIA Director Ratcliffe to Moscow. Not only does the presence of Witkoff and Kushner soften the impact of whatever warning Ratcliffe delivered to Putin’s inner circle, but it also shows that the American government is divided in its own objectives and strategic vision for approaching Russia.
Voices like Ratcliffe and Rubio, who have historically been hawkish on Russia, must now contend with the short-sighted diplomatic initiatives of Trump’s son-in-law and a real estate investor. The Washington Post reported that Ratcliffe warned Russian officials that continuing the war could backfire and that Russia’s position would deteriorate further.
This isn’t a strategy for peace. It’s a recipe for chaos.

Nearly half of world’s migratory bird species in decline, report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:52:51 UTC
22:52:51 KST

Nearly half of the world’s migratory bird species are experiencing population declines, while one in nine is threatened with extinction, according to a global assessment released Friday.
BirdLife International’s State of the World’s Birds 2026 report found that 45% of the 1,843 migratory species assessed had declining global populations. Thirty percent were considered stable, 14% were increasing and the trends of the remaining 11% were unknown.
The sixth edition of the report, which focuses on migratory species and the routes they follow, combines BirdLife’s data with findings from broader scientific research.
It identified 200 migratory species, or 11%, as threatened with extinction. Of those, 32 were classified as critically endangered, 57 as endangered and 111 as vulnerable.
A further 111 species were listed as near threatened, meaning around 17% of all migratory birds are considered to be of significant conservation concern.
The report found particularly severe declines among birds that depend on marine and coastal wetlands. Some 54% of migratory shorebird species and 49% of migratory seabirds are declining, as are between 47% and 51% of species associated with marine habitats, forests and coastal wetlands.
The East Asian-Australasian Flyway had the highest proportion of declining species among the four major land-based flyway systems, at 53%. Half of the species using the world’s six marine flyways were also in decline.
Regional monitoring indicated that long-distance migratory birds traveling between Europe and Africa had declined by around 35% since 1980. In North America, 419 migratory species experienced a net loss of approximately 2.5 billion birds between 1970 and 2017, according to studies cited in the report.
Migratory shorebirds have been among the most severely affected. In North America, 26 of the 28 shorebird species monitored between 1980 and 2019 experienced declines, with more than half losing over 50% of their populations.
The slender-billed curlew, a migratory shorebird last reliably recorded in Morocco in 1995, has been declared extinct. Researchers described it as the first known global bird extinction of a species native to mainland Europe, North Africa and West Asia.
Worldwide, seven migratory bird species have been confirmed or are suspected to have become extinct over the past 150 years.
The assessment showed that the extinction risk facing migratory birds continues to increase. A total of 102 species moved into a higher-risk category because of a genuine deterioration in their status, compared with 34 that moved to a lower risk category following improvements.
Human activity was responsible for nearly all the principal pressures identified in the report. Invasive species and diseases affected 139 threatened migratory species, while agriculture and climate change each affected 103.
Hunting and trapping affected 99 threatened species, followed by pollution at 96, urban development at 71, human disturbance at 65, fisheries at 62, energy infrastructure at 55 and logging at 39.
“Migratory birds are sentinels, and their declines reveal growing pressure on the natural systems that sustain us,” said Stuart Butchart, BirdLife International’s chief scientist.
Butchart said coordinated conservation efforts had prevented extinctions and helped some populations recover, but action needed to be implemented across entire flyways rather than in individual countries.
Flyways are migration corridors connecting birds’ breeding, feeding and wintering grounds across countries and continents. The loss of a single important wetland, forest or coastal resting site can therefore affect populations across a species’ entire range.
The report called for stronger international cooperation to protect and restore habitats, prevent illegal killing, reduce seabird deaths caused by fishing, control invasive species and make agriculture, forestry and infrastructure safer for wildlife.
It warned that progress toward biodiversity targets adopted by 196 countries for 2030 remained “far too slow.”
The report was launched during the Global Flyways Summit in Nairobi, Kenya, where governments, conservation groups, scientists and financial institutions adopted the Nairobi Flyways Declaration, pledging greater cooperation along migratory routes.
The declaration was accompanied by plans involving the Asian Development Bank, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, and the World Bank to integrate flyway protection into development financing and mobilize about $6 billion for habitat conservation and restoration.

What Role Does Denuclearization Have in North Korea-US Dialogue Today?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:50:00 UTC
22:50:00 KST

With his surprise decision to scale back the recent Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercise on the Korean Peninsula, U.S. President Donald Trump clearly signaled his intent to rekindle dialogue with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. However, rather than receiving praise for the goodwill measure, the effort drew rebuke from the North Korean government, which reiterated its position that it has no interest in renewing engagement as long as the United States holds onto denuclearization as a policy objective.
This exchange has renewed debates over long-standing denuclearization policies, particularly as Trump continues his overtures toward the Kim regime in hopes of a possible meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in November. Some have argued it is time to abandon denuclearization as a policy goal and shift to arms control, while others contend that such a concession would undermine the global nonproliferation regime and place further stress on allied relationships.
Rather than a binary “should they, shouldn’t they” approach, the issue requires a more nuanced examination of the constraints and interests at play. For example, what does the Kim regime mean when it demands that foreign governments drop denuclearization as a precondition for talks? What does the Trump administration hope to achieve by renewing engagement? Further, would dropping denuclearization even be politically sustainable for this administration or other governments?
It’s useful to break down the denuclearization debate, examining the knowns and unknowns for the two sides.
Trump’s Overtures and North Korea’s Response
On August 16, Trump announced the shortening of the annual South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercise, reiterating his usual claim that the exercises are costly and adding that they “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea. He claimed that the Kim regime has been “unthreatening and respectful” during his presidency.
North Korea’s response came on August 19 in the form of a statement attributed to Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s high-ranking sister. The statement declared that Pyongyang regarded the reduction of exercises as “unworthy of comment” and has “no interest in it at all” due to “the nature of the military drill with a provocative and offensive feature.” North Korea followed that up two weeks later with another statement attributed to an unnamed Foreign Ministry spokesperson, noting “it is pointless to expect any détente in the region” as the “U.S. remains committed to the complete denuclearization of the DPRK” (an abbreviation of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea).
But this may be changing. In other contexts, the White House has demonstrated a willingness to abandon status quo policies and pursue rapprochement with authoritarian governments. As a result, the administration may consider shifting from denuclearization-first diplomacy to an approach that de-emphasizes denuclearization through arms control and risk reduction measures, or even eliminates it as a policy objective altogether.
The Knowns and Unknowns of North Korean Demands
The Kim regime has clearly set a precondition for renewed engagement with the United States: drop denuclearization from the agenda. What is less clear is what North Korea actually expects with this precondition.
Pyongyang’s rejections of denuclearization evolved following the brief period of diplomacy in 2018-19. After the failure of Kim Jong Un and Trump to reach an agreement at the February 2019 Hanoi Summit, Pyongyang hardened its stance against denuclearization. In December 2019, North Korean Ambassador to the United Nations Kim Song stated that “denuclearization is already gone out of the negotiation table.” Based on numerous statements since, North Korea’s position has become more absolute: denuclearization is not up for negotiation and Pyongyang has no intention to relinquish its nuclear arms.
Despite the hardline position, the Kim regime has not shut the door completely on potential engagement. North Korea has continued to highlight the “excellent” relationship between Kim Jong Un and Trump, referencing Kim’s “good memories and feelings” towards the U.S. president. Although positive inclinations in a personal relationship do not necessarily translate to rapprochement between governments, these are notable signals that may compel Washington to pursue status quo-changing pathways to engagement.
A challenge for Washington is that the scope of the required policy change is not yet clear. What specific actions would Pyongyang expect from Washington to signal the end of denuclearization? Does this mean a policy pronouncement, rescission of United Nations Security Council resolutions, or something else?
It is also unclear whether the Kim regime would be willing to offer concessions in return. There is no indication thus far of what may be negotiable with denuclearization off the agenda, whether it be arms control or other tradeoffs such as reducing North Korea’s military aid to Russia. This creates a risk: if the United States does give ground on denuclearization, Pyongyang could simply walk away from dialogue since it has already met one of its key policy objectives.
The U.S. Debate Over Denuclearization
On the U.S. side, there is a growing recognition that North Korea’s nuclear capability is now an established reality. Three decades of efforts to persuade Pyongyang to relinquish its nuclear weapons have not curbed the Kim regime’s ability to develop a nuclear weapons program of considerable scale and capability. Trump recently said North Korea has 57 warheads, while the South Korean Ministry of National Defense estimated it to be somewhere between 80 and 120.
From the outset, the United States’ goal has been to achieve a nuclear-free peninsula through diplomatic means. This has contributed to a substantial body of policies, sanctions, and international resolutions aimed at constraining and ultimately eliminating the North Korea nuclear program. Thus, there are significant legal and political considerations that affect the extent to which Washington can pursue alternate approaches.
One consideration is the global nonproliferation regime. A shift in U.S. policy would have ripple effects across the framework designed to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, including the Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference and the International Atomic Energy Agency. Experts have pointed out that abandoning denuclearization would signal a de facto acceptance of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state, and that risks not only undermining the Non-Proliferation Treaty but setting a precedent for other rogue states to pursue nuclear armament.
Also, the United States and the U.N. Security Council have imposed numerous rounds of sanctions on North Korea in response to its nuclear development and testing activities, in part to mitigate the increase in nuclear weapons while also deterring others from pursuing similar programs. A formal policy shift that accepted North Korea as a nuclear-armed state would raise questions about the status of existing sanctions and internationally agreed-upon resolutions. At the U.N. level, alterations to the North Korea sanctions program would require Security Council action, potentially requiring the modification or termination of existing resolutions that could easily be blocked by a veto from France, the United Kingdom, or any of the other five permanent members of the Security Council.
A second consideration is the response from U.S. allies. Most American allies and partners have established policies supporting a nuclear-free North Korea, so any unilateral U.S. decision will have cascading effects, forcing other governments either to adapt to a policy shift or oppose the U.S. approach. This will be particularly important for South Korea and Japan.
Although Seoul has already placed denuclearization as the last step of its “END” strategy (“Exchange, Normalization, Denuclearization”) it has not dropped it as a goal altogether. Meanwhile, Japan’s commitment to North Korea’s complete denuclearization remains a pillar of its security designs. A change would push Tokyo to assess how much policy space exists within its current framework to move closer to Washington’s or Seoul’s approach. It may be possible for the three to retain a formal commitment to denuclearization while also pursuing nuclear risk reduction and arms controls, but there will invariably be an impact to trilateral cooperation that requires close coordination.
Further, any pursuit of diplomatic engagement with North Korea without addressing the Kim regime’s ongoing support for Russia’s war effort against Ukraine will invariably face opposition from the United States’ European allies. These partners may withhold support outright unless the White House is willing to leverage issues related to the Russia-Ukraine War in pursuit of engagement with Pyongyang.
The third factor is domestic politics. While the Trump administration was able to move forward on controversial decisions in the first half of his term, the forthcoming midterm election could bring to power a Democratic-controlled Congress, which would attempt more restraint. Additionally, groups across the political spectrum are opposed to altering denuclearization policy, calling into question the sustainability of such a change. Notably, Trump cannot run for re-election; the coming change in presidential administration after 2028 could result in an outright policy reversal.
What This Tells Us About the Denuclearization Debate
These knowns and unknowns reveal a few key considerations for the denuclearization debate.
To start, it would be useful to canvas North Korea about what it actually means by dropping denuclearization as a policy objective. In other words, if the White House is seeking meaningful engagement, a starting point can be inquiring about the Kim regime’s expectations for moving forward past denuclearization. This can be communicated through direct lines of communication or signaled through talking points in the media.
It is also essential to identify the two sides’ goals if preconditions are met and talks happen. Right now, there is no clear indication of what the White House would be seeking to achieve through another summit between Trump and Kim Jong Un. Conversely, after more than 30 years of focusing on denuclearization, it is unclear what the Kim regime would be prepared to discuss in direct dialogue with the United States. Focused examinations and debates on these issues would be helpful in charting a course forward for any potential engagement.
Finally, it is necessary to determine how to translate goals into sustainable policy adjustments. The reality is that the U.S. and North Korea governments are different in nature, and while the Kim regime may be willing and able to institutionalize a permanent change to the status quo, conditions for a democratically-elected government are different. Unilaterally dropping denuclearization as a U.S. policy objective for a photo op will almost inevitably result in significant political pushback and challenges, both domestically and abroad.
Ultimately, the denuclearization debate must be resolved if dialogue with North Korea remains an objective. However, if the goal is to ensure that the dialogue actually produces meaningful outcomes, the debate will require more nuance and structure than currently exist. What would this policy shift mean in practice? Can the White House build an engagement strategy that is realistic enough to produce useful dialogue with North Korea, ambitious enough to reduce nuclear risks, and durable enough to overcome the inevitable obstacles along the way?
A clear understanding of both parties’ expectations and goals will be essential for coordinating with allies and multilateral agencies and institutionalizing any agreements to safeguard against collapse.

Russian assets are not the focus now, Brussels says as calls for action grow louder

2026-09-11

22:49:43 KST

The European Commission is not willing to reopen the contentious debate on the immbolised Russian assets, at least not without a guarantee of success. "Now, the focus is somewhere else," the executive insists.
The immobilised assets from the Russian Central Bank are not "the primary focus" at the moment, the European Commission said on Friday amid growing calls to channel the €210 billion into additional support for cash-strapped Ukraine.
Sweden, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain, backed by the Baltics, have asked the executive to devise new legal options to tap the assets.
Ukraine has endorsed the initiative and pitched creating an EU-owned custodian to hold the assets kept at Euroclear, a depository in central Brussels.
And this week, a cross-party group of 122 members of the European Parliament sent a letter to the Commission, pleading to "reopen the political discussion" on the assets and advance the custodian pitch to "overcome" the Belgian objections.
But on Friday, the Commission sought to tamp down the momentum.
"That's not the primary focus," Paula Pinho, the Commission's chief spokesperson, said. "We had worked extensively on this, and now the focus is somewhere else."
The Commission's priority, Pinho explained, is twofold.
On the one hand, to continue the gradual disbursements of the €90 billion loan, which covers financial and military assistance for Ukraine.
On the other hand, to engage with the Ukrainian government and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to figure out the exact scope of the budget shortfall.
Last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy caught allies off guard when he asked them to plug a $27 billion (€23 billion) deficit in the Ministry of Defence. Kyiv has also flagged €32.6 billion in uncovered budget needs for next year.
Since then, EU and IMF officials have been scrambling to understand the nature and the origin of the eye-popping number.
Zelenskyy's request laid bare the enormous task that Europe faces in helping a country under invasion without US contributions. It also helped revive the push to tap into the Russian assets, which supporters say would spare European taxpayers.
The Commission tried to use the assets last year through an inventive, multi-layered legal proposal that fell apart in December at a make-or-break summit. The executive, which invested a great deal of political capital defending the scheme, met furious resistance from Belgium and strong reservations from Euroclear.
"We left it in December at a very important discussion at the European Council. We never said that it was out of the table. It remains there as a tool," Pinho said.
The Commission, she added, needs to gauge Ukraine's additional financial needs "before we can speak of concrete possible tools to address them".
Separately, Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told Euronews that his services were ready to "re-engage" on the assets and "help find a way forward".
But he stopped short of committing to a new legal text, noting the Commission would wait for guarantees that an "agreement can be reached among member states".
Belgium has already said its objections had not "magically disappeared". Meanwhile, Euroclear is battling a legal challenge from the Russian Central Bank.

French ESA astronaut Thomas Pesquet: Europe must 'maximise scientific return' from ISS before closure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:49:40 UTC
22:49:40 KST

The French astronaut urged Europe and his home country to "maximise the scientific return" from the European Space Agency's next mission to the International Space Station, while stressing the importance of spaceflight for Europe’s strategic sovereignty in space.
French astronaut Thomas Pesquet told Euronews that Europe and France must "maximise the scientific return" from ESA's next private mission aboard PAM-6 to the International Space Station (ISS), which he will lead in summer 2027.
Speaking to Euronews at the International Space Summit held in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday, Pesquet said "we know the ISS is coming to an end soon and we don't know when Europe and specifically France's next turn, will come again, given that long-term missions to the ISS are assigned on a rotating basis."
The ISS is scheduled to retire and be deorbited in 2030 due to its ageing hardware and maintenance issues, as well as the space sector's shift towards commercial activities.
Russia and the US launched the first segments in late 1998, and astronauts moved in two years later. Europe and Japan added their own modules, and Canada provided robotic arms.
Pesquet is part of the European Space Agency's (ESA) Astronaut Corps, which selects, trains, and provides crew members for US and Russian space missions.
The International Space Summit — co-hosted by France and Germany — gathered space industry leaders, heads of state and astronauts to call for greater European sovereignty and investment in the space sector.
At present, ESA does not have its own operational crewed spacecraft or crewed launcher.
For Pesquet, the move towards greater European space sovereignty is a step in the right direction, given that consistent partnerships on the world stage have become a "challenge".
"Given the upheavals in the geopolitical landscape, without getting into the details, it’s clear that it’s difficult to rely on long term partners, consistency has become a rare commodity on the international stage. We believe we must first do things ourselves first."
"That is something that will not change in coming years," he added.
Europe's push to build up its military space assets has been driven by Russia's war in Ukraine, as well as a decision to distance itself from its longstanding dependence on the US in the space domain.
Kyiv's reliance on Elon Musk's Starlink has shown the strategic importance of space services in war, given that satellite networks can provide connectivity even when infrastructure is damaged or destroyed.
"Going forward, maybe there will be more small stations rather than one large station — a European station. I’d really like to see American, Indian, and Chinese stations. We’re also preparing for that world, which is coming very quickly," said Pesquet.
Despite this, he assured that once astronauts lift off, geopolitics down on Earth usually get left behind. A single space crew can include astronauts and cosmonauts from several agencies — from Europe's ESA, Russia's Roscosmos and the United States' NASA.
"I remember the early days of my career, around 2011, when we already tended to focus on the things we had in common, on the very things that brought us together — rather than talking about the things that divided us."
"When you’re part of a crew — on a boat, in a plane, or in a submarine, it's part of collective intelligence, so we keep this attitude. Obviously, relations between organisations aren't always easy. But at least at our level we don’t want that to affect our work, we don’t want it to affect safety, so we maintain healthy relationships."
Europe 'needs' a new space strategy
ESA significantly increased its funding in November 2025, approving a record-breaking €22.3 billion budget for 2026–2028, with €35 billion for space for security and defence.
For Géraldine Naja, director of space transportation at ESA, Europe has "understood" that it needs a change of strategy after typically investing far less than the US and China in space.
"If you compare GNP and the number of people, we are spending six times less than the US," she said.
For Naja, the successful launch of the first commercial rocket — Spectrum — to orbit from mainland Europe by German startup Isar Aerospace on Saturday marked a significant step in the right direction.
"Spectrum is a rocket built and developed by Isar Aerospace, which was incubated in Bavaria, which benefited from several ESA programmes that aim to support new companies and help them commercialise their products."
"Space is very important to defence because the technologies are different and also we have now realised that space tools are absolutely necessary for any defence policy."
"When you look at what is going around us, unfortunately, most of the weapons require communication, navigational tools, which can only be provided by space. Space itself can become a theatre for war," she said.

Houthis seize key Yemen port and island near global shipping route
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
16:47:25 EEST
22:47:25 KST

Yemen’s Houthi movement has reached Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea after seizing the port of Mocha, extending an offensive that has brought its forces to one of the main shipping routes between Asia and Europe.
Four Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Friday that Houthi forces had reached Perim, also known as Mayyun, which lies inside the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Two government sources said Saudi-backed forces had withdrawn from the island. The Houthis also took Dhubab, a coastal town facing Perim, according to the sources.
The reported advance came a day after the Iran-aligned movement captured Mocha, about 75km north of the strait.
The offensive has changed control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast within days and placed Houthi forces near a maritime route whose role in energy exports has increased since the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Bab al-Mandab connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean. Ships travelling between Asia and Europe use the passage to reach the Suez Canal.
Perim sits inside the strait and divides the waterway into two channels. A Yemeni government official told AFP that boats carrying Houthi fighters reached the island after government forces withdrew.
The Houthis have said international commercial shipping faces no threat from their forces, while maintaining threats against Saudi-linked vessels.
The development carries added consequences for Saudi Arabia. The kingdom has shifted crude exports towards its Red Sea coast since the US-Israeli war against Iran disrupted the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia earlier diverted as much as 70 per cent of its crude exports from the Gulf through its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the BBC reported.
Oil prices were heading towards a weekly close above $100 a barrel.
The International Energy Agency said Saudi crude supply fell by 2.3 million barrels a day in August to about six million barrels a day, its lowest level in more than three decades. Saudi figures reported through OPEC put August production at 6.24 million barrels a day, compared with 8.14 million in July.
Attention has also turned to the East-West pipeline.
Satellite images from the European Space Agency showed black smoke near a pumping station south of Medina on Thursday. Saudi authorities and Saudi Aramco had not confirmed an incident.
The Houthi offensive began on 3 September and advanced through western Taiz, southern Hodeidah and the Mocha area. Government-aligned National Resistance forces later withdrew from positions around Mocha, clearing the way for the Houthis to take the city.
Yemeni government forces have signalled plans for a counter-offensive. Military spokesman Majed al-Nazili called on civilians to avoid the road between Taiz and Mocha and stay away from Houthi military equipment.
Axios reported, citing two US officials, that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked US President Donald Trump during two calls on Thursday to order strikes against the Houthis. Trump rejected the request, according to Axios.
The military offensive has also driven another wave of displacement in a country where more than a decade of war has forced millions from their homes.
At least 46,000 people have fled since fighting intensified last week, the International Organization for Migration said on Friday.
“Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left,” IOM Director General Amy Pope said.
The latest displacement includes families leaving areas around Mocha, Taiz and Hodeidah.
Mocha also carries a place in the history of international trade. The port became a centre of the coffee trade under Ottoman rule, exporting Yemeni beans through the Red Sea to Egypt and European merchants. The word “mocha” derives from the city’s name.
Its role in the present conflict rests instead on its position near Bab al-Mandab and the supply routes connecting government-held territory along Yemen’s southwest coast.

BRICS 2026: India charts its own course between Russia and the West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:46:30 UTC
22:46:30 KST

BRICS 2026: India charts its own course between Russia and the West
The 18th BRICS Summit, opening in New Delhi on Friday, will test not only the geopolitical resilience of the largest grouping in the non-Western world, but also the maturity of Indian diplomacy.
India has set itself an extraordinarily difficult task of trying to pour the oil of reconciliation onto the increasingly stormy waters of world politics.
The theme of its 2026 BRICS presidency, “Building for Sustainability, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainable Development,” might sound hopelessly optimistic as the Ukraine conflict and sanctions against Russia continue, the US and Iran remain locked in confrontation, Western pressure on China is growing, Africa and Latin America face what BRICS countries regard as neo-colonial practices, and while trade and technology wars are multiplying.
Against such a background, talk of innovation and sustainable development can seem detached from reality, yet this is precisely where India sees a role for itself; as divisions between rival centers of power deepen, New Delhi is attempting the diplomatic equivalent of walking a tightrope. It believes its longstanding principle of “strategic autonomy” will allow it not merely to keep its balance, but to make a wider contribution to international stability.
That approach is central to understanding India’s BRICS presidency, given that among the BRICS states, India occupies a unique position. It maintains strategic partnerships with the United States and Western European countries whose policies increasingly seek to contain Russia and China, while, at the same time, New Delhi has refused Western demands to distance itself from Moscow.
India consequently doesn’t regard BRICS as an anti-Western alliance. For sure it sees the grouping as non-Western, but not inherently antagonistic towards the West, and this leaves New Delhi caught between two fires.
Some within BRICS may accuse India of being insufficiently willing to confront the West, while Western governments repeatedly criticize India for maintaining close relations with Russia, often invoking its status as the world’s largest democracy.
Shortly before the summit, Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar offered a characteristically pointed defense of this strategic autonomy at an international forum in Finland.
Asked by a British moderator whether cooperation with Russia was immoral, Jaishankar replied that no European country had ever been attacked with Indian weapons, while European weapons had been used against India.
The exchange neatly captured New Delhi’s position as India has no intention of allowing either side to dictate its foreign policy.
Being caught between two fires is rarely comfortable, but India’s strategy isn’t simply to avoid getting burnt; instead, it intends to draw warmth from both while retaining the freedom to choose its own course.
That is both the risk and the ambition behind India’s BRICS presidency.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was translated and edited by the RT team.

13:45:36 UTC
22:45:36 KST

A renewed attempt to legalise assisted dying has been voted down by MPs in a decision that is likely to scupper the idea for a political generation, sparking anger among supporters after an earlier bill was blocked by the Lords.
A private member’s bill put forward by Labour’s Lauren Edwards, which would have permitted assisted dying in England and Wales in certain limited circumstances, was defeated by 286 to 270 at second reading, the first chance MPs have to vote on a measure.
After the decision some MPs cheered and hugged in the Commons chamber, while anti-assisted dying activists celebrated in Parliament Square. But supporters of the measure said a public which, according to polling, generally supports the idea would be baffled by the inability of politicians to enact it.
An earlier private member’s bill to permit assisted dying, spearheaded by another Labour MP, Kim Leadbeater, was approved by MPs in the last parliamentary session but ran out of parliamentary time in April after a handful of peers thwarted it in the Lords, tabling hundreds of amendments.
In a statement after the vote, Edwards said voters wanted change and “will not understand why that couldn’t happen because a minority in the House of Lords used procedural devices to block it and MPs balked at insisting that they do their job”.
She added: “Assisted dying will come in this country, as it is already doing all across the world, but not soon enough. Parliament has dropped the ball today. It will be picked up again, as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand.”
Leadbeater said she felt “really sad”, adding: “I feel really disappointed – not for me but for the many people who’ve campaigned on this issue long before I came along and the terminally ill people who are quite simply asking for choice, asking for compassion, asking for dignity in their dying days.”
A number of MPs and peers were “deeply upset” at events and would attempt to bring the issue back, she predicted, while saying she did not know when this would be.
In another statement after the vote, three Labour MPs who voted against the plan, Ashley Dalton, Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, insisted their decision was purely based on practicalities.
They said: “MPs have voted against this bill because it wasn’t an abstract debate but a decision about a real bill that was unsafe and unworkable. But this is not a moment for celebration. We understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law.
“But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill.”
Much of the other reaction was split along more entrenched lines, with John Sherrington, the Catholic archbishop of Liverpool, thanking MPs for the vote.
In contrast, Andrew Copson, the chief executive of Humanists UK, said: “This vote provides not one extra penny for palliative care or disability support. On the contrary, it makes it less likely. And terminally ill people will still suffer, travel to Switzerland, and take their own lives in increasing numbers, while today’s inequalities continue.”
Friday’s debate before the vote saw some emotionally charged speeches, including from Dalton, who needs lifelong treament for terminal metastatic breast cancer. She argued that the bill did not adequately protect people with treatable depression who also had a terminal illness.
Another Labour MP, Claire Hazelgrove, who supported the bill, said her mother chose to end her life aged 61 while suffering a late-stage terminal illness. Hazelgrove said: “She had access to good palliative care, but what we learned, the hardest of ways, is that not all pain can be palliated. I will never forget seeing her writhing and screaming in pain at points for weeks.”
With many of the arguments for and against the bill being repeats of those made when Leadbeater’s version was approved, the defeat appeared to be a product in part of less motivation among supporters of the plan.
Leadbeater’s bill was backed by 330 votes to 275 on its second reading, and by 313 to 291 at the third reading. Friday’s result thus saw the totals for both sides falling, but with a greater drop-off among supporters.
Some MPs had said they were lobbied notably less by pro-assisted dying campaigners this time than with Leadbeater’s bill.
There was also a more sceptical view of the issue from Andy Burnham’s Downing Street than there had been under Keir Starmer.
With Burnham and his ministers staying officially neutral in what was seen as a matter of conscience, the prime minister announced he would not vote on the bill – his predecessor voted in favour – and said he believed the debate on assisted dying should be paused until social care was improved.
Another factor was the possibility of using the Parliament Act to force the bill through the Lords if peers tried to stop it again, under provisions that prevent the upper house from indefinitely blocking measures backed by MPs. This idea had brought concerns from some MPs.
Closing Friday’s debate, the health minister Alison McGovern said the government would enact the plan if it became law, but reiterated concerns about social care. She said: “In my opinion, social care has been ignored for far too long, both the 1.5 million people, mainly women, who work in it, and the families who need it, and we heard that across the house today.”

Diplomatic tensions between Algeria and UAE: The new reality of a stormy relationship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:44:25 UTC
22:44:25 KST

Abdennour Toumi is a Senior Consultant at Middle East & Africa Strategic Institute (MEA).
For five decades, relations between Algeria and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) evolved from cautious diplomatic cooperation into a broad economic partnership. Nowadays, that relationship has entered a fundamentally different phase. The deterioration of Algiers-Abu Dhabi relations is not simply the product of a bilateral dispute. It reflects a broader struggle over competing visions of a new regional order in North Africa, the African Sahel, and the wider Middle East. Algeria's foreign-policy doctrine remains anchored in sovereignty, non-interference, territorial integrity, self-determination, and the preservation of state institutions.
The foundations of Algerian-Emirati relations were laid shortly after the establishment of the United Arab Emirates in 1971. During the 1970s and 1980s, political relations benefited from high-level contacts. These exchanges created a framework for political dialogue at a time when both countries sought to consolidate their respective positions in the Arab and African worlds.
The relationship acquired a stronger economic dimension during the 2000s under the late Algerian President Abdelaziz Bouteflika. Emirati companies became increasingly visible in Algeria's infrastructure and commercial sectors. For a period, economic engagement provided a useful buffer against political differences. But that buffer gradually weakened as the strategic environments of the two countries began to diverge.
The UAE's decision to establish diplomatic relations with Israel fundamentally altered its position within the regional political landscape. Algeria, however, has consistently rejected normalization with Israel and has maintained a strong political commitment to the Palestinian cause. The same period witnessed a series of developments that transformed the Maghreb's geopolitical environment. The United States recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in December 2020, while France and Spain subsequently adopted positions viewed in Algiers as increasingly favorable to Rabat.
For Algeria, Western Sahara is not merely a dispute between two neighboring states. It is closely connected to its conception of self-determination, regional balance, and national security. Algeria's decision to sever diplomatic relations with Morocco in August 2021 was a clear example of this dynamic. Algeria's strategic culture is deeply influenced by the experience of colonialism and by the belief that the fragmentation of neighboring states can ultimately threaten its national security.
Yet, the convergence between Abu Dhabi and Rabat, particularly in the context of Morocco's expanding relations with Israel, has reinforced Algerian perceptions that a broader strategic alignment is emerging across its western, eastern, and southern security environments. For Algiers, the concern is therefore less about the UAE itself than about the emergence of a network of actors and policies that it views as disruptive and potentially capable of generating destabilizing effects, while obstructing Algeria’s strategic objectives in a sub-region that it considers vital to its humanitarian, stability, and development diplomacy.
The UAE has adopted a considerably more interventionist regional posture. In Libya, Abu Dhabi became a major supporter of Khalifa Haftar and the Libyan National Army during the country's conflict. In Sudan, the UAE has repeatedly faced allegations of supporting the Rapid Support Forces during the country's devastating civil war. Abu Dhabi has denied allegations of providing military support to the RSF.
Whatever the validity of individual accusations, the strategic perception in Algiers is important. Algeria increasingly sees the UAE as a regional actor willing to seed influence through political, economic, and security networks beyond its immediate borders. In January 2024, Algeria's High Security Council expressed concern about what it described as "hostile behavior" originating from a "brotherly Arab country," widely interpreted in Algerian political and media circles as a reference to the UAE. In March, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune referred to Emirati financial interests in several regional conflict zones, including Mali, Libya, and Sudan.
The most consequential development came when the dispute began moving from the regional arena toward Algeria's domestic political space. In February 2026, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune stated that an unnamed Arab country attempted to interfere in Algeria's presidential elections and described that country as a “pseudo-state.” Algerian media widely interpreted the remarks as a reference to the UAE.
The same month, Algeria reportedly initiated procedures aimed at terminating an air transport agreement with the UAE signed in Abu Dhabi in 2013. Taken together, these developments suggested that the dispute was no longer confined to diplomatic disagreements over Libya, Sudan, Palestine, or Western Sahara. Bilateral tensions were beginning to affect practical cooperation and, more importantly, to become a national-security concern for Algeria.
The country shares over 3,200 kilometers of borders with Mali, Niger, and Libya. These are not distant geopolitical theaters for Algiers; they constitute Algeria's immediate security environment. For decades, Algerian diplomacy has sought to prevent instability in the African Sahel and North Africa from spilling across its borders. Algiers has frequently favored mediation, political reconciliation, and engagement with local actors rather than political interference or direct military intervention. This approach has gradually become part of a broader foreign-policy doctrine centered on stability and development. The UAE's growing influence in Libya and its relationships with political and security actors in the African Sahel therefore carry implications that extend beyond traditional diplomacy.
Algeria has historically considered the region part of its important geo-strategic depth. Instability in Mali, Niger, Libya, and the wider African Sahel directly affects Algeria through terrorism, arms trafficking, migration, organized crime, and political instability. The political upheavals that have transformed the region in recent years have complicated Algeria's traditional diplomatic and military approach. Military coups, changes in the regional dynamics and balance, the emergence of new security partnerships, and competition among external regional powers have created an increasingly fragmented geopolitical environment.
In response, Algeria has sought to strengthen its relations with neighboring states, including Tunisia, Mauritania, Mali, and Niger, while reinforcing its border-security posture. It has increased military cooperation and training with those countries. Military allocations for 2025 reportedly reached the equivalent of approximately €23.8 billion, representing a substantial increase compared with 2022 and roughly one-fifth of the national budget.
For Algeria, military preparedness is increasingly linked to diplomatic credibility. A state surrounded by unstable neighbors and competing regional powers cannot rely exclusively on political reconciliation and mediation. The reported failed coup attempt in Niger on Aug. 28, 2026, has added another layer to an already volatile regional environment. Algeria has long regarded political instability in the Sahel as a potential security threat to its southern borders and national security.
In 2023, Algeria exported approximately $10.7 million worth of goods to the UAE. The relatively modest scale of bilateral trade, compared with the strategic importance of the relationship, illustrates the limits of economic interdependence as a mechanism for preventing political confrontation.
The Algeria-UAE relations have crossed an important threshold. The central question is no longer whether Algeria and the UAE have disagreements, which they clearly do. The million-dollar question is whether their competing regional strategies can coexist without producing a permanent strategic confrontation.
In sum, the deterioration of Algeria-UAE relations should therefore not be seen simply as another episode of intra-Arab diplomatic rivalry. It is part of a larger restructuring of power in North Africa and the African Sahel. Algeria today is a major North African rising state with substantial military and economic capabilities, extensive borders, and deep influence in the African Sahel, leading through diplomatic example.

Russia has sustained its one and a half millionth military casualty since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with half a million of those confirmed dead, the Chief of the Defence Staff has said.
Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton said the figure, drawn from Ukrainian General Staff data published on Wednesday, marks a grim milestone highlighting the vast cost and enormous impact of what he called President Putin’s frankly flawed decision to invade.
The proportion killed was confirmed by defence intelligence. “Amongst that one and a half million, defence intelligence have confirmed that 500,000, that is half a million, are dead,” he said.
What that number represents was something he chose to spell out, saying “That means half a million photographs hanging on the walls in devastated, darkened homes around Russia. That means half a million families who will never see their father, their son, their brother, or husband again.”
Of the one and a half million, 1.4 million have been sustained since January 2023 in order to gain just two per cent of Ukraine’s territory.
“I think these numbers illustrate clearly the senseless and futile waste of human life for such little progress, and against such an illegitimate aim of President Putin,” he said.
The Chief of the Defence Staff was careful to separate the Russian state from the Russian population, echoing the Defence Secretary’s statement to the Commons the previous day that Britain has no quarrel with the Russian people. He could not echo those comments more loudly, he said. The purpose was to highlight the cost to Russia and its people of Putin’s decisions, “but we by no means celebrate those costs”.
He named the people bearing them, saying Britain is no more keen to see the Russian population continue to carry the cost of the war than “the beleaguered Belgorod small business owner, or the petrified recruit press gangs in St Petersburg, or the terrified Muscovite family seeing their parent, partner, or child rushed to the front line”.
Putin could end the illegal war tomorrow and stop the killing, he said, and for as long as he continues to fight, Britain will stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine, as the Prime Minister and the Defence Secretary have both said.

Russia ‘open to working with the whole world’ – Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:42:01 UTC
22:42:01 KST

Russia ‘open to working with the whole world’ – Putin
Russia is open to cooperation and doing business with “the whole world,” President Vladimir Putin has said. This includes both Western economic powers – despite what he described as their “ugly forms of competition” – and the growing economies of the Global South and East. 
“We are ready to cooperate with all our partners,” Putin told the BRICS Business Forum panel at the 18th BRICS summit in India, adding that they could be “old or new.”
Putin said that the shared goal is to unlock the development potential of Russia and its partners through “business diplomacy,” making it easier for companies and entrepreneurs to cooperate.
“We do not want to impose any restrictions on ourselves or turn inward – whether at the national, corporate, or even the broader level of our partnership,” he stated. “We are not building our cooperation against anyone. We stand for ourselves and our interests.”
Russia is seeking to expand practical business cooperation with its partners in industry, trade, and tourism, Putin said, noting that Moscow has established a national business cooperation committee bringing together more than 40 of the country’s largest companies.
He also highlighted plans to develop major logistics routes, such as the Trans-Arctic and North-South transport corridors, and proposed creating a new investment platform based on the BRICS New Development Bank to attract private capital and boost competitiveness.
“Together with our partners, we stand ready to contribute to global energy and food security,” Putin said.
Putin noted that the world is undergoing “deep structural shifts,” with traditional economic powers being displaced by new engines of growth – a natural process that he insisted “cannot be stopped.” He argued, however, that Western economies facing growing competition increasingly resort to unsavory methods.
“Sometimes competition takes ugly forms,” he said, citing the destruction of pipelines, attempts to block international transport routes, unilateral “illegal restrictions,” and secondary sanctions against countries “unwilling to follow others’ interests.”
Russia has faced more than 30,000 sanctions since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict – twice as many as all other countries combined, Putin said. Moscow nevertheless weathered the unprecedented pressure by relying on domestic business, science, and engineering while redirecting trade toward “reliable partners,” he stated. Russia’s economy has become more resilient, with growth outpacing the global average over the past three years, he added.
The president noted that against expectations the sanctions had instead hurt those imposing them, pointing to rising budget deficits, public debt, and industrial decline. Leading eurozone economies have seen industrial output fall by around 8% in recent years, he claimed.
Speaking of BRICS, Putin described the group as an increasingly powerful force in the global economy.
“Through our combined efforts, BRICS is building a resilient and viable platform for global growth,” he said. “This is not being imposed on us from the outside by the so-called ‘golden billion’, nor are we trying to impose anything on anyone else.”
Putin noted that BRICS countries generated more than 40% of global GDP over the past five years, compared with 29% for the G7, while contributing more than half of global economic growth against just 18% for the G7. He attributed the momentum to the grouping’s vast population, dynamic domestic markets, and rapidly expanding national companies with global ambitions.
The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi runs through Sunday, bringing together leaders of the expanded grouping to discuss economic cooperation, energy and food security, global governance, and geopolitical challenges. Putin, who arrived in India on Friday, has already held talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the gathering. He is also expected to hold talks with other leaders attending the gathering.

Giant armored crustaceans survive thanks to a gene stolen from bacteria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:41:14 UTC
22:41:14 KST

When scientists refer to the deep sea as Earth’s most alien environment, they’re not exaggerating. Among the cast of bizarre characters are enormous armor-covered crustaceans with large triangular compound eyes and long antennae. Researchers have long wondered how these strange creatures pull off one extreme feat: surviving more than five years without food.
It turns out that millions of years ago these deep-sea isopods most likely co-opted a gene from bacteria that—paired with a large stomach—lets them gorge on rare meals and slow their metabolism to endure long-term starvation in the ocean depths. “This is surprising because bacteria and animals are very different, and such [gene] transfers are rare,” says Jianbo Yuan, a marine biologist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Oceanology and co-author on the new research published in Cell.
Giant marine isopods, which are related to garden pill bugs, live across a wide range of ocean depths, from a comparatively shallow 170 meters to the deep, dark sea around 2,100 meters down, where food and light are scarce. Some deep-sea isopods are supergiant, reaching up to half a meter in length. To understand what separates the deep-sea species from their shallower cousins, the researchers sequenced full genomes from specimens found at 300 and 800 meters and compared their energy demands, enzyme activity and oxygen use.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
They found a key gene called ND1 expressed much more strongly in the deep-sea isopods that looked more like a gene found in bacteria than in an animal: it lacked filler genetic segments called introns and produced very tiny proteins, both signs of a bacterial gene. The researchers theorize that more than 16 million years ago genes from bacteria living in an isopod’s stomach may have been incorporated into its genome in a way that was then passed along to future generations.
The many copies now in deep-sea isopods’ genomes seem to slow down energy production when the creatures are in cold conditions. Inserting the gene into zebra fish, nematode worms and human cells, the researchers found, lowered those organisms’ metabolic rates, too.
The finding “opens a completely new window to study the evolution of deep-sea gigantism and the role of microbiome in deep-sea adaptation,” says Torben Riehl, a marine biologist at the Senckenberg Ocean Species Alliance in Frankfurt, Germany, who was not involved in the study. Deep-sea ecosystems cover more than 50 percent of Earth’s surface and are vital to the planet—so every little bit we learn, Riehl adds, may help us understand the benefits these ecosystems provide and how to preserve them.

'High in protein' – marketing trick or healthy nutrition trend? New study reveals what Latvian consumers really think  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:39:48 UTC
22:39:48 KST

Products labelled “high in protein” have become one of the fastest-growing and most widely discussed food categories in recent years. But is this simply an effective marketing approach, or a well-founded healthy nutrition trend? A sociological survey commissioned by “Agrova Baltics”, part of the European agri-food group “Agrova”, and its functional egg protein brand “Fiteg²” reveals an interesting contradiction: while 72% of Latvia’s population understand what the “high in protein” label means, only 6% know precisely how much protein they need to consume as part of their daily diet. The study’s findings and their significance in the context of dietary habits are commented on by Olga Stepanova, creator of “Fiteg²” products and R&D expert at “Agrova”.
Protein popularity is growing faster than knowledge about it
The study shows that only 6% of respondents know precisely how much protein they need to consume daily. Another 31% believe they have an approximate understanding, while 62% of Latvia’s population overall do not have a clear idea of how much protein their bodies require. Of these, 38% admit that they do not know at all, while 24% say they have heard about the topic but cannot name a specific amount.
Knowledge also differs significantly across age groups – younger respondents are generally better informed, while older people are considerably more likely to admit that they do not know how much protein they should consume on a daily basis.
“The study clearly shows that ‘high in protein’ is not simply a marketing trick. It is a trend that reflects people’s growing interest in a balanced diet and higher-quality food products. At the same time, however, we can see that knowledge about the role of protein in the diet does not always keep pace with this interest. Many people still do not know how much protein they actually need or how to incorporate enough of it into their daily diet,” says O. Stepanova.
Protein products are not just for athletes
While 72% of respondents know that the “high in protein” label indicates a higher protein content than in similar products, some misconceptions about the purpose of these products still persist.
Some 12% of respondents cannot explain what the label means, while another 11% believe that such products are primarily intended for athletes.
O. Stepanova emphasises: “Protein is not only needed by professional athletes or people who regularly work out at the gym. It is one of the most important nutrients for everyone – children during periods of growth, adults with active lifestyles, seniors seeking to maintain muscle mass, people recovering from illness, and anyone who wants to maintain a balanced diet. Our task is to challenge the stereotype that protein products are intended only for a narrow audience.”
The “high in protein” label is no longer enough
The study shows that consumers are becoming increasingly demanding. When choosing protein products, people consider not only the amount of protein, but also the product’s ingredients, taste and price. This demonstrates that consumers are looking not for bold marketing claims, but for products that naturally fit into a healthy everyday diet.
“Being labelled ‘high in protein’ does not, in itself, make a product healthy. It is important to consider the overall composition – the source of protein, as well as the amount of sugar, fat and salt, and the product’s place within a balanced diet. This is also the approach we follow when developing the “Fiteg²” product range. Our goal is not to create products only for athletes, but to offer functional egg protein products to anyone who wants to easily supplement their diet with high-quality protein. The “Fiteg²” range currently includes egg protein powders and egg white protein bars, and we continue to expand the product range as we see that interest in functional nutrition in Latvia continues to grow,” says O. Stepanova.
About “Agrova”
“Agrova” is a European agri-food brand and group whose principal shareholder is “Agrova International”. The group specialises in egg production and processing, as well as the development of egg products and functional nutrition products. The “Agrova” group was established in Riga, Latvia, in 2025 by entrepreneur Jurijs Adamovičs with the ambition of building a globally competitive egg and egg products production platform rooted in Latvia’s agricultural excellence, science and responsible practices throughout the value chain. Today, Agrova operates production facilities in Latvia and the United Kingdom, providing sustainable supply to retail chains, the foodservice sector and food industry companies across Europe.

Real Estate and Continuity Planning for Companies in Latvia  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:39:28 UTC
22:39:28 KST

For companies in Latvia, real estate can be much more than a place where employees work. Offices, warehouses, production facilities and retail premises often support essential business processes, making their availability closely connected with operational continuity. A property-related problem can therefore affect employees, customers, inventory and delivery schedules at the same time.
When a company plans to purchase or develop premises, financing should be considered alongside long-term business needs. Commercial real estate financing can form part of that planning, but the appropriate structure depends on the company's financial position, property type, intended use and broader investment plans. Comparing available options and reviewing the associated obligations can help management understand how a property purchase would fit into the company's finances.
Property decisions should follow the business strategy
Before committing to a commercial property, companies can assess how the premises will serve their operations over the coming years. A growing logistics business may need additional storage capacity, while a professional services company may prioritize office location and accessibility. Manufacturing businesses, meanwhile, may have specific requirements concerning utilities, loading areas, equipment and regulatory compliance.
Location is another practical consideration. Access to transport routes, proximity to customers and suppliers, availability of employees and local infrastructure can all influence the usefulness of a property. A building that appears suitable at the time of purchase may become less practical if the company's activities or workforce change significantly.
Financing is only one part of the investment calculation
The purchase price does not represent the full financial picture. Companies should also account for maintenance, utilities, taxes, renovation, equipment, security and other ongoing costs associated with owning or operating commercial premises.
Cash-flow planning is particularly relevant when property financing is involved. Management should consider how regular financial commitments would interact with seasonal revenue fluctuations, planned investments and unexpected expenses. Reviewing several financing structures can provide a clearer picture of the available alternatives without assuming that one approach will suit every business.
Commercial property needs protection beyond physical security
Security systems, maintenance schedules and access controls can reduce certain operational risks, but they cannot eliminate every possibility of loss. Fire, water damage, severe weather, theft and other unexpected events can disrupt the use of business premises and damage property or equipment.
Commercial property insurance can be considered as part of a broader risk-management strategy. The relevant cover depends on the property, its use and the risks identified by the company. Before selecting a policy, it is sensible to review the scope of cover, exclusions, deductibles and claims procedures rather than focusing solely on the premium.
Companies should also check whether the chosen arrangement reflects the actual value and contents of the premises. Changes such as renovations, new equipment or expansion may alter the company's risk profile and create a reason to review existing arrangements.
Business continuity starts before an incident occurs
A continuity plan does not need to be complicated to be useful. Companies can identify essential functions, determine which premises or equipment are critical, and establish alternative arrangements if access to a building becomes temporarily impossible.
For example, an office-based business may need procedures for remote work, while a warehouse operator could require alternative storage capacity. Contact lists, supplier information, backup systems and clearly assigned responsibilities can also make decision-making easier when normal operations are disrupted.
Regular reviews keep plans aligned with reality
Real estate and continuity planning should not be treated as a one-time exercise. Business models evolve, property values change, new equipment is introduced, and operational dependencies can emerge over time. Each of these developments may affect both financing requirements and the company's exposure to property-related risks.
Before making a new commitment or renewing existing arrangements, companies can compare available financing and insurance options and examine their conditions carefully. A periodic review helps ensure that property decisions, financial obligations and risk-management measures remain aligned with the company's actual operations and longer-term plans.

Can India Exploit China’s ‘Malacca Dilemma’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:39:00 UTC
22:39:00 KST

India faces one of the most challenging security environments in the world, confronting not one but two adversarial neighbors: Pakistan and China. While New Delhi retains the conventional military upper hand over Islamabad, in Beijing it confronts a militarily and economically superior power that has repeatedly used force to alter the status quo along their disputed border.
Since the 1962 border war, India and China have faced a series of military confrontations, including the 2017 Doklam standoff and the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020. More recently, Beijing reportedly provided Islamabad with critical intelligence support during the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, raising the likelihood that any future Indo-Pak crisis will unfold against the backdrop of Chinese support for Islamabad.
Given this geopolitical reality, India must prepare to deter and, if needed, confront future Chinese aggression. Although formidable, India’s military remains conventionally weaker than China’s. At $92 billion, New Delhi’s defense spending is just over a quarter of Beijing’s. Despite India’s efforts to procure advanced Western fighter jets and develop its own indigenous capabilities, China still enjoys a 3:1 advantage in airpower, and its naval modernization far outpaces India’s own efforts.
Fortunately for India, it does not need to match China’s military capabilities one-to-one to establish credible deterrence. The ongoing conflict in the Gulf presents yet another lesson in how it can use asymmetric warfare to its advantage. Over the past six months, Iran has demonstrated its ability to threaten commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting global energy markets and imposing disproportionate costs on conventionally superior military powers.
China, too, has a major maritime vulnerability. Nearly 80 percent of its total energy imports, worth $312 billion, pass through the Strait of Malacca – the shortest sea route between the Middle East and East Asia – creating a critical maritime chokepoint. Recognizing this, China has invested heavily in mitigating the so-called “Malacca Dilemma,” but despite these efforts Beijing remains deeply exposed. Alternative waterways like Sunda and Lombok increase travel time, fuel costs, and logistical complexity, while land-based routes linked to the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are expensive and vulnerable to political instability. It is still critical for China that this vital sea lane remains open.
If it invests in the right maritime denial capabilities, New Delhi could exploit Beijing’s dependence on the Strait of Malacca to offset its conventional disadvantage, whether in a major conflict involving Chinese military aggression against India, or in a situation with more direct military involvement from Beijing in an Indo-Pak crisis. If it finds itself pulled into a broader Indo-Pacific contingency, New Delhi could even work in coordination with Western naval forces.
Disrupting traffic through the Malacca Strait would carry considerable military and political risks. However, India need not close the strait to strengthen deterrence. The ability to credibly threaten such disruption could force Beijing to account for severe economic costs, underscoring the need for India to invest in maritime-denial capabilities now. To address regional concerns, India would need to frame these capabilities as part of a broader effort to strengthen deterrence in the Indo-Pacific, ideally in coordination with regional partners rather than over their heads.
Such a strategy would hinge on a layered maritime-denial architecture. India’s control of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands means it does not need to rely on expensive aircraft carriers to threaten shipping through the Malacca Strait. Instead, it could use low-cost unmanned systems of the kind Iran has employed to deter Chinese vessels and alter the cost-benefit calculus for China.
Similarly, India could utilize inexpensive naval mines to complicate maritime access; the psychological impact of a mined waterway alone can be sufficient to deter vessels carrying expensive cargoes.
The Indian Navy’s submarines operating from the Bay of Bengal would be another valuable asset in such a scenario, not simply because they would put vessels at risk, but also because their presence would force Beijing to devote scarce resources to complex anti-submarine warfare operations.
New Delhi’s growing anti-ship cruise missile arsenal would add to the efficacy of such a layered area-denial architecture. India’s BrahMos and new long-range hypersonic anti-ship missile could threaten Chinese ships from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands without putting expensive naval destroyers in harm’s way.
To make the strategy credible, however, India would need more than just these individual assets. It would need persistent intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance across the eastern Indian Ocean; resilient command-and-control networks; and regular military exercises that demonstrate an ability to integrate drones, submarines, mines, and missiles into a coherent maritime denial strategy.
While New Delhi has invested in expanding its arsenal of these individual assets, it still lacks a coherent maritime denial strategy for the Strait of Malacca. Such an objective would be better served, for one, by fortifying the Andaman and Nicobar Command with credible military capabilities – an undertaking that should not be conflated with the Great Nicobar Island Project. The project has evident dual-use dimensions, but it remains primarily a commercial infrastructure initiative and should not be treated as a substitute for hard military power.
China has spent decades trying to resolve the Malacca Dilemma because Beijing understands its vulnerability. India should recognize that same reality. It need not match China ship for ship or aircraft for aircraft. By investing in credible maritime denial capabilities around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, New Delhi can ensure that any Chinese aggression carries costs Beijing cannot ignore.

2026-09-11
13:38:28 UTC
22:38:28 KST

Addressing the BRICS Business Forum in New Delhi on Friday, President Pezeshkian said the grouping’s real strength will emerge when the economic capacities of its members are transformed into practical networks of trade, investment and financing. He stressed that economic resilience requires diversification of trade partners, financing sources and payment mechanisms.
The Iranian president said the growing use of economic tools for political pressure, along with geopolitical uncertainty and disruptions to supply chains, have made the global economic environment more complicated. He urged BRICS to develop mechanisms that would prevent any country from disrupting legitimate trade by monopolizing financial or technological instruments.
Pezeshkian also proposed greater digitalization and integration of customs procedures, the removal of regulatory and administrative barriers, expansion of cross-border markets and facilitation of joint private-sector investment. He also called for stronger cooperation on standardization so that BRICS could move beyond raw-material trade toward integrated value chains and joint industrial production.
He described food and energy security as key pillars of economic security and said Iran, given its major energy reserves and strategic geographic position, is ready to serve as a strategic partner in BRICS energy, food and transportation supply chains.
Pezeshkian identified expanding the use of national currencies in intra-BRICS trade as one of the most important steps, saying it should be accompanied by mechanisms for managing currency risks and facilitating mutual settlements. He also proposed that the New Development Bank become a major source of financing for infrastructure and energy projects through special credit lines, local-currency financing and guarantees to attract private investment.
He further proposed establishing a joint BRICS reinsurance company with initial capital of $10 billion to cover risks associated with major infrastructure and energy projects and increase private-sector confidence.
Turning to emerging technologies, Pezeshkian said BRICS should not merely consume artificial intelligence technology but should contribute to knowledge production and the development of digital-economy standards, while also strengthening cybersecurity for critical infrastructure.
He called on the BRICS Business Council to move from being a forum for dialogue to an executive engine of economic cooperation, with its working groups setting concrete and measurable projects based on indicators such as intra-BRICS trade growth, the share of national currencies in trade and the volume of private investment.
The Islamic Republic of Iran is ready to work alongside all BRICS members to build a more open, resilient, and equitable economy, President Pezeshkian underlined.
