Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:57:00 UTC
21:57:00 KST

Uber leaves two African markets — and drivers in despair
September 11, 2026
A week ago, Uber unexpectedly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending more than a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also said it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect.
With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda, Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — namely Egypt, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa.
"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition," without sharing details on what this assistance would entail.
In the last year, the multinational company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania, while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.
Africa a difficult market to crack
Uber has not managed to grow across much of the African market despite its massive global scale. The profit-driven ride-hailing app faces stiff competition from rival platforms, including Bolt, inDrive and SafeBoda, which operate in the Nigerian and Ugandan markets and beyond.
However, it's not only Uber that is having to deal with its frustration over the current situation: Many of its drivers across Africa have been raising complaints about shrinking profit margins amid rising fuel costs, inflation and currency volatility, especially in markets like Nigeria.
In their view, Uber's business model of pocketing around 20% — 25% of any trip fare in commissions is no longer tenable.
Discontent, discombobulated and disregarded drivers
Abbas Olamide, an Uber driver in the Nigerian capital Abuja, said the company's overall service was "good," while firmly stressing that the high commission rates were adding greatly to his existing woes.
He told DW that a ride of 30,000 Naira (€20) "to the airport means the ride-hailing app would deduct 6,000 Naira as commission," still leaving him to "then pay a gate fee at the airport."
"Probably because you do not want to go back to town empty-handed, we also pay to park at the airport [to pick up another client]," he explained.
"At the end of the day, what's left is no longer enough."
Samuel Olatunji, an Uber-driver in the megacity Lagos, also shared his concerns with DW following the abrupt announcement of Uber's exit, saying he will now have to recalibrate his own business model.
The 43-year-old driver says he'll have to join hundreds of other drivers who "have to depend on other [ride-hailing] apps now" to ensure any steady stream of income.
"But the amount I take home won't add up like before again."
In recent years, drivers like Olamide and Olatunji have staged several strikes and protests over soaring operating costs, low fares and working conditions, as well as Nigeria's fuel hikes, which this year have also been worsened by the surge in prices at the pump following the war in Iran.
Their pleas and concerns, however, remain largely unheard, as they find themselves having to prepare for a bumpy ride ahead.
Dollars versus naira
Uber meanwhile did not provide a detailed explanation for its decision; however, it comes against the backdrop of double-digit inflation in many places across Africa, which has eroded the purchasing power of millions of people while pushing them deeper and deeper into poverty.
This also makes consumers less likely to use the transport company.
Ikemesit Effiong, partner at SBM Intelligence, a consulting firm based in Lagos, explained that "[r]ising costs for such things as fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance, coupled with a currency that is less valuable now than in 2014 means that fares were climbing faster than the average Lagos or Abuja rider's willingness or ability to pay for the convenience."
Effiong added that while Uber's cost base is dollar-linked, the drivers' revenue is the shrinking naira, leading to the overall maths not working anymore, and forcing Uber to operate under unsustainably thin profit margins.
This is despite the fact that Nigeria's ride-hailing market alone is estimated to be worth around $450 million per year.
"These platforms are trying to hold fares low enough to retain price-sensitive riders, while the driver take-home shrinks in real terms. This pushes drivers toward multi-apping, off-platform negotiation, or exit altogether," he noted.
Effiong further highlighted that one of Uber's local competitors, InDrive, does actually operate under a negotiated-fare approach, resulting in "less reliance on the capital-heavy, standardized-fare template that works in wealthier markets."
The complex economics of ride-hailing
There are some striking similarities between the Nigerian and Ugandan markets: Both countries have huge populations and a growing demand for more transport solution. But both across both Kampala and Lagos, Uber's exit also creates a loss of a service many users had considered a safe and reliable option — more so than some of the other options.
Mary-Esther Anele, a Lagos resident, told DW that she knows that she is "going to start looking for alternatives."
"But most importantly, I'm going to travel less anyway now because transportation costs are going to increase," she added.
There also are questions about any knock-on effects beyond the current decision by Uber:
Will the California-based multinational leave its remaining African markets? Will its pricing dynamics change in order to bring in more money from the continent? And how will competitors respond?
In some other African countries like South Africa, ride-hailing apps like Uber have also long been a thorn in the side of taxi companies and minibuses, whose operators say they don't want to compete against those drivers, even resorting to violence at times as part of ongoing local taxi wars.
Will Uber's shrinking footprint in Africa impact these kinds of developments in other markets?
As countless drivers prepare for an unknown future, the end of their partnership with Uber might — for many — spell their journey's end.
Frank Yiga from Kampala contributed to this report.
Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

Poland investigates desecration of UPA monument by controversial politician, but no charges filed

Poland investigates desecration of UPA monument by controversial politician, but no charges filed
Polish prosecutors are investigating the desecration of a monument and burial site for Ukrainian Insurgent Army The UPA was a nationalist paramilitary organisation that fought for Ukrainian independence during and after World War II, primarily against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union (UPA) fighters who were killed in a battle with the NKVD (the Soviet People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs) in 1946 in the village of Białystok in Hrubieszów County, but no charges have been filed against anyone.
Source: Polish news portal RMF24, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The Hrubieszów District Prosecutor's Office is investigating the vandalism of a monument and burial site of 41 UPA fighters in the village of Białystok.
MEP Grzegorz Braun posted a video showing him and other people striking the stone obelisk with a heavy tool.
The preliminary proceedings concern "insulting a group of Ukrainian ethnicity by damaging the resting place of people who died in battle with NKVD officers" in the village of Białystok in the Dołhobyczów municipality.
Prosecutor Rafał Kawalec, spokesperson for the Zamość District Prosecutor's Office, said investigators have seized the video recording of the incident and questioned witnesses.
The spokesperson added that no one has been charged. He did not rule out that proceedings could be launched to have parliamentary immunity waived if necessary.
The granite obelisk commemorates Ukrainians who were killed fighting against the Soviet NKVD. It stands in the village of Białystok, in the Dołhobyczów municipality (Hrubieszów County), where the Ukrainians were buried in 1946. The monument was erected directly above a mass grave.
The memorial site has existed since the 1990s and has been in its current form – a stone bearing the engraved names of those killed – since 2019. The obelisk has been vandalised several times. In the summer of 2026, it was spray-painted and an arch decorating the stone was cut away. The Ukrainian Embassy officially condemned the act of vandalism at the time.
The Lublin Voivodeship Office has explained that the grave of UPA members located in the Dołhobyczów municipality is not listed in the register of war graves and cemeteries maintained by the voivode.
Background:
- Commenting on the latest incident, Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said: "Political fringe figures in Poland can think of nothing better to do than wage war on graves at a time when a real war is going on."
- The monument was also vandalised on 6 September, and police are searching for those involved.

Inflation persisted in August, potentially locking in a Fed interest rate hike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:54:21 UTC
21:54:21 KST

Prices for a wide swath of goods and services continued to climb in August, according to a report Friday that raises the specter of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike next week.
The consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, putting the 12-month increase at 3.4%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Both readings were in line with the Dow Jones consensus.
However, stripping out volatile food and energy prices, the core CPI posted a 0.3% monthly gain, or 0.1 percentage point higher than forecast. The core annual rate came in at 2.4%, matching the estimate.
The report is the final major inflation indicator the Fed will see before it holds its policy meeting next week, concluding Wednesday with a vote on its key interest rate.
Traders responded to the numbers by ramping up bets that the Federal Open Market Committee will increase its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point. Odds for a hike jumped to nearly 90%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tracker of fed funds futures prices.
"There's no guarantee that the Fed will hike next week, but it's hard to see how the central bank can justify leaving rates on hold," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.
Stock market futures nonetheless surged as oil prices plunged in morning trade. Treasury yields were mixed, though the policy-sensitive 2-year note jumped 4.6 basis points to 4.594%. One basis point equals 0.01%.
Energy propelled the headline number higher, as gasoline prices jumped 3.9%, accounting for more than one-third of the index's gain. The energy index broadly rose 2.1% amid pressure from escalating tensions in the Middle East and was up 16.3% from a year ago. Gasoline rose 27.4% and fuel oil surged 52% on a 12-month basis.
Food prices edged 0.1% higher as food at home costs held flat. The food index accelerated 2.7% annually.
Another significant factor was a 0.3% climb in shelter costs, which had moderated over the prior two months. Transportation services saw a 0.5% increase. Used cars and trucks rose 0.4% and new vehicle prices were up 0.3%, part of what appeared to be broad-based gains for the index. Tariff-sensitive apparel prices were flat and motor vehicle insurance fell 0.8%.
Heading into the CPI release, markets already were pricing in a nearly 70% probability that the central bank would vote to increase its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point.
However, there have been differing views on which way the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will tilt, with some speculating that the difference could come down to hundredths of a percentage point in the CPI reading.
Chairman Kevin Warsh has expressed a commitment to getting inflation back down to the Fed's 2% target and said recently that if the numbers don't improve, "we have work to do." His comments were widely interpreted as advocating a rate hike, though several key officials over the past few weeks have counseled a more patient approach.
"Chair Warsh and others signaled that interest rates can remain on hold only if disinflation continues and today's August report did not deliver that," said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide. "Further, the renewed march higher in oil, gasoline and diesel prices add to concerns that higher energy prices could spill over to other goods and services and inflation expectations."
Nationwide now expects a quarter-point hike next week. The fed funds rate, a benchmark for multiple consumer loans, is currently pegged in a range of 3.5%-3.75%, where it has been for all of 2026.

Putin Meets Modi as India Hosts BRICS Summit

2026-09-11
12:52:00 UTC
21:52:00 KST

President Vladimir Putin arrived in India early Friday for a three-day visit to attend the BRICS leaders’ summit and deepen strategic ties with New Delhi.
On Friday afternoon, Putin met with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi for bilateral talks focused on trade and energy.
Sources cited by Indian media said the two leaders would discuss expanding Russian-Indian trade to $100 billion by 2030, supported by increasing cooperation in rail transit, steel production, critical minerals, fertilizers and nuclear energy.
The Kremlin said earlier this week that the possible sale of Russian Sukhoi Su-57 stealth fighter jets to India is also on the agenda.
A delegation of more than 300 Russian executives is accompanying Putin to New Delhi to negotiate supply chains and food security contracts.
Putin is scheduled to give a speech at the BRICS business forum later on Friday. The main plenary session of the bloc’s leaders will take place on Saturday, followed by an expanded session the following day with partner states and international organizations.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in global affairs. BRICS has since expanded beyond its original group of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa to include Ethiopia, Egypt, Indonesia, Iran and the UAE.
This year’s BRICS summit seeks to lift the bloc’s global profile even as the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran splits its nembers, with Tehran and Abu Dhabi on opposing sides of the conflict.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that the differences between the UAE and Iran had a “negative impact” on the organization, hindering the drafting of a joint declaration. However, he expressed hope that leaders would be able to find a phrasing in the declaration that would be acceptable to all member countries.
Russia remains one of India’s largest energy suppliers. However, New Delhi has tried to balance its longstanding strategic partnership with Moscow against pressure from Washington over its purchases of Russian crude.
Putin and Modi last met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan earlier this month, when Modi told Putin that the Ukraine war needs to end for humanity’s sake. The Indian leader said he would support any effort to stop the war.
Reuters and AFP contributed reporting.

“The Taste of Time” – a classic of Bulgarian rock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:51:53 UTC
21:51:53 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
News
Highlights of Bulgarian musical culture
“The Taste of Time” – a classic of Bulgarian rock
Friday 11 September 2026 15:25
Friday, 11 September 2026, 15:25
PHOTO Balkanton
Font size
Since it emerged in the 1950s, rock has been the voice of youth – of protest and the desire for freedom. It carries the energy of being young and the right to ask uncomfortable questions about the big issues of the day. Around the world, rock has stirred the minds and emotions of generations of intelligent and sensitive people, becoming a challenge to the established order – loud and rebellious, poetic or lyrical, but always distinctive.
In Bulgaria, rock music is almost synonymous with Shturtsite – the legendary band that came to embody the classic rebellious spirit in Bulgarian popular culture. Formed in 1967 by Kiril Marichkov, Petar Tsankov, Petar Gyuzelev and Veselin Kisyov, the group appeared at a time when rock had already become the language of an entire generation around the world. For young Bulgarians, it was a window onto another world and another way of thinking.
Kiril Marichkov (October 30, 1944 – October 11, 2024)
PHOTO shturcite.github.io
At first, Shturtsite followed the international models. The musicians later admitted that their early steps were marked by imitation of the Beatles. But they also believed they needed solid ground to build on before something genuinely their own could emerge. The real challenge was to find their own musical language. And Shturtsite did. As different musicians joined the band over the years, they gradually turned the aesthetics of international rock into part of Bulgarian culture.
Shturtsite believed wholeheartedly in their mission to create Bulgarian rock. Their music used the universal language of the genre, but spoke about Bulgarians, in Bulgarian. In his book The Ambition Called Bulgarian Rock, Rumen Spasov describes rock as a particular synthesis of music, poetry, contemporary folklore and modern technology. He argues that everywhere in the world rock challenges those in power, while in countries without genuine democracy that challenge is suppressed by every possible means and inevitably takes on a particular significance.
PHOTO shturcite.github.io
In this sense, Shturtsite were part of a culture that questioned and rebelled. Their songs from different periods trace the evolution of Bulgarian rock. Many different lyricists wrote for the band, yet the lyrics share a recognisable spirit and character. The result was a Bulgarian phenomenon that both resembled and differed from the international models that had inspired it.
One of Shturtsite’s most memorable songs, “The Taste of Time”, has remained a landmark of Bulgarian popular culture for more than four decades. The music and arrangement are by Kiril Marichkov, while the lyrics were written by a poet described as “harsh and uncompromising”.
Volen Nikolaev (September 9, 1954 – March 15, 2011).
PHOTO Facebook/ Volen Nikolaev
Volen Nikolaev  wrote more than 600 song lyrics. They were sung by stars such as Lili Ivanova and Vasil Naydenov, but Nikolaev is remembered as one of Shturtsite’s closest collaborators. Among the band’s hits based on his lyrics are “20th Century”, “Juliet”, “Farewell”, “The Staircase” and “Hamlet”.
“We are searching again for the taste of time” – the characters rush through life, chase success, put on “new clothes” and try to stop life in its tracks with the wave of a hand. But at what price? Volen Nikolaev’s lyrics are about a generation, growing older and the value of the years that have passed. “The taste of time is salty” – time takes much away, but also gives us the chance to discover who we are.
With songs such as “The Taste of Time”, Shturtsite created rock with a character of its own, bringing together international music culture, Bulgarian poetry and a personal point of view. Today, Shturtsite is much more than the name of one of Bulgaria’s most popular rock bands. The group is proof that a global genre can take root in Bulgarian soil without losing its energy – and without ending up as just another copy.
Editor: Desislava Semkovska

Yemen's Houthis take over vital Bab al-Mandeb strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:50:23 UTC
21:50:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis take over Bab al-Mandeb strait vital to global shipping
The Houthis seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast and captured three strategic islands on Friday, in a lightning offensive that cemented their hold on a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia.
The developments are likely to deepen the US-Israeli war's impact on international commerce, as Saudi Arabia shut down an oil pipeline following attacks, and after months of Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Following a week-long offensive that has left hundreds dead, government officials said the Iran-backed group seized the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
A local official with Yemen's Saudi-backed government said on Friday that the Houthis had "completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandab area and Mayyun Island".
A government military official later reported the group had also seized Greater and Lesser Hanish, the last two islands in the narrow waterway not under their control, as well as all of the neighbouring Red Sea coastline.
"Everything that was under our control on the western coast has fallen," the military official added.
A witness told AFP that gunmen were "deploying along the Bab al-Mandab shore and are driving around in military vehicles".
The capture of the islands, particularly Mayyun in the middle of the strait, heightens the Houthis' ability to attack Saudi tankers, which they have been targeting since July.
Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea ever since Iran's Hormuz blockade choked off its shipments via the Gulf.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated the Houthis on their "resounding victory" on Friday.
Farea Al-Muslimi, research fellow at Chatham House, told AFP: "Now the Iranians don't only control... the Strait of Hormuz, but they control the other most strategic chokepoint in the Middle East."
Oil prices have soared past $100 a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday -- a potential headache for President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said navigation through the Bab al-Mandab Strait was "safe" for all but Saudi Arabia following the latest advances.
'Great victories'
The Houthi offensive has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
It has also displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
It is part of renewed hostilities in Yemen's civil war that began with the group's takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014.
Houthi supporter Abdulhamid Dhaifallah lauded the group's "great victories" in and along the strait.
"They have been preparing for this front for four years," the Sanaa resident said.
Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline that carries Saudi oil to its Red Sea coast.
The Saudi energy ministry on Friday announced that attacks led to the closure of the pipeline -- which it had been increasingly using to bypass Hormuz -- adding that injuries were recorded.
"The East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions was subjected to several attacks on Thursday morning," a ministry official told the SPA news agency, adding: "The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries."
Before the Red Sea offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen's north.
They have recently attacked government-held areas in Hodeida and Taiz provinces and swept down the coast, seizing the port city of Mocha and Zuqar Island, north of Bab al-Mandab, on Thursday.
Mohamed, 46, who fled Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an "apocalyptic" atmosphere in the historic city.
Dangerous conflict
On Friday, the spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majed Abdullah Al-Nazili, said they had begun shelling areas along the Taiz-Mocha road, while residents told AFP they heard airstrikes.
While Saudi Arabia has also hit back with airstrikes and ordered troop reinforcements from Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based, it has failed to stop the Houthis' advance.
Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha's airport on Friday, while a local official said the city's seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
"I think the Saudis have tried everything they can to avoid this war, but I don't think they have any more choice," said Al-Muslimi.
The ongoing exchanges risk reviving a war that killed hundreds of thousands of Yemenis and sparked one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Sanaa and forcing out the government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

"They have been preparing for this front for four years," the Sanaa resident said.
Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline that carries Saudi oil to its Red Sea coast.
The Saudi energy ministry on Friday announced that attacks led to the closure of the pipeline -- which it had been increasingly using to bypass Hormuz -- adding that injuries were recorded.
"The East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions was subjected to several attacks on Thursday morning," a ministry official told the SPA news agency, adding: "The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries."
Before the Red Sea offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen's north.
They have recently attacked government-held areas in Hodeida and Taiz provinces and swept down the coast, seizing the port city of Mocha and Zuqar Island, north of Bab al-Mandab, on Thursday.
Mohamed, 46, who fled Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an "apocalyptic" atmosphere in the historic city.
Dangerous conflict
On Friday, the spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majed Abdullah Al-Nazili, said they had begun shelling areas along the Taiz-Mocha road, while residents told AFP they heard airstrikes.
While Saudi Arabia has also hit back with airstrikes and ordered troop reinforcements from Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based, it has failed to stop the Houthis' advance.
Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha's airport on Friday, while a local official said the city's seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
"I think the Saudis have tried everything they can to avoid this war, but I don't think they have any more choice," said Al-Muslimi.
The ongoing exchanges risk reviving a war that killed hundreds of thousands of Yemenis and sparked one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Sanaa and forcing out the government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

The combined toll stands at 1,428 dead and more than 5,649 missing, including about 800 foreigners, among them tourists and pilgrims.
Nepal, a country of about 30 million people, contributes only a small share of global greenhouse gas emissions. Scientists say rising global temperatures are accelerating glacier melt in the Himalayas and increasing the risk of such disasters.

Why tens of thousands of Hasidic Jews are flocking to Ukraine – and why they are dancing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:49:41 UTC
21:49:41 KST

Why tens of thousands of Hasidic Jews are flocking to Ukraine – and why they are dancing
Tens of thousands of Hasidic Jews are flocking to central Ukraine, praying, singing, and dancing as they prepare to mark the Jewish New Year.
The annual pilgrimage draws thousands of visitors from around the world.
But who are they, why do they travel to a relatively small Ukrainian city every year, and are they still coming despite the conflict?
Who are the Hasidic Jews?
Hasidism is a movement within Orthodox Judaism that emerged in Eastern Europe in the 18th century. Over time, it developed into a number of groups with their own traditions and religious leaders.
Most of those making the annual journey to Uman are followers of the Breslov branch. Their connection to the city goes back to the man who founded the movement more than 200 years ago – Rabbi Nachman.
Who was Rabbi Nachman?
Nachman was born in 1772 in what is now Ukraine and was a great-grandson of Israel Baal Shem Tov, who is regarded as the founder of the Hasidic movement.
He founded the Breslov branch and emphasized prayer, simplicity, and joy. He also placed particular importance on his followers gathering with him for Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year.
Large groups of Hasidim are crossing into Ukraine and heading to Uman for Rosh Hashanah. Several thousand are already there. By September 11, when the Jewish New Year begins, organizers expect up to 40,000 pilgrims from Israel, the US and around the world. War, missile risk,… pic.twitter.com/eklA9ZzENB
— Iuliia Mendel (@IuliiaMendel) September 8, 2026
Nachman died in Uman in 1810 and was buried there. His followers continued gathering in the city after his death, beginning a tradition that eventually developed into today’s mass annual pilgrimage.
How did Uman become a pilgrimage center?
Uman is a relatively small city in central Ukraine’s Cherkasy Region, around 200km south of Kiev. Its population stood at just over 80,000 before the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, while the annual pilgrimage brings tens of thousands of additional visitors.
Nachman moved to Uman only months before his death. Historical accounts say he chose the city because thousands of Jews had been killed there during a massacre in 1768 and wanted to be buried near the victims.
Uman later became home to a large Jewish community. Jews accounted for 59% of its population by 1897. The community was devastated during World War II, when around 17,000 Jews were killed after Nazi forces occupied the city.
Visits to Nachman’s grave continued on a much smaller scale during the Soviet period before growing substantially after the collapse of the USSR.
What is Rosh Hashanah?
This year, Rosh Hashanah begins at sunset on September 11 and ends after nightfall on September 13. Unlike the secular New Year, it is primarily a religious holiday centered on prayer and reflection.
The holiday has particular importance for Breslov followers because Nachman considered their annual Rosh Hashanah gathering especially important. After his death, his followers continued meeting in Uman during the holiday, explaining why the city sees its largest influx of pilgrims at this time of year.
Why all the dancing?
The singing and dancing seen on Uman’s streets are not required Rosh Hashanah rituals.
Music and dancing are common at Hasidic gatherings, while Rabbi Nachman placed particular emphasis on joy. His followers therefore often combine prayer with communal singing and dancing during their time in Uman.
Do pilgrims still come despite the conflict?
Yes. Tens of thousands have continued making the journey despite the hostilities and official travel warnings.
Around 35,000 pilgrims visited Uman in both 2023 and 2024, while more than 35,000 traveled there in 2025, according to Ukrainian officials and media reports. Ukrainian authorities expect as many as 40,000 this year.
Ukraine travel warning
Last week, the US Embassy in Kiev issued a security alert recommending that Americans not travel to Uman, citing the risk of airstrikes, martial law, and movement restrictions. The embassy also warned US-Ukrainian male dual nationals that they may be unable to leave the country and could be subject to conscription. Ukraine has ended an exemption that previously allowed certain Ukrainian men living abroad to leave the country.
Security has been stepped up for this year’s gathering. Israeli police officers have arrived in Uman to work alongside Ukrainian law enforcement in areas where pilgrims are staying and gathering, according to police in Ukraine’s Cherkasy Region.
The pilgrimage has persisted through earlier disruptions as well. In 2020, pilgrims attempted to reach Uman despite Covid-19 border and travel restrictions.

‘Odd couple’ black holes can find each other in space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:47:24 UTC
21:47:24 KST

When two black holes find each other in the vastness of space, they can form a binary odd couple—and it’s more common than researchers expected.
Scientists think most black holes are born when a star dies and its core collapses. This is also the case for binary black holes, pairs of black holes that orbit around each other and slowly move closer together. These pairs are often the remains of stars that lived together, died together and continued to coexist following their collapse. Eventually these two draw close enough together to merge into one faster-spinning black hole that sometimes shoots off into space.
Now research is suggesting that these whirling loners can find love again. New work suggests many black hole pairs are so-called hierarchical mergers: one large, fast-spinning black hole born from a previous merger and the partner it somehow found in the cosmos. This picture of black holes’ origin stories could help clarify how supernova physics work and how galaxies evolve, scientists say. Knowing how black holes form and change is also crucial for understanding general relativity and the history of the universe.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In two studies released recently in Physical Review Letters, scientists describe how they used published data from the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, which tracks merging black holes through the spacetime ripples they release, and other observatories to identify this subpopulation. Each team used a different technique to track the black holes’ mass, spin and tilt, and both captured a distinct group of binary black holes that have “strong signatures” of hierarchical merging—one of the pair is much larger, is spinning faster and orbits out of alignment with its partner.
“At minimum, we’re finding evidence that there are these highly spinning and weirdly tilted black holes in the dataset, and the most straightforward way to interpret that, the Occam’s razor answer, is that these black holes probably came from previous mergers,” says Cailin Plunkett, lead author on one of the recent studies and a Ph.D. candidate at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Her study suggests about 14 percent of black hole duos may be hierarchical mergers.
Physicists had previously predicted that the offspring of black hole mergers in dense stellar environments would find future partners to merge with. And their different astrophysical history would make them operate “in weird and wonderful ways”—a sign that researchers have now spotted, says Paul Lasky, co-author of the other recent study and an astrophysicist at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia.
The fact that two different technical processes both found evidence of these black hole origins is “a concrete example of us moving astrophysics forward,” says Maximiliano Isi, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, who was not involved in either study but has worked with LIGO data in the past. “It’s kind of like trying to see on the road when there’s fog,” Isi says. “We’re all squinting in different ways and looking from different angles and trying to determine what is the landscape of what’s out there, and we are converging into a very nice picture that somewhat aligns with theoretical expectations.”

The Netherlands, Spain push for EU-wide minimum age on social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:46:06 UTC
21:46:06 KST

The European Commission is expected to announce a social media ban for minors next week. The Netherlands and Spain want it harmonised, EU-enforced, and extended to video games and AI chatbots.
The Hague and Madrid are pushing for an EU-wide minimum age for social media use, potentially extended to other online services, as the European Commission prepares to announce its own proposal next week.
The social media ban should be harmonised and enforced at European level, and extended to video games, AI chatbots and other risky digital services, the two countries said in a non-paper circulated on Friday.
Restricting minors' access to social media has become an increasingly hot topic in the EU and beyond. France, Greece, Austria, Denmark, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Germany, Poland and the Netherlands are all considering or advancing national legislation to that effect.
Under pressure to head off a patchwork of national approaches, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced in May that an EU proposal was coming and is now expected during her State of the Union address next week.
Ahead of that announcement, the Dutch and Spanish governments circulated a document meant to shape the upcoming proposal, stressing that "the introduction of a minimum age for social media is a measure that must necessarily be added to existing and upcoming legal frameworks."
The two countries argue that the measure must be proportionate and respect fundamental rights, including freedom of expression, information, and data protection — and be underpinned by a comprehensive impact assessment.
In August, the French Constitutional Council struck down a national law banning social media access for under-15s, ruling the measure was too broad and insufficiently proportionate because it infringed on constitutional rights.
The Dutch-Spanish paper makes the case for tackling addictive algorithms and harmful design across all digital services through a risk-based approach, not social media alone, extending its scope to video games and AI companions.
"There should be a possibility for online providers to obtain an exemption from the age requirement if they can demonstrate that their service is sufficiently safe," the paper reads.
For the two countries, harmonised, EU-level enforcement is essential, as national fragmentation would blunt the measure's effectiveness. They point to the Digital Services Act, under which the Commission already acts as regulator for online services such as Google, Instagram and TikTok, as the model to replicate.
The paper also argues the upcoming proposal should be wary of leaning on parental consent as a mitigating measure, since it would be difficult to implement and would introduce additional privacy risks.
For the ban to work in practice, an age verification app is essential. Spain and the Netherlands want the upcoming legislative proposal built on the EU's age verification framework, with the app's function limited strictly to confirming a person is above a given age, to minimise the privacy impact.

US Patriots Fired at Full Force—But Iran Still Damaged Eight F-15s and an A-10
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:45:48 UTC
21:45:48 KST

- Category
- World
US Patriots Fired at Full Force—But Iran Still Damaged Eight F-15s and an A-10
A massive Patriot response failed to completely shield US aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, where an Iranian ballistic missile barrage damaged roughly eight F-15 fighters and left an A-10 Thunderbolt II missing a wing, according to CBS News reporting cited by Defense Express on September 10.
Iran launched around 20 ballistic missiles at the US-used airbase overnight on September 8-9. Jordan later said its air defenses intercepted 18 of the incoming missiles, while the remaining two fell in unpopulated areas.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Defense Express, however, pointed to another striking aspect of the engagement: the sheer number of Patriot interceptors fired.
Based on available videos, the outlet estimated that US-operated Patriot batteries launched at least 60 PAC-3 interceptors, either MSE or CRI variants, within minutes. Some estimates circulating online have put the number closer to 100, though Defense Express considers that figure likely exaggerated.
Even the more conservative estimate would amount to roughly three Patriot interceptors fired for every Iranian ballistic missile.
Defense Express described the batteries as effectively operating in “machine-gun” mode during the barrage, underscoring how quickly stocks of expensive and limited PAC-3 missiles can be consumed during a concentrated ballistic attack.
Yet the airbase was not left untouched. CBS News reported, citing people with direct knowledge of the damage, that approximately eight F-15 fighter jets sustained light damage. The aircraft were repaired and returned to service relatively quickly.
An A-10 Thunderbolt II suffered much more severe damage and was left missing a wing. For the aging A-10 fleet, such damage could prove particularly consequential, Defense Express notes.
Production ended decades ago, and the US Air Force has been moving toward retiring the aircraft rather than investing heavily in rebuilding severely damaged examples.
No photographs of the affected aircraft or detailed satellite imagery of the damaged section of the airbase have yet been publicly released.
That leaves an important question unanswered: what exactly reached the aircraft parking area?
Defense Express noted that the relatively minor damage to the F-15s would be unusual for a direct ballistic missile impact. One possibility is that fragments from an intercepted missile struck the aircraft.
Another is that the damage came from submunitions carried by an Iranian cluster-warhead ballistic missile. Defense Express said cluster effects appeared visible in footage of the attack.
The episode is particularly notable because these were not inexperienced foreign Patriot crews.
Jordan does not publicly operate Patriot batteries of its own, while the United States deploys the systems in the country to protect American forces and critical facilities.
US air defense personnel have also spent months responding to Iranian ballistic missile attacks, making it harder to attribute the high interceptor expenditure simply to inexperience, according to Defense Express.
The engagement therefore highlights a difficult reality of ballistic missile defense: even a highly successful interception rate can require dozens of scarce interceptors—and still leave enough leakage, debris, or submunitions to damage valuable aircraft on the ground.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine faced a severe shortage of air defense interceptors, leaving advanced Patriot launcher units idling in rural fields.
A system spotted near Kyiv has 16 tubes showing signs of past use, but its unit chief engineer, Dmytro, noted the launcher had not fired in six weeks.

12:43:43 UTC
21:43:43 KST

Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, the US’s war on terror has largely defeated the two global terrorist groups – Al Qaeda and Daesh – following prolonged wars in Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria that saw the deployment of tens of thousands of American troops in different theatres.
Washington used its superior military power to oust regimes in Kabul and Baghdad, claiming their backing for terror groups allegedly planning attacks on American soil, like 9/11.
However, the so-called war on terror strategy adopted following the 9/11 attacks has also left a trail of death and destruction across a vast swathe – crippling nations from Afghanistan to the energy-rich Middle East.
Afghanistan proved a classic example of American duplicity. Two decades after the US ousted the Taliban from power, it facilitated the return of the same group in 2001 following the hasty and chaotic US withdrawal from the Asian nation.
Saddam Hussein’s ouster from the Iraqi leadership also produced dangerous results, leading to armed resistance and internal clashes, which paved the way for the emergence of Daesh across the country. The US invasion also led to the empowerment of pro-Iran armed groups in a country with a large Shia population, helping Tehran increase its influence over Iraq.
Currently, the US is engaged in another Middle East war on Iran, a country which Washington sometimes describes as a terror regime, signalling the continuation of America’s post-9/11 strategy.
While President Donald Trump appeared to want to end the conflict in the short term, there is no clear indication that the unpopular US war will reach an end quickly.
Even top American officials have recently warned Trump that the conflict, which has led to large disruptions in oil trade due to the Hormuz blockades, might continue through the rest of his presidential term, signalling that Washington might face another “forever war”.
Military power alone not enough
In the face of mixed outcomes from Afghanistan to Iraq and most lately Iran, experts see many gaps, disorientation, and implementation problems in America’s post-9/11 strategy, which has fluctuated as Washington has occasionally tried to seize opportunities to pull back from turbulent regions.
As long as the objective was to dismantle terror networks, it seemed to work to some extent for the US, says Iftikhar Firdous, a senior Pakistani investigative journalist with a focus on Afghanistan and militant groups.
“But the problem began when the objective expanded from counterterrorism into state-building, regime change and political engineering,” he tells TRT World.
“Once you start trying to engineer societies through military power, you enter a completely different strategic environment. The US had overwhelming military superiority, but military superiority does not automatically translate into political legitimacy or sustainable political outcomes. That is really the central contradiction of the post-9/11 era,” he adds.
As the Iran war meanders on, the US has come to terms with a grim reality: the tech-powered American military supremacy is unable to bring down the Iranian power structure backed by the powerful IRGC.
“Many of the difficulties emerged from the gap between American military capabilities and the political objectives that developed around them,” says Ali Mammadov, a PhD researcher in political science at George Mason University's Schar School of Policy and Government.
“The US could remove hostile governments and severely weaken terrorist organisations relatively quickly, but establishing durable political orders afterwards proved considerably more difficult,” Mammadov tells TRT World.
Afghanistan and Iraq, the two Muslim states, have complex ethnic, tribal and sectarian structures with different competing local actors, which “military superiority alone could not resolve,” he says,
US government reviews of the country’s conduct in Afghanistan identified many policy problems, including “incoherent strategy, unrealistic timelines, weak sustainability and insufficient understanding of local conditions,” he adds.
“Repeated interventions also generated political backlash within parts of the region. At the alliance level, NATO unanimously invoked Article 5 after 9/11, but divisions became more pronounced as the broader agenda expanded, particularly over Iraq.”
Dania Koleilat Khatib, an expert on Arab-US relations, is more direct about the consequences of the post-9/11 strategy. “It definitely failed, which got the US into endless wars affecting its image worldwide, and created a huge financial burden with the spiralling debt,” Khatib tells TRT World.
From deterrence to uncharted territories
Experts also say that launching a war on terror without well-defined objectives has proven to be more difficult than dealing with a country like the former communist Soviet Union, against which the US Cold War strategy employed a strategy based on the combination of deterrence, containment and ideological arguments promoting democracy, freedom and free markets.
“The war on terror has never attracted that kind of international allegiance,” wrote Rabart Kagan, a well-known scholar of geopolitics, referring to differences between Cold War-era attitudes sympathetic to the US and a generally muted global response to American post-9/11 policies.
Since the end of the Cold War, the US has developed no overarching strategy in foreign policy, and after 9/11, Washington all of a sudden decided to adopt a preemptive military strategy, moving away from its traditional deterrence and containment policies.
Matthew Bryza, a former top US diplomat, who was in the White House working as a National Security Council official on September 11, does not see a single post-9/11 policy which has “really assembled a clear strategy”. He says that launching the Iraq war right after the war on the Taliban led the US to lose focus on Afghanistan’s reconstruction, bogging down American forces in the Middle Eastern state for two decades.
While the US effectively prevented terrorist attacks on American soil, criticism has increased against the US’ policies of regime change and ‘nation-building’ that have “unleashed new instabilities”.
Bryza says the numerous wars have proven “very difficult to control”.
Critics also see the current war on Iran as “an outgrowth” of this pos- 9/11 US approach, he adds.
“The very difficult situation the US has found itself in Iran will lead to a new debate whether the US should be engaged in these sorts of attempts to overthrow governments in the Middle East.”
While Bryza believes that leaving nation-building efforts behind and shifting American focus to the Asia-Pacific region might be a better approach for the US, he adds that unpredictable “events” have repeatedly pulled Washington back to the region.
Empowering China and Russia
Experts also draw attention to the fact that the forever wars not only drained the US of huge resources and cost many lives, but also distracted the country’s leadership from the great power rivalry with China and Russia.
“Twenty-five years later, the irony is that Washington’s post-9/11 wars diverted strategic attention and resources,” says Firdous, referring to how the US strategy has left American power vulnerable to China and Russia.
Geopolitical analysts note that US focus on the Middle East has left Eastern Europe and Caucasia unguarded against Russian operations, allowing Moscow to exert its power in the breakaway regions of Georgia and attack Ukraine.
More importantly, China, the world’s second-largest economy, has steadily increased its hold on global politics by using its big pockets and deepening ties with countries from Africa to Latin America and Asia. Beijing has also improved its ties with Middle Eastern states, from anti-Western states like Iran to oil-rich Arab Gulf states and Egypt.
“There was a broader strategic opportunity cost: the US devoted enormous attention and resources to counterterrorism and the Middle East during a period in which China was steadily accumulating economic and military power,” Mammadov says.
A recent Wall Street Journal analysis also concludes that the US post-9/11 strategy has empowered Chinese and Russian challenges to American global supremacy, quoting Kagan: “China and Russia have welcomed it because it has distracted the United States’ strategic focus away from them.”

Learning Chinese Sign Language
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:42:00 UTC
21:42:00 KST

Learning Chinese Sign Language is a bewildering experience. To begin with, Chinese Sign Language (CSL) is in itself best understood as an umbrella term rather than a well-defined language.
You have Signed Chinese, shoushi hanyu, which is one-to-one transcriptions of the written standard Chinese into signs, replete with interpuncation such as signed question marks. Then there is Natural Sign Language, ziran shouyu, the language that is actually spoken between native deaf signers in China. It has syntax and grammar markedly different from Chinese, makes extensive use of abbreviations and, like all natural sign languages, incorporates facial expressions.
Besides these, there are yet other types of CSL described in the academic literature, such as Literary Sign Language (wenfa shouyu) and Society Sign Language (shehui shouyu). All the more confusing is how these terms often seem to overlap or even are used interchangeably.
Since 2018, the government has been actively promoting a type of sign language titled Guojia Tongyong Shouyu, sometimes translated into English as Chinese General Sign Language (CGSL). According to the Chinese Ministry of Education, CGSL can be seen as the sign language equivalent to Standard Mandarin. Having moved away from a standard based on spoken or written Chinese, CGSL incorporates elements from the natural sign languages and thus appears to be less alien to native deaf speakers. While this standardized variety has been described by some Chinese academics as a “natural sign language,” it is, however, uncertain if it is viewed as such by deaf Chinese themselves.
For the prospective learner, there is a surprisingly user-friendly app based on the official CGSL lexicon. There are daily quizzes, signed demonstrations of the words, targeted tests, themed glossaries, and other useful tools for learning. Unfortunately, all of this does not compensate for the staggering lack of lexemes in the dictionary. Basic and commonly used words such as “curious” or “already” are missing.
Sometimes the all too familiar top-down perspective of Chinese officialdom shines through with its clear political priorities: while there is an entry for “Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League,” the arguably far more useful word “weekend” is not listed. Even more striking is how words pertaining to sexuality or “taboo” body parts are missing altogether. For example, how would a sign language interpreter fare at a client’s gynecologist visit when the CGSL has no official terms for a woman’s genitalia?
A couple of years ago, I was myself trying to learn Chinese Sign Language. I began by signing up to an online class, taught for free three nights a week. The teacher, however, was of the old-school, pre-CGSL era. Each lesson he stiffly taught us how to sign Chinese words and characters, without any facial cues and without teaching any grammar. Knowing enough about sign language to recognize that this was not the way deaf Chinese actually speak to each other, I quickly abandoned this approach and figured that the best way would be to befriend native speakers and simply learn from them.
What I had not foreseen was how the natively spoken natural sign languages not only vary from region to region, but seemingly even from speaker to speaker. Without classroom instruction and with different speakers signing in different ways, it soon became hard to know which was the “correct” way to sign. Apparently, I was not the only one with this problem: one of my deaf acquaintances said he would often not understand what other native deaf speakers were saying.
In fact, not only do deaf Chinese sometimes have a hard time understanding each other, but most of them struggle to understand the sign language used in official Chinese media. In one study exploring this issue, up to 84 percent of the deaf participants reported having trouble understanding the signed Chinese in television programs.
Phenomena such as these – official use of sign language that is unintelligible for actual deaf persons – might, in some part, be ascribed to what in Chinese is called xingshi zhuyi, or pointless formalism. The 2008 Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Protection of Disabled Persons stated that there should be sign language available for television shows, and state-owned broadcasting companies might simply want to check that box – without bothering to produce content that is relevant for or even comprehensible to a deaf audience.
With this said, there is an apparent growing interest among Chinese academics, and clear signs of growing awareness of sign language issues in Chinese society in general. My experiences with learning Chinese Sign Language might already be outdated. In 2023, a long article with the title “The Sign Language Used by Interpreters Is 90 Percent Incomprehensible to Deaf People” ran in the well-renowned Shanghai-based publication The Paper. According to state media, a national standard for proficiency and testing in CGSL has been implemented since March last year. Things are looking up.
Some of the most exciting developments, however, are taking place on social media. On platforms such as WeChat and Xiaohongshu (RedNote), there are countless content creators discussing the differences between different types of sign language, teaching sign language to others, or poking fun at the stiff, unnatural mimicry of hearing learners.
Surprisingly enough, some deaf users are also openly discussing governmental policies, seizing a rare opportunity for a marginalized group to talk about the political reforms directly affecting them. That these topics apparently have a low level of political sensitivity might, however, not be something to view entirely as a positive. Perhaps it simply speaks to the level of neglect of the deaf community.
Nevertheless, the days of “Signed Chinese” seem to be numbered, and younger generations of media-savvy deaf Chinese might quickly become a force to be reckoned with. One could venture to say that the future is looking bright for new learners of Chinese Sign Language.

Kyiv • UNN
An official at a pretrial detention center in occupied Simferopol is suspected of beating a civilian from Kherson. The man was beaten to intimidate and humiliate him.
An official of a Russian pre-trial detention center is suspected of inhumane treatment of a civilian from Kherson - as a result of the beating, the man suffered severe physical pain and significant psychological distress, UNN reports, citing the Prosecutor General's Office.
Under the procedural guidance of the Prosecutor General's Office, the deputy head of the Regime and Supervision Department of Russian Pre-Trial Detention Center No. 2 in temporarily occupied Simferopol was notified of suspicion in absentia
Details
According to the investigation, the official used physical violence and psychological pressure against civilians, including for reasons of hatred toward Ukrainians. One of the victims was a resident of Kherson.
In December 2022, during a walk, the man found a SIM card and took it with him. Later, detention center employees found it among his belongings.
On the official's orders, the man was taken from his cell to a utility room on the third floor of the detention center, which inmates called the "baulny room," where there was no video surveillance.
The civilian was forced to face the wall, lower his head, and press his hands, palms down, against the wall. After that, according to the investigation, the official personally began beating him - striking his torso with his hands and his lower limbs with his feet.
As a result of the beating, the man suffered severe physical pain and significant psychological distress. According to the investigation, the violence was deliberate - to intimidate the victim and humiliate his human dignity.
These actions were classified as inhumane treatment of a civilian who was under the control of the occupying authorities, and as a violation of the laws and customs of war (Part 1, Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).

Elbit Systems Deutschland told Reuters on Friday that it continuously evaluates opportunities for further expansion in Germany but no locations have yet been selected for future expansion.
"As a long-standing partner, the company operates across several locations in Germany, employs hundreds of German employees and continues to strengthen its local industrial presence," it said.
DEPORTATIONS 'FROM THE FIRST MINUTE'
The anti-immigration AfD, which is seeking to form a state government after winning a historic election victory just short of an outright majority, has pledged deportations "from the first minute", citizen patrols and separate classrooms for refugee children.

Any backing for the project could complicate talks with the left-wing populist BSW, the only party not to rule out cooperation with the AfD.

Gökhan Ergöçün
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
Consumer prices in the US rose 3.4% on an annual basis in August, while monthly inflation accelerated to 0.4%, official data showed Friday.
 
The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the monthly consumer price index gain accelerated following a 0.1% increase in July.
A 3.9% surge in gasoline prices accounted for over one-third of the total monthly increase in overall consumer prices.
The energy index grew 2.1% over the month after falling 1.5% in July, pushing its annual advance to 16.3%.
Core consumer prices, which exclude volatile food and energy items, rose 0.3% in August following a 0.2% gain in the previous month.
On an annual basis, core inflation slowed slightly to 2.4% in August from 2.5% recorded in July.
Food prices ticked up 0.1% over the month and posted a 2.7% increase compared to the same period last year.
Shelter costs increased 0.3% in August, while indexes for communication, lodging away from home, and airline fares also recorded monthly gains.

Swedbank Economic Outlook: Resilience amid global uncertainty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:37:31 UTC
21:37:31 KST

The Swedish and global economies have shown resilience despite continued turbulence in the Middle East. Swedish growth is expected to stabilise at around 2 per cent in the coming years, driven mainly by domestic demand. As the recovery continues and inflation rises, the Riksbank will start hiking the policy rate at the end of this year. Regardless of the outcome of Sweden’s upcoming election, the scope for fiscal reform will remain limited, meaning that the election result is expected to have no material impact on economic conditions, according to Swedbank Economic Outlook.
“Swedish household consumption has been increasing since 2024, driven by rising real incomes. We expect this trend to continue. At the same time, we’re seeing a rapid rise in public consumption and investments, mainly because of the ongoing defence build-up. But exports will also support growth in the years to come, making an important contribution to the recovery alongside stronger domestic demand,” says Mattias Persson, Group Chief Economist at Swedbank.
Overall, Swedbank forecasts that Swedish GDP will rise by about 2 per cent annually during 2026–2028. The economic recovery is anticipated to lead to a clear improvement in the labour market from next year, and unemployment is expected to decline to 7.3 per cent by the end of 2028.
The Riksbank will hike the policy rate
Swedish inflation is low but will rise gradually during the next six months. Underlying inflation, excluding energy and temporary fiscal measures, will rise to just over 2 per cent at the end of this year and 2.7 per cent at the beginning of next year. Accordingly, Swedbank expects the Riksbank to hike the policy rate by 0.25 percentage points in November 2026 and again in February 2027, bringing it to 2.25 per cent.
“As inflation rises and the Swedish economic recovery continues, we anticipate that the Riksbank will want to normalise monetary policy. Indicators point to increased price pressure, and delayed impacts of the war in the Middle East are expected to contribute to higher prices for goods and services going forward. Freight prices have also risen, and extreme weather is cause for concern. As inflation approaches a level above the target, we see the Riksbank hiking the policy rate in November and again at the beginning of next year,” says Mattias Persson.
Swedish housing prices rise at a moderate pace
The Swedish housing market has stabilised, with both prices and the number of housing transactions rising. Housing prices are expected to increase by about 4 per cent this year.
“Next year, we expect to see somewhat lower activity in the housing market, as housing demand will be held back by higher mortgage rates resulting from a higher policy rate. We forecast that housing prices will rise by about 2 per cent per year in the next two years,” says Mattias Persson.
The Swedish election will have only a limited impact on the economy
Swedbank expects around SEK 15 billion in unfinanced reforms next year and SEK 25 billion in 2028. This would entail a public-sector budget deficit throughout the two-year forecast period. Sweden’s Maastricht debt will rise gradually but will remain below the debt anchor’s upper limit of 40 per cent of GDP.
“Even though Sweden will replace the surplus target with a balanced-budget target from 2027, the scope for unfinanced reforms will be much more limited than it has been in previous electoral terms. Sweden has an advantage over many other countries thanks to its low public debt, but maintaining that advantage requires a return to the fiscal framework we have established. That’s especially clear if you look at the increase in long-term rates that we’ve seen in recent weeks,” says Mattias Persson.
Climate change is affecting the economy
This summer’s record-breaking heat has affected both the Swedish and European economies. In Sweden, higher electricity prices will cause inflation to rise by 0.2 percentage points this year. Other climate-related risks, such as disruptions to supply chains and global food production, represent a clear upside risk to inflation. In Europe, efforts to restore areas affected by recent fires will be costly, putting additional pressure on already strained public finances.

UK chancellor urged to remove ‘hidden taxes’ from energy bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:37:01 UTC
21:37:01 KST

More than 120 organisations including big businesses and charities have called for the removal of “hidden taxes” added to energy bills to help reduce costs for consumers and prevent businesses closing.
In a letter to the chancellor the signatories – including Energy UK, business trade body the CBI, End Fuel Poverty and Age UK – called for levies amounting to 10% of energy bills that fund policies to be paid for by the government. John Healey is to present his first budget on 28 October.
The signatories want the remainder of the levy funding the building of renewable energy projects to be scrapped. The former chancellor, Rachel Reeves, shifted 75% of the funding to government taxation last year.
The organisations also called for an end to levies to help build nuclear power plants, the funding of the warm homes discount scheme and the feed-in tariff programme, which was closed in 2019 but continues to pay businesses and customers with ongoing contracts for generating their own energy and supplying excess back into the grid.
The letter argues that moving levies off bills would lower the total average household bill by as much as £250 a year, including the £150 saving from Reeves’s moves to cut some levies funding green energy schemes, and lower electricity prices for businesses by 20%.
“The UK is actively sabotaging its own efforts to bring down energy costs by taxing electricity,” said Ed Matthew, director of UK programme at thinktank E3G, which co-authored the letter alongside Energy UK. “Any credible plan to tackle the cost of living and enable reindustrialisation needs to include removing these taxes from bills to the exchequer.”
Last year, Britain’s biggest energy supplier, Octopus, said bills were on track to increase by 20% over the next four years, even if wholesale prices were to drop, because of the increasing amount levied due to the rising cost of government policies.
The outbreak of the Iran war has pushed gas and electricity prices up with households facing the highest energy charges in three years this winter. The energy consultant Cornwall Insight forecast that Ofgem, the UK regulator, will increase its quarterly price cap again in January, putting the average annual bill at £1,872.
The government faces growing pressure to tackle the UK’s energy costs, which are some of the highest in the developed world, after its pre-election promise in 2024 to cut energy bills by £300 a year by 2030.
The letter, which has been backed by 123 organisations, including energy companies, business bodies, banks, retailers and campaigning groups, says UK energy bills are 70% higher now than they were in 2021.
In July, Andy Burnham announced a cut to VAT on domestic energy bills from October, an average saving of £45, although this reduction is currently set to stay in place only until April.
“High electricity prices hurt all of us,” said Dhara Vyas, chief executive of Energy UK. “By taking levies off the bill, the government can show it is serious about tackling fuel poverty and the cost-of-living crisis, growing the economy, and bringing down inflation. Cheaper electricity would have an outsized impact across the economy.”
The letter also warned of the impact on companies, saying: “High energy costs are widely recognised as a significant constraint across the economy, driving business closures and job losses, while simultaneously deterring investment in the UK.”

RNLI lifeboats launched 9,058 times in 2025 but only 109 of those call-outs were to small boats in the Channel, representing 1.2% of its rescue work. Almost 95% of those who crossed the Channel in small boats last year were picked up by the UK Border Force, it said.

Digested week: royal hairlines – Prince George’s hair has such brio as he starts at Eton | Emma Brockes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:35:21 UTC
21:35:21 KST

Monday
In a news cycle to make everyone older than gen Z feel ancient, we start the week anticipating the 25th anniversary of 9/11 at the end. Social media floods with poignant interviews and images from lower Manhattan that day, triggering memories for the rest of us of where, who and how young we were. Ridiculously, I was having my eyebrows done in Hendon, north London, and came out to find a white van pulled over at a crazy angle to the curb, doors flung open, radio cranked up, and people stopped in the street to listen. I remember looking over the city and wondering if I’d seen jets, or explosions.
And just as we’re wrestling with that marker of time, photos of Prince George starting at Eton college come out, juxtaposed with photos of his father doing the same at that age. This triggers an even worse sense of whiplash, as we bob back and forth to 1995. How nice Prince George looks, I think; happier, or at least more confident, than his father had been at that age. After which – and I apologise for this – the main focus of my interest is his hair.
I wonder if the young prince has been bothered by thoughts of the male pattern baldness in his family. The royal men age awkwardly, as we know; sooner or later they all wind up looking like the Spitting Image puppet of Prince Philip (there’s a reference to age me). But here comes the cavalry, in the form of Kate Middleton’s fun, less tightly bred genes, which might send the royal bloodline in a different direction!
“Look, his hair’s standing up on its own,” says a friend, as we scrutinise pictures of the young George. She’s right; while William at that age had the floppy posh fringe, George’s hair has such brio! “I reckon he might keep it,” we conclude, a sure example of generational progress.
Tuesday
How will you spend the remaining decade or so we have left of human life on this planet? As forecasts of an extinction-level event via AI tussle with headlines about the climate feedback loop, I find myself considering, for example, taking out a giant mortgage I won’t have to pay off owing to my own and everyone else’s extinction; pulling out pension money, given retirement isn’t going to happen; or, within easier reach and requiring less decision-making, taking (another) nap, since, times being what they are, we may as well do what we want and to hell with the rest.
The AI thing is scary, not least because of my total ignorance and the sense of powerlessness to do anything – not even throw a bottle, pyrrhically, in the recycling. This latest round of AI doom-mongering kicked off when Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, posted on social media on Tuesday that Open AI and Anthropic were both wantonly ushering humankind towards destruction. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
Coxon is 27 and recently unemployed. I mean, he’s probably just trying to audience-build before launching a podcast, right? On the other hand, a few years ago I met a consultant whose job it was to go into companies and teach people how to formulate better prompts for AI. He told me, half-jokingly but not, that he had taken the precaution of embedding a bunch of code in [insert wherever bunches of code go], in which he identified himself and prompted future AI armies: “If you’re going to go on a murdering spree, leave this guy alone, OK?”
Wednesday
More quotidian ways of being brought down, this week: your toilet flush can give you norovirus and watching TV with your laptop on your stomach can give you something called “toasted skin syndrome”, which I would recommend you don’t Google for images.
First, the toilet. Particles released during a “turbulent” flush cycle can leave microbes floating in the air for up to 20 seconds, according to new findings from Flinders University in Australia. Researchers reviewed 22 studies of toilet-generated aerosols, which sounds like a niche area even by the standards of niche areas. There was, said researchers, a lack of clarity as to whether or not closing the toilet seat might help with this, but, at the risk of sounding anti-intellectual, I think we can deploy our common sense here, right? That, or campaign for the reintroduction of outside toilets.
And then, toasted skin syndrome. In the British Medical Journal, doctors from University hospitals of Leicester NHS trust warned against prolonged contact between your abs and your laptop, citing a fishnet pattern on the skin caused by heat from the device. Customarily, they said, this injury would be seen in older people using hot water bottles or heating pads, but is increasingly showing up in school-age children addicted to their screens. For the avoidance of a scabby and painful mess, you’re advised not to use your midsection as a desk!
Thursday
Two forthcoming documentaries causing excitement this week: Alex Gibney’s four-hour opus about Elon Musk, about which its subject has been whining all week on X; and You Can See Everything, the Elizabeth Holmes documentary, which sounds even wilder. In it, the Theranos founder, currently serving an 11-year prison sentence for fraud, gives startlingly intimate access to Nathan Fielder, better known for his comedy, and the documentary-maker Lance Oppenheim. The trailer alone suggests that despite all the hoopla, it isn’t over-hyped.
After the film’s opening at Telluride, the review site RogerEbert.com said it was “like no other film I’ve ever experienced”. CBS News called it “the wildest documentary ever seen”. Variety called it “a shameless, fascinating, reality-TV-eats-its-tail look at entitled duplicity”. In the trailer, Holmes stares at Fielder while rocking a baby in a bouncer with her foot, the little-girl hair and big Kewpie-doll eyes a reminder of what an uncanny figure she is. Fielder, meanwhile, doesn’t seem fully to have recovered from meeting her. “I’m really struggling to this day to understand what I experienced,” he said in a Q&A after the film, making the whole thing sound like a horror movie I can’t wait to see.
Friday
A beat late, but worth drawing attention to: the presence at Manchester Pride, recently, of a drag rendition of Linda, AKA Ann Droid, from the brilliant BBC show of that name written by Diane Morgan and starring her and Sue Johnston. The figure in lilac fatigues raised a huge cheer, and it’s interesting to note how quickly it has been taken up by camp culture.
This is something you can’t engineer. For example, I have a feeling the creators of Riot Women, a show most lesbians I know disliked and a lot of straight women loved, thought it had queer energy, but I would be surprised if anyone dressed up as those characters at Pride. Diane Morgan, on the other hand, has a sensibility that puts her in a very gay-adjacent zip code and, with antique robotic moves and a shout-out to “Sue! Sue! Sue!”, we love and appreciate her accordingly.
