Behind closed doors: What Washington and the Middle East are saying about Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:34:36 UTC
21:34:36 KST

The fourth annual MEAD Conference, which brings together participants to discuss regional security cooperation, was held this week in Washington at one of the most sensitive and consequential moments since the forum was established.
The gathering came amid uncertainty over the future of the confrontation with Iran, continuing threats across the region and ahead of two elections likely to shape the next phase of relations between Jerusalem and the White House: Israel’s election and the U.S. midterm elections.
This year, representatives from 24 countries traveled to the U.S. capital, including officials and experts from the United States, Israel and other countries across the Middle East — the largest number of countries represented since the conference was founded.
Several countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel also sent representatives, taking advantage of the confidentiality rules that have governed the conference since its inception.
In recent years, MEAD has emerged as an influential forum for shaping ties among Washington, Jerusalem and capitals across the region. Discussions have covered security, intelligence, technology, business, energy and governance, as well as energy security and maritime shipping routes — issues that over the past year have shifted from primarily economic concerns to matters of critical regional security.
One of the keys to the conference’s success is its adherence to the Chatham House Rule, which allows participants to speak candidly without having their remarks or identities publicly attributed. That arrangement has become particularly significant at a time when virtually every public statement in the region is closely scrutinized.
Participants made a number of extraordinary remarks during the conference’s various panels that, because of those confidentiality rules, cannot be reported.
One speaker who drew particular attention was Maj. Gen. Tomer Bar, the former commander of the Israeli Air Force, making his first appearance at an international forum since leaving the post. Several other former senior officials who played central roles in the war with Iran also participated. Their accounts offered striking insights into the conflict that cannot be disclosed under the conference rules.
On the sidelines of the conference, two notable assessments emerged from officials who asked not to be identified.
A former senior Biden administration official offered a bleak assessment of Israel’s standing in American politics. The former official said Democrats, as well as many younger Republicans, are increasingly distancing themselves from Israel, while American Jews are becoming increasingly alienated from the country.
In the former official’s view, Israel’s current government is “erasing Israel’s value” in the eyes of broad segments of the American public.
The official also expressed concern about the future of U.S.-Israel relations if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu forms another government. A different prime minister, the official said, could help “reset” the relationship and ease Israel’s difficulties in the United States — even someone relatively unfamiliar to Americans, such as former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot.
‘Netanyahu has lost credibility’
People close to U.S. President Donald Trump said on the sidelines of the conference that he and his closest advisers are deeply disappointed with Netanyahu.
According to the officials, Netanyahu has “lost credibility” in their eyes over Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. They said frustration with Netanyahu is growing behind the scenes, even if it has not spilled into public statements. As evidence, they pointed to the U.S. administration’s decision not to condemn Britain over sanctions it imposed on Israel.
The Trump associates also expressed anger over Netanyahu’s handling of the U.S. president’s 20-point plan to end the war in Gaza, which they said was drawn up in coordination with the Israeli prime minister. They accused Netanyahu of now seeking to undermine the plan.
On Trump’s support for a pardon for Netanyahu, who is on trial in Israel on corruption charges he denies, the officials said the president’s position was not part of any deal. Rather, they described it as a reflection of Trump’s personal identification with what he views as the persecution of a political ally, with no quid pro quo being sought.
A substantial portion of the conference was devoted to conditions in the Gaza Strip and implementation of the 20-point plan. Participants described some improvement compared with a year ago: Humanitarian aid has increased significantly, the rate of casualties has fallen sharply and, according to some speakers, about 90% of Gaza residents now oppose Hamas, whose popularity is declining.
At the center of the proposed framework is a Palestinian technocratic committee intended to provide services and temporarily administer Gaza, alongside an international body overseeing implementation of the plan.
The proposal calls for recruiting and training a Palestinian police force of between 10,000 and 12,000 officers. Israel is screening a pool of about 220,000 candidates, according to information presented at the conference, and has so far approved about 16,000.
Meanwhile, an international stabilization force is taking shape. It is expected to initially include about 2,500 troops from several countries before expanding with additional personnel contributed by countries in Africa, Asia and Europe.
However, sharp criticism of Israel was heard at the conference over allegations that it is blocking the international force from entering Gaza, preventing the entry of the technocratic committee, which is waiting in Cairo, and preventing 4,000 Palestinian police officers from leaving Gaza for training in Egypt.
The international community also came under criticism. Participants said many countries blame Israel for conditions in Gaza while themselves refusing to accept students or refugees from the territory.
The discussions indicated that Israeli officials see little chance of Hamas voluntarily disarming, but believe the diplomatic route should be exhausted before other measures are taken. That assessment comes amid warnings from the IDF that Hamas is rebuilding its strength and removing weapons from storage.
Iran weakened, but collapse could take years
Much of the conference focused on Iran’s condition in the six months since the latest round of fighting began.
A broad assessment emerged that the government in Tehran has been severely weakened. Participants said Iran’s economy is in dire condition, with the local currency falling to about 2.3 million rials to the dollar and official inflation at roughly 88%, though some believe the actual rate is considerably higher. The government is also struggling to pay public-sector salaries.
Assessments presented at the conference suggested that about 80% of Iranians oppose the government and that signs of internal fractures are emerging within both the political establishment and the military.
Participants stressed, however, that they did not expect an imminent collapse. Rather, they described a gradual process that could take one to three years.
Meanwhile, some pointed to troubling signs surrounding Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, saying he has surrounded himself with some of the most extreme figures in the Iranian establishment amid growing paranoia and fears for the government’s survival.
A person familiar with the matter said on the sidelines of the conference that the memorandum of understanding signed in June between Washington and Tehran had been a “terrible” document that would have funneled hundreds of billions of dollars to Iran, helping preserve the mullah rule and potentially advancing its path toward a nuclear weapon.
The person said hard-liners in Tehran, intoxicated by what they saw as their own strength, ultimately failed to implement the document because they sought complete U.S. capitulation. That refusal, the person argued, prompted Trump to reassess the situation and recognize whom he was dealing with.
Behind the scenes, representatives of several Middle Eastern countries agreed that the region ultimately needs to be rid of Iran’s extremist government, according to discussions at the conference. But there was also an acknowledgment that such an outcome is far from guaranteed and would require considerable patience.
Participants also said that if Iran attacks Israel, Israel’s response would be severe and would focus on Iranian oil infrastructure — a move that some at the conference believe could accelerate the government’s collapse.
Cautious optimism over Lebanon and Syria
The mood surrounding Lebanon was one of cautious optimism. Assessments presented at the conference described Hezbollah as significantly weaker than in the past, though Lebanon’s government is still seen as too weak to confront the Iran-backed terrorist group directly.
Participants also described the trajectory in Syria as positive, though far from ideal.
Some in Israel view Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa as a pragmatist and believe Jerusalem should give him a chance, seeking a security agreement with his government while proceeding with “caution and suspicion.”
Others regard al-Sharaa, a former Islamist insurgent leader, as little more than “a terrorist in a suit.” Both camps, however, agreed that full normalization between Israel and Syria is less realistic for now.
Discussions of the Gulf states revealed a shared concern over Iran as well as sharp criticism of the Muslim Brotherhood. In some sessions, participants described the Islamist movement as more dangerous than Iran itself, arguing that dialogue with Tehran remains possible despite the threat it poses.
Participants also voiced fundamental opposition to allowing any single actor to control strategic shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandab Strait. Control of the waterways, they argued, is a global problem rather than merely a regional one.
Discussions also touched on a long-term U.S. strategy to develop an oil pipeline that would bypass the Strait of Hormuz and expand refining capacity on U.S. soil, reducing dependence on the strategic waterway.
Israel-Saudi ties ‘better than they appear’
The outlook for expanding the Abraham Accords, the U.S.-brokered normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab states, was mixed.
There was skepticism that Saudi Arabia would normalize relations with Israel in the near future, but participants stressed that relations between Jerusalem and Riyadh remain better than public appearances suggest.
The Trump administration has not abandoned its ambition to expand the Abraham Accords, participants said, and developments underway behind the scenes could potentially bear fruit after the elections.
The discussions also emphasized that current military and intelligence cooperation between Israel and the United States is at an unprecedented level — even when compared with Washington’s historic alliance with Britain.
Israel’s domestic political situation also featured prominently. Participants assessed that after the coming election, Israel will need to form a broad government capable of addressing two major unresolved issues: legislation governing military conscription for Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, men and the government’s efforts to overhaul the judiciary. Both were described as potential “time bombs” if no solution is found.
Participants also noted that, for the first time in years, there is no significant public pressure within Israel to withdraw from territory its forces currently hold — whether in Lebanon, Syria or Gaza. Some at the conference viewed that situation as an opportunity to shape a new diplomatic reality in the region before other actors fill the vacuum.
China’s role was another subject of discussion. According to assessments presented at the conference, Beijing is no longer purchasing Iranian oil, though it previously supplied Tehran with raw materials for its missile industry in exchange for oil.
Participants said Washington has been sending Beijing clear messages on the issue while continuing to impose secondary sanctions on entities accused of helping Iran circumvent restrictions, including banks in Turkey and other actors in India.

Will Arab parties play the kingmaker in fractured Israeli polls Netanyahu is expected to lose?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:34:14 UTC
21:34:14 KST

The numbers game has intensified in the run-up to next month’s general election in Israel, seen as one of the most consequential in the country’s history.
Pre-election public polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ultra-right bloc is unlikely to win a 61-seat majority in the 120-member parliament, known as the Knesset, to form a government.
The Zionist opposition, led by former chief of Israeli occupation forces Gadi Eisenkot and ex-premier Naftali Bennett, is also expected to fall short of the 61-seat threshold required for government formation.
In other words, basic arithmetic shows either political bloc will need support from Arab parties – which are typically backed by Palestinian citizens of Israel comprising one-fifth of the country’s population of 10.3 million – to form a government.
According to a Channel 12 survey, Netanyahu’s allies are projected to win 52 seats, while the anti-Netanyahu camp is expected to win 57 seats. Arab parties are likely to win 11 seats.
This shows the Arab parties – long treated by Zionist parties as radioactive – may hold the key to government formation after the October elections.
Israeli elections are based on nationwide proportional representation, which means voters don’t vote for a particular member of the Knesset.
Instead, they vote for a “list”, which is the official slate of candidates that a party submits to the election-holding body.
A party winning 10 seats means the first 10 names on that party’s list will become members of the Knesset.
Sometimes, several parties make an alliance and contest polls under a “joint list”. The strategy helps small parties reduce the risk of falling short of the 3.25 percent vote threshold – the minimum percentage of total votes that a party must receive to enter the Knesset.
Gokhan Batu, a Levant studies analyst at the Ankara-based Centre for Middle Eastern Studies, tells TRT World that Arab parties have little chance of formally joining the new cabinet.
“There is almost no prospect of the Arab parties, either individually or through a joint list, formally joining the government,” he says.
Two main Arab-majority lists are contesting the October election.
The first is a Joint List representing an alliance of three mostly Arab groups – Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad.
These parties merged to avoid falling short of the electoral threshold of 3.25 percent total votes.
The other is the United Arab List or Ra'am, which is led by Mansour Abbas.
According to Batu, Ra’am “clearly supports the opposition bloc” and does not appear at risk of falling below the 3.25 percent threshold.
The Hadash-Ta’al-Balad joint list is also expected to safely cross the threshold, he says.
“Together, the Arab parties could win around 10 to 12 seats,” he adds.
Nimrod Goren, president and founder of the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies (Mitvim), tells TRT World that the Arab parties will be “of importance” if current polling numbers materialise on election day.
“But not in the sense of picking either side (Netanyahu or an opposition leader) to form the coalition,” he notes.
Supporting Netanyahu is something that Arab parties are “not considering at all”.
He says the real question is whether Jewish opposition parties will accept Arab support – or even abstention – to sustain a minority coalition government, one that is formed by a political bloc that collectively holds fewer than 61 seats.
“Arab parties aren’t likely to actually join the coalition. At the moment, the opposition is split on the issue,” Goren says.
Are Arab parties radioactive?
Zionist parties don’t usually treat Arab parties like ordinary coalition partners. In fact, opposition groups use the inclusion of Arab parties in the cabinet as a weapon to delegitimise the ruling coalition in the name of national security.
After the October 7, 2023, attacks, there is even less appetite among most Israeli Jews to include any Arab parties in a coalition.
Batu says the issue is more complicated than a simple refusal by Zionist groups to cooperate with Arab parties.
“Netanyahu himself previously sought Ra’am’s support,” he notes.
Ra’am joined the 2021-22 Bennett-Lapid government as a coalition partner, becoming the first Arab party in decades to join a ruling coalition.
“Ra’am’s participation also became one of the main political vulnerabilities of the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021,” Batu notes.
“Arab support may be strategically valuable when forming a coalition, but it can also carry a considerable political cost,” he says.
“The main obstacle lies in the attitudes of the wider public and the parties’ electoral bases,” he notes.
Bennett, the former premier and one of the main opponents of Netanyahu, has said that any future government that he leads will include only Zionist parties. This is despite the fact that his previous coalition included Ra’am.
Similarly, Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the right-wing party Yisrael Beitein, has ruled out forming a minority government that would depend on Arab votes.
According to Goren, the Arab parties are motivated first by a desire to remove Netanyahu and his ultra-nationalist partners.
“Some of the leading Arab politicians indicated that they will be ready to do whatever it takes politically to enable a different coalition to be formed,” he says.
“So, it is not likely that there will be much give-and-take on policy issues to enable it,” he adds.
What’s on Arab parties’ agenda?
One common assumption is that Arab seats, seemingly indispensable for government formation, would force Zionist parties to extend concessions on Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Both experts disagree.
“Frankly, a coalition established with Ra’am’s support would be unlikely to produce meaningful gains concerning Gaza or the occupied West Bank,” Batu says.
That’s because Ra’am doesn’t treat these issues as the “central purpose of its participation”.
Abbas of Ra’am justified joining the 2021-22 Bennett-Lapid government to his electorate purely in terms of the benefits it could secure for the social, economic and infrastructure needs of Arab citizens of Israel, Batu notes.
Israeli-Arab parties advocate for a two-state solution. They view the establishment of an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel – based on the 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital – as the only viable path to lasting peace.
Parties like Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad consider this solution as a core ideological and national goal.
Even the more pragmatically focused Ra'am party believes that Palestinian self-determination in Gaza and the occupied West Bank is essential for resolving the broader conflict.
Both Bennett and Lieberman currently rule out a coalition with Arab parties anyway, Batu notes.
“The situation is, therefore, considerably more complicated than the parliamentary arithmetic alone suggests,” he says.
Given that the immediate goal of Arab parties seems to be the end of a Netanyahu-led government, any room for bargaining over headline issues like Gaza and the occupied West Bank is limited.
“The right thing to do is to have Jewish-Arab cooperation within the opposition, to enable Israel a better government and prospects for a brighter future,” Goren says.

No vaccine-autism link, finds WHO review
Unknown

21:33:22 KST

WHO found no causal link between vaccines and autism after reviewing studies from 2010 to August 2025.
NEW DELHI: At a time when the debate has resurfaced in the United States, a 15-year review by the World Health Organization (WHO) has reaffirmed that there is no causal link between vaccines and autism. The findings not only dismantle persistent myths but also underscore the safety of vaccines, reinforcing the critical role immunisation plays in public health worldwide.Autism spectrum disorder is a group of neurodevelopmental conditions that can affect social interaction and communication skills, with signs typically emerging in early childhood.
The controversy began in 1998, when a study led by British doctor Andrew Wakefield claimed that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine could be linked to autism. The study was later retracted byThe Lancet, but the claim continued to spread.The issue gained fresh attention in the US on Aug 10, when President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking changes to childhood vaccine recommendations and raised the issue of autism during the signing ceremony. Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has long questioned vaccine safety, backed the move. However, WHO’s Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety has repeatedly examined the issue and found no evidence of a causal relationship.
The findings are particularly relevant for India, where measles-rubella vaccination is part of the national immunisation programme, with the govt working towards measles-rubella elimination by 2026. The Union health ministry launched the National Zero Measles-Rubella Elimination Campaign 2025-26 in April 2025, with children up to five years targeted for two doses of the vaccine. Its 2025-26 annual report puts first-dose coverage at 98.6% for April-Dec 2025.The WHO review, published on Sept 3, assessed peer-reviewed studies from 2010 to Aug 2025. It included 31 primary studies and five meta-analyses, along with 21 narrative reviews. Methodologically the most rigorous studies did not support a causal association between vaccines, including those containing thiomersal, and autism spectrum disorder.
Studies reporting a positive association were rated as having very low strength of evidence and high risk of bias, while none of the meta-analyses supported a causal link. The review also found no convincing evidence that thiomersal, an organomercury preservative, causes autism. WHO said the overall evidence supports the safety of current vaccines.WHO also cautioned that the rise in autism diagnoses should not automatically be attributed to vaccination. Improved identification, broader diagnostic criteria and greater awareness could be contributing to higher diagnosis rates.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Marine Le Pen’s secret weapon: why three presidential losses have not stopped her rise
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:33:00 EEST
21:33:00 KST

Marine Le Pen’s secret weapon: why three presidential losses have not stopped her rise
Marine Le Pen enters the 2027 presidential race in a position that would once have seemed difficult to reconcile.
She has already lost the presidency three times.
In July, the Paris Court of Appeal upheld her conviction over the misuse of European Parliament funds. Her party, the far right Rassemblement National, or RN, has meanwhile produced Jordan Bardella, a younger leader who can poll as well as she does and increasingly cultivates a political identity of his own.
Yet Le Pen begins the campaign far ahead of every other potential candidate.
Defeates that change you
There is an irony at the heart of Emmanuel Macron's political legacy.
His victory in 2017 broke the party system that had governed France for decades. The Socialist Party and the traditional right had alternated in power throughout most of the Fifth Republic. Neither reached the presidential runoff that year. Macron instead assembled much of the moderate centre left and centre right behind a new political force and argued that the old division between left and right had become obsolete.
By weakening the parties that had traditionally occupied the space between the governing centre and the extremes, Macron also strengthened the position of the forces opposing him from outside it.
Macronism and Le Penism consequently became mutually structuring political poles. Macron could present himself as the European, liberal and republican barrier against nationalism. Le Pen could present herself as the principal alternative to a political order increasingly identified with Macron.
This suited both sides electorally.
Macron defeated her twice, but every campaign in which the Élysée portrayed Le Pen as the principal threat also reinforced her status as its principal competitor. By 2022, their second consecutive runoff no longer looked like an accident. It looked like the new structure of French presidential politics.
The contrast with Jean Marie Le Pen is revealing.
His qualification for the second round in 2002 was treated as a national political emergency. Jacques Chirac subsequently won with more than 82% of the vote. Marine Le Pen qualified in 2017 and again in 2022. Her repeated defeats should, in principles, have weakened her. They also produced something more useful: presidential familiarity.
For an ordinary candidate, losing three times can signal exhaustion. For Le Pen, those defeats also demonstrate that she repeatedly gets closer to the Élysée than almost anyone else.
The system around her has meanwhile become less coherent. The French party system is fragmented but increasingly characterised by the dominance of one political force, the RN, because none of its competitors possesses a comparable electoral position. The old governing parties remain diminished, Macron's camp has struggled to become a durable political organisation independent of its founder, and the left remains divided over both leadership and strategy.
Le Pen is therefore no longer merely the candidate of an outsider movement trying to force its way into French politics. She represents its most consolidated electoral bloc.
Macron will leave the Élysée in 2027 because the Constitution prevents him from seeking a third consecutive term, and Le Pen has never been closer to be the next resident of Elysée’s Palace.
The economic explanation for Le Pen's strength requires more care than the language of French "decline" sometimes suggests.
France is not an economy in collapse. It remains one of Europe's largest economies, with strong infrastructure, high productivity in many sectors, major industrial capabilities and significant foreign investment. Even after a difficult year, France remained Europe's leading destination by number of foreign investments projects in 2025.
Yet the direction is less reassuring.
EY recorded a 17% fall in such projects last year, while several European competitors gained ground, and investors increasingly identified political stability, regulatory predictability and costs among France's weaknesses.
Meanwhile, France's political problem is not the absence of resources or potential weaknesses identified by financial analysts. It is increasingly the distance between the resources the country possesses and what citizens believe they receive from them.
France combines high taxes and extensive public spending with correspondingly high expectations of the state. Citizens expect functioning hospitals and schools, reliable transport, pensions, policing and a degree of equality between territories.
When these services appear less reliable while debt remains high and successive governments struggle to pass budgets or sustain parliamentary majorities, dissatisfaction questions whether the state remains capable of delivering what it promises.
Despite a court conviction and a younger rival
Marine Le Pen has spent much of her leadership pursuing what the French call dédiabolisation, the attempt to remove the stigma inherited from her father and the old Front National. She expelled Jean Marie Le Pen from the party, abandoned some of his most provocative language, changed the organisation's name and professionalised its public presentation.
The RN continues to defend positions on immigration, nationality and "national preference" that remain far outside much of the old governing consensus.
Normalisation has gradually become reciprocal.
French political life has also changed its relationship with the RN. Fifteen years of presidential campaigns, television appearances, parliamentary debates and electoral victories have progressively gave the RN institutional legitimacy. The RN then acquired something the old Front National rarely possessed: institutional legitimacy.
It won municipalities. It sent 89 MPs to the National Assembly in 2022. Its parliamentary presence became larger again after the 2024 elections. Its politicians became regular participants in institutional life rather than permanent outsiders to it.
French voters have watched Marine Le Pen’s debate two presidential elections against Macron. They have watched her lose. They have watched her return.
The RN has not necessarily become moderate, but it has become ordinary.
Le Pen's legal situation should, in theory, have interrupted this progression.
The Paris Court of Appeal upheld her conviction in July over the misuse of European Parliament funds and sentenced her to three years' imprisonment, two suspended and one to be served under electronic monitoring, alongside a €100,000 fine.
The court reduced her ineligibility sentence to 45 months, 30 of them suspended, meaning that the effective portion had already been served and no longer prevented her from running in 2027. Le Pen immediately confirmed her candidacy and appealed to the Court of Cassation.
As things stand, she remains eligible, although the legal process is not over.
The outcome leaves her in a politically peculiar position. She was not acquitted, but neither was she removed from the election.
That allows loyals supporters to interpret the proceedings through an existing populist narrative in which institutions seek to prevent voters from making their own choice.
Le Pen increasingly presents institutional constraints in precisely these terms, treating popular sovereignty as a competing source of legitimacy. Yet the evidence does not justify assuming that conviction has created a broad martyr effect.
The September Ipsos poll instead suggests polarisation. Her electoral base remains exceptionally loyal, but almost half of voters continue to say that she worries them a great deal.
Jordan Bardella creates a different challenge to her personal position.
His ascent initially appears to undermine the idea that Le Pen herself retains an exceptional appeal. He is younger, carries less of the Le Pen family's historical baggage and has demonstrated that he can match or occasionally outperform her in presidential polling. The RN's further normalisation may eventually require Marine Le Pen to recede.
But Bardella's emergence can work in both directions.
For most of the Front National's history, the movement appeared inseparable from one family. Bardella demonstrates that the RN can produce a nationally recognised leader without the Le Pen surname.
The party consequently looks less like a family vehicle and more like a durable political institution with a succession mechanism of its own.
The man who proves that Marine Le Pen is replaceable may therefore also make her candidacy appear less risky, because an RN victory no longer implies entrusting the country to a movement entirely dependent on one individual.
Their relationship is not without tension.
Bardella has recently distanced himself from elements of Le Pen's programme on pensions and the proposed ban on Islamic headscarves in public, reinforcing the impression that he is developing a somewhat different, more economically orthodox profile. But that divergence also reveals how far the RN has travelled. It can now contain different political styles within the same national leadership.
Bardella is Le Pen's successor, insurance policy and increasingly her rival.
He is also evidence that the RN's electorate is no longer reducible to personal loyalty towards Marine Le Pen.
Le Pen does not need France to love her
This is perhaps the most important point in understanding her position seven months before the election.
A French presidential candidate does not need majority enthusiasm in the first round. Le Pen needs her political bloc to remain more cohesive than those competing with it, qualify comfortably for the second round and then prevent the rest of the electorate from coordinating effectively enough to stop her.
That is where her current advantage becomes structural.
Data gives her between 34% and 36% in the first round while her competitors remain far behind and and divided among several political families.
Her support is unusually transferable from one election to the next: more than nine out of ten of her 2022 voters currently intend to return to her.
Her position is therefore strong, but victory is not inevitable.
A large part of the country still rejects her.
Her conviction could become more damaging during an actual campaign. Bardella may eventually prove a stronger RN candidate. A credible opponent from the centre, centre right or left could still consolidate voters who currently share little except their opposition to Le Pen. Le Pen's greatest advantage is not that a majority of French voters actively want her, but that her opponents may struggle to organise a majority against her.
For much of Marine Le Pen's career, the burden rested on her.
She had to persuade enough voters that she and her party were acceptable enough to govern France. After three presidential defeats, the institutionalisation of the RN, the collapse of the old party system and years of economic and political frustration, part of that burden has moved elsewhere.
Her opponents must now persuade voters not only that Marine Le Pen represents a risk, but that uniting to prevent her presidency still offers something safer and more credible in return.
Le Pen’s advantage is not that France has embraced her, but that the old machinery for stopping her has weakened. In 2027, her opponents may find that fear of the RN is no longer enough to build a majority.
Charlotte Guillou-Clerc,
Journalist (France)

Memo to King Charles: you can’t stop the Sussexes’ reality show bandwagon. You only spice up the script  | Marina Hyde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:31:49 UTC
21:31:49 KST

Once again, it has been a lively week for the Real Housewives of Windsor franchise, with Harry and Meghan back in the UK for precisely 12 days before the king fired out a letter via the lord chamberlain on Monday, reminding viewers that the Sussexes are “private citizens” and not to treat them as working royals. You have to say the producers on this unscripted reality show are truly at the top of their game with these targeted provocations. Harry and Meghan duly took the bait and issued an intemperately hurt rejoinder – but we’ll get to that in a bit.
First, let’s deal with King Charles’s missive to “relevant senior stakeholders across government, the military and Lord Lieutenancies”. Ugh. Not to be too aesthetically sensitive, but I think we can all live without the sovereign being reduced to the ghastly language of “relevant senior stakeholders”. What next? Seeking “buy-in” for ribbon-cutting events and referring to posies as “high levels of audience engagement”? It does all rather reinforce the idea that the Windsors’ cringe-makingly self-styled “the firm” really is some dreary mid-range company with a wan Meet Our Team page on its website, in which Prince William – carefully photographed without a tie – explains that he “enjoys long walks with the dog and is a passionate Aston Villa supporter”.
Either way, the letter sent on Charles’s behalf was guaranteed to send the plot into overdrive, much as it does in any Real Housewives franchise when one of the cast sends a cease-and-desist letter to one of the others. (An event that basically feels like it can occur weekly.) Typically these letters then become dramatic drivers. Far from suppressing stories as supposedly intended, they always end up sparking whole new public debates and plotlines in themselves. This is what happened with the Windsors this week – and, indeed, was always going to happen, given the appearance of a pre-emptive slapdown.
The royal household must be able to see that the key thing about the Sussexes is that they are forever desperate to be taken seriously, like a music act that was put together on a TV talent show but now wants you to think they’re up there with Patti Smith and Nick Cave.
And so it was that Meghan and Harry’s spokesperson immediately hit back in public, announcing that the couple “were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance”. Ouch. Never show weakness, guys! A briefing given to the Telegraph added that: “The Sussexes prefer the term ‘public figures’, and would have liked an acknowledgment that, on a personal level, they remained members of the royal family, despite no longer receiving public funding.”
As indicated, this all hints at a season of endlessly messy dramas to come, given it took less than a fortnight of the pair being back in the country before a public blow-up occurred. In terms of the kind of bizarro unintended consequences you might see on a Housewives episode when someone’s kicked off at a girls’ spa day, the military chief of Uganda promptly announced his country was pulling out of Prince Harry’s Invictus Games because they didn’t want to participate in something “that does not have His Majesty’s approval”. What can you say? Other than: deploy the reaction gifs.
You don’t have to be a reality TV obsessive to spot the faultlines here that should guarantee that the Sussexes’ unexpected return to the UK will result in endless drink tosses. It’s all there in their immediate reaction. Harry and Meghan are really wholly formed reality TV stars now. Not only do they do the tit-for-tat media release to move the plot along, but they also let you know what they were feeling when they read the original press-released letter from the king. In reality TV, moments like these are gleaned from “master interviews” (MIVs), filmed at the end of a season to provide useful retrospective commentary that the producers can cut the main action with. So you’ll see Hell’s Kitchen contestants helpfully reflecting on the scene you’ve just watched, and going: “And I’m standing there thinking – Chef Ramsay is going to go crazy when he sees this.” Or, in this case, “I was a little surprised not to have been told by Chef Ramsay about this in advance.”
This is precisely how the Sussexes now conduct public life, and it remains incompatible with the way the royal household does it. For all their supposed desire for a quiet life, Harry and Meghan have done that thing that the Beckhams – and indeed the secessionist Beckham-Peltzes – seemingly cannot help but do, where they claim to enjoy privacy but in fact live life out loud in a way that has come to feel normal to them but is really anything but.
Which brings us back to the burning question of why on earth you’d move back somewhere you are on the record – multiple times – as absolutely loathing in all its aspects. Increasingly, and faster than predicted, it feels like the answer to that is “for content” – scripted or otherwise. It’s fairly difficult to see the Sussexes’ relocation as anything other than laying the groundwork for a sequel to the only story of theirs that has ever rated with audiences: their own struggle with the forces of the British establishment/media/enemies within the royal household. Or as Real Housewives of Beverly Hills star Lisa Rinna once put it – and her head would be right up there on the franchise’s Mount Rushmore – “you better believe I’m gonna talk about it”.

The RDIF will support the initiative by leveraging its investment expertise and international partnership network, he emphasized.

European Commission pushes for all-English trade deals despite French opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:31:23 UTC
21:31:23 KST

France's umbrage at the anglophone-only presentation might complicate the ratification of the EU-India trade deal, even though it supports the deal itself and considers India a strategic partner.
The European Commission transmitted the EU-India trade deal, clinched last January, to EU member states for ratification on Friday – but only in English, despite opposition from France.
The EU executive wants to fast-track the ratification process for trade deals by skipping the translation of agreements into the bloc's 24 official languages.
“When President von der Leyen went to India in January to conclude negotiations for this landmark trade agreement, she made a commitment to try to get it over the line within this calendar year,” Commission Deputy Chief Spokesperson Olof Gill said on Friday. “That is still our ambition.”
However, as first reported by Euronews in March, Paris is rejecting the idea of providing single-language documents for fast ratification, arguing that translation is an obligation – and not only into French, one of the working languages of the EU institutions.
Access for EU and national lawmakers to EU trade deals in all languages is a concern for the French, who consider that those agreements contain technical provisions whose nuances can only be understood once translated.
However, the approval of the European Parliament is necessary for the ratification of EU trade deals, and sometimes also that of EU national parliaments.
Translation before the European Parliament's vote
The Commission said on Friday that the EU-India trade deal will be translated after the signature process by EU countries, before it is transferred to the European Parliament. Once ratified, it will then be published in the Official Journal in all the official EU languages.
“What we are proposing to do is that the agreement will be signed in the language of negotiations, i.e. English, and all EU language versions will become available as soon as possible during the process and certainly before the agreement will be voted in the European Parliament," Gill added.
It is not clear whether the Commission’s commitment will be enough to ease French opposition to this new style of ratification procedure.
Paris already led opposition to the EU-Mercosur agreement, clinched in December 2024, but for trade reasons. EU farmers feared unfair competition from Latin American products on the EU market.
Since then, ratification of the deal with the Latin American countries has been suspended after MEPs seized the Court of Justice of the European Union with a legal referral.
This time, French opposition might be driven by non-trade-related considerations, as France supports the EU-India trade deal in principle.
The deal does not target farm products and was clinched with a partner seen by Paris as the most strategic one in the Asia-Pacific region.

At least 46,000 displaced as fighting escalates in Yemen: UN migration agency

Rania Abushamala
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
At least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Friday, warning that the figure is rising “by the hour.”
The UN agency called on all parties to the conflict to guarantee safe humanitarian access and protect civilians, aid workers and humanitarian assets on the ground.
“Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left,” IOM Director General Amy Pope said in a statement.
“As fighting spreads, reaching people with lifesaving assistance is becoming harder. We urgently need safe, unimpeded access,” she added.
Pope urged all parties to protect civilians and humanitarian personnel, as well as the supplies, vehicles and facilities used to deliver aid.
The displacement figure covers Yemen’s western coast and Taiz province as of Thursday and continues to rise, according to the agency.
Large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving the strategic port city of Mokha overnight, carrying their belongings.
The IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix team is working to compile updated figures to guide the humanitarian response, but widespread telecommunications disruptions have made communication with affected areas extremely difficult.
New arrivals have been reported in the southern provinces of Lahj and Aden, while others are reportedly moving north toward Ibb province.
Entire villages in Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi and Al-Ma’afer have reportedly been emptied as clashes moved closer to populated areas, the agency said.
The Mokha–Taiz road, a key supply route, has also reportedly been cut off, placing additional pressure on host communities receiving displaced families.
The IOM said it had been assisting displaced people through its shelter, land and property teams, Camp Coordination and Camp Management operations, and other field units since the beginning of the conflict.
However, all operational movements were temporarily suspended Friday because of the “deteriorating security environment.”
The agency urged the warring parties to guarantee safe and sustained humanitarian access, protect aid workers, facilities and assets nationwide, and restore communications and transport routes needed to deliver assistance.
Emergency supplies have already been depleted by the response to last month's floods, while the most urgent needs include shelter, food, water, household items, healthcare and protection services, according to the IOM.

Italian liberal politician Emma Bonino died Friday at the age of 78, prompting tributes from across the political spectrum for the civil-rights activist and former European commissioner.

Advertisement
A veteran of Italy’s fight for civil and women’s rights, Bonino played a key role in the campaigns that led to the legalization of divorce and abortion in the country during the 1970s.
In 2017, she co-founded the liberal More Europe party, which paid tribute to her on Friday. “Activist, parliamentarian, minister, European commissioner. Always radically free,” party leader Riccardo Magi wrote on X. “Her life was a long struggle against everything that denies freedoms.”
Carlo Calenda, leader of the liberal Italian Action party, said: “The last great protagonist of the civil battles that led to the modernization of this country,” adding that “a piece of Italian and European political history is passing away.”
Bonino’s endeavors extended beyond Italy. She served as a European commissioner in the 1990s, notably overseeing an increase in humanitarian aid to countries and regions affected by some of the most devastating conflicts of the decade, including the Balkans, Rwanda and Afghanistan.
“Emma Bonino has never waited for the world to be ready. She has always chosen to move forward, showing the way to others,” wrote European Parliament President Roberta Metsola. “The Europe she fought for will miss her.”

Beijing can rewrite China’s property rules, but it can’t undo the damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:30:05 UTC
21:30:05 KST

Beijing can rewrite China’s property rules, but it can’t undo the damage
A narrower supply pipeline, industry consolidation and years of balance-sheet repair are inevitable as China seeks stability, rather than a perpetual housing boom
Michael Han is assistant president and Shanghai general manager at Yuepu Technology Group.
Financial markets are notoriously prone to mistaking a fundamental institutional shift for a temporary liquidity crisis. The futurist Roy Amara is often credited with the observation that people tend to overestimate the short-term effect of a transformation while underestimating its long-term impact. China’s real-estate sector is furnishing a textbook case of an analogous dynamic.
On August 28, Chinese housing authorities and financial regulators announced a package to overhaul the commercial housing sales system. The measures include a gradual shift towards sales of completed homes, tighter supervision of presale escrow accounts, new project-based financing arrangements and extended mortgage terms. The announcement initially sparked excitement among global financial centres eager for another round of sweeping property stimulus.
Equity markets quickly delivered a far more complicated verdict. When trading resumed on Monday, shares of major property developers plummeted. China Jinmao and Greentown China dropped by more than 10 per cent; China Resources Land and other major builders also suffered losses. This whiplash – early optimism followed by a punishing sell-off – underscored a disconnect between policy intentions and investor expectations. The market initially misinterpreted Beijing’s intent, only to reprice as the reality of structural deleveraging set in.
Global investors often evaluate Beijing through a simple binary lens, expecting either aggressive credit expansion or policy neglect. The recent regulatory actions reveal a more deliberate objective. By reshaping the architecture of project sales and commercial credit, Beijing is not attempting to revive the speculative boom of past decades. It is rewriting the institutional rules for an industry that has entered a mature, lower-growth era.
For over two decades, real estate expanded through a high-leverage feedback loop. After the 1998 housing reforms that ended state welfare housing allocation, rapid urbanisation created immense demand. Municipal governments relied heavily on land sale proceeds for revenue, while state commercial banks provided abundant credit. Developers acquired land with borrowed capital, sold flats long before completion, used presale proceeds to clear debt and buy more land, and repeated the cycle.
10:57
Boom, bust and borrow: Has China’s housing market tanked?
That expansion produced vast urban infrastructure but also built a financial system dependent on rising land values, high leverage and rapid inventory turnover. Once housing prices softened, the machine operated in reverse.

Russia’s central bank left its key interest rate unchanged for the first time in a year and a half, holding it at 14% after a meeting of its board of directors.
The bank noted that Russia’s economy is “growing at a moderate pace” in the third quarter of 2026, though price pressure has “increased significantly” in recent months. “Underlying price growth accelerated to an annualized 5–6%, primarily due to the effect of a temporary reduction in production capacity in certain industries. As these effects fade and aggregate demand growth remains restrained, the decline in underlying inflation will resume,” the regulator stated in a press release.
Under its baseline scenario, the central bank expects inflation to run 6.0–7.0% in 2026 and return to 4.0% in 2027 if current policy holds.
The bank had cut the key rate 10 times in a row before this, a cycle that began in June 2025. The last two reductions were 25 basis points apiece: the rate fell from 14.5% to 14.25% in June 2026, then to the current 14% in July.
Days before this, Vladimir Putin, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum on September 3, said that Russia does not have an “overly tight monetary policy,” adding that flooding the economy with money is dangerous and that the government and the central bank are deliberately suppressing inflation, and that this goal is being achieved.
Earlier in the summer, Putin twice publicly called for the central bank to lower its rate; others made the same demand, including Sberbank CEO German Gref, who spoke of Russia’s economy “overcooling.”

Anthropic reveals five biological weapon risk cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Anthropic reveals five biological weapon risk cases
Anthropic says it has caught scientists using its AI models for research that could help develop biological weapons, including work aimed at making dangerous pathogens more transmissible and harmful.
Five cases of biological researchers using Claude raised serious security concerns, according to a company threat intelligence report published on Thursday.
One case, to be carried out at a military research institute, involved gain-of-function research aimed at making the chikungunya virus more transmissible and better able to evade the immune system.
Another scientist used Claude while researching highly dangerous bird flu and ways the virus could adapt to mammals. Other cases involved work on viruses related to smallpox and the redesign of dangerous toxins.
Anthropic said some of the researchers went to considerable lengths to get around its restrictions, including hiding their identities, routing traffic through other countries and using services designed to bypass safety controls. The accounts involved have been banned while the services used to get around the safeguards have been shut down.
The company stopped short of saying the scientists were definitely trying to build biological weapons. However, it warned that sophisticated actors may deliberately hide malicious aims behind legitimate-looking research.
Anthropic acknowledged that its AI is becoming more capable, saying older models were too weak to meaningfully assist sophisticated users with dangerous biological research, but that it can no longer make the same assurance about today’s systems.
The findings come just weeks after US scientists used AI to design complete viral genomes and successfully created 16 functioning viruses that did not previously exist in nature. Although those viruses infected bacteria rather than humans, researchers have warned that the experiment demonstrates how quickly AI’s biological capabilities are advancing.
Anthropic’s report also detailed other alleged misuse of Claude, including cyberattacks, surveillance, propaganda, fraud and assistance with conventional weapons such as missiles, armed drones and bombs.
Just days before the threat assessment was published, Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger publicly stated that he believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade, adding that the company still has no clear plan for safely controlling superintelligence.
His admission came after another Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, resigned, accusing Anthropic and OpenAI of ignoring the “civilizational stakes” and “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He separately warned that sufficiently advanced AI could hack critical infrastructure or help create “extinction-level bioweapons.”

"This is a shameful and immoral behavior that can elicit nothing but shame and condemnation from any normal human being," the ministry said.

In Ukraine, the underground resistance organization is remembered primarily for its fight against Soviet rule during and after World War II.
In Poland, the group is mainly remembered due to its role in the Volyn massacres, a mass killing of tens of thousands of Poles in what is today western Ukraine, then under Nazi occupation. Thousands of Ukrainians were killed in retaliatory attacks.
The UPA monument is "offending the (Polish) victims" of the Volyn massacres and "must be dismantled," Braun said in a post on social media.
The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry, in turn, denounced Braun for turning "remembrance and respect for the dead into a circus show to score political goals."

Ukraine's reaction came just as Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski was visiting Kyiv.
Braun, representing Poland in the European Parliament, is known for ultranationalist, antisemitic positions and provocative political stunts, as well as sharp criticism of the current Polish government. Braun's party polls around 8% ahead of Poland's parliamentary elections next year.

FACTBOX: BRICS association profile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:26:56 UTC
21:26:56 KST

TASS-FACTBOX. The 18th Summit of the BRICS interstate association will be held in New Delhi, India, on September 12-13. The event will be held under the motto "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability." Among the issues on the agenda of the summit are the creation of mechanisms for settlements in national currencies, cooperation in the field of artificial intelligence, technologies, energy and critical infrastructure. This year, India is hosting the BRICS summit for the fourth time.
TASS editors have prepared a special feature on the history of BRICS and its evolution.
Creation and goals
The organization was established in 2006 upon Russia’s initiative. The organization’s co-founders were Brazil, Russia, India and China. The acronym BRIC was derived from the names of the association’s member countries in English. After South Africa joined them in 2011, the association was renamed to BRICS.
At the first summit in Yekaterinburg in June 2009, its goal was defined as "the development of consistent, active, pragmatic and open dialogue and cooperation between countries." Later, BRICS declared it was not a bloc or antagonist to any third parties.
BRICS expansion
At a remote meeting of the quintet’s foreign ministers in May 2022, China came up with an idea to launch the process of expanding BRICS, with the aim of increasing its membership and influence in the world. By August 2023, about 20 countries had applied to join the organization. According to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, all BRICS members were in favor of admitting like-minded countries "that believe in multipolarity and in the need for more democratic and fair international relations."
At the 15th summit held in Johannesburg (South Africa) on August 22-24, 2023, it was announced that six countries - Argentina, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE - would join the organization. However, in December 2023 Argentina changed its mind (after President Javier Milei came to power). Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has retained the status of an invited country.
Ethiopia, Egypt, Iran, and the UAE became full members of BRICS on January 1, 2024, while Indonesia joined the association on January 6, 2025, bringing the total number of members to ten. The expanded group has been informally referred to as BRICS Plus.
At the 16th BRICS Summit, held in Kazan in October 2024, a new format of participation was introduced - the BRICS partnership - which became a mandatory step before becoming full member.
On January 1, 2025, Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Thailand, Uganda, and Uzbekistan received BRICS partner status, followed by Nigeria on January 17, and Vietnam on June 14. Therefore, the organization has as of today 10 permanent member countries while 12 more enjoy the partner status.
Summits and ministerial meetings
BRICS does not have a headquarters or a charter. It is essentially an informal club, or rather a platform for collaboration. The rotating presidency is held by the summit’s host country. Since 2013, the presiding country has been inviting countries close to it geographically and geopolitically to participate in the summits. Regular negotiations are held at the level of foreign ministers, finance, health, education, science and agriculture ministers, and secretaries of security councils. Since 2015, the BRICS civil, parliamentary and youth forums, as well as media summits have been held. Today there are more than 20 negotiating platforms within the BRICS framework, covering such areas as energy efficiency, climate change, food security, poverty alleviation, sustainable development, and the activities of international financial institutions.
Since hosting its first BRICS event in June 2009 in Yekaterinburg, Russia has chaired the association three more times and hosted multiple meetings of BRICS participants.
In July 2015, Russia hosted the 7th BRICS Summit in Ufa. In November 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it held the 12th summit via video link, with cameras set up in the presidential residence in Novo-Ogaryovo near Moscow for Putin. Russia also hosted the 16th summit on October 22-24, 2024, held in Kazan, the capital of the Russian Republic of Tatarstan.
The most recent 17th BRICS Summit was held in Rio de Janeiro (Brazil) on July 6-7, 2025. During the summit, participants expressed their views on the most pressing international issues, including the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East and outlined directions for the further development of the association. The final declaration included statements on international politics, economics and trade, international security, climate and sustainable development, reducing the risks of natural disasters, issues related to the development of artificial intelligence and cooperation in space exploration.
BRICS activities
To date, the BRICS countries have established several structures in the business and financial sphere, including the Exchange Alliance (2011), the Business Council and the Council of Centers of Expertise (2013). Since 2011, the BRICS Business Forum has been organized to strengthen trade, business, investment and production ties among the BRICS member countries. In 2014, the BRICS New Development Bank was established with its headquarters in Shanghai (China). Its shared capital is $100 billion.
The Bank is designed to finance infrastructure and sustainable development projects in the BRICS nations and developing countries. Since its launch, it has approved 120 projects worth $39 billion. The Bank works in conjunction with the BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement (the agreement was signed in July 2015).
Since 2015, the summits have been adopting a key document in the field of economic interaction - the five-year Economic Partnership Strategy. This document is still under consideration.
Moreover, the BRICS countries are also developing cooperation in the fields of science, education, healthcare, space exploration, culture, sports and other spheres. The Scientific Council has been functioning since 2013. In September 2017, the BRICS Network University (established in 2015), which includes about 60 universities (among them 12 Russian, including Moscow State University, St. Petersburg State University and Urals Federal University), began operating. The main subjects of educational and research programs are economics and energy; IT and information security; ecology and climate change and water resources. This educational institution is headquartered at the Urals Federal University in Yekaterinburg.
BRICS has been holding film festivals since September 2016, and theater school festivals since 2017. In August 2020, at Russia’s initiative, the first meeting of sports ministers was convened. It approved a memorandum of cooperation, envisaging BRICS sports games, cooperation in the field of sports and organization of sports recreation and leisure. The first BRICS Games were held in Kazan on June 12-23, 2024, with 27 sports included in the program.
Statistics
The population of the BRICS+ countries accounts for 49.5% of the world’s 8.2 billion people. In 2025, the combined GDP of BRICS countries, according to World Bank data, reached 30%, compared to 43% for G7 member states. The combined GDP of BRICS members measured by purchasing power parity (PPP) accounted for 39.2%, compared to 28.3% for the G7 countries. China accounts for 70% of the global economy, India for 13%, Russia for 8%, Brazil for 7% and South Africa for 2%.
On July 4, 2025, Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov stated at the Board of Governors meeting of the New Development Bank that the total financial assets of BRICS countries exceed $60 trillion, representing more than 50% of the global total. In June 2025, Kirill Dmitriev, head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, announced that trade between BRICS countries had reached $1 trillion.

EU approves additional $7B for Ukraine defense, including drones, Patriot missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:26:15 UTC
21:26:15 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
The European Commission on Friday approved an additional €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) for Ukraine to procure defense products, including air and missile defense systems, ammunition, drones and electronic warfare equipment.
The funding is aimed at strengthening Ukraine's ability to counter intensified Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks.
“Today, we have approved €6.1 billion to help Ukraine procure different defence products in the field of air and missile defence, ammunition, drones and electronic warfare,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on US social media company X.
“With this approval, Ukraine can now also purchase the Patriot equipment it needs to better protect its skies from Russia’s indiscriminate attacks,” she added.
The package will finance purchases from both EU and Ukrainian defense companies and allow Kyiv to procure PAC-3 missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
The funding comes under the EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026-2027, of which €60 billion is earmarked for defense and €30 billion for budgetary assistance.
With Friday's decision, the €28.3 billion allocated for Ukraine's defense support in 2026 has been fully assigned, covering specific equipment, suppliers, quantities and implementation timelines.
The bloc has already disbursed €8.35 billion in defense funding for Ukraine this year.
The announcement came as the EU and Ukraine also held the first board meeting of a new defense industry initiative aimed at jointly developing drone and counter-drone technologies.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said the initiative seeks to strengthen Europe's drone capabilities by drawing on Ukraine's battlefield experience.
Kubilius said Europe must learn from Ukraine not only about drone technology and production but also about accelerating manufacturing processes and rapidly scaling up production capacity.
The EU currently produces around 1.5 million drones annually, compared with roughly 10 million each in Ukraine and Russia, he said.
Europe should be prepared to increase its production to 10 million drones or more annually in the event of a crisis or war, Kubilius added.
The initiative's board includes representatives from nine EU member states and nine Ukrainian companies, selected from around 400 applications.
Its priorities include accelerating joint ventures between EU and Ukrainian companies, securing supply chains, expanding testing capabilities and speeding up research, development and procurement.
Kubilius said the initiative should go beyond being a consultation platform, with the first concrete results expected by the end of the year.

One proposal would move Russian assets held by Belgium’s Euroclear depository, where the vast majority of the frozen reserves are located, along with assets held at other European financial institutions, into a separate EU-controlled structure, the Financial Times reported on Sept. 11, citing two sources familiar with the discussions.

But Sweden and other EU countries have recently urged the European Commission to restart work on transferring frozen Russian reserves to Ukraine.
The effort was halted in December 2025 after Belgium opposed the plan over concerns about legal and financial liabilities.
Sweden has argued that using the frozen Russian funds could help cover Ukraine’s financing gap without adding an extra burden to the EU budget or member states’ finances.

AI’s rapid rise expected to boost economy at expense of widening income inequality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
12:24:09 UTC
21:24:09 KST

Sevgi Ceren Gokkoyun, Bahattin Gonultas and Emir Yildirim
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to grow the economy but also lead to the unequal distribution of wealth, with income shifting toward capital owners rather than labor, according to a recent report.
AI firm Anthropic warned that AI would boost the American economy by 32% and create massive prosperity by 2030, but it would also widen the income gap.
The firm’s economics team praised AI’s massive potential to drive economic growth to unprecedented levels while advising that it would also lead to historic job losses for white-collar workers.
The report outlines three key scenarios for the US economy based on the pace of AI development, adoption rates and task-based automation capabilities.
An extreme scenario shows that virtually all jobs are performed autonomously, leading US annual gross domestic product (GDP) to grow as much as 15%, causing the economy to double around every five years.
US GDP is projected to rise as much as 32.4% compared with previous projections without considering AI, reaching $44.4 trillion. This radical scenario foresees AI outperforming humans in most white-collar tasks, such as those of engineers, software developers and accountants.
The same scenario also warns that the overall unemployment rate would rise to a whopping 12%, exceeding a typical level in a recession.
White-collar employment would decline more than 20%, and wages for the group would fall more than 10%. Meanwhile, income distribution would fall to 45.2% for labor, while the share of capital would rise by 14.8 points to 54.8%.
Under the current economic system, this share is divided 60% to labor and 40% to capital.
Even if the economy grew by one-third, the total wages paid to workers still would not exceed the level seen in a potential world where AI does not exist, the report showed.
The economic gains derived from AI would mostly be in the hands of capital owners who already have the AI models, data and computing resources, the model revealed.
Meanwhile, wage increases may be seen in occupational groups less affected by AI, such as technical trades, electricians or nursing, as these rely on physical strength and interpersonal skills, potentially becoming more valuable.
At the same time, a more moderate scenario in which AI plays a less prominent role showed a more controlled market movement.
This projection expects AI to take on only 4% of tasks across the US economy, with the country’s GDP anticipated to rise 1.6% compared with a scenario without AI, totaling $34.1 trillion. Employment and unemployment in this projection remain within historical norms, while AI has a gradual impact on markets like the global rollout of the internet.
Under a more pronounced, medium-term scenario in which AI takes over around half of white-collar tasks, US GDP is expected to rise 8.3% above the baseline scenario to $36.3 trillion, while unemployment approaches 4.6%-5%, white-collar employment declines around 4% and white-collar wages stagnate.
The report authors say these scenarios are not definitive, as their model excludes external macroeconomic factors like economic crises, market shocks, government policies, disruptive AI failure modes or other advancements in robotics that could automate manual labor.
The report surveyed around 11,000 US adults, showing that the public’s median expectations generally align with the more pronounced medium-term scenario.
Anthropic economist Peter McCrory said the goal is to ensure that institutions and governments can make strategic decisions against potential future risks.
Meanwhile, billionaire Elon Musk said the extreme scenario outlined in the report, forecasting 15% annual growth once humanoid robots enter mass production, will happen.
He said AI will likely grow the global economy by up to 30% given the current productivity gains.

The suspects are accused of both corporate raiding and money laundering.
Stolar, Mudra and Myktytas are accused of illegally seizing real estate by hacking the corporate register, forging documents, and bribing judges and law enforcement agencies.
Apart from that, Mudra and Mykytas are also are accused of laundering Hr 150 million ($3.4 million) and transferring the funds through Sense Bank to post bail for former Justice and Energy Minister Herman Halushchenko.
Halushchenko was charged in February in a case involving state nuclear power monopoly Energoatom — the largest corruption investigation of Zelensky’s tenure.
In June, Mykytas said that Timur Mindich, a Zelensky ally and a suspect in the Energoatom case, had delivered cash for Halushchenko's bail to "Kyrylo Oleksiyovych" — an apparent reference to Zelensky's Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov, according to alleged transcripts of NABU tapes published by the media outlet Hromadske.
"Let the court sort it out. You know, it (his name) comes up in a lot of places," Budanov told Hromadske on Aug. 27 when asked about alleged references to him in the tapes.
Stolar represented the pro-Russian Opposition Platform-For Life faction in parliament until it was banned amid Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Now he represents the Restoration of Ukraine group, an offshoot of the Opposition Platform-For Life.
Stolar has been linked to several controversial construction projects in Kyiv, as well as a scheme that allegedly defrauded hundreds of homebuyers during the 2000s, according to investigative journalists. He has denied the accusations of wrongdoing.
Under former President Petro Poroshenko, Ukrainian media labeled Stolar the “de facto mayor of Kyiv” due to his influence in the city.
Stolar has also partnered up with Artem Kolyubayev, a former business partner of Zelensky's former Chief of Staff Andriy Yermak, according to the Bihus.info investigative project.

Despite that conflict and economic pressure from the US to cut trading ties, India has sought to balance maintaining its relationship with Tehran and with Israel and Arab Gulf states.

In the meeting, the leaders also exchanged views on "key regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region which have impacted maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers."

Pezeshkian arrives for BRICS Summit

WATCH — India's difficult BRICS chairship
With BRICS nations now representing nearly 3.7 billion people and close to 40% of global GDP, leaders are meeting amid rising geopolitical tensions, trade disputes and energy challenges.
While the expanded bloc is seeking a stronger voice in the global economy, disagreements over an alternative payment system and China's dominant role could test unity. Renewable energy and green infrastructure financing are emerging as key areas to watch.
Former UN diplomat: BRICS is 'voice of Global South,' but 'contradictions remain'
Speaking to DW about the BRICS Summit, former UN diplomat Shashi Tharoor said that the expansion of the bloc has made it the voice of the Global South.
The BRICS coalition started out with four member countries; Brazil, Russia, India and China but now has 11 members and partner countries after the economic bloc decided to open up membership for more countries in 2023.
Tharoor noted that while Iran joined the coalition, US strategic partners Egypt and Ethiopia also joined
"The expansion that took place in Johannesburg turned out to be one in which both sets of geopolitical points of view were accommodated," Tharoor noted in an interview with DW.
He argued that, "in some ways the expansion has made it much more the voice of the global south."
However, he also said that while the majority of the world is represented in the new 11-member BRICS, the chances of having a consensus has also decreased.
"I would say that BRICS is functioning, but the contradictions remain, and some contradictions have become even more apparent," he said.
He said that when BRICS leaders met this year, they "could not agree on any particular language, and so the chair, India, issued a chair statement instead… it wasn't just Iran, it was also Ukraine that they couldn't agree on."
Tharoor noted that the bloc has a "built-in set of geopolitical divergences which will crop up whenever issues divide the members."
Piyush Goyal proposes 'borderless' digital trade at BRICS
Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Friday urged BRICS member countries to link their payment systems, encourage trade in local currencies, and make digital trade more accessible globally.
Addressing the opening ceremony of the BRICS Business Forum on Friday, Goyal highlighted India's digital payments ecosystem, including the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), as a potential foundation for deeper cross-border financial cooperation among BRICS economies.
"Today, it is also accepted in 11 countries and I would urge the Brics member countries and partner countries to link our payment systems, trade in each other's local currencies, make digital trade global and build together for the future emerging technologies," Goyal said as reported by Indian newspaper Deccan Herald.
Modi, Putin to meet on the sidelines of BRICS
Russian President Vladimir Putin landed in Delhi on Friday to attend the BRICS Summit being held at the Bharat Mandapam on September 12 and 13.
He will be meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the afternoon. Talks are expected to focus on enhancing cooperation in a range of areas, including defence, energy, technology, pharmaceuticals and people-to-people exchanges.
"Warmly welcome President Vladimir Putin of Russia for the 18th BRICS Summit. He was received by MoS K V Singh at the airport. India and Russia share multifaceted and longstanding ties anchored in Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership," Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a post on X.
This is Putin's first in-person participation at a BRICS Summit held outside Russia since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Later in the evening, Modi will also be holding a bilateral talk with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian.

Loui was born in 1964 and enjoyed an entertainment career spanning more than three decades across TV, radio and film and included his work as a filmmaker.
