President in shelter, and ‘armaggeddon’ on TV: here’s how Lithuania met 9/11 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

It was early morning in the US. President Valdas Adamkus, who was visiting Washington, was hurried to a secure shelter, while in Vilnius, senior officials gathered for an unscheduled meeting to discuss the country’s security situation.
Based on archive reports from Panorama, this article reconstructs the issues that dominated life in Lithuania in September 2001, the country’s response to the terrorist attacks and how Lithuanians assessed the situation.
‘Armageddon’
"It was like a science-fiction film about Armageddon. But this was really happening, in the very heart of the democratic world’s financial centre, next to Wall Street,” Vykintas Pugačiauskas said as he began his dramatic report on September 11, 2001.
“As panic-stricken people tried to escape the area around the World Trade Centre, oil and gold prices rose around the world, while the dollar fell," he added.
The terrorist attacks also caused concern in Lithuania. That same day, Lithuanian officials and heads of the country’s security and law-enforcement institutions gathered for an unscheduled meeting with then Prime Minister Algirdas Mykolas Brazauskas.
Although it was decided not to declare a state of emergency in Lithuania, then parliamentary speaker Artūras Paulauskas told journalists there was "some worrying information", but declined to elaborate. Prime Minister Brazauskas said at the time that the situation was not dangerous, but additional measures would be taken.
Following the meeting, security at strategic sites was increased. The biggest security operation was at the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant: access to the surrounding area was restricted without special permits, while armed officers carried out regular patrols.
Increased attention was also given to the Port of Klaipėda and the international ferry terminal, while ships patrolled the waters. Following the attacks, additional security measures were also introduced at Vilnius Airport.
The terrorist attacks brought transatlantic air travel to a halt both in Lithuania and around the world. As a result, large numbers of passengers were stranded at airports. Lithuania was no exception – at the time, an average of about 50 people travelled to the US every day on connecting flights.
The terrorist attacks also pushed up fuel prices. According to the report, the price of petrol rose by five cents. A petrol station representative said fuel sales had increased by 25%. However, no major economic shocks were observed in the first few days.
Banks also saw increased demand for European Union currencies and, somewhat surprisingly, the Lithuanian litas. During this period, people were exchanging US dollars for litas.
Adamkus' US visit
In 2001, Lithuania was making major efforts to join NATO. It was therefore not surprising that visits by the country's leaders to the US were frequent. Before the trip, President Valdas Adamkus said he expected his visit to Washington to be one of the most challenging of his entire presidency.
That morning, Adamkus and the Lithuanian delegation attended a working breakfast with representatives of American Jewish organisations, where the threat of terrorism was also discussed. It was during this breakfast that news of the attacks first broke.
The presidential delegation was taken to a shelter in the basement of the hotel. Later, the entire delegation moved to the Lithuanian embassy in Washington, which was considered a safer location.
Because of the situation, the planned visit was cut short by four days. Interestingly, the delegation was also among the first passengers to be allowed to board a transatlantic flight from the US after the attacks.
The delegation became passengers on the first transatlantic flight after the terrorist attacks. The US authorities also provided a military aircraft to fly the delegation to Reykjavik. From there, they transferred to a Lithuanian Airlines aircraft and reached Vilnius Airport at 04:00 on September 13.
After returning to Lithuania, Adamkus said the attacks would not make Lithuania’s path to NATO more difficult and could, on the contrary, make it easier.
The day after his return to Lithuania, the president issued a special address in which he spoke about the events of September 11 and their significance for Lithuania. The president also expressed his full support for US action and spoke about changes in international politics.
"September 11 shook and changed the world. We, the people of Lithuania, also need to fully understand these changes. In a single day, our world became more fragile and vulnerable, as even the most powerful country in the world proved to be vulnerable," Adamkus said in his address to the nation on September 14.
The speech prompted a range of reactions. People interviewed in the streets of Lithuanian cities disagreed with the position expressed by the president and pointed to the theme of revenge in his speech. Many of those interviewed also referred to Lithuania’s small size and limited influence.
"I would say we should refrain from that. We are a small country, and no one will defend us. We will exhaust our own strength for the sake of others, and there will be nothing left for us," one woman told reporters.
Opinions and assessments varied. It is important to remember that at the time, Lithuania’s prospects of joining NATO and the European Union were viewed in very different ways.
While some saw membership as Lithuania’s steady return to the West, others associated it with an increased threat.
Nevertheless, the government at the time continued the integration process and supported the implementation of Article 5 of the Washington Treaty.
But it was the possibility of further attacks that caused the greatest concern. As reports spread about the possible use of biological weapons, Panorama journalists looked into the situation in Lithuania’s laboratories.
What was Lithuania living through before the attacks?
Events often overshadow one another. The scale of the September 11 attacks pushed some of the major stories of the time out of the spotlight.
September 2001 saw teachers in Telšiai and other cities begin a week-long strike. They were unhappy about delays in the payment of salaries to education-sector workers. They were warned that the strikes would continue for as long as their wages remained unpaid.
Teachers interviewed for the report said they earned 350 litas at the time (around 100 euros). School pupils interviewed were unsure whether the protest would achieve anything – some welcomed it, while others worried about their exams.
The sporting world was dealt a painful blow, which people interviewed in the streets described as a tragedy. Lithuania’s run at the 2001 European Basketball Championship in Turkey ended in the last 16 with a defeat by neighbouring Latvia.
"We praised them too much, glorified them too much. The men were flying high, but you need to keep your feet on the ground," one passer-by said.
Following the fiasco, coach Jonas Kazlauskas resigned. This period in Lithuanian basketball came between the euphoria of the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney and Lithuania’s European championship triumph in 2003.
After the defeat, Adamkus even joked about severing diplomatic relations with Latvia.
Lithuania continued preparing for integration into NATO and the EU. In September 2001, joint exercises involving Lithuanian and NATO forces, called Amber Hope, were held in Rukla. Almost 3,000 troops took part.
Rukla residents welcomed the increased activity in the town, while the commander of the Land Forces, Colonel Valdas Tutkus, cautiously spoke about the positive assessments expected from Lithuania’s future allies.
Local residents were pleased that turnover at shops and cafés had increased tenfold.
Minsk troubles
Meanwhile, Lithuanian journalists and international observers were closely following events in Belarus. The country was preparing for its second presidential election.
The vote was originally due to take place in 1999, but while serving his first term, A. Lukashenko changed the constitution and extended the presidential term to seven years.
"The elections in Belarus confirmed the thesis of the classic of authoritarianism, Joseph Stalin: 'It does not matter who votes how. What matters is who counts the votes and how'," journalist Jolanta Paškevičiūtė said as she began her report from Minsk.
Lukashenko won the election. He was challenged by the opposition, which accused the authorities of holding a fraudulent election and claimed that Vladimir Hancharyk, who came second, had received about 40% of the vote, compared with 46% for Lukashenko.
But international attention shifted from the election to the US the very next day.

India and Russia are building something big in space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:44:44 UTC
20:44:44 KST

India and Russia are building something big in space
Space exploration and satellite navigation are fragile, failure-prone and enormously expensive. Yet they offer something few other fields can match: technological superiority and strategic prestige.
The main players in space remain Russia, the United States, and China, followed by India, the European Union, and Japan. Newer entrants include the United Arab Emirates, Iran, and a range of states in South America and West Asia. Because the sector is so costly and high-risk, cooperation is highly valued – it brings redundancy, speeds up technological progress, and cuts the price of getting there.
Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov earlier this week, in the runup to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to New Delhi, noted that Russia and India are considering the possibility of cross-flights involving mixed crews to their future national orbital stations. He said that this cooperation could eventually extend to joint scientific experiments and research.
In May this year, Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval visited the Roscosmos Joint Industry Information Center, while in August, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar traveled to Moscow to co-chair the 27th session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation (IRIGC-TEC).
Increased collaboration between Moscow and New Delhi within the space sector is occurring within the backdrop of three larger yet interlinked trends: first, the United States’ active dismantling of the remaining international order; second, the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and Iran; and third, the advancement in drones and defense technologies.
The current US administration has upended the established decades-long US foreign policy by targeting longstanding allies with tariffs and sanctions in the attainment of its goals. India has become a target more than once of American tariffs and economic pressure. Attempts to reach a deal with the Trump administration have failed to produce long-term tangible gains.
This, however, has had a deep impact on the Indian populace. Since the normalization of Indo-US ties, the Indian public had forgotten that historically, American interests had been antagonistic to India during the entire Cold War period. These buried emotions have been surfacing lately with public skepticism regarding American intentions. Deepening cooperation with Russia and attempts to normalize ties with China are New Delhi’s way of signaling its displeasure toward American actions.
Recent developments in Indo-Russian cooperation have involved mutual deployment of ground stations, co-production of engines, and development of national orbital stations. These will allow Russia to offset vulnerabilities by outsourcing joint-production capabilities of critical components to India out of Ukraine’s reach.
The astronomical advancements in drone and smart defense technologies have underscored the significance of satellite-based constellations in warfare. A variety of Russian munitions and weapon systems employ GPS/GLONASS and the upcoming Rassvet system in precision guidance and control. UMPK-equipped glide-bombs, cruise missiles such as the Kh-101, drones like the Shahed-136, Geran-3 & -4, and Orlan-10, along with ballistic missiles such as the Iskander-K, witness a significant increase in accuracy and precision with minimal falloff over large distances.
Furthermore, despite the destruction of existing Viasat infrastructure in Ukraine during the conflict’s opening days, the rapid deployment of Starlink prevented the complete collapse of Ukrainian command and control structures. These attributes make the systems vital to any future operational requirements against adversaries with both limited and significant electronic warfare capabilities.
India’s worst-case military scenarios stipulate for a two-front war. The ability to deploy these munitions and weapon systems may provide its forces with definite tactical and strategic advantages in critical sectors along and beyond the lines of engagement. However, all these require the backbone of GPS/GLONASS capabilities and/or the Rassvet/Starlink low-orbit constellations on which these systems rely. Russia is currently in the process of operationalizing its Rassvet constellation to full functionality.
India’s own NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is in dire straits. The indigenous satellite navigation system has dropped below the critical threshold of satellites required for accurate geolocation. Simultaneously, the quest for a reliable low-orbit satellite navigation system over the Indian subcontinent has led to multiple contenders, including the French-TATA venture Eutelsat, the American Starlink and Viasat systems, Reliance’s own planned constellation, and possibly the Russian Rassvet system in the near future.
Space-based cooperation need not be limited to the bilateral level. In August 2021, BRICS space agencies signed an agreement for cooperation in remote sensing satellite data sharing. In May of the following year, the BRICS Joint Committee on Space Cooperation was officially launched. This year, BRICS+ engaged in advanced discussions of cooperation with calls for a BRICS Space Economy being made. Whether civilian cooperation in satellite data constellation ultimately advances to include sensitive military collaboration remains to be seen. What is already clear, however, is that low-orbit constellations are set to become a major disruptor in both civilian and military technology, and this is one area in which the Russia-India partnership could deepen further.

Beijing freezes plant approvals for energy-storage  batteries amid overcapacity fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:43:05 UTC
20:43:05 KST

ExclusiveBeijing freezes plant approvals for energy-storage batteries amid overcapacity fears
‘Dozens of new projects in the pipeline sparked policymakers’ fears about redundancies,’ analyst says
Companies had not been allowed to add new capacity since May, as key regulators like the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) stepped in to curb a construction spree that risked creating severe overcapacity despite rising demand from renewable-energy projects around the world, the sources said.
The temporary ban could be lifted if the supply-demand balance changed, they added.
“The decision to suspend construction of new ESS [energy-storage system] battery factories was made because dozens of new projects in the pipeline sparked policymakers’ fears about redundancies,” said Ivan Li, a researcher at Loyal Wealth Management in Shanghai.
“The ministry-level authorities apparently looked to take pre-emptive measures so that sustainable growth could be achieved.”
Energy-storage systems, comprising batteries along with battery management, power conversion and control equipment, store excess energy generated from renewable sources like solar and wind farms while providing backup power during outages and helping stabilise electricity grids.
The MIIT, which is mainland China’s top economic planning agency, the National Development and Reform Commission and provincial-level regional governments are jointly responsible for drafting policies about ESS projects.

U.S. Army orders more of its M110 sniper systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:43:03 UTC
20:43:03 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Knight's Armament Company a five-year contract worth up to $49,997,842 for M110 Semi-Automatic Sniper Systems through September 2031.
- The award continues a sole-source arrangement dating back years, even as the Army has separately fielded the lighter M110A1 as a planned replacement.
The U.S. Army has handed Knight’s Armament Company, run by founder Charles Reed Knight Jr., a new five-year deal worth nearly $50 million to keep building M110 Semi-Automatic Sniper Systems.
The firm-fixed-price contract covers the rifle, its variants, accessories, spare parts, special tools and training, and runs through September 10, 2031.
Only one company bid, and Knight’s Armament won it, a pattern the Army has followed with the M110 for years. Army Contracting Command in Newark, New Jersey, is overseeing the deal. Work locations and funding will be worked out order by order rather than locked in today.
The M110 fires 7.62x51mm NATO ammunition and grew out of Knight’s Armament’s SR-25 design, which the Army picked in 2007 after a competition. Unloaded, it weighs about 6.27 kg (13.8 lb). It sends a 175-grain round downrange at roughly 783 meters per second (2,570 feet per second) and can hit point targets out to about 800 meters (875 yards). Both the Army and Marine Corps have fielded the rifle, and it saw heavy use in Afghanistan and Iraq.
The Army has spent nearly a decade trying to replace the M110 with something lighter. In 2016 it picked Heckler & Koch’s G28-based M110A1 for up to 3,643 rifles, in a deal worth up to $44.5 million, aimed at giving snipers a weapon that doesn’t stick out the way the longer M110 does. That didn’t end M110 purchases. The Army ordered more in 2018 for about $16.5 million, then kept buying under a five-year contract that ran through last September. This week’s award picks that supply line back up rather than closing it out.
The Army has also been buying M110s for Ukraine. In September 2025, it gave Knight’s Armament a separate $21 million contract to build M110 systems for Ukraine’s armed forces, paid for through the Ukraine Security Initiative and Partnership Capacity Building program, with deliveries due by January 30, 2027. Ukrainian special forces, the National Guard and International Legion volunteers have reportedly carried the rifle.

Russia may exhaust its resources for the war against Ukraine by 2028 — HUR
Kyiv • UNN
The HUR estimates that Russia will exhaust its military and economic resources by 2028 at the current rate of losses. Every day, Russia loses up to 1,500 military personnel.
Russia may exhaust its resources for the war in Ukraine by 2028 if the occupiers’ military losses remain at their current level. This was stated by the head of the Main Intelligence Directorate, Oleh Ivashchenko, in his first interview with international media, including The Times, reports UNN.
Russia has military and economic resources for the coming year, but according to our estimates, they will be exhausted in 2028 if military and economic losses continue to increase at the same rate
He noted that Russia recruits around 1,000–1,200 people every day, while its daily losses on the front amount to 1,400–1,500, with about 60% of them killed.

Ivashchenko emphasized that these figures are causing a lack of support for Putin’s war effort.

The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine has codified the Steppe Wind (Stepovyi Viter) strike unmanned aerial system developed by domestic company Unwave.
Official codification enables government procurement and the delivery of these UAVs to Defense Forces units, the company told Militarnyi.
The mid-range UAV was jointly developed with partners from Sky Composite Engineering to hit stationary targets, armored vehicles, and personnel.
The strike system has a tactical range of up to 70 km, a maximum route length of more than 90 km, and a flight endurance of up to 65 minutes.
The UAV can carry a 5-kg payload and is equipped with an optical terminal guidance system.

Unwave first spoke about the Steppe Wind in February this year at the MITS x Azov Corps: Defense Technology Horizons 2026 conference.

Fact check: Which EU economy is performing the best?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:42:00 UTC
20:42:00 KST

Recent comments by Portugal's prime minister have prompted discussion about which EU country currently has the best-performing economy and employment growth rate.
Portugal's economy and employment growth are the best-performing in Europe, according to the country's Prime Minister Luís Montenegro. But how true is that?
Montenegro made the comments while speaking to the Assembly of the Republic, Portugal's parliament, on 8 September. Here, MPs were debating a motion of no confidence in the government put forward by the far-right Chega party.
The motion came about after Montenegro refused to sack Interior Minister Luís Neves over allegations of misconduct while he was head of Portugal's Judiciary Police between 2018 and 2026.
Other opposition parties came together to support the centre-right minority government and vote down the motion, in an effort to avoid further political instability. The country has, after all, held three elections in three years.
During the debate, the prime minister told MPs that Portugal had the best economic performance and the top rate of employment growth in Europe.
To find out whether his claims held any weight, The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, looked at the most recent Eurostat figures on member states' GDP growth.
They reveal that the EU's GDP as a whole was up by 0.7% in the second quarter of 2026, compared to the previous quarter.
Ireland was the main driver of this, with far and away the highest jump in GDP at +10.2%. Analysts say its strong growth, a sharp upward revision from previous estimates, was largely driven by major output surges from global firms, particularly in technology and pharmaceuticals. Because of this, economists view it as an unreliable metric.
Slovenia and Lithuania came in second and third place, with a growth of 1.8% and 1.7%, respectively.
Portugal came in joint seventh place with Cyprus, with both countries' GDP's rising by 0.8%.
So it's fair to say Portugal is ranking among the best of the 27 member states, but it’s not the best, according to Eurostat data.
Austria was the only country that recorded a decline, with its GDP contracting by 0.1%.
When it comes to employment, the same Eurostat dataset shows that employment had gone up by 0.1% in both the Eurozone and the EU in the second quarter of 2026.
Around 221.4 million people were employed in the EU during that time.
In this case, Montenegro would be correct: When broken down by member state, Portugal came in first place with a 1% growth in employment in the second quarter of 2026.
It was followed by the Czech Republic and Malta in joint second place, at 0.9% growth.
Several countries saw a decrease in employment, notably Finland (-0.8%) and Greece (-0.4%).

Philippine rescuers recovered 30 bodies from a burned-out ferry on Friday, raising the death toll from the blaze to 35, authorities said.
Firefighters found the remains after they gained access to the vessel for the first time, having extinguished a fire that had hampered search and rescue efforts since Wednesday night.

Sweden's fractured left holds slim lead in polls before Sunday election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:41:04 UTC
20:41:04 KST

Sweden's fractured left holds slim lead in polls before Sunday election
STOCKHOLM, Sept 11 - Sweden's centre-left opposition bloc holds a narrow lead ahead of Sunday's parliamentary election, three opinion polls showed on Friday, two days before what is seen as a referendum on the incumbent right-wing government's alliance with the far-right.
Across Europe, far-right parties have been on the rise, with Alternative for Germany, which opposes immigration and backs closer ties with Russia, winning a state election and Marine Le Pen leading polls for next year's presidential vote in France.
In Sweden, Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson narrowly remains favourite to become prime minister again after four years in opposition and replace Ulf Kristersson of the centre-right Moderates.
Sweden's four left-leaning parties between them have support of between 49.3% and 50.8%, giving them from 175 to 180 seats in the 349-seat parliament, according to the surveys conducted by the Ipsos, Demoskop and Indikator Opinion polling firms.
Backing for the coalition government and its far-right support party, the Sweden Democrats, stands at 47.6% to 49.0%, corresponding to between 169 and 174 seats, the polls released by Swedish Radio and dailies Aftonbladet and DN showed.
Kristersson has overseen a shift in Sweden away from the liberalism for which the country was once known, introducing some of Europe's toughest policies on immigration.
Andersson's bloc, which has pledged higher public spending, has retained a majority in every poll published this year, with most of the recent surveys pointing to a winning margin of around 10 seats.
But one of the surveys on Friday showed a margin of a single seat, mirroring Sweden's close-fought election of 2022.
In mid-August, the centre-left held a 10 percentage point lead in several polls, which political scientists at the time said was a nearly insurmountable gap to bridge before election day.
Kristersson says that if his bloc wins, the Sweden Democrats, which has apologised for its past links with neo-Nazism, would join the government for the first time.
DIVIDED LEFT
The centre-left remains divided over which parties should be included in a government headed by the Social Democrats, with the Centre Party and the Left Party each ruling out taking part if the other is in.
The parties also differ on key policies, from a tax on billionaires to whether Sweden should build new nuclear reactors.
This may in turn lead to lengthy negotiations and the formation of a minority government including some, but not all, opposition parties if the left wins.
The rival blocs both support Ukraine in its fight against Russia's invasion as well as military rearmament at home and relief for households hit by the rising cost of living.
But while the campaign focused on a range of issues including Sweden's welfare state, immigration and crime, there was no single dominant issue, experts said.
"Nothing has really stuck, it's been sort of unsatisfactory in that sense," said Nicholas Aylott, an associate professor at Sodertorn University.
The Social Democrats remain Sweden's biggest single party with support between 27.4% and 29.7%, down from 30.3% in the 2022 vote, the polls show.
The anti-immigration Sweden Democrats party maintained its position as the governing bloc's biggest group with 18.3% to 19.0% support, down from 20.5% since the 2022 election, the polls showed.
The party has been propping up the ruling coalition without being part of the cabinet. REUTERS

French activists seek bigger probe on Israel Gaza flotilla raid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:40:53 UTC
20:40:53 KST

Breadcrumb
French activists seek expanded probe into Israel's abduction of Gaza flotilla
Twenty-six French activists who sailed as part of the Global Sumud Flotilla to break the Israeli blockade of the Gaza Strip have filed a joint complaint in Paris seeking to expand French investigations into violations they accuse Israeli forces of committing against them.
They are calling for investigations on the abduction and seizure of flotilla boats in international waters, followed by the forced transfer of participants to Israel and their detention.
Previous investigations were limited to charges of torture and war crimes.
Alongside their personal testimonies, the complaint draws on reports prepared by forensic doctors and psychologists after the activists returned to France, activist Yasmin Skoula told The New Arab.
The complaint was filed against an unknown person or persons on 7 September with France's National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office in the capital and covers the Israeli army's seizure of flotilla boats in international waters and the subsequent transfer, detention and assault of their passengers in October last year and in April and May this year.
The plaintiffs are asking for an investigation into nine charges, including the diversion of vessels, arbitrary detention and violence committed against them by Israeli soldiers, police officers and prison guards.
The charges also include torture, war crimes, death threats, sexual assaults, obstruction of medical evacuations and the deliberate damaging of one of the boats during a coordinated drone attack.
Speaking to TNA lawyer Raphael Kempf, one of eight lawyers who prepared the legal file, said the most important addition the complaint makes to the ongoing investigations in France is "new legal classifications".
The prosecutor's office has so far opened investigations based on charges of torture and war crimes, without including the diversion of vessels or arbitrary detention.
He added that the Israeli army's interception of the flotilla boats in international waters falls under the crime of vessel diversion under French criminal law, while taking passengers to Israel and imprisoning them there constitutes arbitrary detention.
According to Kempf, the complaint is not limited to acts of violence committed by Israeli soldiers against the participants but considers the interception of the boats a crime in its own right.
"We are not only challenging the consequences of this operation in terms of violence, assault and torture, but also its very nature," he said, adding that what the plaintiffs want to challenge is "the Israeli army allowing itself to detain people in international waters and then illegally take them to prisons on its territory".
To prove that the boats were in international waters, the lawyers are relying in particular on location data showing where they were when they were intercepted.
Kempf stressed that the location of the boats when the Israeli army intercepted them is "certain and beyond doubt".
The evidence also establishes that participants were taken to the port of Ashdod and then detained in Israeli prisons.
He added that the participants did not want to enter Israel but to travel to the Gaza Strip. Therefore, it cannot be said that they entered Israeli territory "illegally", as Israeli authorities tried to force some of them to acknowledge it while they were detained.
The French lawyer said the investigation should identify the soldiers and others who took part in the assaults, paving the way for arrest warrants to be issued against them and for their arrest if they enter French territory or another European country.
He did not rule out responsibility extending to those who ordered the interception of the boats and detention of their passengers but said determining the chain of responsibility remains the task of the investigation.
"Ultimately, those with the authority to issue arrest orders must be held accountable," he said, alongside those who directly carried out the assaults.
Kempf expects the complaint to be joined to the preliminary investigations opened by the National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office in June and assigned to the Central Office for Combating Crimes Against Humanity.
But for the lawyers, joining the cases is not enough.
They are calling for the file not to remain solely in the hands of the prosecutor's office but to be handled by an independent investigating judge.
This would allow the plaintiffs to become civil parties in the case and request that witnesses be heard and evidence gathered outside France.
The complaint is no longer based solely on the plaintiffs' testimonies, after medical and psychological reports that were not available immediately after their return to France were added to the file.
When Yasmin Skoula spoke to TNA in May, hours after her arrival, the activists had not yet undergone the necessary examinations.
Since then, several of them have seen forensic doctors and psychologists, and reports on their physical injuries and psychological effects, some of which continue to this day, have been added to the file.
Regarding sexual violence, Skoula previously told TNA that the activists had documented at least 16 cases, including accounts of gang rape.
This figure included participants of all nationalities, while the complaint filed in Paris covers five French plaintiffs who reported being subjected to sexual assaults by Israeli forces.
These included being forced to remove their clothes during searches and being touched sexually.
Their testimonies are included in the file, alongside medical and psychological documents collected after their return.
Among the incidents included by the lawyers in the joint complaint is an account previously given by Skoula to TNA about far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir entering the tent where she was being searched after Israeli female soldiers forced her to remove her clothes.
She said the incident was included based on her testimony and those of other participants who were present.
In May, Ben-Gvir himself published a video showing activists kneeling on the ground with their hands tied at the port of Ashdod.
The Central Office for Combating Crimes Against Humanity has begun contacting French participants in the flotilla to hear their testimonies, according to Skoula, who has not yet received a summons to give hers.
She said investigators are calling people in turn in alphabetical order, and all participants intend to comply with requests to give testimony.
Shortly after being deported to Turkey, Skoula gave testimony before Turkish lawyers, which was intended to support an investigation at the International Criminal Court, but she has received no information about that case since.
Months after the Israeli assaults, some plaintiffs continue to suffer from injuries sustained during the incidents.
Skoula noted a French participant in the flotilla is still receiving medical care for a serious injury to her cervical vertebrae, while others who suffered broken ribs needed about two months to recover.
Skoula said her physical injuries have left no lasting effects after she suffered bruising and tingling in her hands for several weeks, but she continues to have difficulty sleeping and recurring nightmares.
Despite this, the activist noted that the participants were able to receive treatment, talk about their suffering and seek legal recourse, unlike Palestinians who are continuously subjected to more severe violations and often have no opportunity to receive treatment, have their complaints heard or seek legal recourse.
The plaintiffs and their lawyers are most concerned that the French prosecutor's office could close the case without further action.
"If this case is closed without further action, the decision will be political because it is based on a solid legal foundation. Such a choice would once again entrench Israel's impunity," Skoula said.
Kempf, for his part, said he expects the prosecutor's office to add the complaint to the ongoing investigations and investigate its allegations.
But he is concerned about what happens afterwards, as French law allows prosecutors to close a case even when its legal elements are established. He believes that any closure, if it happens, would not be because of weaknesses in the case legally but as a result of a political decision.
Skoula also said she heard some Israeli soldiers speaking French, leading her to suspect that some of them hold both Israeli and French citizenship.
She said some French participants in the flotilla were, to the best of her knowledge, able to identify the soldiers more clearly than she could, which could help the investigation establish their identities.
The French activist is calling for prosecution of everyone found responsible for or involved in the incidents, whether they carried them out, issued the orders or helped implement them.
She believes the case does not concern the flotilla participants alone.
"I expect all those responsible and complicit to be held accountable, and for this complaint to once again draw attention to what Palestinians are experiencing. We can today give our testimonies, speak to journalists and seek legal recourse, but this is not available to Palestinians. I hope the complaint will also contribute to securing justice for them," Skoula concluded.

Vertska noted that the heaviest restrictions are found in southern Russia, a region frequently subjected to Ukrainian strikes.
Vertska added that it cannot track all notifications because expired ones disappear from the system.
Russia’s ongoing fuel crisis
Ukraine has struck Russian refineries hard throughout 2026, triggering an unprecedented fuel crisis for Russia, the world’s third-largest oil producer.
Russia’s Recruitment of Foreign Fighters for Ukraine War ‘Amounts to Human Trafficking’
Jet fuel, like gasoline and diesel, is also refined from crude oil and is therefore affected by the refinery strikes, as Russia can extract the oil but struggles to refine it. Ukraine claimed to have put 43% of Russia’s refining capacity offline by July.
In June, Russia introduced an export ban on jet fuel running from June 1 to Nov. 30, with limited exceptions. It also imposed similar export bans on diesel and gasoline.
In July, Russia was reportedly importing jet fuel from Japan via intermediaries.
The Kremlin has since tried to downplay the crisis, with top officials assuring the public in July that the fuel crisis would not last, but Russian President Vladimir Putin recently acknowledged at a forum that the crisis is real and might last for some time.
Putin tried to downplay the impact on Russia’s economy by claiming that it is more “profitable to export crude oil than to process it domestically.” The claim was countered by a recent think tank report suggesting that both Russia’s export revenues and volumes dropped in August.

Wasps are disappearing this summer, and scientists are worried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:38:35 UTC
20:38:35 KST

Wasps are disappearing this summer, and scientists are worried
Britain’s wasps are mysteriously disappearing, and this summer’s extreme heat may be a major reason why.
- Date:
- September 11, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Britain’s wasps have become mysteriously scarce this summer, and scientists suspect an unusual combination of temperature swings, heatwaves, and food shortages may be responsible. Even the wasps that remain appear unusually small, potentially offering a glimpse of how extreme heat could reshape insect populations.
- Share:
Summer can be lovely – until a wasp turns up. Whether they present as an irritating picnic visitor or an uninvited loft guest, common social wasps are as much a part of our summer as festivals, sun cream and the growing despair of how to entertain children who’ve forgotten how to be bored.
But summer 2026 is breaking the norm, and there don’t seem to be many wasps about. As a wasp biologist, I’ve noticed it acutely, because my students need wasps for their experiments, and we simply can’t find them.
A second sign that something is wrong is the absence of wasp stories in the media. Wasps tend to be more active in warmer weather. Their colonies grow faster and bigger, and they end up making news headlines by bothering humans. This time last year – also a warm spring and hot summer – the media airwaves were filled with “plagues of wasps” stories. Now, even professional pest-controllers tell me it’s a quiet year with very few requests to remove wasp nests.
Admittedly, these are anecdotes not data: the Big Wasp Survey – the only national wasp monitoring survey – is yet to start sampling this summer. But the signs are not good.
If data back this up, their absence worries me greatly because – love them or hate them – wasps are important in ecosystems as pest-controllers, pollinators and decomposers.
So what’s happening?
Spring started well for wasps. In the warm, dry spring a glut of glorious foundresses – new queens – emerged from hibernation to start their nests alone, carrying out all the nest building, egg laying, foraging and brood rearing. This nest-founding period is a risky time. If a new queen survives until her first brood emerges as adult workers, though, then the odds are in her favour as she no longer needs to undertake risky foraging.
But spring 2026 was strange: the warm, dry start should have been good. Warm, dry spring weather improves a nest’s chance of survival as it ensures a good nectar supply for the queen to develop her ovaries and good prey populations for her to feed the brood. But we experienced unprecedented heat for the time of year, punctuated by cold, damp days and followed by unexpectedly chilly nights.
Such weather extremes may have caused queens to abandon their nests or die, reducing the initial spring queen bounty to a more modest population.
Temperature tolerance
And then came the heatwave. And another. And another. Some insects may benefit from this. Wildlife charity Butterfly Conservation is hoping 2026 could be a “bumper summer of butterflies” because warm, dry days mean uninterrupted foraging, mating and egg-laying.
But all insects have a thermal tolerance called critical thermal maximum (CTmax). If their CTmax is exceeded, insects succumb to desiccation, muscle spasms and eventual stupor.
For honeybees, this is around 49°C – which might sound high, yet ground surfaces exceeded 50°C in the UK heatwaves this summer. But the temperature doesn’t need to reach an animal’s CTmax to affect their productivity and behaviour. For example, bumblebee cognition and foraging efficiency are impaired by heatwaves of 32°C.
Bumblebee Conservation Trust raised concerns that 2026 may exacerbate a declining trend in bumblebee populations as flowers wither and bees fail to forage effectively.
Wasps are thought to be quite resilient to extreme weather. They are one of the most successful invasive species around the globe. And as a social insect, their thermoregulation behavior (such as wing fanning to cool the larvae) and nest architecture (which has insulating envelopes surrounding the brood combs) may help buffer any environmental perturbations.
Insects also have waxy molecules called cuticular hydrocarbons that coat their exoskeletons protecting them from desiccation. Social wasp cuticular hydrocarbons change structure in response to heat, better protecting them from desiccation in excessive heat.
Their varied diets should also buffer them from imbalances in prey populations. However, their CTmax may be lower than other social insects – at around 45°C (113°F) – which may have made them especially vulnerable to the high ground temperatures of the 2026 heatwaves.
Why are the wasps so small?
There’s something else that I’ve noticed: the few wasps I’ve seen are rather small. The adult size of many insects is fixed during their development, depending on the quality and quantity of food they receive as larvae. Wasps don’t get bigger once they’ve pupated.
The first workers to emerge in spring are usually small because the queen is limited in how much food she can provide for them alone. But by early August, the foraging capacity of the colony has increased exponentially, brood are better fed and the emerging workers are substantially larger.
So why are we still seeing “spring-sized” wasps? It’s possible that limited diversity and abundance of prey may mean their nutrition is restricted. The problem may also be more directly linked to heat. Insect larvae reared at higher temperatures will develop faster and reach pupation at a smaller size.
Global warming is thought to explain the trend in social wasps shrinking in size over the last 100 years. We could be seeing this in real-time this year.
How can you help wasps?
Share your alfresco meal with a wasp. When it approaches, don’t flap it away. Watch to see what it wants. In the absence of wild prey, it might be desperate for some protein (your picnic ham) to feed her brood. In the absence of flowers for nectar, it might be in need of something sugary (some jam) for her own nutrition.
My research team would also like you to share your wasp observations with us, so that we can better understand these important insects. Snap a photo of her eating and submit your data to the Wasp Picnic Survey 2026: Ham or Jam?. Keep the observations coming all summer. The wasps (and wasp scientists) will thank you.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Seirian Sumner, Professor of Behavioural Ecology, UCL. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The Russian Orthodox Church has sent a fragment of a medieval warrior prince’s right hand to Russian troops in occupied Ukraine, saying the relic will strengthen their morale.
The remains of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy were uncovered this summer during restoration work at Moscow’s Cathedral of the Archangel, inside the Kremlin.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Donskoy, who died in 1389, is revered by Russian nationalists for defeating forces of the Golden Horde at the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380.
Russian President Vladimir Putin personally inspected the remains in August, describing their discovery as “absolutely unique and marvelous” and saying it “reinforced the foundations of Russian history.”
Donskoy’s name was given to a Soviet tank column funded by the church during World War II. The Russian Orthodox Church canonized him in 1988.
Critics accused the church of breaking religious protocol by opening the tomb. Although Donskoy’s burial place had long been broadly known, no attempt had been made to recover and venerate his remains during the nearly four decades since his canonization.
Despite the objections, the church removed a fragment of Donskoy’s right hand and placed it in an ornate reliquary protected by reinforced glass.

On Tuesday, Sept. 8, senior Orthodox clergy held a prayer service around the relic at the Saur-Mogila war memorial in occupied Donetsk Oblast. Russian military representatives and Kremlin-installed officials also attended.
The relic will now be displayed to Russian combat units along the more than 1,000-kilometer (620-mile) front line.
“The very same right hand with which he wielded his sword ... has been sent to the front,” the church said, claiming the relic would strengthen the soldiers’ spirits.
The church referred to Donskoy as its “holy commander” and said he would stand “shoulder to shoulder” with Russian troops.
The Russian Orthodox Church has strongly supported the Kremlin’s aggression, sending priests to military units, ordering prayers for a Russian victory and portraying the war against Ukraine as a religious struggle.
Earlier this year, relics of Alexander Nevsky, another medieval prince revered by the Russian Orthodox Church and Russian nationalists, were also sent to the front.

Germany charges 7 suspected Hamas members over attack plot
September 11, 2026
German federal prosecutors on Friday charged seven suspected members of the Islamist militant group Hamas.
The men allegedly plotted to carry out a deadly attack on Israeli or Jewish targets in Germany or Austria.
What are the charges?
The men are accused of helping procure weapons, membership in a foreign terrorist organization, and taking part in preparations for act of violence endangering the state, the Federal Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe said on Friday.
Investigators believe the suspects, who were arrested in Germany and abroad over recent months, were already pursuing a concrete attack plan.
The men are accused of helping obtain guns and ammunition for an attack targeting representatives of Israel, Jewish people or people regarded as pro-Israel.
The plot allegedly became concrete by July 2025 and was intended to take place on the second anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel.
Prosecutors say that one of the suspects recorded a video claiming responsibility in advance and announcing the planned attack in the name of Hamas.
All seven men also face weapons charges, while three are additionally accused of violating Germany's War Weapons Control Act.
What weapons had allegedly been obtained?
By the time three of the suspects were arrested in Berlin on October 1, 2025, prosecutors say the group had obtained:
- one functioning fully automatic rifle
- 13 functioning handguns
- more than 700 rounds of ammunition
Part of the arsenal was allegedly moved to Vienna and stored there by another suspect who is being prosecuted separately.
According to prosecutors, all seven belonged to Hamas and several were tasked by senior Hamas officials with securing the weapons.
The suspects were arrested between October 2025 and May 2026 and remain in pre-trial detention.
Another alleged participant, Mohammed A., was arrested in London on November 3, 2025, at the request of German authorities.
He has not yet been transferred to Germany and is being prosecuted separately.

Hamas planned Berlin-Vienna attacks for Oct. 7 anniversary, indictment shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:35:43 UTC
20:35:43 KST

Visitors view rows of empty chairs bearing photos of Israeli victims and hostages displayed in front of the Brandenburg Gate during a memorial vigil in Berlin, Germany, on October 7, 2025. | Stefan Frank/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — Hamas planned coordinated terrorist attacks in Berlin and Vienna to mark the second anniversary of the Oct. 7 massacre in Israel, according to a 214-page indictment filed by Germany’s federal prosecutor.
The attacks were to take place simultaneously or in close succession around Oct. 7, 2025, targeting Israeli and Jewish interests in the two European capitals, according to the indictment, obtained by WELT, which — like POLITICO — is part of the Axel Springer Global Network.
The plot was supported by an international weapons-procurement network that moved pistols, an automatic rifle and hundreds of rounds of ammunition through Denmark, Germany and Austria.
Advertisement
Federal prosecutors said last year that they had arrested men linked to the Palestinian militant group who were suspected of planning attacks on Israeli and Jewish targets in Germany. The indictment, which has not been made public, reveals that Vienna was also an intended target — and that the attacks in the two capitals were to be coordinated. The principal targets included Israeli diplomats, Jewish community centers and pro-Israel demonstrations.
Seven men have been charged in connection with the plot and remain in pretrial detention, according to the indictment. One of the accused was working as a confidential informant for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. The files show that the informant continued reporting to his intelligence handler while allegedly failing to disclose the full extent of his own involvement in obtaining ammunition for the group.
The indictment portrays the plot as part of a broader shift in Hamas’ operations in Europe. Intelligence assessments cited in the filing say plans existed even before the Oct. 7, 2023 attack to establish and train operational cells on the continent, using Turkey as a base and directing attacks remotely from abroad.
The prosecutors alleged the weapons operation was also coordinated from Lebanon, where a Hamas operative allegedly oversaw one of the procurement channels linking members of the network across Europe.
According to the indictment, the objective was to move beyond the fundraising, propaganda and logistical activity that had long characterized Hamas’ presence in Europe and develop the capability to carry out attacks against Israeli and Jewish targets in the West.
The plot began to unravel on Oct. 1, 2025, just six days before the planned attacks, when German authorities arrested three suspects in Berlin during the handover of a cache of weapons that prosecutors say had been assembled for the operation.
Advertisement
In the courtyard of a residential building on Turmstrasse in Berlin’s Moabit district, investigators seized a fully automatic Crvena Zastava assault rifle, eight Glock 26 pistols and more than 600 rounds of ammunition, according to the indictment. The weapons had been transported to Berlin through a procurement chain stretching across Germany and Denmark.
Investigators say the group operated two distinct but coordinated weapons channels. One supplied the Berlin arsenal, while the other moved five handguns and ammunition from Copenhagen through Berlin to Vienna, where they were stored in a rented unit together with clothing and other equipment.
The indictment also says one of the suspects recorded a claim-of-responsibility video in Vienna in August 2025, weeks before the planned attacks. Masked and armed in front of a Hamas flag, he threatened acts of revenge in Europe in the name of the Al-Qassam Brigades, Hamas’ military wing.
The case is now before the state-security division of Berlin’s highest state court and is expected to become one of Germany’s most significant terrorism prosecutions in recent years.

U.S. Navy hires small firm for drone-mimicking planes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:35:33 UTC
20:35:33 KST

- The Navy awarded KestrelX up to $9,987,285 for low-observable target aircraft and support services for military training exercises through March 2028.
- The contract extends an SBIR program that began with a $725,000 Air Force award to the company in 2021 for threat-replication aircraft.
The U.S. Navy has awarded KestrelX, a small Florida-based aviation company, a contract worth up to $9,987,285 to supply low-observable target aircraft and engineering support for Navy and Department of War training exercises.
The Navy did not obligate any funds when it signed the deal, and will instead pay KestrelX as it issues individual task orders. Work will be split across the company’s Lake Mary, Florida headquarters (60%), Driggs, Idaho (20%) and New Bern, North Carolina (20%). Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division at Lakehurst, New Jersey, awarded the contract without competition, and it covers fleet exercises, ship training and aircrew training, along with flight operations, technical integration and equipment support tied to those events.
The award falls under a Small Business Innovation Research program topic called “Unmanned Aerial Vehicle and Cruise Missile Threat Replication Aircraft.” KestrelX first won SBIR funding for that same work from the U.S. Air Force in 2021, a contract worth about $725,000. This week’s Navy award represents a Phase III follow-on, extending the company’s threat-replication work to a second military branch.
KestrelX was founded by Don Moseley, a former Navy F-14 Tomcat and F/A-18 Super Hornet pilot who later served as a developmental test pilot for the F/A-18 at Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 after graduating from Navy Test Pilot School. Moseley has said the idea for the company took shape in 2019, while he was flying an adversary jet at the Nevada Test and Training Range and watched an F-117A stealth fighter pulled out of storage to serve as a low-observable adversary aircraft in the same exercise.
The company’s aircraft have since stood in for real-world threats in several military exercises. At Northern Strike 24-2 in Michigan, KestrelX flew two small JSX-2 microjets built by Sonex Aircraft out of Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center. More recently, at Sentry South 26.1 off the coast of Savannah, Georgia, the company flew two Risen KX-2 propeller aircraft, which it describes as the world’s fastest ultralight, to replicate Iranian-designed Shahed-136 loitering drones for U.S. forces practicing detection and intercept tactics.
The Navy’s new contract specifies low-observable aircraft, a step beyond the microjets and propeller planes KestrelX has flown in past exercises. The Navy has not said which aircraft in the company’s current or future lineup will meet that requirement, nor has it disclosed how many training events the contract is expected to cover before it expires in 2028.

How US-Iran war is impacting the global oil sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:34:28 UTC
20:34:28 KST

The US war on Iran is disrupting oil production and shipping routes across the Middle East, tightening global crude supplies and pushing energy prices higher as the conflict increasingly affects major production and export corridors.
Saudi Arabia's crude oil production plunged to 6.24 million barrels per day in August, its lowest reported level since 1990, according to data the kingdom directly reported to OPEC.
Saudi production fell by around 1.9 million barrels per day from 8.1 million barrels per day in July, reversing a sharp recovery from 7.1 million barrels per day in June. The decline came despite plans by Saudi Arabia and other OPEC+ members to increase output during the month.
The impact of the war has extended beyond the immediate conflict zone, affecting both the Gulf and alternative export routes through the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia has relied heavily on its western export infrastructure, particularly the Red Sea port of Yanbu, as instability around the Strait of Hormuz complicated traditional Gulf shipping routes.
That alternative corridor has also come under pressure after Yemen's Houthi group declared a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia on July 20, describing it as a new front in the conflict involving Iran and the United States.
The group subsequently claimed attacks on Saudi-linked vessels and energy facilities, including infrastructure around Yanbu and the Jazan refinery. Tankers have responded by switching off their Automatic Identification System signals to reduce exposure to attacks.
Ship-tracking data showed a sharp deterioration in Red Sea flows during August, with Saudi crude and condensate loadings from Yanbu falling to a six-month low. Vortexa estimated August loadings at 3.2 million barrels per day, while Kpler put them at 1.5 million barrels per day.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has also come under pressure. Vessel transits through the waterway fell to just seven on Wednesday, compared with a 10-day average of 14, according to preliminary ship-tracking data.
Despite the fall in production, Saudi Arabia supplied 7.1 million barrels per day to the market in August, according to its direct communication with OPEC, significantly above its reported production of 6.24 million barrels per day.
The disruption has contributed to tighter global crude supplies and higher oil prices. Brent crude climbed above $100 per barrel this week as renewed fighting between the United States and Iran and attacks on shipping heightened concerns over Middle Eastern energy supplies.
Further sign of the impact
By Friday, Brent futures stood at $106 per barrel as of 0800 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate traded at $101. Crude oil prices had risen by around 10 percent on a weekly basis.
In a further sign of the impact on consumers, diesel prices in the United States exceeded $6 per gallon for the first time, reaching $6.05 on Friday, according to American Automobile Association data.
The energy shock has also weighed on financial markets. Asian shares declined on Friday, tracking Wall Street losses, while oil prices continued to rise.
Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 percent, South Korea's Kospi lost 2.3 percent, Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 0.8 percent, China's Shanghai Composite declined 1.8 percent, and Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 1.2 percent.
Higher energy prices have also added to inflationary pressures. US producer prices rose 5.4 percent year-on-year in August, accelerating from 4.8 percent in July, while US Treasury yields have remained above pre-war levels amid concerns over energy prices, inflation and rising government debt.
Diplomatic efforts are meanwhile expected to focus on keeping energy shipping routes open. Iran and Gulf states are expected to meet on Monday in Oman to discuss a temporary arrangement for managing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, Yemen's western coast has seen rapid military developments, with media reporting Houthi advances on several fronts towards areas near Mocha and the Bab al Mandeb Strait.
With disruptions affecting production, the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, the US-Iran war is increasingly placing pressure on the global oil sector, with continued fighting and shipping risks keeping crude prices elevated.

Hundreds of asylum seekers removed from UK to France have disappeared, say NGOs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:33:24 UTC
20:33:24 KST

Hundreds of asylum seekers including at least 41 age-disputed children who were removed to France under the “one in, one out” deal have disappeared, human rights organisations have said.
The pilot scheme was hailed as “groundbreaking” by the former prime minister Keir Starmer when he and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, announced it in July 2025. Under a treaty drawn up for this agreement, it forcibly returns small-boat asylum seekers to France in exchange for others brought legally to the UK from France.
The deal is due to expire on 1 October and at the moment it is not known what, if anything, will replace it.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is reportedly pushing for the deal to be extended and scaled up, and the French government has indicated it wants the scheme to be expanded Europe-wide rather than France having to accept small-boat returnees alone.
One French politician told the Guardian that so far France’s overtures to other countries to take back a share of small-boat asylum seekers had received a negative response.
About 1,400 small-boat arrivals have been returned to France since September 2025, just 4% of 32,000 who have crossed the Channel since the deal was signed. These figures do not include the significant minority who have come back to the UK a second time, some of whom are now living under the radar here. The UK and France amended the treaty to allow for people returning to the UK in lorries to be sent back to France a second time.
At a meeting in parliament this week chaired by Mike German, a general rapporteur on asylum and migration policy for the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe, and Alex Sobel, the new chair of parliament’s joint committee on human rights, parliamentarians were told about the disappearances and other concerns about the scheme by NGO representatives working on the ground.
Maddie Harris, the director of the Humans For Rights Network, said several NGOs had between them compiled a list of at least 41 age-disputed children and young people whom they claimed had been unlawfully returned to France. It is unlawful to detain lone children in adult immigration detention centres, and they are excluded from the one in, one out treaty.
The Home Office disputed this and told the Guardian: “This is categorically untrue. Nobody has been returned to France where their age is in dispute.
“Every detained person is advised of their right to legal representation and how they can obtain such representation within 24 hours of arrival at an immigration removal centre. Age assessments are carried out to maintain the integrity of our border, while ensuring those genuinely under 18 receive the appropriate support.”
However, the prisons and detention Independent Monitoring Boards have reported that almost a hundred children had been identified as unlawfully detained as adults for the scheme. The IMBs’ interim chair, Jane Leech, attended the meeting and raised concerns that some people were being unlawfully detained for the scheme because the Home Office was “detaining more people than they can remove”.
French politicians have told the Guardian that only 200 people forcibly returned to France were still in contact with the authorities there, with hundreds of others having gone underground in countries across Europe.
The Guardian has interviewed dozens of returnees who are no longer in contact with the French authorities and are living underground in Europe. They say they have disappeared due to hostility from the French authorities, pressure to return to their home countries where they believe they will be unsafe, or the threat of being forced back to other European countries such as Bulgaria that they passed through on their journeys.
Home Office sources said that what happened to people once they were returned to France was a matter for the French authorities. France’s interior ministry declined to comment on the disappearances.
Harris said the forced return of lone children to France was “shameful”. She said: “We support many children detained under this scheme and attempt to secure their release. However, at least 41 children have been removed from the UK to France and their whereabouts is currently unknown. The vast majority of these children have experienced acute violence and exploitation and are now without protection somewhere in Europe.”
Nihal Osman, a programme coordinator for Médecins Sans Frontières, told the parliamentary meeting that asylum seekers were returned to France from the UK in a “deeply concerning” condition, with many displaying severe psychological symptoms such as flashbacks, acute anxiety, self-harm, suicidal thoughts and psychological breakdown.
“What we are witnessing is the accumulation of trauma on trauma,” she said.
Sobel said he was “deeply concerned” about the ongoing securitisation of the French border to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel to the UK. “The French police are doing things it would be unacceptable for British police to do,” he said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Power Company will begin releasing more than 30 years of marine ecological monitoring data next year through the Taiwan Biodiversity Information Alliance to support conservation and research.
Taipower said Thursday it signed a memorandum with TBIA to add its survey records to the alliance’s biodiversity platform for public access, per CNA.
The state utility said major power facilities are located along the coast and rely on seawater for cooling, prompting the company to assess environmental impacts, per UDN. Its first large-scale study focused on waters around Kuosheng Nuclear Power Plant in New Taipei.
Taipower said its efforts follow the international Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures approach, which promotes conservation beyond legally protected areas. It has incorporated conservation into its power facilities and received recognition for land and marine conservation efforts.
Adding survey records to TBIA’s network will expand their use beyond environmental management into scientific research, Taipower explained. TBIA integrates biodiversity data from government agencies and research institutions through a query system, making the information available to the public.

In Germany, they want to restrict the AfD&apos;s access to classified data

In Germany, they want to restrict the AfD's access to classified data
Kyiv • UNN
Interior ministers are discussing restricting the future AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt's access to intelligence data. No decision has been made yet.
Germany’s interior ministers are discussing how to restrict the access of the as-yet-unformed government of the "Alternative for Germany" in Saxony-Anhalt to sensitive information held by law enforcement and intelligence agencies. Bild reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication, this was the subject of a closed video conference involving the heads of the interior ministries of all 16 federal states and the federal interior minister.
The main concerns are related to the possible control of the "Alternative for Germany" over the state Office for the Protection of the Constitution. If a government is formed, the party will gain control over Saxony-Anhalt’s Interior Ministry, which oversees approximately 6,500 police officers and 123 intelligence officers. Information about operations related to Russia and right-wing extremism is causing particular concern.
The publication learned that several measures are being discussed: restricting the automatic exchange of intelligence data with Saxony-Anhalt, reducing the state’s access to the Nadis database, which stores intelligence data on individuals, organizations, and cases, as well as abandoning the principle of unanimity at the conference of interior ministers. In the latter case, 13 of the 16 votes may be sufficient to adopt decisions.
According to sources cited by the publication, the Federal Ministry of the Interior has already examined the legal possibilities for such restrictions. However, there is no unity among the federal states: Hamburg, Thuringia, North Rhine-Westphalia, and Bavaria support a tough approach, while others fear that reducing the exchange of information would, in itself, weaken security.
The new Landtag of Saxony-Anhalt will convene on October 6.
To remind you
The far-right "Alternative for Germany" party achieved a historic victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Taichung Power Plant to remove partial coal burning installations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:30:12 UTC
20:30:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Economic Affairs said Thursday that it approved the demolition of structures housing coal generators 1 and 2 at Taichung Power Plant.
The power plant located in the city's Longjing District is the biggest in the world. It has been blamed for severe air pollution in the region, prompting the government to favor gas over coal-burning.
The economics ministry held the evaluation meeting. State enterprise affairs Director-General Hu Wen-chung (胡文中) hosted the event, joined by Taiwan Power Co. Vice President Lu Ching-hwang (盧景煌) and city officials.
Hu said that all parties have agreed to remove the compartment and one smokestack. He noted that work will begin in October.
Hu urged Taipower to take special precautions, especially when removing the 252-meter-tall smokestack. Taipower said that it has made all preparations.
The ministry said improving air quality is a nationwide consensus. The ministry also urged the city to speed up Taipower's application to build the gas turbine generators.
The decision came after Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) inspected the power plant on Sept. 4. Cho said the plant's total emissions have dropped by 80% compared to 2014.
Cho said the first gas turbine unit is expected to become operational in late September. The second unit will be onsite in late October.
Cho reiterated the government's commitment to have the plant run on gas by 2034, with coal generators reserved for emergencies. He said the old generators will only function during maintenance tests.
Taipower said the move is part of the plant's phased transition from coal to gas. It noted that six new gas turbines will be added by 2034, with four coal burners removed.
The utility was to reassign four coal burners for emergency use in 2018. Former economics minister Wang Mei-hua (王美花) negotiated with the city to instead have coal generators 1, 2, and a smokestack removed, and generators 3 and 4 moved to reserves.

U.S. Navy orders full production of new Growler jamming unit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
11:29:39 UTC
20:29:39 KST

- The Navy awarded General Dynamics Mission Systems a contract worth up to $184.25 million for full-rate production of the EA-18G Growler's NGEAU electronic warfare unit.
- About $40 million was obligated at award, with work running through September 2032 at the company's Bloomington, Minnesota facility.
The U.S. Navy has awarded General Dynamics Mission Systems a contract worth up to $184.25 million to move a new electronic warfare component for the EA-18G Growler into full-rate production. The contract covers manufacturing of the Next Generation Electronic Attack Unit, known as NGEAU, along with sustainment support for the unit and future sustainment work on the jet’s Advanced Capability Mission Computer.
The Navy issued the award as an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract mixing firm-fixed-price and cost-plus-fixed-fee terms, with work to be performed at General Dynamics Mission Systems’ facility in Bloomington, Minnesota, through September 2032. That $184.25 million figure is the contract’s ceiling rather than a guaranteed payout. The Navy obligated just over $40 million at the time of the award, split between fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds ($29,691,536) and fiscal 2025 funds ($10,365,451), with additional money to follow as the Navy places orders against the contract.
The Navy awarded the contract without competition, citing federal rules that allow a sole-source purchase when only one contractor can meet the requirement. Naval Surface Warfare Center Crane, in Crane, Indiana, is managing the contract on the Navy’s behalf.
NGEAU upgrades the Electronic Attack Unit already built into the EA-18G Growler, the Navy’s dedicated electronic warfare jet, as part of a broader update called Growler Block II. The unit works alongside the ALQ-218 Airborne Electronic Attack System Enhancement to help the aircraft detect and respond to unfamiliar radio signals on its own in a crowded electromagnetic environment, a capability the Navy has said it needs to keep the Growler fleet effective until a future aircraft eventually replaces it.
Boeing, which builds the EA-18G, holds a separate contract covering NGEAU testing and hardware kits. A 2023 order worth $95.9 million tasked Boeing with developmental and operational test support and the production of 25 NGEAU A-Kits, 25 gunbay pallet A-Kits, 15 NGEAU B-Kits and nine B-Kit spares, with work split across St. Louis, Missouri; Minneapolis, Minnesota; Bethpage, New York; and Linthicum, Maryland. The Minneapolis-area work on that earlier contract points to General Dynamics Mission Systems’ existing role supplying NGEAU hardware before this week’s move to full-rate production.
NGEAU is a separate system from the Next Generation Jammer pods that mount externally on the Growler’s wings, which Raytheon and L3Harris are building to eventually replace the aircraft’s older ALQ-99 jamming pods. NGEAU instead upgrades processing hardware built into the aircraft itself.

French gov't cuts 2026 economic growth forecast to 0.5 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
19:29:26 CST
20:29:26 KST

PARIS, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The French government has cut its 2026 economic growth forecast to 0.5 percent from 0.7 percent previously, the country's Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said Friday.
Lescure announced the forecast at a press conference on the government's updated macroeconomic outlook, adding that the government expects the economy to grow 1 percent in 2027.
The government also expects inflation to reach 2.1 percent in 2026 and 1.8 percent in 2027, Lescure said.
It was the government's third downward revision to its 2026 growth forecast this year. It lowered the forecast to 0.9 percent from 1 percent in April, before cutting it again to 0.7 percent in July.
Overall, "we have therefore halved the growth estimates for this year," Lescure said, noting that against this backdrop, the target of limiting the budget deficit to 5 percent of GDP in 2026 "is no longer an option." "France will have a deficit above 5 percent in 2026," he added.
The government's new forecast remains slightly higher than the latest estimate from the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Insee), which lowered its forecast to 0.4 percent from 0.7 percent in its latest economic outlook report released Thursday.
Compared with its neighboring countries, France's economy is lagging behind, mainly due to a sharp downturn in public works activities linked to the municipal election cycle, the impact of heatwaves, a weaker labor market and less favorable fiscal stimulus measures, Insee said. ■

Cambodia's fuel, oil imports surge 40 pct to 3.38 bln USD in first 8 months of 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
19:29:16 CST
20:29:16 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's imports of mineral fuels, oils, and distillation products increased 40 percent year-on-year in the first eight months of 2026, driven by robust domestic economic growth and rising global energy prices, official data showed on Friday.
The Southeast Asian country spent 3.38 billion U.S. dollars on these commodities between January and August, up from 2.41 billion dollars during the same period last year, according to a report from the General Department of Customs and Excise. The import category encompasses mineral fuels, mineral oils, distilled products, bituminous substances, and mineral waxes.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said the expanding import volume reflected accelerating domestic economic momentum.
He cited rising industrial production, expanding transport and logistics networks, and heightened electricity demand as key drivers.
"The significant increase in spending on fuels and oils was also driven by rising global fuel prices caused by ongoing conflicts in the Middle East," he told Xinhua.
Mengdavid said the global price spike has trickled down to local consumers.
On Friday, the Ministry of Commerce reported that the price of regular gasoline rose 9 percent over the last 10 days to 4,800 riels (1.18 dollars) per liter. Diesel prices also climbed 6 percent to 5,450 riels (1.34 dollars) per liter.
Cambodia remains entirely dependent on imported petroleum and diesel, as its domestic offshore oil reserves remain unexploited. ■

VIENTIANE, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The Lao weather bureau has issued a heavy rainfall warning, urging the public to remain vigilant as continued rain is forecast across the country from Sept. 12 to 14.
The Department of Meteorology and Hydrology under the Lao Ministry of Agriculture and Environment issued the warning on Friday, saying a low-pressure trough extending across central and southern Laos toward a strong low-pressure system over the central South China Sea is expected to strengthen on Sept. 12 and may develop into a tropical depression.
The system, combined with strengthening southwest monsoon winds, is expected to bring widespread light to moderate thunderstorms across Laos, with rainfall affecting areas from the northeast to the central and southern regions.
Heavy to very heavy rainfall is expected in some areas, particularly in Bolikhamxay, Khammuan, Savannakhet, Salavan, Sekong, Champasak and Attapeu provinces.
Authorities and residents are advised to remain alert and prepare for prolonged rainfall, which could trigger flash floods, landslides, river flooding, and urban inundation. ■

The country aims to vaccinate over 30 million children against polio during the upcoming nationwide campaign from Sept. 21 to 27 and in all subsequent campaigns.
