Mathernova: Russia acts in Ukraine just like terrorists did during Sept 11 attacks
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:47:30 EEST
19:47:30 KST

European Union Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová believes that the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks—which destroyed the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York—and Russia's terror in Ukraine share common features.
“The attacks have much in common. Terrorists and criminals are behind them. russia acts like a terrorist state in Ukraine,” Mathernova wrote in a post published on the social network X.
She noted that 25 years ago, she was in an office in Bratislava in front of a television screen and saw the second plane crash into the Twin Towers live on air.
“I saw the second plane crashing live on TV. The explosion. People desperately jumping from the burning towers. A huge cloud of dust engulfing New York City,” the ambassador said.
According to Mathernova, she did not think back then that she would ever again witness such horror in her life. Yet now, 25 years later, she is experiencing the same thing during Russian attacks on Kyiv.
“During the explosions of drones and missiles. The air stops moving for a moment when we run to shelters during the sirens and listen to the deafening explosions. Then I see images of dead bodies, bloodied people, and dust, rubble and emptiness everywhere,” Mathernova said.
She recalled that the September 11 terrorist attacks claimed the lives of 2,977 people.
“The attack on America united the democratic world in the belief that terrorism must never be appeased. In Ukraine, the UN has already officially verified the deaths of more than 16,800 civilians. According to the UN, the actual number is likely substantially higher,” the ambassador noted.
Mathernova emphasized that 25 years ago the world realized that terrorism is not the internal affair of a single country, and called for a renewed recognition of this fact.

“Modi ji, who has been showcasing his international clout by calling Donald Trump his 'friend' and who even coined the slogan 'Abki Baar Trump Sarkar' among Indian-Americans, is now seeing continuous insults against Indians and people of Indian origin under his administration,” Ramesh said.“Yet, the Modi government is behaving as if it is a silent partner in this entire episode. An extremely offensive poster targeting 'Mr Singh' was issued from the official handle of the US Department of Homeland Security, in which a turbaned Indian was threatened with lines like 'Get off our roads' and 'Self-deport or find out',” he said in a post in Hindi on X.
Ramesh said the episode was not merely an insult to an individual or community but to “the dignity of all Indians”. He said the government should have strongly rebutted what he described as racial stereotyping and “this level of governmental rudeness”.The DHS later removed the advertisement following protests in the US, Ramesh said. However, he alleged that the department continued to defend the campaign and its language through other official posts.“The question is: Why has there been no strong public rebuttal from the Modi government on this insult to Indians?” Ramesh said.The Congress leader also linked the controversy to earlier instances in which he accused the government of failing to defend Indian interests before the US administration. He recalled the deportation of Indians on US military aircraft in handcuffs and leg shackles and the imposition of additional US tariffs on India.“Why has our diplomatic strength become so feeble during the tenure of the Modi government, which boasts of being the 'vishwaguru', that India's interests and sovereignty are facing one blow after another?” Ramesh said.“Why is the Modi government silent? Why does the Government of India keep proving itself weak time and again?” he said.Ramesh questioned whether the government's relationship with US President Donald Trump meant that Washington could continue to target Indians while India remained silent.“Friendship is important in foreign policy, but national interest, the dignity of Indians, and India's sovereignty are paramount, and there can be no compromise on them,” he said.The controversy erupted after DHS used AI-generated imagery as part of a campaign against unlicensed commercial drivers. The advertisement showed a brown-bearded man and referred specifically to “Mr Singh”.The reference drew criticism from advocacy groups, including the Hindu American Foundation (HAF) and Sikh Coalition, which accused the US agency of racial profiling.“Singhs are Hindu, they are Sikhs, they are American and they drive. Racist, un-American, anti-Indian profiling/trolling by @DHSgov should shock our nation's collective conscience,” the HAF said on X.“This is a discriminatory post by a federal agency that is far beyond political messaging, and we welcome an investigation,” the organisation said, tagging Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K Dhillon and FBI Director Kash Patel.The Sikh Coalition said the incident showed that Sikhs continued to face profiling based on their appearance.“Twenty-five years after 9/11, Sikhs are still being targeted and profiled for how we look,” it said.“Millions of Sikhs in the United States have the last name Singh, which means lion. We will defend ourselves. We will defend Americanism. We will defend our home,” the DHS said in a post on X.
Another post featured Optimus Prime with a DHS arm patch confronting the brown-bearded man alongside the message: “Self-deport or find out”.The controversy comes amid the DHS campaign to promote its CBP Home programme, which allows eligible undocumented migrants to register their intention to leave the US voluntarily. Those opting for self-deportation can receive travel assistance and an exit bonus of USD 2,600, according to the DHS.

Military Court Centres
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

11:47:16 BST

Military Court Centres
The Service Justice System is supported in the UK by two designated Military Court Centres at Bulford (Wiltshire) and Catterick (North Yorkshire).
Hearings at both court centres are open to the public unless directed otherwise by a Judge Advocate.
The courts are located on the perimeter of a military establishment. This design provides public access to the Service Courts. The public entrance is staffed by the personnel from Military Provost Guard Service who employ security screening checks as a condition of entry.
Each court centre has two court rooms with all courts holding the capability to manage any type of case within the Service Justice System. Case are listed between the hours of 9.30am to 4.30pm, Monday to Friday. The courts do not sit on Saturdays, Sundays and on public holidays.
Each court is fitted with the latest Digital Audio Recording technology, Assistive Listening devices, Digital AV/IP Evidential Presentation Systems and the latest Section 28 recording capability. We are leading the use of in-court technology for the Board members and defendants and are developing our use of AI court transcription technology throughout 2025.

Russia has threatened Lithuania with nuclear weapons as the Baltic nation is eyeing a lift of its nuclear weapons ban.
Lithuania’s parliamentary parties provisionally agreed to the constitutional amendments in July, and the parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs voted 7-2 on the proposal on Wednesday, Sept. 9, paving the way for a final decision in early 2027.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The lifting of the ban would allow NATO, of which Lithuania has been a member of since 2004, to deploy nuclear forces on its territory.
On Friday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov threatened Vilnius over the plan by saying the Baltic nation – once under Soviet occupation – will be “in the sights of our nuclear weapons.”
“And if there are nuclear weapons on the territory that are aimed at us, then the territory of this country will also be in the sights of our nuclear weapons,” Peskov told Russia’s Channel One on Friday, as reported by state media RIA Novosti.
Lithuania, one of Ukraine’s strongest backers in Europe, borders Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad to the west and staunch Moscow ally Belarus to the south, with Vilnius a mere two-hour drive from Minsk, Belarus’s capital.
Russia began deploying nuclear weapons to Belarus, a non-nuclear nation, in June 2023. In December 2025, Russia also deployed its nuclear-capable Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM) to Belarus, whose combat use in Ukraine marked the first combat use of its kind in history.

“The geopolitical situation is getting worse… Our constitution was written when geopolitical circumstances were totally different,” Nauseda said.

Houthis complete takeover of Bab al-Mandab area

This handout satellite image from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Sept. 10, 2016, shows black smoke billowing over the desert southeast of Medina along the general route of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline (Petroline).(Photo by Handout / 2026 Copernicus Sentinel Data / AFP)
Yemen’s Houthis took over on Sept. 11 a Red Sea island in the middle of the Bab al-Mandab shipping lane, completing their push to control the area, a local government official and eyewitnesses told AFP.
“Boats carrying armed Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island after government forces withdrew from it yesterday,” the official said, referring to an island also known as Perim that divides the strait into lanes.
“The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandab area and Mayyun Island, which is located in the middle of the strait,” he added, speaking to AFP on condition of anonymity.
An eyewitness said gunmen were “deploying along the Bab al-Mandab shore and are driving around in military vehicles.”
Hundreds of people have died since the Iran-backed Houthis launched last week an offensive against Riyadh-backed Yemeni government forces around Bab al-Mandab.
The waterway has gained importance as a transit route since the start of the wider Middle East war, which saw Iran blockade the Strait of Hormuz.
The local government official said the number of fighters on Mayyun is “not large”, adding that they would probably opt to deploy on hills overlooking Bab al-Mandab.
The waterway, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports, includes four strategic islands: Zuqar, seized by the Houthis on Sept. 10, Mayyun, and the two Hanish islands.
Government military sources told AFP that the Houthis have besieged government troops on the Hanish islands.
They said they were unsure about the status of their troops, which number more than 2,000, but believe the Houthis have ordered them to surrender.
A senior military official told AFP that the besieged forces have appealed to authorities for “rescue, food and water, and the lifting of the siege, which would require air support.”
The news outlet Axios reported that U.S. President Donald Trump rejected a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for strikes against Houthi fighters in Yemen.
The Saudi crown prince called Trump on Sept. 10 to tell him about the deteriorating military situation in Yemen as Houthi forces approached the coastal city of Mokha, Axios reported, citing two unidentified U.S. officials.
The crown prince reportedly called Trump again a few hours later to request strikes on the Houthis, but the American president declined.
Washington will provide Saudi Arabia with intelligence on the Houthis and targeting data, and more than 200 U.S. military personnel are already in Saudi Arabia providing “non-kinetic support,” according to a U.S. official cited by Axios.

MOSCOW, September 11. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces carried out one massive strike and six group strikes, targeting, among other things, defense industry enterprises, logistics centers, fuel, energy, and transport infrastructure facilities, as well as a data center used by the Ukrainian military over the course of the week, the Defense Ministry reported.
"On September 5-11, the Russian Armed Forces carried out one massive strike and six group strikes using high-precision weapons and long-range drones, resulting in the destruction of military-industrial complex enterprises, logistics and distribution centers for military cargo, fuel, energy, and transport infrastructure facilities, a data center used for the purposes of the Ukrainian military, production facilities and storage sites for drones and their components, ammunition, fuel, and supply depots, radio and electronic intelligence centers, as well as temporary deployment sites for Ukrainian servicemen and foreign mercenaries," the statement said.
Russian air defenses intercept 5,673 Ukrainian UAVs in past week
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 5,673 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and four Flamingo cruise missiles over the week, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down 48 guided aerial bombs, 14 rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, four Flamingo long-range cruise missiles, two Neptune long-range missiles and 5,673 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 233,403 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 30,888 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,777 multiple rocket launchers, 36,423 field artillery guns and mortars and 71,589 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.
Russia’s Battlegroup North makes Ukraine lose over 1,400 troops in past week
Ukraine lost over 1,430 troops in the area of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North in the past week, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"The enemy lost a total of over 1,430 service members, 12 armored combat vehicles, 83 motor vehicles, five field artillery pieces, and eight electronic warfare systems and counter-battery radars," the statement reads.
Russia’s battlegroup West wipes out over 1,395 Ukrainian troops over week
Russia’s battlegroup West eliminated more than 1,395 Ukrainian troops and destroyed ten enemy armored fighting vehicles over the past week, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Enemy losses in this area totaled more than 1,395 servicemen, ten armored combat vehicles, 108 vehicles, 12 field artillery guns, and seven electronic warfare and counter-battery stations," the statement noted.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates over 290 Ukrainian troops last week
Ukraine lost over 290 troops in the area of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr in the past week, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Over the past week, over 290 service members were eliminated, along with six armored combat vehicles, 122 motor vehicles, and eight electronic warfare systems and counter-battery radars," the statement reads.
Black Sea Fleet destroys 12 Ukrainian unmanned boats over past week
Russia’s Black Sea Fleet destroyed 12 Ukrainian unmanned boats over the past week, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Black Sea Fleet forces destroyed 12 unmanned boats of the Ukrainian navy in the Black Sea," the ministry said.
Russian forces liberate settlement of Novogrishino in Donetsk People’s Republic
Units of Russia’s Battlegroup Center have liberated the settlement of Novogrishino in the Donetsk People’s Republic, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"The settlement of Novogrishino in the Donetsk People’s Republic was liberated as a result of active offensive operations by units of Battlegroup Center," the statement reads.
Russian forces liberate Zorevka in Zaporozhye Region
Russia’s Battlegroup East has liberated the settlement of Zorevka in the Zaporozhye Region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Units of the Battlegroup East continued advancing deeper into enemy defenses and liberated the settlement of Zorevka in the Zaporozhye Region over the past day," the ministry said.
Russian forces hit 19 vessels operating for Ukrainian military over past week
Over the past week, the Russian Armed Forces struck 13 dry cargo ships, as well as two tankers, two tugs, and two motorboats that were operating in the interests of the Ukrainian military, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Over the past week, 13 dry cargo ships, 2 tankers, 2 tugboats, and 2 motorboats operating in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces were struck," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces liberate three settlements in past week, take control of five others
Russian forces liberated three settlements over the past week and took control of five others, according to TASS calculations based on Defense Ministry data.
The settlements of Kurtovka and Novogrishino in the Donetsk People’s Republic and Zoryovka in the Zaporozhye Region were liberated, the ministry reported. In addition, the Russian army took control of the settlements of Berezniki, Ozyornoye, Dolgenkoye, Zarubinka and Goptovka in the Kharkov Region.
Russian army disables several Ukrainian port infrastructure facilities this week
Over the past week, the Russian Armed Forces disabled a number of infrastructure facilities at Ukrainian ports used for receiving and storing military cargo and fuel and lubricants for the Ukrainian military, the Russian Defense Ministry has said.
"A number of infrastructure facilities at Ukrainian ports that facilitated the receipt and storage of military cargo, as well as fuel and lubricants intended for the Ukrainian military have been disabled," the ministry stated.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 2,215 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 2,215 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 12 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week in the special military operation in Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The Ukrainian armed forces lost more than 2,215 personnel, 12 armored combat vehicles, 56 motor vehicles and two electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week," the ministry said in a statement.
Two Ukrainian battalions trapped near Olkhovatka in Kharkov Region
Two Ukrainian battalions have been trapped near Olkhovatka in the Kharkov Region, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Two enemy battalions have been trapped near the settlement of Olkhovatka in the Kharkov Region. All their attempts to break out have been disrupted," the statement reads.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 2,820 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 2,820 casualties on Ukrainian troops in its area of responsibility over the week in the special military operation in Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The enemy losses amounted to more than 2,820 personnel, 20 armored combat vehicles, 64 motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and 10 electronic warfare and counterbattery radar stations in that frontline area over the week," the ministry said in a statement.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 1,330 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 1,330 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 11 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week in the special military operation in Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The Ukrainian armed forces lost more than 1,330 personnel, 11 armored combat vehicles, 127 motor vehicles and 11 field artillery guns in that frontline area over the week," the ministry said in a statement.
Liberation of Zorevka in Zaporozhye Region expands control west of Kommunarovka
The liberation of Zorevka has expanded the zone of control west of Kommunarovka and created conditions for the further advance of the Battlegroup East in the Zaporozhye Region, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
"The liberation of Zorevka has enabled units of the Battlegroup East to expand the zone of control west of Kommunarovka and create conditions for further advance in this sector of the Zaporozhye Region," the statement said.
Battlegroup North continues encirclement of Ukrainian forces in Kharkov Region
Russia’s Battlegroup North continued encircling Ukrainian formations while expanding the outer perimeter of the encirclement in the Kharkov Region over the past week, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Over the past week, units of the Battlegroup North in the Kharkov Region continued tightening the inner ring and expanding the outer ring of the encirclement of enemy formations," the ministry said.

The Ukrainian armed forces suffered losses amounting to up to two platoons. Two armored combat vehicles, five vehicles, three ground-based robotic systems, and more than 20 heavy Baba-Yaga hexacopters were destroyed," the statement said.

EU Approves €6.1 Billion Ukraine Defense Package, Unlocking PAC-3 Patriot Purchases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:45:44 UTC
19:45:44 KST

The European Commission approved a €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) tranche of defense funding for Ukraine on Sept. 11, including exemptions allowing Kyiv to use the money to purchase US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
The approval allows Ukraine to draw on the EU’s €90 billion ($104 billion) support loan to purchase PAC-3 interceptors, among the few weapons capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The decision does not, however, mean the missiles will be delivered immediately. Ukraine faces a global shortage of Patriot interceptors as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius confirmed the decision at a press conference in Brussels on Friday, according to a Ukrinform report, the Commission had formally approved the package after EU member states backed the measures earlier this week.
“Today, the Commission officially approved €6.1 billion for Ukraine for air defense, drones and missiles from the Ukraine Support Loan,” Kubilius said.
The latest approval means the EU has now allocated all €28.3 billion ($32.9 billion) earmarked for Ukraine’s defense under the sprogram.So far, €8.4 billion ($9.7 billion) has been disbursed. Kubilius said another €4.7 billion ($5.5 billion) is currently being processed.
Fires, Explosions Reported Across Russia as Ukrainian Drones Target Refineries, Ozon Hubs
The €90 billion support loan, approved by EU countries in April, is intended to cover around two-thirds of Ukraine’s defense and budgetary needs in 2026 and 2027 and will be delivered in tranches.
PAC-3 missiles global shortage
This latest decision allows Ukraine to bypass some of the loan’s standard procurement requirements.
Under the rules, weapons purchased with the loan are generally required to come from the EU or Ukraine sources, with equipment containing more than 35% of components sourced from third countries requires explicit approval.
Kubilius said the Commission had granted five such exemptions: three for Ukrainian companies to source drone components from outside the bloc and two for US-made equipment, including PAC-3 interceptor missiles.
“Ukraine’s military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical products in the required quantities and within very short time frames,” Kubilius said.
The commissioner said speed is particularly important for air defense, given Ukraine’s immediate needs and the limited global supply of Patriot interceptors.
The European Commission estimates that Ukraine needs around 2,000 PAC-3 interceptors annually to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks, while global production is only gradually increasing.
Kubilius said allies are exploring ways to provide Ukraine with missiles from existing stockpiles while waiting for new production.
One option under discussion is for EU member states that already have PAC-3 missiles to transfer them to Ukraine immediately and receive replacement missiles under agreements planned for 2027.
EU relaxes sourcing rules for Ukrainian drones
Three of the five exemptions approved by the Commission relate to Ukrainian drone manufacturers.
The Commission did not specify from which countries the components covered by the exemptions would be supplied. However, an earlier exemption approved in April allowed Ukraine to source drone components from China.
The remaining two exemptions cover US-made equipment, including PAC-3 missiles, with purchases potentially coordinated through NATO.
The decision comes as Ukraine and its allies seek to strengthen air defenses before winter, when Russia is expected to again target Ukraine’s energy infrastructure with large-scale missile and drone attacks.

Flamingo Missiles Strike Sanctioned Chemical Plant Volgogradpromproekt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:45:20 UTC
19:45:20 KST

In the early hours of September 11, Ukrainian long-range FP-5 Flamingo missiles attacked the Volgogradpromproekt specialty chemicals plant in Volgograd, Russia.
The incident was reported by Flamingo manufacturer Fire Point.
The governor of the Volgograd region confirmed that the city had come under a missile attack. According to him, debris fell on the grounds of an industrial facility in southern Volgograd.
Volgogradpromproekt is located in the Kirovsky district of the city. It is a research and production company operating in the field of low-tonnage chemicals and manufacturing organophosphorus compounds, flame retardants, resins, and other specialty chemicals.
According to Exilenova+, the manufacturer’s products are used in the production of polymer and composite materials for Russia’s aviation, shipbuilding, and defense industries. Organophosphorus compounds and flame retardants, in particular, provide these materials with fire resistance and other required performance properties.
One of Volgogradpromproekt’s key products is OSF, an organosilicon ferrocene derivative containing iron compounds. It is used as a catalyst and combustion-rate modifier for composite solid rocket propellants.
A Russian patent states that the iron content of the OSF product is about 10%. Adding this component makes it possible to regulate the burn rate of rocket propellant while maintaining its required properties.
In December 2023, the United States added Volgogradpromproekt to its sanctions list along with companies supporting Russia’s military-industrial base. The U.S. Department of the Treasury specifically cited the production of ferrocene-containing combustion catalysts in its sanctions rationale.
The manufacturer’s ties to Russia’s military-industrial complex are also confirmed by a court ruling. According to it, in 2018, Volgogradpromproekt signed three contracts with the Perm Powder Plant to supply 15 tonnes of OSF worth a total of ₽97.836 million ($1.1 million), excluding VAT.
The Perm Powder Plant is one of the key producers of solid rocket propellants and propellants for Russia’s military industry.
Court documents explicitly state that these products were supplied as part of Russia’s state defense procurement program, with Volgogradpromproekt acting as a contractor.
Today, a possible Ukrainian drone attack on the Volgograd Oil Refinery was reported, which is also located in the southern part of the city. During the strike, local residents heard explosions and the distinctive sounds of drones flying overhead.

I Fixed a Tractor Using John Deere’s Self-Repair Service. Farmers Aren’t Sold on It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

There is something wrong with the tractor. The water-in-fuel sensor, a small device embedded in the John Deere machine that monitors the integrity of its diesel engine, is disconnected. And I’ve got to fix it.
I’m not a mechanic or a farmer. I’m poking at a laptop at John Deere’s corporate office in Santa Clara, California. There’s a cable connecting the computer to a 5130ML tractor sitting on the grass nearby. A bright red notification sits on the screen, telling me something is wrong. I type in a question and the software pulls up instructions and a few images from the user manual that matches the serial number of the machine.
I wander over to the tractor and find the parts modeled on the screen. I spot the sensor, with two very obvious dangling wires that need to be connected together. I press them together, hear a little click, then step away and look back at the screen. The notification has cleared. Everything seems to be fine. In just a couple minutes, all by myself, I’ve fixed the water-in-fuel sensor. This fix was an easy one. It's a WiF, really.
The John Deere employees surrounding me offer their congratulations. They’ve all been very patient with me, someone who has written several articles for WIRED about their company’s seemingly steadfast reluctance to let anyone but its official technicians repair its products.
In the group is Jahmy Hindman, senior vice president and chief technology officer of John Deere, who has flown in from Illinois. Hindman has worked for the company for 30 years. In that time, John Deere has thrived in an era of technological advancement. He’s here now to show off the company’s self-repair software Operations Center Pro Service, a system that pairs with nearly every electronic-enabled machine John Deere has made.
“It is owner-friendly,” Hindman says. “I think that's always been our intent.”
Lots of farmers would beg to differ.
Oh Deere
John Deere is the largest agricultural machine manufacturer in the US. In the past couple decades, machines of this ilk have become far more technologically advanced, loaded up with controllers, radios, and sensors. Many newer machines are equipped with 4G wireless connections that enable the collection of precise location data and other metrics. Some tractors can even run without a human operator at all, guided by built-in software systems to run autonomously on predetermined paths.
Over the last decade, John Deere has become a big target of the ever-growing right-to-repair movement. The company’s high-tech software systems also come equipped with digital locks, which require official, dealer-sanctioned approval to access. If you want to fiddle with a part, or replace it with an aftermarket alternative, those software restrictions can block those attempts.
That frustration has manifested in multiple lawsuits and even federal action. In April, the company agreed to pay out a $99 million settlement to its equipment owners to pay back burdensome repair costs. In July, the company settled a separate lawsuit brought by the US Federal Trade Commission that would require the company to make its products more repairable. John Deere did not admit wrongdoing in either case. Repair advocates say the two measures have been insufficient, both in financial terms and as requirements that will actually change Deere’s behavior. (Both settlements are not yet final until a judge issues a final ruling.)
Pro Tip
John Deere disagrees, of course, citing its recent efforts to make the case that its self-repair program works just fine.
The company introduced its Pro Service in 2025. Prices start at an annual cost of $195 per individual machine. For bigger operations or independent repair shops, the price to access every machine in John Deere’s fleet starts at $4,995 a year. That access for agricultural and turf services costs $5,995 per year.
Pro Service lets owners connect Deere’s software to their equipment via Wi-Fi or cable. Based on the serial number of the machine, the software can be used to find information from manuals and John Deere’s broader data services to diagnose any maintenance the machine needs. John Deere also recently introduced an AI chatbot called JD to its Operations Center self-repair software tool, but I did not have a chance to use that version during my visit. The AI features are meant to make it easier to find information about the components in any given machine.
“As the tractor products grow in size, they also grow in number of controllers that are necessary in order to make it all work,” Hindman says, noting that in some cases tractors can have upwards of 50 controllers. “So it can be super complex.”
Theoretically, Pro Service is the ultimate platform to find any equipment information and diagnose any problem. If something goes wrong, the software will guide you through a fix. Some features in Pro Service can be downloaded and used offline in case a connection isn’t working when something needs fixing. You can customize the layout to your liking and keep track of the full history of the software updates on each machine. If you need a new part, the software will helpfully serve you a link to the product in John Deere’s shop. It feels as smooth as scrolling through an Amazon page.
Kelli Sullivan, a group product manager of marketing automation and governance at John Deere, is the person leading the demo. She says owners are in full control of their data and can choose whether to share it with John Deere or an independent repair shop, or keep it private.
Data as a Service
The thing John Deere does seem to struggle with is enticing people to use its Pro Service, or even making its customers aware of it. (That’s the reason I’m here at this demo.) A year on, John Deere says its service has about a thousand daily users—a relatively small number, given that there are somewhere around 1.8 million farms in the US.
“We’re just trying to get the word out,” Sullivan says. “We have a suite of tools that are already available in our customers’ hands that allow them to do those things.”
Jared Wilson is a farmer in Missouri who uses Deere machines to care for his 3,000 acres of corn and soybean crops. He is also a named plaintiff in the $99 million lawsuit against John Deere who has called that payout ruling “fundamentally flawed.” When I describe my demo experience to Wilson, he laughs, saying the service works best on particularly simple repairs.
“If you have multiple failures, you have to figure out where to start,” Wilson says. “If you have three different or four different diagnostic codes, where do you start in the tree to figure out what's wrong?”
Wilson does not use Pro Service. He doesn’t know anyone who does, saying the farmers he knows tend to use cracked versions of the software they find on gray markets instead of giving their money to John Deere. Even with Pro Service, he says, farmers don’t always trust that John Deere will give farmers the tools they really need to fix their stuff.
“It's taken a class action lawsuit and FTC action to get them to come this far,” Wilson says. “If you believe what they're saying now—that this is actually it and we're getting everything we've asked for—then I've got some oceanfront property in Arizona to sell you.”
One of Wilson's biggest concerns with using a service like Pro Service, he says, is that it’s almost impossible to compare the dealership version of the software with the customer version of the software for parity. (Hindman says the versions of the software are all the same.)
Part of the problem are PIPs, or product improvement plans, which is a term John Deere uses to identify potential or existing problems in its machines. John Deere can issue a PIP, which then goes out to let people who own a particular piece of equipment know there’s an issue with the machine. But those missives only go out after the system has gathered the information that an improvement might be needed in the first place.
If a user faces a novel problem with how a machine works, it would still take time for that issue to get back to John Deere, which would verify it, then issue a PIP in Pro Service. In the meantime, the person dealing with the broken tractor won’t have the needed information to figure out exactly what is going on. Ideally, many of them would like to be able to troubleshoot the problem themselves, without having to use the company’s proprietary software.
“They're still not giving us access to that next level that we have to have for some of the most difficult problems that we encounter,” Wilson says.
Willie Cade, a board member of the advocacy group Repair.org and frequent critic of John Deere, takes that a step further.
“They're just monopolists that want to make money and as much as they possibly can,” Cade says. “Their real customer is not the farmer. Their real customer is Wall Street.”
At the demo, I ask about the repair advocates and what they get wrong about John Deere. Hindman says he doesn’t mind the pressure.
“We have the best intentions of making sure that we have the ability to give customers the tools that they need to keep their equipment up and running,” Hindman says. “We share that goal in common. Are there things that we need to continue to work on? I'm sure that there are. But let's not forget that we are a long way towards moving the needle to a much better state.”
The repair advocates are still pushing on John Deere. Agricultural equipment like tractors are some of the most durable goods, built to last for years and even decades of hard manual labor. If society isn’t able to establish a precedent to let people fix these machines, advocates argue, it becomes harder to pass legislation or judicial rulings that would solidify people’s rights to fix their own personal devices.
“This is an issue that's concerning agricultural equipment,” Wilson says. “But it's really the vanguard of a much bigger and persistent problem that affects every aspect of our society.”
Update, September 11 at noon: Additional information about the status of the two legal settlements was added to the story.

Timothy Snyder: how US failed after 9/11 and what Ukraine should learn from its mistakes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:45:00 EEST
19:45:00 KST

Timothy Snyder: how US failed after 9/11 and what Ukraine should learn from its mistakes
On September 11, 2001, when I taught my third class as a professor of East European history at Yale, I knew what the subject had to be: provocation.
The Russian imperial secret services, and then the Soviet secret services, had perfected the art of convincing adversaries to do what they wanted them to do while making them think it was for their own reasons.
When something terrible happens, as it had that day, suffering, though no doubt desired by those who caused it, is not the point. The point is to get you into a frame of mind that leads you to do something that hurts yourself even more.
History is full of acts of terror. The real question, I told the students that day, is what you do next. You cannot prevent every terrible thing from happening. But your freedom begins with your response.
Sadly, we Americans responded exactly as the terrorists would have wanted.
Indeed, we likely exceeded their expectations, making the world much worse for ourselves and everyone else.
Why Trump emerged
The obvious response to 9/11 should have been to liberate ourselves from fossil fuels.
Without our dependence on oil, we would never have been entangled in the Middle East in the first place. Had we funded clean-energy sources, we could have headed off global warming, prevented further Middle East wars, and prevented the rise of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s hydrocarbon oligarchy.
It was not to be. President George W. Bush, the feckless scion of an oil family, had no interest in intensifying the search for safe energy.
The terrorists attacked us, he claimed, because "they hate our freedoms." Yet our own government then acted to limit our freedom.
A new Department of Homeland Security placed a grab-bag of agencies, including border management, under a single authority, treating them all as a matter of security. This set the stage for a domestic politics that divides people living in America into "legals" and "illegals," us and them, and builds concentration camps.
The notion of a "homeland," which echoes the Nazi fascination with Heimat, was even more dangerous. At the time, it was an exotic label for a government department, not really in keeping with American English or institutional traditions. But the word has since been normalized in an essentially fascist sense.
Under President Donald Trump’s administration, the main threats are deemed to be domestic,
from those who do not truly belong. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth treats the armed forces as a site of culture wars: men against women, whites against Blacks. Troops’ future task is "homeland defense." The armed forces are to become the personal militia of a ruler, used to quash resistance to Trump.
Of course, one of the major causes of Trump’s rise was the US invasion of Iraq in 2003 – a war of choice that was the worst possible foreign-policy response to 9/11. The war left Americans traumatized and vulnerable to a candidate who would exploit the issue to gain power (only to launch more wars and make us vulnerable to more terrorism).
It would also entrench a political economy dominated by military spending and debt. Instead of addressing wealth inequality, social immobility, and family insecurity, we poured blood (mainly of others) and treasure into the sand.
As a people, we followed a script that could have been written by the terrorists themselves. Worse, our elected leaders became that script’s co-authors.
The Bush administration invented the links between Iraq and the 9/11 terrorists, which eventually led Americans to distrust their government, enabling the rise of someone like Trump. And these invented pretexts set the stage for violating the most basic precept of international law: the prohibition of unprovoked wars of aggression.
The Russians followed America’s lead
With that, the post-Cold War era of democratic revival in 1989–91 drew to a close. In preparation for the invasion of Iraq, Americans claimed that just as liberation had been possible in Eastern Europe, so it was possible in the Middle East.
The situation was, of course, very different; it is one thing to oust a dictatorship from within, and quite another to do so by foreign invasion. And while Europe’s post-communist leaders had ideas about what would come next, the Americans in Iraq had none, imagining that simply destroying a bad regime would bring about a better one.
It would be wrong to say that the US-led invasion of Iraq caused Russia to invade Ukraine over a decade later, in 2014.
But the American war certainly made life easier for Putin,
who concluded that great powers could invade other countries with the help of extravagant lies.
One reason I warned in 2013 and early 2014 that Russia could invade Ukraine and seize Crimea was the surreal propaganda being deployed in Russian media. Like the US propaganda of 2002 and early 2003, it made no sense.
The Americans claimed that fighting terrorism required ousting a regime that, while horrible, suppressed the Islamism that was behind 9/11. The Russians escalated the nonsense: Ukrainians were all gay, all Nazis, and all Jews. Their state did not exist, but oppressed Russians. Despite being an authoritarian regime, Russia would bring democracy to Ukraine, though it already was one.
Not long after the invasion began, I participated in a public discussion in Prague. Emotions ran high. One person wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with a Russian fascist slogan took the microphone and asked why Russia should obey any rules when the Americans had not done so in Iraq in 2003. (I replied that rules were rules: the American invasion had been illegal, but two wrongs did not make a right.)
The question exemplified an approach that arose from the internal logic of an oligarchic regime, but also one that the US had facilitated: there was no truth, no right and wrong, and no rules.
Respond like Ukrainians
In late 2021 and early 2022, as Russia was preparing its second invasion of Ukraine, the shadow of Iraq still loomed. Two decades earlier, the US lied about the rationale for invading Iraq.
Now, it was sharing the truth about Russian plans to invade Ukraine. In general, although the facts were clearly there.
It was easier to doubt the Americans in 2022 because of the lies they told in 2002. As a result, everyone was less prepared than they might have been when the big war (as the Ukrainians call it) came.
Having been provoked in 2001, America responded as the terrorists wanted, helping to create a world in which terrorism is so normal that we hardly know when to use the word.
Putin and Trump use it to define their enemies, though they are themselves state terrorists. Trump himself normalized terrorism by seeking to stay in power by force in January 2021.
And Putin’s criminal war of aggression in Ukraine features widespread rape, abduction of children, and the mass execution of activists in occupied territories. But what is most obviously terroristic is the daily launch of drones and missiles targeting Ukrainian civilians.
I am writing this underground in Kharkiv, where the air raid sirens are sounding for the third time tonight. The Ukrainians shoot down most of the drones, but the missiles simply fall, explode, and kill, because Americans have chosen to deny them Patriot missiles.
This partly reflects the solidarity of terrorists: Trump’s emissaries were just in Moscow praising Putin's "goals." It is also a side effect of Trump’s doomed war of choice against Iran. The US has pointlessly fired munitions in the Middle East that might have saved lives in Ukraine.
Trump’s Iran war enables Putin’s Ukraine war.
And yet Trump’s war is extremely unpopular–and obviously lost. He stays in it, even as the US midterm elections approach, perhaps because he is hoping the Iranian regime will do him the favor of striking inside the US.
Then he can try to suspend elections or deploy more American troops in more American cities and remain in power indefinitely.
That is one way of wanting the terrorists to win:
fight a big war in the Middle East, deplete your own defenses, and hope for the worst. Iran might take the bait by launching a murderous action, or Trump could simply claim that it had.
Given all the provocations and lying and terror since 9/11, it would be foolish not to take this scenario seriously. And if it happens, the answer will be the same as it was in 2001: your freedom begins with your response. Above all, do not do the thing that the terrorist wants you to do.
From where I sit, in the dark hours of the early morning, I recall Ukrainians I saw last night, meeting underground for a public event, smiling, drinking wine, and talking about ideas, not doing what the terrorists want, not giving in and going along, but thinking for themselves about the future.
That is what Americans must do today, on this terrible anniversary. Do not be provoked; do not enter the mental world of the terrorist; think for yourself.
Only then can we hope to make this next quarter-century better than the last one.
This article originally appeared on Project Syndicate and is republished with permission from the copyright holder.
Timothy Snyder,
the inaugural Chair in Modern European History at the University of Toronto

The notion of a "homeland," which echoes the Nazi fascination with Heimat, was even more dangerous. At the time, it was an exotic label for a government department, not really in keeping with American English or institutional traditions. But the word has since been normalized in an essentially fascist sense.
Under President Donald Trump’s administration, the main threats are deemed to be domestic,
from those who do not truly belong. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth treats the armed forces as a site of culture wars: men against women, whites against Blacks. Troops’ future task is "homeland defense." The armed forces are to become the personal militia of a ruler, used to quash resistance to Trump.
Of course, one of the major causes of Trump’s rise was the US invasion of Iraq in 2003 – a war of choice that was the worst possible foreign-policy response to 9/11. The war left Americans traumatized and vulnerable to a candidate who would exploit the issue to gain power (only to launch more wars and make us vulnerable to more terrorism).
It would also entrench a political economy dominated by military spending and debt. Instead of addressing wealth inequality, social immobility, and family insecurity, we poured blood (mainly of others) and treasure into the sand.
As a people, we followed a script that could have been written by the terrorists themselves. Worse, our elected leaders became that script’s co-authors.
The Bush administration invented the links between Iraq and the 9/11 terrorists, which eventually led Americans to distrust their government, enabling the rise of someone like Trump. And these invented pretexts set the stage for violating the most basic precept of international law: the prohibition of unprovoked wars of aggression.
The Russians followed America’s lead
With that, the post-Cold War era of democratic revival in 1989–91 drew to a close. In preparation for the invasion of Iraq, Americans claimed that just as liberation had been possible in Eastern Europe, so it was possible in the Middle East.
The situation was, of course, very different; it is one thing to oust a dictatorship from within, and quite another to do so by foreign invasion. And while Europe’s post-communist leaders had ideas about what would come next, the Americans in Iraq had none, imagining that simply destroying a bad regime would bring about a better one.
It would be wrong to say that the US-led invasion of Iraq caused Russia to invade Ukraine over a decade later, in 2014.
But the American war certainly made life easier for Putin,
who concluded that great powers could invade other countries with the help of extravagant lies.
One reason I warned in 2013 and early 2014 that Russia could invade Ukraine and seize Crimea was the surreal propaganda being deployed in Russian media. Like the US propaganda of 2002 and early 2003, it made no sense.
The Americans claimed that fighting terrorism required ousting a regime that, while horrible, suppressed the Islamism that was behind 9/11. The Russians escalated the nonsense: Ukrainians were all gay, all Nazis, and all Jews. Their state did not exist, but oppressed Russians. Despite being an authoritarian regime, Russia would bring democracy to Ukraine, though it already was one.
Not long after the invasion began, I participated in a public discussion in Prague. Emotions ran high. One person wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with a Russian fascist slogan took the microphone and asked why Russia should obey any rules when the Americans had not done so in Iraq in 2003. (I replied that rules were rules: the American invasion had been illegal, but two wrongs did not make a right.)
The question exemplified an approach that arose from the internal logic of an oligarchic regime, but also one that the US had facilitated: there was no truth, no right and wrong, and no rules.
Respond like Ukrainians
In late 2021 and early 2022, as Russia was preparing its second invasion of Ukraine, the shadow of Iraq still loomed. Two decades earlier, the US lied about the rationale for invading Iraq.
Now, it was sharing the truth about Russian plans to invade Ukraine. In general, although the facts were clearly there.
It was easier to doubt the Americans in 2022 because of the lies they told in 2002. As a result, everyone was less prepared than they might have been when the big war (as the Ukrainians call it) came.
Having been provoked in 2001, America responded as the terrorists wanted, helping to create a world in which terrorism is so normal that we hardly know when to use the word.
Putin and Trump use it to define their enemies, though they are themselves state terrorists. Trump himself normalized terrorism by seeking to stay in power by force in January 2021.
And Putin’s criminal war of aggression in Ukraine features widespread rape, abduction of children, and the mass execution of activists in occupied territories. But what is most obviously terroristic is the daily launch of drones and missiles targeting Ukrainian civilians.
I am writing this underground in Kharkiv, where the air raid sirens are sounding for the third time tonight. The Ukrainians shoot down most of the drones, but the missiles simply fall, explode, and kill, because Americans have chosen to deny them Patriot missiles.
This partly reflects the solidarity of terrorists: Trump’s emissaries were just in Moscow praising Putin's "goals." It is also a side effect of Trump’s doomed war of choice against Iran. The US has pointlessly fired munitions in the Middle East that might have saved lives in Ukraine.
Trump’s Iran war enables Putin’s Ukraine war.
And yet Trump’s war is extremely unpopular–and obviously lost. He stays in it, even as the US midterm elections approach, perhaps because he is hoping the Iranian regime will do him the favor of striking inside the US.
Then he can try to suspend elections or deploy more American troops in more American cities and remain in power indefinitely.
That is one way of wanting the terrorists to win:
fight a big war in the Middle East, deplete your own defenses, and hope for the worst. Iran might take the bait by launching a murderous action, or Trump could simply claim that it had.
Given all the provocations and lying and terror since 9/11, it would be foolish not to take this scenario seriously. And if it happens, the answer will be the same as it was in 2001: your freedom begins with your response. Above all, do not do the thing that the terrorist wants you to do.
From where I sit, in the dark hours of the early morning, I recall Ukrainians I saw last night, meeting underground for a public event, smiling, drinking wine, and talking about ideas, not doing what the terrorists want, not giving in and going along, but thinking for themselves about the future.
That is what Americans must do today, on this terrible anniversary. Do not be provoked; do not enter the mental world of the terrorist; think for yourself.
Only then can we hope to make this next quarter-century better than the last one.

the inaugural Chair in Modern European History at the University of Toronto

Gateway or outpost? Inside Israel's growing footprint in Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11

Breadcrumb
Gateway or outpost? Inside Israel's growing footprint in Cyprus
On the southern coast of Cyprus, the signs of a growing Israeli presence are becoming harder to miss.
There are new housing developments marketed to Israeli buyers, large parcels of land changing hands, political posters, and a network of schools, synagogues, kosher businesses, and other institutions serving a community that is no longer made up solely of tourists and second-home owners.
The result is an increasingly visible Israeli footprint on an island that has long relied on foreign capital to drive its property market.
Yet the scale and concentration of some projects have prompted a debate on the island: is this simply another wave of foreign investment, or is something more permanent taking shape?
A new wave of foreign investment
Cyprus’s economy has long depended on third-state investment, with successive schemes – including the controversial “golden passports” and golden visas – designed to attract capital, particularly into property.
Historically dominated by the United Kingdom and Russia, capital has more recently come from Lebanon, Ukraine, and Israel.
The golden visa scheme enables non-European Union (EU) nationals to obtain residency by investing €300,000 in property or a company, raising concerns over transparency and regulation.
Direct investment vis-à-vis Israel stood at around €3.5 billion in stock in 2025, with €308 million in transactions, according to preliminary data from the Central Bank of Cyprus.
Recent Israeli investments have involved large land purchases and projects combining housing developments with resorts and gated communities. In 2023, liberal Israeli newspaper Haaretz wondered whether Cyprus was becoming the “second Israel?”
Israel's growing exodus
The trend coincides with rising Israeli emigration. Since 2023, political tensions surrounding judicial reforms proposed by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition government, followed by the Gaza war, have fuelled mounting insecurity and pessimism about the country’s future.
“The justice reform from January 2023 was the first turning point. Many lost hope in the future of Israel. October 2023 confirmed this trend, and many decided to move,” Michael Harari, Israel’s former ambassador in Cyprus, told The New Arab.
Between 2023 and 2025, 270,000 citizens left Israel, a recent study based on data from the Israel Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) found, highlighting particularly substantial emigration among highly educated and economically strong groups.
In Cyprus, this movement has translated into both relocation and investment – helping turn what was once largely a tourism and property relationship into a more visible presence.
Cyprus as a haven
In this troubled landscape, removed from regional convulsions, Cyprus has become “Israel’s favourite island escape” – less than an hour away by plane, relatively affordable and safe.
“Cyprus offers the closest escape,” Louisa Varaclas, director of the Israel Office within the Cyprus Tourism Ministry, told The New Arab.
Israel was Cyprus’s second-largest tourism market in 2025, accounting for 13% of all arrivals, or 600,000 visitors. The Israeli Embassy estimates that around 15,000 to 20,000 Israelis currently live in Cyprus, compared with 6,500 in 2018, although the exact number is difficult to determine because many hold European Union (EU) passports.
Geographical proximity, political ties, a favourable tax regime, business opportunities, and a sense of security have helped make the island attractive for residence and investment.
“Cyprus is a security partner,” Roee Kibrik, Director of Research from the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies (Mitvim), told The New Arab. For Israel’s strategic logic, he argues, the island can almost be understood as an extension of Israel’s security space - while the partnership also serves Cyprus’s security interests.
“Given that political and economic relations between Israel and Cyprus deepen, there will also be growing Israeli interest in tourism, residence, and investment in Cyprus,” Zenonas Tziarras, a lecturer in the Department of Turkish and Middle Eastern Studies from the University of Cyprus, told The New Arab.
Cyprus also offers a “gateway” to the European Union (EU), its market, its electricity and gas infrastructures and sea routes, but also its institutional structures and political channels, Kibrik argues.
From property to communities
The growing Israeli presence is particularly visible in coastal areas around Larnaca, Limassol, and Paphos, where Israelis have purchased property and marketed dedicated housing complexes. Jewish institutions, kosher businesses, and Hebrew-language services have expanded alongside them.
“Some definitely left Israel. Some others live in Cyprus while continuing to work in Israel, while others are moving part of their assets or establishing companies in Cyprus,” Kibrik says.
This trend has also fueled concerns over housing affordability. Property prices rose by 11.7% in Larnaca and 10.7% in Limassol between 2025 and 2026, with the Central Bank of Cyprus attributing part of the inflation to stronger demand from third-country investors, alongside construction and labour costs.
Harari admits there are tensions. “This migration is a natural process and contributes largely to the local economy. But of course, for a small place as Cyprus, these numbers are substantial, and you can also understand concerns from local populations because there is influence on property prices.”
The island’s role as a refuge during crises has further deepened these connections. In October 2023, 5,000 Israelis landed in Cyprus. During the Israel-Iran conflict in June 2025, 15,000 Israelis were stranded after airspace closure.
Chabad centres provided accommodation, food, and emergency assistance, illustrating how a network initially serving religious and tourist needs has also become part of the infrastructure supporting a growing Israeli community.
Chabad, a global Hasidic Jewish movement, operates around 4,000 centres in 100 countries. Publicly apolitical, recent investigations have documented support from parts of the movement for Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power), the far-right party led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
In Cyprus, Chabad operates six centres, alongside a synagogue, kindergarten, mikvah, kosher certification agency, a cemetery, and summer programmes. Its founder and Cyprus’s chief rabbi, Zeev Raskin, also promotes the development of resorts and tourist complexes designed to comply with Jewish law.
Gated communities and contested projects
Several projects have sparked controversy over planning and environmental regulation, the role of national and local authorities, and the longer-term character of this presence.
In Latchi, a large hotel complex completed the final stages of construction while licensing issues remained unresolved. In Polemidia, a €50 million Jewish school designed for up to 1,500 students has generated concerns over traffic and planning, while the municipality had not been involved in the process.
Its slated director, Rabbi Yehoshua Smukler, has described the project as the future “cornerstone” of Cyprus’s Jewish community.
In Trozena and Gerovasa, Hungarian-Israeli businessman Uriel Kertesz has proposed redeveloping abandoned villages into an “ecotourism” project combining homes, vineyards, a wellness centre and restored ruins. The project has faced environmental scrutiny, as the area falls within the Natura network of protected natural areas.
In Zygi, a 60,000-square-metre luxury development is marketed as a gated complex of residences serving the Jewish community. When announced in 2024 by property entrepreneur Daniel Morris Goldberg and Rabbi Ziv Raskin, the project was promoted as a “kosher slice” of Cyprus.
“Do we have closed communities, rather than absorbing individuals into the local culture?” Kibrik asks, pointing to an emerging debate over housing, culture, and the transformation of some areas.
The speed and concentration of Israeli investments distinguish them from the longer-established Russian presence, notes Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, Assistant Professor in Transitional Justice and Human Rights from the University of Central Lancashire - Cyprus.
“Russians have had a very long-standing presence on the island, which developed gradually, whereas Israelis have been much more sudden and economically aggressive, with entire areas being purchased. Russians are primarily based in Limassol and live within the city, whereas some Israelis have begun constructing gated communities, separating themselves within exclusive areas," Hadjigeorgiou tells The New Arab.
"There is also an oversensitivity here because of what is happening in Israel and Palestine and the history of Israelis settling on land, accompanied by violence and displacement, while the local history of occupation vis-à-vis Türkiye adds another layer.”
Theodosis Pipis, a doctoral candidate in History from the University of Leiden, puts the question more bluntly.
“Given these projects and the high concentration of land purchases happening swiftly in coastal and port cities, could Cyprus be falling under the auspices of some form of permanent or semi-permanent Israeli expansionism?”
Growing influence and public outrage
In July 2026, campaign posters for Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief-of-staff and candidate in Israel’s elections, popped up along highways around Larnaca airport, generating an unusual debate over Israel’s growing influence in Cyprus.
This event echoed wider concerns. “Israeli buyers are purchasing significant land parcels and strategic economic assets. This cannot but sound the alarm for us,” Stefanos Stefanou, a spokesperson for the Progressive Party of Working People (AKEL), warned in June 2025.
And this trend has become a significant issue across the political spectrum, from the election posters to the redevelopment of abandoned villages.
“It’s a topic most circles on the island discuss - no matter though you are from the left, the far-right, the centre, we can all see the growing Israeli presence on the island,” Pipis tells The New Arab.
Growing economic connections also involve powerful business interests. Cypriot-Israeli real estate businessman Yakir Gabay, whose fortune is estimated at around $4 billion, has become a prominent figure in Cyprus.
He is involved in an €856 million investment project around Limassol and recently purchased a 950,000-square-metre plot from the Bank of Cyprus for €28 million.
In February 2026, he also joined the executive committee of the 'Board of Peace'. He visits Israel frequently, operates behind the scenes, and has close personal and business ties to Jared Kushner and, as early as November 2023, reportedly submitted a reconstruction plan for Palestine.
Cyprus, alongside Greece, has recently become an essential part of Israel’s strategic environment. The relationship spans defence, military cooperation and energy, and has developed into a deeper strategic partnership.
Since June 2017, the Israeli military has regularly conducted exercises on the island, including air force, naval, and ground forces units, and intelligence and evacuation drills. The exercises have included simulations relevant to operations in southern Lebanon, making Cyprus a uniquely accessible training environment for Israel’s military.
“Of course, the deepening strategic relationship between both states has made Cyprus an attractive place to Israeli citizens, as a place to invest and live. Both come together,” Harari says.
Sylvain Henry is a writer based in Samos, Greece, and a master's graduate in sociology and political philosophy. He recently worked with the Cyprus Refugee Council

Regulator suspends Plastic Surgery Center operations in Helsinki
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
13:42:53 EEST
19:42:53 KST

Finnish regulators have suspended healthcare services at two Plastic Surgery Center companies operating from the same premises in central Helsinki after inspectors found serious risks to patient safety.
The Licensing and Supervisory Agency, LVV, carried out an unannounced inspection at the Aleksanterinkatu premises of Plastic Surgery Center Helsinki Oy and Plastic Surgery Center Tampere Oy on 9 September. The agency ordered both providers to stop healthcare services with immediate effect.
The action comes as police investigate the death of 27-year-old social media influencer Olivia Oras, who had been a patient at the clinic.
Police are investigating the case as aggravated negligent homicide. Helsinki Police received a request for an investigation on 6 September and conducted a special search of the Aleksanterinkatu clinic on Thursday.
The regulator has not disclosed the specific patient safety problems identified during its inspection.
“We cannot provide further details about the suspension decision at this stage. We will provide more information once the written decision has been completed,” Niina Oresmaa, head of a unit at LVV’s social and healthcare division, said in the agency’s statement.
LVV plans to release further information on 18 September.
The suspension is the latest regulatory action involving private aesthetic healthcare providers in the Helsinki region.
Earlier this week, LVV ordered Medical Centre Estetic Oy in Helsinki to stop healthcare services after an inspection found unauthorised medicines and treatments, along with problems involving patient records, medical devices and medicine storage.
Regulators have also taken action against Nordicshape this year. Healthcare services at its Espoo clinic were suspended in April following findings involving medicines, medical supervision and medical devices. Its Helsinki clinic was ordered to halt healthcare services in July over separate patient safety deficiencies. The Espoo company filed for bankruptcy in July.

California tightens child safety rules for social media, AI chatbots
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
18:41:55 CST
19:41:55 KST

SACRAMENTO, the United States, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- California Governor Gavin Newsom on Thursday signed 13 bills to strengthen protections for children against online risks, particularly those involving social media and artificial intelligence (AI) companion chatbots.
The measures prohibit covered platforms from providing users under 16 with addictive features, including addictive feeds and autoplay, according to the governor's office. They also remove the parental-consent option for such users and require platforms to verify users' ages before providing the features.
Newsom also signed Senate Bill 1119, known as "Adam's Law," which establishes new safeguards for children under 18 who use companion chatbots. The law is named after Adam Raine, a 16-year-old California teenager who died by suicide in 2025 after interacting with ChatGPT, according to State Senator Steve Padilla, one of the bill's authors.
The law requires child-safety risk assessments, crisis protocols addressing suicidal ideation and self-harm, parental controls, notices informing children that they are interacting with AI, and measures to prevent chatbots from encouraging children to rely on them for emotional support.
The law also requires independent child-safety audits. By default, chatbots must limit children's continuous use to one hour and daily use to two hours, while parents can adjust the settings or disable access for children under 16.
Under another measure, a social media platform that generates more than 100 million U.S. dollars in annual gross revenue can be held liable for statutory damages if it fails to exercise ordinary care and causes injury to a child. The damages are the greater of 5,000 U.S. dollars per violation, capped at 1 million U.S. dollars per child, or three times the child's actual damages.
The other signed bills address areas including children's privacy, age assurance, school-issued electronic devices, student data, digital wellness and digitally altered or AI-generated material depicting child sexual exploitation, according to the governor's office. ■

International symposium explores new approach to folklore protection

NANCHANG, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Participants at the 2026 International Symposium on Intellectual Property and Traditional Cultural Expressions this week said China's experience in protecting folklore provides a strong reference as the world explores new paths for folklore protection.
Nearly 400 Chinese and foreign guests from the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) and more than 30 countries and regions attended the event held in Fuzhou, east China's Jiangxi Province.
During the event, participants also visited ancient streets and intangible cultural heritage sites in Fuzhou, gaining first-hand insight into China's efforts to protect and promote traditional cultural expressions.
Edward Kwakwa, WIPO assistant director general, said the symposium provided an important platform for mutual learning and exchange.
Differentiated national practices and open multilateral dialogue will jointly contribute to improving global folklore copyright governance and safeguarding world cultural diversity, Kwakwa said.
Tempa Tshering, an intellectual property (IP) officer at Bhutan's Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Employment, spoke highly of China's full-chain service model covering folklore IP rights confirmation, utilization and protection.
Tshering said that protection and commercialization are not at odds, but rather mutually reinforcing. He explained that offering creators reasonable incentives can encourage the inheritance and protection of traditional culture.
Holton Faasau, an official with Samoa's Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Labour, shared similar views. A copyright service system that reaches grassroots workshops and ordinary cultural inheritors can ensure cultural protection truly benefits the creators, Faasau said.
Lucille Anak Awen Jon, a jewelry designer from Malaysia, said China's grassroots IP service experience is worth learning. She noted that IP is not an obstacle to innovation but a tool that helps traditional folk art enter the modern market.
Modernization should create new value while preserving the cultural essence of traditional art, she added.
Afsana Mirzazada, an official with the Intellectual Property Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan, said legal protection should not seek to freeze traditional culture at a particular point in time.
Instead, it should prevent the misuse of traditional cultural expressions while allowing them to survive and evolve as a living cultural phenomenon, Mirzazada said. ■

China to raise gasoline, diesel prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
18:41:50 CST
19:41:50 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- China will raise the retail prices of gasoline and diesel from Saturday, based on recent changes in international crude oil prices, the country's top economic planner announced Friday.
Under the adjustment, gasoline and diesel prices will increase by 260 yuan (about 38.38 U.S. dollars) and 250 yuan per tonne, respectively, according to the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC).
Based on the current pricing mechanism, the ceiling retail prices of gasoline and diesel should have been raised by 435 yuan and 420 yuan per tonne, respectively, this time, according to the NDRC.
Preliminary estimates show that private car owners will spend about 7 yuan less than they otherwise would when filling up their tanks, while truck drivers will spend about 75 yuan less per tank, as the increase was smaller than required by the pricing mechanism.
Since China's previous adjustment of refined oil prices on August 28, the conflict between the United States and Iran has escalated again, driving international crude oil prices up sharply, the NDRC said, adding that the increase this time is aimed at cushioning the impact of rising international oil prices on the domestic market.
China's three biggest oil companies -- the China National Petroleum Corporation, the China Petrochemical Corporation and the China National Offshore Oil Corporation -- and other refineries, have been directed to maintain production and facilitate transportation to ensure stable supplies.
Currently, there exists considerable geopolitical uncertainty and close attention should continue to be paid to how the evolving U.S.-Iran situation affects international oil prices, said the NDRC.
China's domestic oil and gas supply is expected to reach 440 million tonnes of oil equivalent by 2030, according to a five-year plan for the sector, which was jointly released by the National Energy Administration and the NDRC in August.
The country's total oil and gas output reached a new record of 420 million tonnes of oil equivalent in 2025, marking a notable improvement in the country's independent energy security capacity, official data showed. ■

‘Blew the hell out of it’: How Iran damaged US bases in Bahrain, Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

10:41:35 UTC

‘Blew the hell out of it’: How Iran damaged US bases in Bahrain, Jordan
US official admits the naval base near Manama sustained heavy damage in the war with Iran.
A Bahrain-based United States military installation has sustained severe damage during recent months of fighting with Iran, the acting secretary of the US Navy has said, prompting Washington to evaluate what to do with its headquarters in the Middle East.
“They blew the hell out of Bahrain,” Hung Cao said in an interview with The Epoch Times on Wednesday, in a rare official admission of the impact of the conflict on a key US facility amid escalating tensions in the Gulf, six months into the US and Israel’s war on Iran.
