China’s young investors embrace risk. Why are their portfolios so safe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:05:57 UTC
19:05:57 KST

China’s young investors embrace risk. Why are their portfolios so safe?
Despite high risk tolerance, millennials and Gen Z invest in safer assets due to a combination of factors, a study shows
Young Chinese investors may be just as willing to take risks as their global peers, but their portfolios remain more conservative against a backdrop of years of relative underperformance in China’s stock market, a prolonged property downturn and deflation, according to a senior researcher at the CFA Institute Research and Policy Centre.
The disconnect between their willingness to take risks and their actual investment choices illustrated what the institute called an “aspiration-implementation gap”, said Rhodri Preece, senior head of research at the institute.
“They want to retire early. They’re willing to take risks, but yet their portfolios [show] the most commonly cited investments are more conservative investments like wealth-management products and money-market funds,” Preece said in an interview on Thursday.
The findings were based on the institute’s latest survey of 400 affluent investors in mainland China conducted in December, with its main analysis focusing on 300 Gen Z and millennial respondents.
Some 72 per cent of Chinese respondents held cash or cash equivalents and 62 per cent owned bank or trust wealth-management products, the survey found. By comparison, cryptocurrencies and mutual funds were the two most commonly owned investments among young investors globally, at 67 per cent and 64 per cent, respectively.

Trump's war cascades into a multifront battle for regional order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:04:25 UTC
19:04:25 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump's war cascades into a multifront battle for regional order
Iran has widened its war in the Gulf. Israel, meanwhile, continues its war in the Arab Levant and is also preparing for a greater role in the Gulf.
Tel Aviv is openly declaring that it will continue its war against Iran and its regional axis, while Benjamin Netanyahu continues to speak of bringing down the Iranian regime. Tehran, weakened and in retreat across parts of the Levant, is seeking to expand its influence in the Gulf, not only through the Strait of Hormuz but also by opening a new front around the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
It has already laid the groundwork through a series of military operations against Gulf states and appears to be preparing for further action if the US blockade continues and military strikes persist.
The world is holding its breath. Donald Trump is threatening to strike Pickaxe Mountain, the heavily fortified nuclear facility near Natanz. Netanyahu, meanwhile, continues to say that Israel is ready to carry out further operations against Iran as Tehran seeks to restore its nuclear programme.
Israel is working to provoke Iran further and draw it into a renewed war. Netanyahu appears to see escalation as the main route through which to fight his electoral battle, and therefore prefers to continue military operations in pursuit of achievements that could improve his political standing.
What Netanyahu wants is a renewed war stretching from Lebanon to Syria, alongside renewed confrontation between the United States and Iran. He is also seeking a greater Israeli role in the Gulf, particularly in the Yemen war.
Israeli reports point to concern in Tel Aviv that the Houthis could consolidate control over Bab al-Mandab and gain greater influence over shipping in the Red Sea. The Israeli military has also conducted exercises in Eilat simulating naval warfare.
Redrawing West Asia for good?
What the United States is doing amounts to redrawing the map of the Middle East, and of a significant part of the wider region. Israel, for its part, repeatedly says that it has already changed the Middle East and intends to continue doing so.
The shared US-Israeli objective is to draw the states of the region further into Israel’s orbit and into the Abraham Accords. Israel will seek to impose this through military pressure, whether in Lebanon, Syria or later on other states, including Gulf countries.
Saudi Arabia is particularly important in this regard, as Trump continues to push for it to join the Abraham Accords.
Lebanon, meanwhile, remains under sustained military and political pressure aimed at pushing it in the same direction.
This cannot be separated from remarks by the Israeli president about his ambition to meet the Lebanese president, visit Beirut and announce a peace agreement. Nor is it different from US statements that openly point towards an eventual peace agreement between Lebanon and Israel.
The framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel is increasingly being presented as the basis for governing that relationship, with Hezbollah’s disarmament across Lebanese territory treated as a central condition.
In this way, Washington is effectively giving Israel political cover to remain militarily active until Hezbollah is disarmed.
The US position coincided with Israel’s destruction of tunnels at Ali al-Taher, north of the Litani River, a clear indication that Israeli military operations may continue in other areas.
Netanyahu himself said that the Israeli army had destroyed tunnels around Beaufort Castle and Ali al-Taher, adding that there would be further operations.
Against this backdrop, the region appears to be approaching another moment of explosion.
It may be delayed, or it may erupt at any moment, particularly as Iran studies the options available to it and considers how to respond to the tightening US blockade, the strikes it is facing and the escalation in Lebanon.
In Yemen, Iran has moved towards an escalation through its allies, with the aim of strengthening control over Bab al-Mandab.
This has come alongside advances by the Yemeni government in other provinces as it seeks to tighten pressure around Sanaa and weaken the Houthis.
Iran’s moves in Yemen therefore constitute one of the most important tests of the Mecca security arrangement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.
Dealing with the situation in Yemen will require renewed activation of the international coalition established by Saudi Arabia to protect navigation through Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea.
Israel is likely to watch from the sidelines initially and wait for an opportunity to impose itself as a central player there, whether through security and intelligence cooperation or through direct military power.
But that would come at a high political price: first through a security agreement with Saudi Arabia, and then through a political agreement, peace deal or normalisation.
Israel as the region's policeman
What Israel wants is clear: to become the “policeman of the region” and the effective successor to US predominance from the Gulf to the Arab Levant.
Israel is presenting itself as a state capable of guaranteeing the security of regional governments and protecting them, on the basis that such protection requires alliance with Israel and acceptance of its conditions.
Israel also wants to demonstrate that the Mecca arrangement, or any other security or defence agreement, cannot provide Saudi Arabia or other regional states with an alternative source of military strength.
Turkey and Pakistan did not intervene militarily in support of Saudi Arabia in the past, have not done so now and may not do so in the future.
Israel, which is increasingly fighting over strategic routes, corridors and crossings, is also unlikely to accept a Turkish military presence around Bab al-Mandab or Turkish intervention in a campaign against the Houthis.
Israel is seeking to widen the war across the region.
It wants to show that it alone is capable of confronting Iran and its allies, and through that confrontation impose itself as an essential party in any regional equation involving the Arab Levant, the Gulf or the Eastern Mediterranean.
This is what Israel has been working towards for years.
It has built partnerships and strategic alignments around the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly with Cyprus and Greece, while also seeking to connect these arrangements to the Gulf.
The same logic is visible in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, or IMEC, which links India to Europe through the Gulf and the Eastern Mediterranean.
Israel wants Saudi Arabia and Egypt to become part of this wider strategic architecture, while gradually drawing Lebanon and Syria into it as well.

Zelenskyy: First results of negotiation process expected by late September

Conditions for negotiations will not exist during the elections in Russia; however, an opportunity to meet with a US delegation in New York may arise at the end of September, and initial results from the talks could emerge by the end of the month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.
"Regarding Russia—when they hear that we are holding negotiations with Europeans, Canadians, or Americans, or anything of the sort, they try to intensify their attacks on us. Simply to derail any negotiations, to destroy any dialogue. But we believe in peace and will move in that direction. There is only one way to stop this war; there is no other path. Therefore, I think we can achieve the first results by the end of September," Zelenskyy said at a press conference alongside Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday.

China angered by Taiwan VP's visit to EU democracy forum
September 11, 2026
China was angered by Italy and the EU on Friday, lodging "solemn representations" with both after news broke that high-ranking Taiwanese officials had traveled to the bloc to attend an annual democracy summit.
Beijing's Foreign Ministry said it firmly opposes official interactions of any form with Taiwan by nations who have ties with China.
Solemn representations is a literal translation of a Chinese term expressing diplomatic discontent.
At issue is a visit by Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim and Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung, both of whom were welcomed to the Ventotene Conference for Freedom and Democracy in Italy.
China sees democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, which it has vowed to "reunite" with the mainland.
Beijing has previously blasted Hsiao as an "independence diehard" and has criticized her Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) as a separatist outfit.
Taiwan's government has not sought formal independence but Beijing has, nevertheless, threatened to take the island by military force.
EU Parliament VP blasts Beijing 'regime' over interference
European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno announced Hsiao and Lin's attendance at the conference early Friday morning, adding that news of the visit had been kept under wraps until they arrived for safety reasons.
The EU's Picierno, who called the visit a "very important message," was defiant on Friday, saying, "No one can decide who is hosted in Ventotene and who is not," and calling out the Chinese "regime" for seeking to interfere.
Though Taiwanese foreign ministers travel abroad, it is rare for an official as high-ranking as the vice president to visit nations with ties to Beijing for fear of fallout for host countries.
Other prominent pro-democracy advocates such as Russian Kremlin critic Yulia Navalnaya, the wife of the late Alexei Navalny, and Belarus opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya are also in attendance.
The conference began on Thursday and is scheduled to wrap up on Saturday.
EU threading needle between support for Taiwan, ties with China
Italy, like most nations, is not among Taiwan's 12 formal diplomatic allies, although the Vatican is.
Still, both Italy and Taiwan have de facto embassies in each other's capitals.
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani will not meet with the visiting Taiwanese officials.
Further details are expected to be made public after the conference concludes.
The EU is walking a fine line between democratic support for Taiwan and relations with China.
Beijing's support for Russia in its ongoing invasion of Ukraine — which also prompted Taiwan to seek closer ties with the EU in 2022 — has been a thorn in the side of EU nations and in Brussels.

A specific facial proportion shapes our assumptions about men’s parenting styles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:00:36 UTC
19:00:36 KST

A new study indicates that people tend to view men with wider faces as more capable of protecting children. The findings suggest that facial proportions guide our assumptions about a person’s parenting style, motivations, and mating strategies. The research was published in Evolutionary Psychological Science.
The study centers on the facial width-to-height ratio, a physical measurement that compares the horizontal distance across a person’s face from cheek to cheek against the vertical distance from the upper lip to the brow. Past research established that wider male faces tend to signal physical strength and aggression. For example, a 2015 meta-analysis found that men with larger facial width-to-height ratios are consistently perceived by others as more physically formidable and dominant.
Building on this, a 2021 study provided evidence that people actively prefer to recruit men with wider faces for group roles that require physical strength and defense. Separate research has also indicated that physical strength translates into specific parenting stereotypes. For instance, a 2022 study found that people judge physically strong men as better suited for protective parenting roles.
The new study merges these lines of inquiry. From an evolutionary perspective, human mothers historically faced intense physical and caloric demands when raising children. Identifying a mate or ally capable of offering physical protection would have provided a distinct survival advantage. The research team tested whether the facial cues that make a man look like a good fighter also lead people to view him as a better, more motivated protector of children.
“What motivated me to conduct this research was a growing interest in the parental motivational systems that clarified the multidimensional nature of parenting that necessitates people to make tradeoffs in some parental decisions,” lead author Mitch Brown, a teaching assistant professor in the Department of Psychological Science at the University of Arkansas, told PsyPost.
“Consideration of the tradeoff between protection and nurturance was the next logical step for formidability research with its own tradeoff logic,” Brown explained. “With facial width-to-height ratio being a common route to infer formidability with the primacy of face-to-face contact, while similarly connoting both anger and strength, the feature seemed to be an ideal way to model this tradeoff in perceptions.”
To investigate this, the researchers conducted four separate experiments. In the first study, 101 undergraduate students evaluated 20 standardized photographs of White male faces displaying neutral expressions. Half of the faces featured high facial width-to-height ratios, and the other half featured low ratios. The participants rated how effective each man would be at protecting and nurturing his children.
The participants rated the men with wider faces as more effective at protection, giving them an average score of 4.23 on a 7-point scale, compared to 3.84 for the men with narrower faces. The difference in nurturing ratings between the two groups was not statistically significant.
The second study tasked 111 participants with building a hypothetical coalition. Viewing the same set of faces, participants were asked to select up to five men who would be best at protecting offspring, and up to five who would be best at nurturing offspring. The participants also rated the faces for physical strength, aggressiveness, and warmth.
When selecting a team for protection, participants chose the men with wider faces much more often, picking an average of 2.78 men with high facial width-to-height ratios compared to just 1.15 men with low ratios. For the nurturing task, choices were evenly split. The tendency to choose wider-faced men for protection was strongly associated with perceiving them as stronger and more aggressive.
The third study, involving 194 participants, investigated how the brain processes these facial cues. Participants evaluated the same faces, but half the images were shown upright, and half were inverted upside down. Turning a face upside down disrupts configural processing, which is how the brain evaluates the overall arrangement of facial features rather than looking at individual parts in isolation.
When the faces were upright, the men with wider faces again appeared more effective at protection. However, when the faces were inverted, this protective advantage was not statistically significant. This suggests that perceiving protective ability relies on taking in the whole facial arrangement at once. In contrast, the men with narrower faces were still seen as slightly more effective at nurturing even when the images were upside down, suggesting that nurturing judgments might rely on specific, independent facial features.
“None of these results particularly surprised me, though I was particularly interested to see that the effects for Study 3 did not provide a clear answer for how perceivers view parental ability when facial process is disrupted,” Brown said. “Although perceivers were still able to infer men’s parental abilities through an inverted face, the effect was substantially muted from when the faces were presented upright.”
“This suggests that perceivers may be inferring a certain configuration of formidability that is based on specific figure,” he continued. “The confluence of these traits could have led selection to favor awareness of the broad constellation of formidability through various features that appears to be a broad judgment instead of many small ones, particularly ones that could be constrained by linguistic differences across cultures.”
However, Brown was careful to note that the facial width-to-height ratio itself is not necessarily a single evolutionary trait linked directly to hormones. “I am not indicating that fWHR itself is selected, nor am I arguing that the total feature is indicative of testosterone,” he clarified. “Rather, there appears to be a broad signal value that is apparent to perceivers through fWHR that is consistently informing perceptions of men’s parental abilities.”
The fourth study focused on the men’s presumed motivations rather than their abilities. A group of 206 participants rated the faces using modified questionnaires to assess how driven the men seemed to protect or nurture children. They also rated the men’s presumed interest in casual sexual encounters versus committed, long-term relationships.
The results indicated that observers assumed the men with wider faces were more motivated to protect children, scoring 3.51 on a 7-point scale compared to 3.40 for the narrower-faced men. Conversely, they viewed the men with wider faces as less motivated to nurture children, scoring 3.11 compared to 3.47. The wider-faced men also appeared more interested in short-term mating strategies, while the narrower-faced men seemed more inclined toward long-term relationships.
“The effects in this study are fairly large, which may reflect an apparently loud signal value in the faces,” Brown noted. “However, perceptions of ability appeared larger than that of motivation. This could reflect that fWHR may itself be a more reliable cue to physical ability rather than motivational states or traits.”
While laboratory settings isolate specific variables like face shape, real-world judgments involve much more context. “Additionally, having more information about a person beyond initial impressions would be informative in broader perceptions (thanks for stating something obvious that ignores the purpose of isolating variables, Reviewer 2),” Brown added. “But ancestral conditions likely saw individuals having to infer information relatively quickly without having the chance for fuller interactions, which may lead to an advantage in forming stereotypes with minimal information.”
These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2022, which found that physically stronger men are perceived as more effective protectors of offspring. The new study echoes this pattern, though it examined facial proportions rather than physical upper-body strength. Similar results were also seen in a 2023 study covered by PsyPost, which found that large neck muscles lead perceivers to rate men as more effective at protecting offspring.
However, the new results stand in tension with research covered by PsyPost later that same year. That 2023 study found no association between facial masculinity and a man’s actual or perceived involvement in paternal care. It is worth noting that the new study specifically evaluated perceptions of a man’s ability to protect offspring based on the facial width-to-height ratio, whereas the earlier study measured general perceptions of direct paternal care based on overall facial sexual dimorphism.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The researchers relied on a specific set of standardized photographs, which only showed faces and provided no information about body size. While facial width is associated with physical formidability, a person’s actual body mass could heavily influence these judgments in the real world.
Additionally, the participants were undergraduate students drawn from Western university populations. People from different cultures evaluate facial features differently, and these specific stereotypes might not translate universally across all societies. Future research could explore whether these facial cues align with reality by measuring men’s actual facial proportions and comparing them to their self-reported parenting styles and actions.
“Despite how informative fWHR may ultimately be for these stereotypes, it remains important to recognize that any kernel of truth may not be enough to make broad inferences for every part of normal life as an imperfect rule,” Brown said. “This research is merely identifying how facial structures connoting physical prowess forms the basis of stereotypes that could have been historically functional to maintain one’s fitness within group living.”
Looking ahead, the researchers hope to see how these initial impressions affect high-stakes, real-world decisions. “My next steps are to apply these ideas into legal domains,” Brown told PsyPost. “Although perceptions could be based in potential kernels of truth and could have an ancestral function, it would nonetheless be inappropriate for perceivers to rely on visual information as the basis of legal decision-making without concomitant evidence.”
“I am conducting research currently seeing how fWHR informs perceptions of whether men should receive custody rights in divorce proceedings,” he continued. “In other words, would the inferred aggression from fWHR impede fair treatment under the law.”
Ultimately, the findings highlight the complex and sometimes contradictory nature of how we interpret physical strength. “This research should reflect an effort to identify ambivalence in the signal value of formidability, which may make research on the topic more challenging to discuss,” Brown concluded. “Formidability is a wide concept with many facets in the broad construct. Future research would benefit from trying to parse those components apart, which may clarify the heterogeneity in the literature.”
The study, “Formidable Facial Structures Inform Perceptions of Men’s Ability to Protect Offspring,” was authored by Mitch Brown, Donald F. Sacco, Nicholas P. Maxwell, Lindsey E. Eagan, and Steven G. Young.

‘less materiality means more humanity’: philippe starck on the designeuropa lifetime award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:00:33 UTC
19:00:33 KST

PHILIPPE STARCK RECEIVES LIFETIME ACHIEVEMENT AWARD 2026
For French designer Philippe Starck, being honored with the Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2026 DesignEuropa Awards in Ljubljana marks more than a celebration of iconic forms. It serves as an active platform to discuss an impending, systemic evolution. From iconic everyday objects widely regarded as modern design classics, to his landmark work in art direction, architecture, interior design, mobility, and spatial and naval engineering, Starck has continually redefined what it means to be a creator. Yet, he enters this milestone with a distinct position: the ultimate destination for industrial design is its complete disappearance. As the creative sector navigates an era defined by resource scarcity and changing human behaviors, his focus remains locked on stripping away mass production to maximize human utility.
‘The future is based on dematerialization,’ comments Starck, opening the conversation with designboom in an exclusive interview. ‘This means the product is disappearing and the more it disappears, the more powerful it becomes. In my own practice — that I encourage and advocate — I consistently strive to create with the minimum of the minimum, because I believe that less materiality means more intelligence and more humanity. This actually questions the role of the designer as we have known it so far.’
DesignEuropa Awards honors Philippe Starck with Lifetime Achievement Award 2026 | all images courtesy of Starck
BIALETTI MOKA, PORSCHE TURBO AND MORE HONORED BY EUIPO
Organized by the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), the 2026 edition marks the 10th anniversary of the DesignEuropa Awards, an international program established to celebrate creators who protect their physical ideas as EU designs. The awards history includes widely recognized designs like the Bialetti Moka pot and the Porsche Turbo, illustrating how legal protection supports an object’s economic value. By bridging this heritage with a modern creative landscape rapidly accelerating under generative AI and automated physical reproduction, the EUIPO aims to protect independent creators from rapid physical replication.
‘Institutions such as the European Union Intellectual Property Office are vital to protect creation and creativity, especially now with the birth and exponential development of artificial intelligence. A.I. can deliver something really good in a second. So, there will be five billion young designers who will never think about creating, they will simply ask an A.I. to do it. The work no longer exists. That is why, when I have the chance, I tell young designers to think twice and that the secret to success is to be alone and have your own idea,’ explains Starck when reflecting on the role of formal design registration today.
Juicy Salif for ALESSI, 1988
SHAPING A MUTATION FROM MATTER TO SERVICE
Starck spent decades working to lower production costs and increase the availability of well-designed goods, a philosophy he termed democratic design. Now that functional industrial goods are widely accessible, he argues that the focus must shift to environmental responsibility. The challenge is no longer to fill empty domestic spaces, but to implement a strategy of positive de-growth. Creators and consumers alike are challenged to dial back output by a calculated, collective ten percent — a marginal shift that remains unnoticeable on an individual level but radically alters global material dependencies.
‘Today, I believe the battle for democratic design is won since almost anyone can afford a quality chair for fifty euros, yet my mission remains unchanged: to give the best service — whatever form it takes — to the maximum number of people and using the minimum of resources from our limited planet,’ shares Starck on his enduring criteria for introducing any new object into a saturated market.
Miss Dior chair for DIOR, 2020
This approach requires rejecting short product lifecycles driven by three-month trend updates. Starck argues that longevity occurs when an object outlasts temporary fashions through a balance of engineering and materials. To achieve this, he collaborates with established manufacturers such as Alessi, Baccarat, Cassina, Duravit, Flos, Kartell, Target, and Emeco, among many more, using their deep technological expertise to test new material limits. Whether spending thirty years perfecting the exact structural curvature of 3D-molded wooden furniture or introducing a punk-like subversion to historical product icons, the goal is always to create a fertile surprise that honors long-term cultural transmission.
‘For creators of my generation, the subject is even more vital because we are not only producers of ideas, but we are also still producers of matter. We have a duty and a responsibility to design sustainably and to create projects that are timeless, honest, and of the highest quality both materially and culturally — to ensure their longevity. To do this, we must challenge trends that consume too much energy, cynicism and contempt,’ he further notes.
LA REDOUTE, Good Goods catalog “The non-objects for the non-consumers of the future moral market”  1994-96
Operating across vastly different scales, Starck uses the same methodology whether designing a plastic chair, a luxury vessel, or a zero-gravity habitation module for Axiom Space. He treats physical spaces as narratives, arranging shapes, colors, and textures to influence how a room feels. By treating physical enclosures as narrative scripts, spaces are transformed into active, stimulating environments designed to guide human emotion. Objects like the Juicy Salif lemon squeezer or the Louis Ghost chair function as focal points within an environment rather than just tools.
‘Whether it is design or architecture, poetic and humorous stories are as important as ergonomics and functionality,’ Starck shares. ‘The Juicy Salif is both a lemon-squeezer and a conversation starter, the Louis Ghost chair is an everyday friend that one can choose to see or to forget… when I imagine new places, I act like a film director, aiming to create stimulating scenarios within which people will be immersed, feeling more creative, more intelligent, and even, I hope, more in love.’
DURAVIT Starck Barrel |  image © Alberto Zanetti, 2024
Looking forward, this narrative approach directly extends to the next generation of creators, who are increasingly tasked with creating systems and services rather than physical goods. As the 10th anniversary of the DesignEuropa Awards highlights this transition, the competition spotlights a diverse cross-section of innovation across the EU. Shortlisted finalists from countries including Czechia, Germany, Latvia, Slovenia, and Spain demonstrate a wide sectorial footprint, stretching from critical healthcare advancements and home or urban appliances to sustainable agriculture, fitness, and sports. The 2026 edition captures the ever evolving design landscape through the Next Generation Design Award, celebrating young creators up to 29, alongside the newly introduced Public Choice Award, which invites the design community to directly cast its vote on these defining benchmarks.
‘The next generation of creators will no longer produce materiality but create service. They will be our coaches, our dieticians, our psychiatrists. This is not a choice, this is our future and the only way to contribute to the great story of our evolution. We, humans, are part of our permanent mutation. There are still unexplored territories, and this empty space will be incredibly fertile for thought and creativity,’ he concludes.
LA ALMAZARA Ronda, 2024 | image © Alfonso Quiroga Ferro

organization: European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO)

Trump Administration Proposes Cutting Grace Period for H-1B and Other Visas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

The Department of Homeland Security has proposed scrapping the policy allowing certain foreign workers—including H-1B visa holders—to remain in the U.S. for up to 60 days after losing their jobs to find a new sponsor, according to a government notice published Friday.
The White House-approved proposal is the latest disruption to the H-1B visa, which sits at the intersection of the Trump Administration’s priorities to restrict legal immigration, put an “America First” policy to work in the labor sector, and increase oversight of tech companies that rely on workers under this category.
Under the new proposal, some foreign workers would be considered immediately removable from the U.S. if they no longer work for an employer linked to their visa status.
The proposal “restores a direct relationship between an alien’s nonimmigrant status and the specific employment or activity that formed the basis of his or her admission or grant of status in the United States and reduces administrative burden,” according to the notice in the Federal Register.
Public comments on the proposal are accepted for 60 days. If adopted, the policy would mark one of the biggest changes to immigration policy, almost a decade after the grace period was created.
Cracking down on legal immigration
In early 2017, during the final days of the Obama Administration, a rule took effect stating that foreign citizens with legal immigration status under the H-1B visa, as well as several other visa categories, would have a 60-day grace period after they lose their job. That leeway allowed these workers to look for a new job or to change their immigration status.
The other visas covered by the grace period are E-1 treaty trader visas and E-2 treaty investor visas; L-1 visas allowing short-term work for executives and managers with international firms; O-1 visas for individuals with “extraordinary ability” in science, sports, or the arts; and TN visas for qualified Canadian and Mexican professionals. The grace period also covers H-1B1 visas for nationals of Chile or Singapore working in a specialty occupation, and E-3 visas for Australian citizens working in a specialized professional occupation.
According to DHS’s calculations, nearly 4,000 workers a year utilize the grace period to submit a new nonimmigrant worker petition after a layoff or resignation. More than 99% of them are H-1B visa holders.
Eliminating the grace period would favor American laborers, the DHS argued. “DHS assumes that almost all these entities would offer the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers, go through the I-129 petition process to sponsor nonimmigrant workers, or reassign the work to other current employees,” the document read.
Its removal would also reduce administrative work, as the existing rule states the DHS could skip or shorten the grace period at its discretion. According to the document, from Oct. 1, 2017, through May 20, 2026, the DHS calculated 1.9 million petitions or applications on which USCIS had to assess whether the 60-day period could have potentially applied.
A ripple effect
The DHS acknowledges that the policy changes would not only affect prospective employers but also families of the workers who may be forced to leave the U.S.
The proposal could also affect the immigration status of dependents of H-1B visa holders. Immigration advocacy group FWD.us estimates about 730,000 H-1B visa holders living in the U.S., plus 550,000 dependents, including spouses and children.
But according to the proposal, the department says it believes “the harm of the up to 60-day discretionary grace period outweighs the potential benefit it provides to the impacted aliens and employers, the alien’s dependents, and the community at large.”
Remaking the H-1B visa
Since 1990, hundreds of thousands of skilled foreign workers have entered the U.S. through the H-1B visa system. Citizens from India make up the bulk of H-1B visa holders, according to an April U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services report, with China a distant second. Tech industry titans like Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, Google’s Sundar Pichai, and even SpaceX’s Elon Musk have stayed in the U.S. with the help of H-1B visas.
Congress has set the current annual cap for new H-1B visas at 65,000, though an additional 20,000 is allotted for those with advanced degrees. Demand for H-1B visas often outpaces the cap.
But the Trump Administration has subjected the H-1B visa to various changes, as Trump claims skilled foreign workers have taken away jobs from Americans.
It has since replaced the traditional H-1B lottery with a weighted system favoring higher-skilled, higher-paid workers. And while a court blocked an attempt to impose a $100,000 fee on certain H-1B employers, the Administration in August proposed a new $103,265 fee for certain H-1B petitions and expanded a $4,000 biometric and security fee to cover extension applications from employers with a large foreign workforce.

One in nine migratory birds threatened with extinction, global report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

One in nine migratory birds are threatened with extinction and 45% of migratory species such as cuckoos, turtle doves and Arctic terns are in decline, according to a global report.
The migratory slender-billed curlew was officially declared extinct last year, the first global bird extinction in mainland Eurasia and Africa in recent centuries. Worldwide, seven migratory bird species have been confirmed or are suspected to have become extinct over the last 150 years.
The threats to migratory birds, which are overwhelmingly caused by humans and include the intensification of farming, unsustainable hunting, pollution, invasive species and global heating, were revealed in the State of the World’s Birds report.
Seabirds and shorebirds, which depend upon marine habitats and coastal wetlands, are faring particularly badly, according to the analysis, which is produced every four years by BirdLife International.
Stuart Butchart, the chief scientist at BirdLife International, said: “Migratory birds are sentinels, and their declines reveal growing pressure on the natural systems that sustain us. But the science is equally clear: conservation works, with coordinated action preventing extinctions and helping populations recover. The solutions exist: what is needed now is their implementation at flyway scale.”
The report was published at the Global Flyways summit in Nairobi, Kenya, where governments, scientists, conservation NGOs and financial institutions signed a commitment to increase efforts to protect migratory birds along their flyways, the routes taken by billions of migratory birds moving between continents and seasons.
The Nairobi Flyways Declaration comes with three development banks integrating flyway conservation into their lending frameworks, providing $6bn (£4.4bn) for habitat protection and restoration along migratory routes.
Threats to migratory birds include persecution, with an estimated 13.1 million to 42.7 million migratory birds illegally killed or taken every year in Europe, the Mediterranean, the Caucasus and the Arabian peninsula. Many of these are songbirds caught in mist nets or on “lime sticks” for human consumption.
Invasive species, such as rodents sometimes accidentally introduced on to small islands where seabirds breed, also threaten migratory birds.
Loss or damage to natural habitats is another prime cause. According to the report, scientific monitoring over the past decade has found that more than half (58%) of 1,099 key biodiversity areas for migratory birds are in poor or very poor condition.
But the report highlights how conservation action, often across national boundaries, is reviving some species.
The eradication of non-native rabbits, cats, rodents and the weka bird from Australia’s Macquarie Island, an important site for breeding seabirds, has led to a resurgence in populations of migratory seabirds including the blue petrel, grey petrel, white-headed petrel and the Antarctic prion.
In China, an ambitious countrywide programme to remove smooth cordgrass, a North American grass introduced in 1979 to stabilise coastal mudflats for development, has restored 37,553 hectares (92,756 acres) – half the total area – in its first year, opening up vital food-rich mudflats to shorebirds again.
In Britain, the restoration of wetlands on agricultural land threatened by coastal erosion at Wallasea Island, Essex, has led to peaks of more than 32,000 waterbirds returning to the site, including 11,270 red knots.
Outlined at the summit were plans by the Asian Development Bank to mobilise $3bn over the next decade to protect at least 50 priority wetlands across the east Asian-Australasian flyway, with the funds also supporting nearly 200 million people who depend on these ecosystems. The Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean is mobilising $3bn-$5bn up to 2050 to safeguard more than 30 landscapes and seascapes. Several billion dollars has also been pledged by the World Bank and BirdLife to support flyways across Africa, Europe and Asia used by more than 2 billion migratory birds.
Princess Takamado of Japan, the honorary president of BirdLife International, said: “Migratory birds do not recognise borders. They connect Asia to Africa, the Arctic to the tropics. The Nairobi Flyways Declaration acknowledges this reality – that it needs international cooperation and coordination to keep migratory birds safe. I am excited and proud to see that the scientific community, conservation organisations and the financial sector are uniting to make this happen. We stand at an important turning point. We have been waiting for this moment for a long time.”
Martin Harper, the chief executive of BirdLife International, also called the Nairobi Declaration a turning point but said governments, businesses and civil society needed to play their part. “Development banks are rising to the challenge. The BirdLife Partnerhip is prepared to act. We now need others to step up to reverse the declines and save the wonder of migration.”

Trump’s clash with Canada is his latest imperialistic embarrassment | Sidney Blumenthal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Trumpism is the lowest stage of imperialism. “We’re not going to invade Greenland. We’re going to buy it,” Donald Trump reportedly told the annual black-tie dinner on 1 February of the private Alfalfa Club, an assemblage of prominent Washington figures, a number of whom he had publicly humiliated, and others he was investigating or suing. “It’s never been my intention to make Greenland the 51st state. I want to make Canada the 51st state. Greenland will be the 52nd state. Venezuela can be 53rd.” The room greeted several of his remarks with dead silence. His cosplay as the Pirate King was not received as a good-humored takeoff from a Gilbert and Sullivan opera. He went on. “So many people in the room I hate,” he said in a display of honesty. “Most of you I like,” he claimed. Then, at his peak euphoria, he flew off to Mar-a-Lago to plan his attack on Iran, which took place 27 days later.
Trump’s imperialism of piracy and plunder is less of a system even than that of the earliest imperialism of 17th-century privateers raiding the Spanish Main, the divine right of kings, and monarchs dividing up the spoils as favors to create their lords and earls. His schemes of aggrandizement operating by threat and force are justified by no larger rationale, nothing as exalted as “the white man’s burden”, marauding wherever and however he can to seize resources.
Describing his actions as some version of colonialism grants him a more orderly and coherent method than he possesses. His pillaging bears not the slightest resemblance to the highly organized administration of Queen Victoria’s British empire. Trump’s predation is calculated to wreck the long-established arrangements of international trade, law and cooperation created after the second world war and the fall of colonial empires, whose guidelines he sees as obstructing his own profit and power. Obsessed with his fortune hunting, he couldn’t care less about the political consequences for ill-fated Republican candidates in the midterm elections who must face the music for the harm he is doing to their states. They are the least of his collateral damage.
Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, offered the most succinct critique of Trump’s intent to usurp the sovereignty of countries in order to make them turn over their wealth to him. Carney said: “Canada is a sovereign, independent nation. We are not a target to be bullied, nor are we a client state to be subordinated … We will not sign an agreement that sacrifices our basic sovereignty, undermines our legal system, or cedes control over our foreign trade to Washington.” He called Trump’s demands a “last-minute power play intended to reduce Canada to an economic subsidiary”.
Trump’s ultimatum abrogated the legal foundation of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which he himself had signed in 2020. He had previously demeaned Carney as the “governor” of Canada. Now, adopting his characteristic pose as victim, Trump claimed Canada had been “ripping off the United States for years” and were among “worst” nations to “deal with”.. “They feel entitled and will be entitled no longer … It’s time to teach Canada you can’t do this anymore…. Someone should get these clowns to fall in line.”
Carney replied that Canada was “at war” and would adopt “counter-measures”, tariffs of its own. “America,” he said, “has changed … If Washington wants to trade, they must come to the table as equals.”
Trump’s answer was to issue an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, the reflexive branding of the real estate operator. The White House put out AI-generated videos of Trump kicking over a sign reading “Lake Ontario” and replacing it with a new one, “Lake America”, and another with a squadron of ducks all with Trump’s hairdo and armed with machine guns patrolling the shore of “Lake America” to the theme music of Hawaii Five-O. The implied invocation of the Marx brothers’ farce of the ludicrous country of Freedonia nonsensically going to war, Duck Soup, seems lost on the busy beavers of Trump’s slop.
Trump’s method has been consistent since he leveraged a mineral resource deal out of Ukraine in April 2025 at a weak point in its conflict with Russia. Rather than pressure Putin, Trump’s agents disguised as diplomats, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate pal Steve Witkoff, the Rosencrantz and Guildenstern of Trump’s imperialism, stand by to negotiate post-sanctions deals on his behalf.
Venezuela became Trump’s template for his piratical adventures. After swooping in on 3 January to capture its strongman, Nicolás Maduro, Trump promised a transition to democratic elections and that the US would play a custodial role over Venezuelan oil for the benefit of its people.
Not long after Trump grabbed Maduro, he declared he needed to acquire Greenland and threatened a tariff war against Denmark and European allies to “get Greenland, including right, title and ownership”. “We probably won’t get anything unless I decide to use excessive strength and force, where we would be frankly unstoppable. But I won’t do that,” Trump said, adding, “I don’t have to use force,” and “I don’t want to use force.” He relented momentarily on 21 January after he claimed he had reached a “framework” agreement to negotiate over natural resources, though he subsequently sent preposterous agents into Greenland to stir up a quixotic annexation movement to no avail.
A month later, he bombed Iran. Trump stated that his true inspiration for the Iran war was the Venezuelan model in a post on 11 June: “At some point in the not too distant future, we will … assume total control of their Oil and Gas Markets, much like we have with Venezuela, which is working out brilliantly for both Venezuela and the United States of America.”
On 31 August, Trump announced that the US would take a stake in 17 oilfields in partnership with North American Blue Energy Partners, controlled by a Venezuelan oilman, Alejandro Betancourt. Betancourt was briefly detained in Britain, which was reportedly linked to a Swiss warrant on suspicion of money laundering. Betancourt has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with any offenses. The Swiss warrant was withdrawn in May and he became a Trump associate.
The Trump administration has already claimed to have received proceeds of $500m from oil sales, initially deposited in an account in Qatar. When the congressman Sean Casten of Illinois and the senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland wrote a letter requesting information, the administration shifted the money to an opaque account managed by the treasury department. In an article published in June by the Council on Foreign Relations, “The U.S. Took Over Venezuela’s Oil Industry. Where Has All the Money Gone?”, Roxana Vigil, a former treasury department expert, observed that in dealing with the “same corrupt regime, different leader … the Trump administration has provided almost no information on the system it has established to sell Venezuelan oil, collect the revenue, and use the funds”.
The countries whose sovereignty, self-interest and rule of law Trump has struck include the United States. His assault on Canada has sent a shock through the whole US economy. The state most affected economically, Michigan, shares with Canada one of the most integrated industrial relationships in the world. More than 38% of Michigan’s exports go to Canada, the Detroit-Windsor corridor handles 25% of all US-Canada trade, and Trump’s tariffs immediately threaten 260,000 jobs with an immensely damaging multiplier effect. As of March, his tariffs had already caused estimated losses of $35bn to automakers. The average cost per Michigan household is estimated to be $5,619 in added expenses due to tariff-induced price increases.
Trump’s tariffs have effectively hamstrung the Republican candidate for the Senate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, leaving him with the Hobson’s choice of either inciting Trump’s rage or submitting to his whim. Rogers has decided to take the latter course. He has called Trump’s economic policies “masterful”. When JD Vance came to the state, Rogers praised the administration. “The impact you have had on our state is phenomenal,” he said. Rogers hurls language about “extremism” against the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that substitutes for discussing Trump’s economic fiasco. Rogers is performing the kind of self-abasing fealty to Trump that Trump wishes he would receive from Carney. If only Rogers were the prime minister of Canada, there would be no trouble about “independence”.
Vladimir Lenin, in his 1917 tract, Imperialism: The Highest Stage of Capitalism, argued in his dogmatic and overdetermined style that imperialism at the turn of the 20th century represented the integration of monopoly, finance and industrial capital, with the great powers dividing the world into colonies, and their conflict precipitating the first world war.
In Trump’s imaginarium, he views himself as omnipotent and omniscient. When the world isn’t pliable, he must resort to greater force to reassure himself that the world acknowledges his self-image. The more he meets resistance to his fixed idea, the more pressure he must exert. He finds himself in a vicious cycle. His power hemorrhages, US power dissipates and he spins in a whirlpool.
Trump’s Venezuelan paradigm, whose conditions cannot be replicated, have quickly descended into questionable business deals. Failed from the start of his Iran war, his pursuit of “total control” recedes over the horizon. His clash with Canada has been confronted with Carney’s fierce defiance. Trump’s quest for a new field to conquer has landed him in yet another quagmire.
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” said Carney. In the meantime, Trump’s outlandish exhibitions of triumphalism in the face of rejection and defeat echo the Marx Brothers more than they echo Marx and Lenin: “Hail Freedonia!”

  Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

Pupils missed 15m hours of school time during UK’s June heatwave, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

The gruelling heatwave that hit the UK in June caused pupils to miss more than 15m hours of lesson time as soaring temperatures forced hundreds of schools to close, according to a study.
The research found that at least 760,000 schoolchildren in England and Wales missed lessons owing to closures during the heatwave – one of five in the UK this summer – as temperatures inside some classrooms topped 40C (104F), leaving pupils and staff suffering from heat stress, nausea and headaches.
“Staff and pupils were fainting and at least one of my colleagues was taken to A&E,” said Jenny Cooper, a teacher and National Education Union safety representative for London at the time of the heatwave. “Schools need to be places where we can learn and teach safely. A place for children whose homes are not safe … these heatwaves and the lack of investment in schools are jeopardising this.”
The heatwave lasted for eight days and triggered a red health alert across many parts of the UK, with hospitals forced to cancel operations, workplaces shortening hours, and people warned not to travel. There were nearly 2,900 excess deaths caused by the May and June heatwaves.
The research by DeSmog, based on reported school closures and official absence rates, gives the clearest picture to date of the impact of heatwaves on schools. It found that during the June heatwave pupils in England and Wales missed at least 15m teaching hours with more than 1,700 schools closing completely or finishing early.
School staff told the Guardian that learning was almost impossible as temperature records for June were broken, with pupil behaviour and attention deteriorating rapidly.
One primary school teacher said: “Everyone was lying or sitting on the floor with their water bottles, sweating, moaning and feeling tired, [complaining of] headaches and nausea.
“The adults barely coped and most of the children were calling for their mummies and daddies. There was no learning, just surviving the best we could.”
Where schools did remain open, the report found that absence rates soared as parents decided it was safer to keep children at home. One parent told DeSmog she took her five-year-old out of school after pupils returned home with severe heat rashes.
Experts say that this level of disruption in schools can have a big affect on children’s education and wellbeing and the wider community – especially for those from more deprived backgrounds.
Nicola Gray, from the University of Huddersfield, who led research into the impact of school closures during the Covid-19 pandemic, said missed school days could come at high costs – from lower exam results to poorer mental health.
“School provides basic social services, social connection, and nutrition [through free school meals],” she said. “We do not want the education and training of our students to dip precisely at the time when they’re going to need new skills and the best possible futures in a changing climate.”
Charlotte O’Regan, from the education charity the Sutton Trust, said the closures put students in the most deprived areas at a disadvantage.
“While some schools or parent organisations are able to pay to ensure that their environments are suitable for study, we know that state school leaders are already having to face difficult decisions when it comes to funding,” said O’Regan.
“We saw a significant widening of the attainment gap during the pandemic, and we have to make sure that the weather doesn’t become yet another barrier holding back those worst off.”
Parents, staff and academics agree that rapid adaptations are needed in schools to keep children safe and able to study – especially with even more extreme temperatures expected next year due to the worsening climate crisis and the supercharged El Niiño.
Cooper, who retired from teaching in September, said: “We really need a complete rethink of our school system. Schools must be properly funded so they can prepare for the rapidly changing climate.”
A Department for Education spokesperson said hot weather could “be a struggle”, adding: “Schools did a fantastic job keeping children learning safely during this summer’s heatwave. Schools put measures in place, so they remained the best place for children to be, even during a heatwave – because every day in school counts.”
They added the department was “investing to make schools more resilient to a changing climate – including through a £710m renewal and retrofit programme and almost £20bn to rebuild over 750 schools.”
DeSmog collected information on more than 1,700 affected schools based on dozens of national and local news reports and with the help of AI. This information was then analysed using census data to calculate the total number of students affected by closures.
The researchers also analysed government data on pupil absences during the heatwave, revealing a big increase in students missing school time in England and Wales.
Additional reporting by Clare Carlile and Brigitte Wear

9/11 entrenched Islamophobia in US politics. But it doesn’t work the way you think | Moustafa Bayoumi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

It’s been 25 years since the terrorist attacks of September 11, and during this time Muslim Americans have learned how to live in that dangerous space between other Americans’ fears and their ignorance.
The fear was clear from the beginning. Immediately following 9/11, Muslim Americans faced what Human Rights Watch called “a severe wave of backlash violence”. A tide of hate rose up against ordinary Muslims and those who appeared to be Muslim, including at least three murders in the immediate backlash after the attacks. The federal government, for its part, began targeting Muslim immigrants in a massive surge of repression that legal experts soon compared to the Palmer Raids of the 1920s.
The ignorance was just as evident. Even Oprah Winfrey did her part to allay it, dedicating an episode of her show in October 2001 to “Islam 101”. The Qur’an leapt on to the New York Times bestseller list that fall. Yet despite these early efforts at education, most Americans still learned little about Islam and Muslims. One 2006 study found that only a third of those polled realized that Muslims worship the same God as Christians and Jews do. Close to 10% of respondents thought Muslims worship a “moon god”.
Much of this fear and ignorance has continued unevenly over the last quarter century, with negative attitudes towards Muslim Americans softening at times and hardening, sometimes into deadly violence, at other times. What’s interesting is when expressions of these attitudes happen. It turns out that predicting when animosity to Muslims will rise and fall may not be quite what you think.
Researchers who study Islamophobia discovered several years ago that anti-Muslim outbreaks in the United States don’t follow highly publicized acts of terrorism. Rather, Islamophobic incidents tend to cluster more routinely around our election cycles. That’s what the New American Foundation found in 2018. That’s what the researcher Dalia Mogahed discovered earlier. And that’s partly what the Brookings Institution’s Shibley Telhami was referencing when he wrote, in 2024, that there was “strong suggestive evidence” that presidential messaging and crisis rhetoric can considerably sway American public attitudes toward Muslims.
Islamophobia, in other words, is better understood not as an irrational fear of a religious other but rather as an increasingly instrumentalized part of our politics, one that is most often activated around our elections. (Needless to say, when Islamophobia is deployed, it’s at the expense of the American Muslim community’s wellbeing.) And since we’re also closing in on a fiercely contested midterm election season, we should take note of the sky-high levels of Islamophobic rhetoric we’re witnessing today from the (mostly Republican) politician class.
Consider Laura Loomer, the far-right activist and Donald Trump’s close confidante. “Ban Muslims from holding office in America,” she posted on Twitter/X in July. Then there’s the South Carolina representative Nancy Mace, who wrote: “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic. We refuse to be silent.” The Florida representative Randy Fine, who has called for the deportation of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, believes: “We need more Islamophobia, not less. Fear of Islam is rational.” And the senator Tommy Tuberville recently stated: “Michigan Democrats just voted to send a TERRORIST to the Senate. Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed is a RADICAL ISLAMIST who will do everything he can to destroy America.” In a thinly veiled Islamophobic comment, JD Vance recently said: “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil. And on the rise in the United States of America today.”
In Texas, the levels of Islamophobia are now stratospheric. Lone Star politicians loudly trumpet anti-Muslim messages and repeatedly introduce versions of anti-Muslim legislation, seeking to forbid everything from sharia courts, which don’t actually exist in Texas, to real estate developments by Muslims. Must be election season.
The Texas governor Greg Abbott, who is up for re-election, has designated the country’s largest Muslim civil rights organization, the Council on American Islamic Relations (Cair), a foreign terrorist organization. This is ludicrous, of course, but as a Muslim organization, Cair’s an easy mark. As the Knight First Amendment Institute points out, “the domestic targeting of dissent starts with groups that those in power deem to be attractive political targets, but it never ends there. Without further opposition to these orders, CAIR is likely only the first of many groups to be in the crosshairs of politically motivated governors.”
And that’s the larger point. Muslim Americans have been weathering these kinds of attacks for decades now, but what we also know is that attacks on Muslims won’t end as attacks on Muslims. For 25 years, we have known what it means to live under a national security state. We have known what warrantless surveillance feels like. We have known what politicized immigration enforcement looks like (remember the Muslim ban?). We have known what it means when our dissenting voices are silenced, especially when advocating for Palestine.
And so, we recognize when those same tools are used by the National Security Agency to spy on ordinary Americans (as revealed by the whistleblower Edward Snowden) or when today’s mass deportations carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement resemble the immigration crackdown on Muslim immigrants decades earlier. Republicans worry loudly about their made-up fantasy of “creeping sharia”, but what all of us should really be concerned about is the reality of this creeping authoritarianism.
Muslim Americans have hardly been silent when facing this repression. Instead, we’ve organized ourselves to oppose it. If the political culture of the United States is poised to deny us our legitimate rights, then the response must be preserving those rights for everybody, not just for Muslim Americans.
That’s exactly what we’re witnessing today. Muslim Americans are more present in the American political scene than ever before. According to a recent study, a record 255 Muslims now serve in elected positions across the country, including 11 mayors, 18 judges and four members of the US House of Representatives. Muslim women account for more than 43% of the total.
Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed are probably today’s most visible Muslim American politicians. What makes them noteworthy is not just their obvious communication skills, but their deliberate attention to policies that enhance the public good for all.
El-Sayed, for example, prioritizes universal access to healthcare and clean water, eliminating medical debt and banning corporate money in politics. Mamdani, for his part, has delivered a pilot program delivering taxpayer-funded childcare for two-year-olds, a rent freeze on rent-stabilized apartments, and a parents’ night out program, where children spend supervised time at city recreation centers so parents can have time for themselves. These Muslim politicians have discovered a simple, timeless truth: Democracy’s best defense is ensuring that everyone lives well.
For the last 25 years, a bevy of political forces have routinely mobilized fear and ignorance against Muslim Americans to peddle the fiction that Muslims will take over the country. Their message has always been that Muslim Americans don’t belong in the United States.
But you know what? We’re paying less attention to them by the hour. Muslim Americans have too much work to do preserving our democracy. The truth is that, while the Islamophobes waste everyone’s time with the ludicrous charge that Muslims and Americans are irreconcilably different, Muslim Americans are just too busy making a difference. For everyone’s sake.
- 
  Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

====================================================================================================

We must pause risky AI research while we still have the power to do so | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

Another day, another horseman of the apocalypse galloping over the horizon. Lately we have heard from so many AI doomers – tech whistleblowers popping up to warn that their work is probably going to kill us – that we’re becoming almost blase about it. Humanity wiped out within a decade? Well, only if another world war or the climate crisis doesn’t get us first. Since it’s never clear whether the tech threat is real, or just a twisted form of hype from an industry that drums up investment by making their products sound more powerful than they really are, most of us settle for trying not to think about it too hard.
But something about the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s very public resignation from the cutting-edge American lab Anthropic, via a post on X arguing that he can’t keep working for companies “gambling with our lives”, has cut through where bigger names have not. Most chillingly, he claimed that colleagues still at Anthropic aren’t staying because they think he’s wrong about the dangers of pursuing self-improving super intelligence – the holy grail of machines that are not just smarter than humans but capable of building their own even more powerful successors, evolving independently of humans – but because they’re afraid of ceding the field to people with fewer scruples. His colleagues, Coxon said, talk routinely about the “endgame” or the “crunch time”, meaning that what they do in the next year or two will decide the fate of humanity. Whether that’s true or simply self-aggrandising techbro delusion, what he describes is an industry now practically begging to be saved from itself.
The frisson of alarm over AI running through Westminster this week was real, sharpened by news of Anthropic – which pitches itself as being more safety-conscious than its rivals OpenAI – declining for the first time to submit a new model for scrutiny by Britain’s AI safety watchdog. We are now entering a far more disruptive era of AI, dominated not by relatively basic chatbots but by agents designed to undertake tasks on humans’ behalf, making their own decisions about how to complete them. Unfortunately, it turns out even basic life admin requires the kind of fine judgments that come instinctively to humans but seem remarkably hard to codify for machines.
Take the over-zealous agent tasked recently by its Australian client with booking him into a pilates class, which responded to finding the class full by hacking the gym’s website and booting other people off the waiting list. Now imagine it blundering into something more life-threatening than a gym class. When Coxon says his industry hasn’t fixed problems with alignment, and when OpenAI’s chief scientist warned last week that no lab had solved them well enough to carry on scaling this fast much longer, what they’re talking about is this failure to replicate in machines the values and assumptions humans apply to decisions without even really knowing they’re doing it – including the sense of how far it’s justifiable to go in getting what you want.
A series of reported escapes by agents supposedly confined to OpenAI’s lab for testing, some of which contrived to access the internet behind their human supervisors’ backs and conduct real-world cyber-attacks, has meanwhile raised serious questions over the industry’s ability even to experiment safely. (Unnervingly, Coxon says newer models seem to know when they’re being tested, making it easier for them to deceive researchers.)
And agents don’t have to acquire anything like super intelligence to threaten human life: think how easily a cyber-attack on air traffic control, or NHS data systems, or even water purification systems could cause mass fatalities.
What’s happening in some frontier AI labs now is arguably the equivalent of the Manhattan Project that built the atomic bomb, but this time led by private companies in a mad dash for wealth and market dominance, not scientists under an elected government’s command. Britons meanwhile got more say in sugar taxes on junk food than we’re getting over regulating something theoretically capable of rendering us extinct.
Given time, of course, it might prove possible to replicate in machines the vast ecosystem of social ties, moral codes, intensive parenting and state policing that humans have developed to stop us behaving like sociopaths. (Only this week, Google’s DeepMind reported an experiment where 100 agents were given a maths problem and told not to cheat: though a minority promptly did cheat, a larger group either snitched on them to the humans or helped devise technical fixes.) But time is the one thing nobody dares to give themselves in the middle of an arms race, which is why it’s high time for governments to act. We need an international agreement to press pause, not on AI research as a whole, but on the riskiest projects, until we better understand whether it will ever be possible to mitigate the dangers or control the results. Since it’s hard to imagine Donald Trump voluntarily sacrificing US geopolitical or commercial advantage over China for the good of humanity, leadership may have to come for now not from above but below, where industry insiders spooked by their own work are making common cause with the rest of us.
More Americans are now concerned than excited about AI, according to polling this summer from the Pew Research Center – and unusually it’s the young who are most hostile, afraid it will not only take their jobs but make it harder to form relationships or think creatively. (That’s what growing up on social media seemingly does for trust in tech.) Even big business seems increasingly sceptical, with almost two-thirds of international executives surveyed by the consultants McKinsey this summer reporting no measurable impact on earnings from using the admittedly basic AI tools now available to them.
Warnings about an AI bubble triggering another 2008-style global financial crash haven’t helped, while plans to build giant, energy-guzzling datacentres are meeting angry local resistance on both sides of the Atlantic from people who can’t see what’s in it for them. Pressing pause on potential Armageddon looks in the circumstances less like the luddite option, and more like a smart way for tech companies to avoid a full-on backlash that will sweep away the good with the bad.
But if the AI doomers are right, then the window to do so may not always be open. It’s time for humans to stop and think about what we’re doing to ourselves – while we alone still have the power to do so.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Press review: Ukraine seeks donors outside EU as Europe faces prolonged fuel price surge

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
