compact forest cabin by wiki world takes shape as a red wooden submarine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:45:40 UTC
17:45:40 KST

Red Submarine Cabin is a modularcabin product designed by Wiki World as a spatial system for remote landscapes in China. Developed around Wiki World’s Digital Wood technology, the cabin combines digital fabrication with a compact, prefabricated construction system. Conceived as a high-performance, zero-footprint, plug-and-play dwelling, it can accommodate different materials and functions while adapting to a range of landscapes. The cabin takes the form of a small red wooden structure, using the visual language of a submarine as a reference for its architecture. Measuring just over 20 sqm, the interior contains a living room with an expansive picture window, a climbing ladder leading to a loft, and a sleeping area positioned beneath a large skylight. Circular portholes reinforce the submarine concept while providing additional framed views of the surrounding landscape. The project takes conceptual inspiration from Fitzcarraldo, the 1982 film by German director Werner Herzog, particularly its depiction of a protagonist who attempts to transport a steamship over a hill and into the Amazon rainforest. The cabin translates this surreal relationship between vessel and wilderness into a small-scale dwelling positioned within the forest.
all images by Li Xiao, Cai Muan, XhotLi Xiao, Cai Muan, Xhot
A timber cabin shaped by the language of a submarine
The submarine reference extends from the exterior appearance into the cabin’s spatial details. Circular windows function as portholes, while panoramic viewfinders frame the surrounding vegetation and changing patterns of daylight. Within the forest, the relationship between the cabin and its setting becomes part of the spatial experience. Wind, trees, leaves, sunlight, and shadows form a constantly changing backdrop to the compact interior. The cabin’s windows establish framed connections with the woodland, while the loft and skylight provide different positions from which to observe the surroundings. The compact scale concentrates domestic functions within a limited footprint. The living room, loft, sleeping area, windows, and circulation are arranged as components of a small spatial system designed for occupation within the forest.
Wiki World’s architects describe the Red Submarine Cabin as part of the studio’s ongoing exploration of natural construction and the relationship between living behavior and the environment. The project questions conventional assumptions about the size required for a home, using a compact footprint to bring occupants into closer contact with materials and the surrounding landscape. The reduced scale also allows everyday activities to become closely connected with the woodland setting. The terrace extends the living environment outdoors, maintaining a direct relationship with the existing ground, vegetation, and seasonal changes.
Digital fabrication and prefabricated timber construction
The entire structure uses glued timber, with each custom-shaped component and joint digitally designed and fabricated. The system achieves 100 percent prefabricated assembly, allowing the cabin to be produced as a coordinated set of customized structural elements. Digital Wood technology forms the basis of this construction approach, combining the precision of digital fabrication with a timber structural system. Customization is applied not only to the individual components but also to their joints, allowing the structure to be assembled from prefabricated parts. The approach forms part of Wiki World’s broader concept of the “Playtime Cabin,” which considers the dwelling as a customizable environment shaped around different understandings of domestic life.
The cabin is designed to minimize intervention on its site. Existing trees and bamboo are retained, preserving the original woodland and the textures of the paths. The houses are entirely elevated, separating the structures from the ground and allowing the existing landscape to remain largely continuous beneath them. This elevated construction forms part of the project’s zero-footprint approach, reducing the need to alter the existing woodland while positioning the cabin directly within the forest. Through its combination of prefabricated timber construction, digital fabrication, compact planning, and elevated placement, the Red Submarine Cabin establishes a modular dwelling system that can be inserted into natural settings while maintaining the existing character of the site.

area: 20 sqm

Iran-backed Houthis seize key port in Yemen, advance on another vital oil choke point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:44:52 UTC
17:44:52 KST

The Iran-backed Houthis reportedly advanced to Yemen's strategic Perim Island on Friday, delivering a major boost to the militant group's push to take control of one of the world's most important shipping choke points.
The capture of Perim Island, which was reported by several news agencies, citing multiple Yemeni government sources, comes just one day after the Houthis seized Yemen's port city of Mokha on the Red Sea coast. CNBC could not independently confirm the report.
The rapid ground offensive is seen as a severe setback to Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni forces it backs and puts Iran and its proxies on course to exercise control over two critically important oil choke points on either side of the Arabian Peninsula: the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Strait of Hormuz.
Perim Island is a small and rocky area of land that divides the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a waterway that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and to global markets.
There are concerns that the Houthis' advance toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could have significant ramifications for global trade, particularly if the militant group ratchets up threats or attacks on Red Sea shipping.
The Houthi advance prompted Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to personally press President Donald Trump for U.S. military intervention, MS NOW reported later Friday, according to a person familiar with the conversations.
The crown prince spoke with Trump twice Thursday and urged him to strike the Iranian-backed group as it closed in on the Bab el-Mandeb. Trump declined, saying the U.S. does not plan to widen its regional military campaign to include the Houthis, according to the person, who was granted anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the conversations. Axios first reported the calls.
A senior administration official told CNBC the U.S. remains focused on protecting core national security interests, including freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, "while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges."
The official added that the U.S. is "in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia."
The capture of Mokha marked a "major blow" to Saudi Arabia as it raises the possibility of the group exerting a tighter grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Hamish Kinnear, principal Middle East and North Africa analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
Mokha is situated about 75 kilometers (46 miles) north of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
"The Houthis were already threatening Saudi shipping from previous positions, but their capture of Mocha opens up the possibility of further advances towards the Bab el-Mandeb coastline and a tighter grip on the chokepoint," Kinnear said in a research note.
As the war continues, Kinnear said both Tehran and Washington believe time is on their side, making a new truce unlikely for now.
"Oil and gas prices, and more specifically refined products such as diesel, will continue to tick upwards while that remains the case – even if US convoys and Strait of Hormuz export alternatives cushion the price impact," Kinnear said.
The strategic importance of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has grown significantly since the start of the U.S. and Israel's war against Iran in late February, with the waterway emerging as an alternative route for crude moving toward Asia.
What next for oil prices?
Oil prices traded sharply lower on Friday, but both major benchmarks could still end the week above $100 per barrel for the first time since mid-May.
International benchmark Brent crude futures with November expiry traded 3.3% lower at $104.21 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with October expiry were last seen 3.4% lower at $99.08.
The resilience of the oil market is being tested by a clearer recognition of the mounting threat to regional supply, strategists at ING said, with energy market participants seen repricing both the duration and severity of the conflict.
Even as flows continue through the Strait of Hormuz, ING's strategists said flows remain well below prewar levels, underlining how fragile the situation has become.
"Saudi energy infrastructure and crude oil exports from the Red Sea are increasingly at risk, with the Houthis in Yemen targeting Saudi Arabia," ING's Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey said in a research note published Friday.
"As the Houthis have taken control of the Red Sea port of Mokha in Yemen, recent events increase the threat to shipping around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," they added.
— Luke Fountain contributed to this report.

2026-09-11

This month, like in September every year, world leaders from the 193 member states of the United Nations are set to descend on the organization’s headquarters in New York for what is termed the “high-level week.”
Discussions will focus on the most important global issues of the day, from climate change to health, as well as international peace and security. At the top of the agenda, most likely, will be the ongoing tensions in the Middle East, the war between the US and Iran, and the war in Gaza.
Like every year, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is slated to address the General Assembly and, like in the past, there will likely be protests from states openly hostile to Israel and possibly even from some of Israel’s friends.
For this edition of The Jerusalem Report, we take a deep dive into the global institution, and look at some of the resolutions against Israel that suggest its inherent biased.
The cover story features an interview with Israel’s Ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon. Now in his second term, Danon told the Report that he has witnessed growing hostility, especially from UN officials.
Ambassador Alan Baker, a former legal officer in the UN’s Office of Legal Affairs and former legal adviser to Israel’s Foreign Ministry, argues that the UN has pushed beyond its legal mandate and needs to undergo reforms.
Asher Fredman, the executive director of the Misgav Institute for National Security and Zionist Strategy, lays out the case for why the US should reconsider its financial backing of a global organization structurally biased against the US and its allies.
Scrutiny of the UN would not be complete without looking at the controversial agency UNRWA. Marcus Sheff, the CEO of the Institute for Monitoring Peace and Cultural Tolerance in School Education, breaks down why the agency is so problematic.
Then there are Jonathan Harounoff, a former spokesman for Israel’s mission to the UN, who takes readers behind the scenes at the institution, and commentator Neville Teller, who highlights how the discredited “Zionism is racism” 1975 resolution is making a comeback.
Meanwhile, Executive Director of UN Watch Hillel Neuer looks at the role of special rapporteurs and why they all turn against Israel.
Pivoting to Israel’s October 27 election, the Report’s staff writer and deputy editor Chani Kaplan asks analysts why there seems to be a dearth of female political leaders. Assaf Shapira, the head of the Israel Democracy Institute’s Political Reform Program, explains why Israel’s electoral system is less representative than in other democratic countries.
Security analyst Dr. Eric R. Mandel interviews award-winning Iran International journalist Negar Mojtahedi about the reality inside Iran.
Sagiv Steinberg, a Middle East geostrategic analyst and communications expert, discusses how a loss of support for Hamas is leaving Palestinian politics with a deepening vacuum.
Abir Gitlin from the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv shares findings of a recent survey that shows how Israelis have reassessed their views on the war with Iran and how the US supports them.
Former Israeli deputy foreign minister and ambassador Danny Ayalon, together with Middle East analyst Moran Alaluf, explore why a ceasefire or agreement can never be enough when an enemy retains the will and capacity to strike again.
Finally, feature writer Dana Ben-Shimon introduces readers to Kulna, a Jerusalem co-existence organization that has stayed strong despite tensions.
While the focus of this edition is on events in Midtown Manhattan, there is plenty here to give you food for thought as you enjoy the High Holy Days with your families.
Chag Sameach

Sinai desalination plant shuts amid fears of contamination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:43:24 UTC
17:43:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Sinai desalination plant shuts amid regional contamination fears from Israeli war on Gaza
Mediterranean water contamination has started threatening drinking water supply to hundreds of thousands of people in North Sinai, after the closure of the largest desalination plant in this north-eastern Egyptian territory.
The state-run North Sinai Drinking Water and Sewage Company was forced to shut down the Kilometre 17 desalination plant earlier this month, citing a rise in Mediterranean water turbidity.
The company said it would take the necessary measures to compensate province residents for the disruption of supply from the plant.
With its annual share from the Nile River, its principal source of fresh water, dwarfed by the growing population and its accelerating agricultural expansion, Egypt has increased reliance on seawater desalination and sewage treatment to satisfy its rising water needs.
The populous Arab country now operates 125 desalination plants, having added dozens of such plants to its desalination capacity over the past decade as part of its water security plans.
These plants include 27 in Sinai which shares borders with the Gaza Strip and Israel.
A brewing problem
North Sinai is home to nine desalination plants that together produce tens of thousands of cubic metres of water each day.
This output meets the basic needs of hundreds of thousands of people in the province.
Kilometre 17 is by far the largest desalination plant in North Sinai. It is designed to produce 300,000 cubic metres of water every day, once its two phases are complete, according to Egyptian media.
Phase I of the plant, which has been shut down because of Mediterranean water contamination, produces 100,000 cubic metres of water every day.
The suspension of the plant's production has caused suffering to people and left them scrambling for alternative sources in a part of the world where bottled water is an unaffordable luxury for many.
"We've been without water from the plant for over two weeks now," Mohamed Nasr, a resident of Arish, the provincial capital of North Sinai, said.
"My daughters and I have to walk a long distance to get the water," he added.
Speaking to The New Arab, he expressed frustration at the current disruption, which compounds the lack of other services in the province.
The North Sinai Drinking Water and Sewage Company said it would distribute drinking water for free in the different cities of the province.
Nasr said, however, that the water trucks operated by the company are nowhere to be found, which adds a layer of financial suffering to people like him, who cannot afford the purchase of water.
"The plant's closure has caused the price of water to surge dramatically in the market," he said.
Nasr revealed that he has to pay 400 Egyptian pounds (roughly $7.8) for a water tank with 2,000 litres in it, from 200 pounds for the same tank earlier.
The tank, he said, meets his family's needs for two or three days only, depending on their consumption.
Located west of Arish, Kilometre 17 plant also serves the other North Sinai cities of Sheikh Zuweid and Rafah, on the border with Gaza.
Gaza connection
North Sinai authorities have yet to determine the reasons for the rise in Mediterranean water turbidity levels.
A technical and environmental team has toured the Kilometre 17 plant on 5 September to investigate these reasons and determine the technical measures needed to re-operate it.
Nobody has succeeded in providing any scientifically-proven reason for the contamination of Mediterranean water off North Sinai.
Some people have, however, linked this contamination, especially the presence of microalgae blooms, to material originating near Egypt's Nile Delta.
Nonetheless, the recent closure of several desalination plants in Israel may point to a common cause.
Israeli scientists are now debating whether sewage flowing from Gaza due to damage by Israel war helped fuel a similar microalgae bloom off the Israeli coast.
Still suffering incessant Israeli attacks, even as the truce sponsored by US President Donald Trump continues to be in effect since October last year, Gaza experiences a severe sewage and sanitation crisis after nearly 90% of its water and waste infrastructure was destroyed.
The war-ravaged territory faces a total collapse of its sanitation system, with tens of thousands of cubic metres of raw sewage flooding streets and displacement camps every day, according to the United Nations.
Regional fallout
If sewage flowing into the Mediterranean proves to be the reason for the contamination of water off the Israeli coast, this would be a problem of Israel's making, political analysts said.
With the same problem causing the disruption of water supply in both Egypt and Israel, it also offers insights into how the effects of Israel's killing and destruction in Gaza cannot be contained inside the Palestinian territory, they added.
"I have seen conditions in Gaza move from bad to worse, with Israel escalating its attacks, despite the ceasefire," Palestinian political analyst Ayman al-Raqab told TNA.
The more such attacks continue, he added, the harder life becomes for the people of Gaza.
He warned against the toll Gaza's destruction would have on neighbouring Mediterranean countries, if action is not taken to rehabilitate the Palestinian territory as soon as possible.
Egypt has been lobbying for reconstructing Gaza to stave off its people's deteriorating humanitarian conditions since the ceasefire came into effect.
With a multibillion dollar reconstruction plan in hand, Cairo has also been exerting tremendous effort–together with other ceasefire mediators–to prevent Israel from derailing the lull in fighting.
On 8 September, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said his country strongly opposed Israeli plans to displace Gaza's population.
He also called for ensuring the entry of sufficient amounts of humanitarian aid into the Palestinian territory.
While the ceasefire continues to hold on paper, the people of Gaza receive a fraction of the humanitarian aid needed, according to international relief organizations, amid reports that Israel blocks up to 65% of the required aid.
These deteriorating humanitarian conditions add to the miserable state of infrastructure in the war-torn territory, something whose effects cannot remain confined to Gaza, analysts said.
"I am confident that the pollution flowing into the sea from Gaza will negatively affect neighbouring countries," al-Raqab said.
"This makes it necessary for the international community to move to improve conditions in the territory before it's too late," he added.

Rebels launch FPV drone attack on Myanmar jets
Unknown

2026-09-11
08:43:20 UTC

- Anti-junta fighters targeted Myanmar's Tada-U Air Base with FPV drones on September 10, 2026, with video showing a hit on a Yak-130 jet's nose.
- Mandalay International Airport, which shares the base's infrastructure, closed for two days as Myanmar's military disputed claims of aircraft damage.
Anti-junta fighters launched a wave of FPV drones at Myanmar’s Tada-U Air Base on September 10, 2026, and video posted online shows one striking the nose of a Yak-130 jet, according to resistance sources.
Myanmar’s military government said the drones were all intercepted before causing any damage.
Journalist Thomas van Linge shared footage on X on September 10 showing an FPV drone hitting the Yak-130’s nose section, which houses part of the aircraft’s onboard electronics and flight controls. Resistance sources said the drones damaged four jets at the base in total, located in Tada-U township roughly 35 km (22 miles) south of Mandalay, Myanmar’s second-largest city.
State-run Myanmar Radio and Television gave a different account, reported by Xinhua. It said security forces detected six FPV “suicide drones” targeting Tada-U’s airfield and surrounding areas, intercepted all of them using counter-drone measures, and safely disposed of the explosives they carried. The report said no one was hurt and no aircraft or runways were damaged.
One fact both sides do not dispute: Mandalay International Airport, which shares infrastructure with the air base, closed for two days starting September 11. Myanmar Airways International and Mingalar Airline canceled flights into and out of the airport as a result.
The Yak-130 is a Russian-made, twin-seat jet built by the Yakovlev Design Bureau as a trainer, though Myanmar’s military has also flown it in ground-attack missions. Myanmar Witness, a London-based group that documents rights abuses in the country, reported in 2022 that it had verified Yak-130s firing unguided rockets and cannon rounds in populated civilian areas.
Thursday’s attack extends a pattern of resistance forces targeting Myanmar’s air power with drones since the military’s 2021 coup. The Kachin Independence Army downed a military Mi-17 transport helicopter with a drone near Shwegu in May 2025. In February 2026, an FPV drone destroyed a radar station at Nant Paung Air Base, and a separate suicide drone struck a Myanmar National Airlines ATR-72 as it prepared for takeoff at Myitkyina Airport.
How much damage the Yak-130s suffered at Tada-U remains unresolved. Resistance groups and Myanmar’s military have given conflicting accounts, and neither side has released footage or evidence that independently confirms the extent of the damage.

The facility’s products are important to Russia’s chemical industry and its associated supply chains.

Berezniki is located approximately 1,500 kilometers in a straight line from Ukraine’s state border. The full extent of the damage to the plant was unknown at the time of publication.
In 2025, the Azot plant was also targeted by Ukrainian drones. The strike briefly disrupted the facility’s production process, after which operations resumed.

Asia’s Economic Integration: A Roadmap for Peacebuilding in the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:43:00 UTC
17:43:00 KST

When the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN, was formed in 1967, the five founding states intended to produce a front against the spread of communism. The venture has since grown to include a total of 11 countries, producing a remarkable set of unforeseen consequences, from becoming the fifth-largest economy in the world to reinforcing peace across a swath of diverse and developing countries.
Instead of pursuing Cold War initiatives, the bloc has become increasingly integrated, tied together through manufacturing supply chains, trade infrastructure, and shared financial institutions like the Chiang Mai Initiative. ASEAN now produces over $4 trillion in GDP and has a population of 678 million people. The collaboration’s biggest success, however, has not simply been increased commerce. With economic integration comes regional stabilization and peace, a consequence further fostered by the signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2020, which includes Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace in the region ever since 1952 with the Treaty of San Francisco, and it serves today as a key example of how market mechanics can drive peacebuilding. In fact, it was ASEAN that eroded tensions from the Konfrontasi war in the early 1960s, and has solidified the climate of peace between the Southeast Asian members ever since.
Economists and politicians have often considered the question of whether trade contributes to peaceful relations between states. The affirmative answer is not novel; however, in the case of ASEAN and the Asia-Pacific, the specifics begin to clarify the theory. Peacebuilding through economic means is more a matter of building economic capacity and trade interdependence than of simply trading goods between nations. This crucial specification turns the Asia-Pacific from a successful case study into a model for peacebuilding elsewhere, and it is one that has been imitated by the Gulf Cooperation Council or, more recently, by the C5 in Central Asia.
Economic interdependence is a consequence of cooperation, occurring over time by building trust and relying on companies that diversify operations across countries. Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize winner in Economic Sciences, has regularly argued for this by pointing out that both prosperity and stability mutually flow from systems or institutions that offer a broad stake in the economic growth of a nation. Thus, when firms create cross-border commerce, war becomes economically unviable and politically undesirable. The principle is not exclusive to the Asia-Pacific, and despite ASEAN’s success, it is clear that outliers perpetuate risks by building up economic barriers instead of interdependence. Examples include relations between North and South Korea or China and Taiwan. The question, therefore, remains: how can peace be built today through economic interdependence, or in other words, how can rivals begin working together in an economic capacity?
Answers learned in the Asia-Pacific could resound further away. In the Middle East, for example, diplomatic efforts for peace in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and Israel and the Palestinian Territories have worked through a long campaign of advocacy; however, it is only with the additional incentives that economic cooperation brings that peace efforts actually remain sustainable and enduring. For Israel and the Palestinian Territories, economic interdependence and a shared aspiration could enhance the ongoing international effort to ameliorate decades-long tensions. Syria offers an immediate test case as well. When the Assad regime fell in 2025 and the United States and the European Union both lifted sanctions, organizations began to move in, building relationships and supporting the fragile new state’s desire for peace. American companies have established power generation projects, the Gulf states and Turkey have signed dozens of economic memoranda of understanding with the new state, and startups like Behti Betak or nonprofit organizations like the Words of Isa are building grassroots relationships aimed at creating a newly integrated Syria, driving peace across the Middle East. Integration leads to interdependence. Interdependence self-reinforces peace.
Peacebuilding of this sort may be especially critical for Israel and the Palestinian Territories, where conflict and violence have persisted for decades before the Gaza War. Reconstruction and reconciliation efforts require that businesses spread their operations across the divide. Organizations like the Portland Trust, based in the United Kingdom, have focused on the region on the basis that economic co-operation and dialogue between the parties is inseparable from diplomatic peacebuilding efforts. And such economic development (alongside political will) can create hope, ambition, and opportunities for Palestinians. The founding Chief Executive of The Portland Trust, Lord Jonathan Kestenbaum, brings a personal history to the work of reconciliation. His family’s own flight from Nazi persecution ultimately led them to the UK, where he grew up, and whilst a student in London, he was General Secretary (mazkir) of Bnei Akiva UK, a branch of the global youth movement. He then studied at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem in the 1980s completing an MA in education, and thereafter helped to build an international training program for young educators. As a dual national at the time, Kestenbaum was conscripted to military service, with this experience influencing his life-long commitment to reconciliation between Palestinians and Israelis with a particular focus on building bridges through economic co-operation.
Lord Kestenbaum returned home to the U.K. after a few years in Jerusalem and gave up his dual nationality, retaining only British citizenship. He helped found the Portland Trust, and spent many years fostering peace efforts between Israelis and Palestinians. This history gave him a grounding in the region, a commitment to co-existence and a familiarity that exemplifies how peacebuilding through commerce is not abstract policy but is instead built through relationships and real-life experiences. The Portland Trust has to date worked extensively to support Palestinians and Israelis through projects like the Palestinian Agriculture Impact Fund and the building of the city of Rawabi.
Personal experiences bring markets together, and when they come together, they accelerate growth and integration among an increasing number of actors. Each of these actors learns to empathize with their business partners, regardless of historical or political differences. The process reinforces peace, builds harmony, and creates trust. In the case of Israel and the Palestinian Territories, the process is needed alongside reconstruction efforts like Trump’s Board of Peace, which aims to produce lasting peace but has yet to break ground.
Peace is not guaranteed through economics; however, throughout the last century, and in the case of the Asia-Pacific, it has become the most reliable mechanism of sustaining peace, cultivating the types of relationships that grow closer instead of farther apart. Private investment adds a financial tie to the process; however, intentional relationships with an empathetic desire for peace fundamentally secure the process. Southeast Asia’s history, compared to Syria’s cautious reopening or Gaza’s Board of Peace, shows that commerce can lay groundwork that politics otherwise cannot. The region will need institutional support, perhaps even at the level of an ASEAN, but the foundation is growing. More inter-state commerce will bring stronger relationships, paving the way forward to a future of peace, stability, and economic growth.

A coach believed to be carrying tourists through one of Switzerland's most scenic Alpine valleys has crashed near the entrance to the country's national park.
A coach overturned on a mountain road in the eastern Swiss canton of Graubünden this week, leaving five people dead and 40 injured, local police said on Friday.
The crash took place on Thursday on a stretch of road linking the villages of Susch and Zernez, deep in the Engadine valley.
"The Dutch coach was travelling from Zernez towards Susch at 4.45 pm. Near the village of Less, it veered off the road in a roadworks area and overturned. Of the 45 adults on board the coach, five died," a police report said.

The Dutch Federation of Travel Agencies (ANVR) told AFP that the coach belonged to the tour company Oad, adding that all passengers were from the Netherlands.
Television footage from Swiss broadcasters showed emergency crews swarming the scene, working around the coach as it lay overturned on an embankment beside the carriageway. Helicopters were seen landing nearby to assist with the response.
According to the ANVR, the coach left the Netherlands on Monday and was on a day trip to Switzerland from Austria when the crash happened.
Zernez sits at the gateway to the Swiss National Park, a rugged Alpine reserve covering more than 100 square kilometres across the Engadine region, and is a popular starting point for visitors exploring the region.
Police say the investigation into the cause of the crash is ongoing.

Reshaping the Mossad: Inside Roman Gofman’s world of spies, Iran, and high-stakes strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:41:11 UTC
17:41:11 KST

Roman Gofman only took office heading the Mossad on June 2 and had little time or opportunity to work a transition with his predecessor. This was because, in a wild twist, David Barnea was part of a lawsuit trying to block his appointment, which only resolved that week.
In that sense and in the sense that the Mossad operates in the shadows, it is hard to talk about Gofman’s accomplishments as the country’s new spymaster.
But in a forward-looking sense, he will likely be one of the most powerful and influential Jews in the world over the coming year. He will have a special focus on the all-important and multi-headed Iran conflict, but also with involvement in Syria, with the US and Russia more broadly, and in combating global terror.
The Jerusalem Post understands that Gofman recognizes that his greatest challenge will probably be calibrating between advancing short-term clandestine kinetic attack or spying operations in Iran versus plans for regime change, which are likely to be a longer-term effort.
Resources will need to be devoted to each, but resources are not endless, and choices and priorities will need to be determined.
If for many years, the Mossad was assigned to thwart and stall Iran’s nuclear program, while such efforts will continue, the agency’s role in tracking and thwarting Tehran’s ballistic missiles program may grow going forward, given the regime’s direct attacks on Israel in recent years. All of this could lead Gofman to push the agency even further into kinetic attack missions, something which has grown in recent years, as opposed to its more traditional role as an intelligence collection agency – though that will still continue.
In addition, Gofman faces a unique fork in the road.
On the one hand, Israel and the US in early 2026 chose to assassinate Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and to go for an accelerated regime change plan, which in a sense broke the ice and has opened up possibilities for more rapid change. On the other hand, the failure of the early 2026 regime change plans means that there will be extra scrutiny on any such future plans, and potentially resistance from Israeli allies, including parts of the Trump administration, to trying again anytime soon.
At this point, presumably Gofman’s view would be that the old Mossad Kurdish revolt plan cannot be reconstituted and that a new plan needs to be rapidly prepared.
Moreover, one of the reasons that Gofman fired the Mossad’s deputy chief “A”, its analysis chief, and its Iran desk chief, was because he believes their former plans for regime change cannot go forward as they were, and must either be heavily modified or entirely altered.
In other words, the Post understands that Gofman did not fire the former Mossad high command officials to transfer blame for the failure of regime change generally to them from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or because of the failure of the Ahmadinejad plan specifically, according to foreign sources. The Ahmadinejad plan was a radical idea attributed to Barnea’s Mossad to replace Khamenei with former Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, who had shifted from arch antisemite, to being willing to cooperate with unexpected partners after being dismissed by the ayatollah.
There has been no formal inquiry into the failure of the Ahmadinejad plan, and looking backward is not a priority for Gofman.
Rather, his focus is on future plans and trying to shift tactics to keep the Iranians on their heels.
His personnel changes were because, generally, the former senior officials’ plan to topple the regime failed and because he needed others with different skills and who could better connect to his mentality for how to operate going forward.
While some have criticized Gofman for not waiting at least six months or so to see how operations and relations with the former Mossad high command members might pan out, his view is that he has no time to waste.
According to his view, the situation with Iran is the most dynamic it has been in decades, and the Mossad needs to be able to jump on any openings that could be to Israel’s advantage, however unexpected, something which new outlooks will help with.
This requires organizational shifts, which can be very difficult to accomplish with any large organization, and often is much easier with some significant high-up personnel changes.
In that sense, the Post understands Gofman will probably adopt a variation of the “death by a thousand cuts” 2021-2022 Naftali Bennett strategy versus Iran, but with more aggressive short-term moves against Iran mixed in to try to accelerate the regime change and threat-reduction process.
He recognizes that Iran 2026 is weaker and more vulnerable than Iran 2021, but is also more ready to directly strike Israel with ballistic missiles, which creates new opportunities and dangers.
So there must be a mix of new versions of the Mossad’s “beepers” sabotage against Hezbollah, which often take 5-10 years to plan and materialize, but also many shorter-term actions with more immediate results (critics will point out that some of these projects may now take longer since Gofman fired three top officials).
Speaking of the “beepers”, the Post has learned that Gofman has a clearer view than ever before that Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, and Iran are really, in one way or another, mostly Iran, and this will also inform how he designs multifront strategic plans.
In addition, Gofman would note that virtually every new Mossad chief makes changes to department heads to assemble new talents and outlooks they deem necessary for strategic shifts.
Exactly where he will take the organization he cannot yet reveal, partially because many actions are classified, and partially because he is still delving into how best to reorganize the Mossad’s structure and processes to optimize the outcomes he is seeking.
But based on his running into the crossfire on October 7, despite being a brigadier general (he ended up being the most senior wounded official of the war), Gofman will be willing to take some risks to achieve certain results which his predecessors might have backed away from.
One area where the Post understands Gofman is likely to continue, and potentially expand, Mossad efforts is the social media influence campaign, which the agency went very public about it versus Iran in 2026.
In fact, the main incident that held up his Mossad appointment approval in court for some months involved a controversy over how, in the IDF, he handled or did not handle a minor-aged Israeli social media influencer, with one of the bottom lines being, regardless of his actions regarding the minor, that he has significant understanding of psychological warfare campaigns.
Some new pieces of Gofman that some are noticing are his resourcefulness and unusual determination to succeed. If his hard work and seriousness were keys to promotion within the IDF, now that he is the first immigrant head of the Mossad since its early years many decades ago, officials are seeing that only a unique character who can adapt to many kinds of roles could reach the top of the pyramid.
At his inaugural event, Netanyahu addressed Gofman and his history as someone who moved to Israel from Belarus at the age of 14, saying, “you paved your own way with 10 fingers,” adding later that Gofman was a successful boxer, finishing second in a competition at age 17.
Will Gofman survive as Mossad Chief if Eisenkot is the next PM
Gofman views himself as a nonpartisan figure politically, and is immediately ready to work to advance the Mossad’s mission, whoever is the next prime minister, whether that be Netanyahu, or Gadi Eisenkot, or Naftali Bennett.
What about the specific, now widely published incident in which Gofman, then a mid-level IDF officer, publicly butted heads with Eisenkot years ago when Eisenkot was the IDF chief?
Gofman would neither back away from his comments in the moment about the need for the IDF to shift to a more aggressive attack posture (comments which he would say were justified after-the-fact of October 7), nor would he view it as having any bearing on their future ability to work together.
Rather, the Post understands that Gofman will pursue the future mission of the Mossad without regard to any past interactions, and even under Netanyahu, he has been willing to voice dissent when necessary.
In June, shortly after taking up his role, when Israel attacked in Beirut against objections (or running into post-attack criticism) from the US, the Post understands that Gofman opposed the strike.
The Israeli attack on Beirut led to a series of additional exchanges between Israel and Iran, and some say led the US to lose focus on the nuclear issue, having lost trust in Israel’s discretion of what attacks made sense on the eve of what many thought would be a major deal between Washington and the Islamic Republic.
Meeting with the CIA, conducting other Mossad foreign relations
On July 22, Gofman made his first trip to the US since being named chief of the Mossad.
Generally, the visit aimed to coordinate US and Israeli positions regarding ongoing negotiations with Iran and the nuclear issue, but the talks were too sensitive to reveal more beyond that at this time.
Broadly speaking, Gofman, like his recent predecessors, recognizes that intelligence cooperation with allies, especially the US, is more critical than ever to achieve Israeli goals.
While critics wondered about how he would handle relations with America, given that his fluency in speaking English (as opposed to reading) is reportedly not at the same level as some recent Mossad chiefs, reviews so far show that Mossad-CIA ties are as strong and effective as ever.
Of course, intelligence chiefs do get even more comfortable with one another over time. Further, Gofman and CIA Director John Ratcliffe are not necessarily expected to immediately introduce their wives to each other as Yossi Cohen and Mike Pompeo did early in their terms in 2017. But plenty of spy chiefs have worked together effectively without such additional pieces.
Gofman also has an edge in some ways, as he had been heavily involved in foreign affairs meetings as Netanyahu’s military secretary. This is something which not all prior Mossad chiefs had as much experience with at the highest levels.
One question which still is unanswered, but regarding which more details will doubtlessly be revealed in the future, is where Gofman stood on the issue of discussions between Israel and the US regarding the nuclear threat at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility.
In July, suddenly Trump and other US officials said that Israeli officials had told them the Islamic Republic was moving toward reassembling and rebuilding aspects of the nuclear weapons program at the site. The US president then used this as a potential reason to return to war and attack specifically at that site.
Various IDF officials have denied that they made claims about any imminent nuclear threat at Pickaxe Mountain.
Besides the US, Gofman is the first Russian-speaking Mossad chief, something which gives him an edge over prior chiefs in conducting aspects of relations with Russia, a country which continues to have a wide variety of impacts on Israeli national security.
Syria and Gaza
The Post previously confirmed reports that Gofman met with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani, as well as the heads of the country’s general and military intelligence services.
Gofman’s involvement in these highly sensitive talks early on in his term only emphasizes both the trust that Netanyahu has in the Mossad chief to handle high-stakes and sensitive issues as well as the idea that even adversaries respect him for being straightforward and not playing games.
More specifically, it is public knowledge that Israel has tried a variety of ways to convey to Syria that it will not quietly ignore any new presence of Turkey in Syrian territory, which could limit Israel’s freedom of action to protect its security interests.
This comes after a recent Israeli attack on a Syrian airport where top Jerusalem officials said that Turkey was setting up a radar and other items.
Regarding Gaza, despite multiple claims in recent months by Innovation, Science, and Technology Minister Gila Gamliel that the Mossad and Gofman had been assigned a project of spiriting Gazans out of the Strip, if they chose to leave willingly, the Post has confirmed for the third time that there is no substance to the claims to date.
Rather, such issues remain in the purview of the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and other agencies. While the Mossad sits in on intergovernmental committee meetings on the issue and may make certain contributions, as all agencies do, it is nowhere near being at the forefront of this project.
As a general matter, it is also worth noting that despite occasional news cycles about Gazans potentially wanting to leave, such as to Somaliland, there are no signs of any large-scale emigration from the Strip. Moreover, the Trump administration has been pushing for some time in the opposite direction, to rebuild Gaza for the Palestinians.
Iran and global terror generally
Another major priority of the Mossad is protecting Jews worldwide from terror plots. In recent years, a large number of these plots – sometimes dozens per year in many different countries – have emanated from Iran.
The Post understands that while obviously the Mossad remains committed to the defensive side of this equation, Gofman sees that changes in the balance of power with Iran may be opening up new opportunities to cut off aspects of these terror plots in a more offensive-minded manner. For Gofman, it will all start and end with Iran.

Hong Kong Tiananmen activists sentenced up to 7 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:40:00 UTC
17:40:00 KST

Hong Kong Tiananmen activists jailed for up to 7 years
September 11, 2026
A Hong Kong court on Friday sentenced three pro-democracy activists who organized annual vigils marking China's deadly 1989 Tiananmen crackdown to between five and seven years in prison under the city's national security law.
The sentences handed down were:
- Lee Cheuk-yan, 69 — seven years
- Chow Hang-tung, 41 — seven years and three months.
- Albert Ho, 74, — five years and two months, after pleading guilty
The three were convicted in August of "incitement to subversion" over their activities with the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, which received a fine of HK$1.5 million ($191,304, €164,768). The alliance had organized annual Tiananmen vigils in Victoria Park.
Defendants deny charges
Judges cited the group's call to "end one-party dictatorship," saying it challenged the legitimacy of Communist Party rule in the Chinese special administrative region.
Lee and Chow denied the subversion charges under Hong Kong's controversial national security law. The defendants also insisted the alliance had not asked people to do anything illegal.
The court rejected arguments that the defendants believed they were acting within the law given Hong Kong's freedoms of speech, which have been severely curtailed since Beijing imposed the law in 2020 following a crackdown mass pro-democracy protests the previous year.
The vigils, once a major annual event in Hong Kong, have been effectively banned under the law.
Chow, a barrister who represented herself, raised both arms and waved at supporters as she was escorted out.
Her mother, Medina Chow, addressed her supporters saying, "For today's verdict, you do not need to be overly saddened. Do not lose heart. And above all, do not feel guilty."
What is the international reaction?
The convictions have drawn criticism from foreign governments and rights groups.
"This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," said Amnesty International's deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks.
Germany and France last month had condemned the verdict against Chow saying that "peaceful advocacy for human rights does not constitute a crime."
Chow was the recipient of Franco-German Human Rights Award in 2023.
Among those arrested under the security law are pro-democracy former media tycoon Jimmy Lai and former student leader Joshua Wong.

CM Suvendu Adhikari tucks into fish-and-pulao bhog at Kalighat temple on the occasion of Kaushiki Amavasya on Thursday
NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Thursday visited Kolkata's Kalighat Temple and partook of the traditional fish and pulao bhog, days after Dhirendra Krishna Shastri triggered a row by asking Bengalis to give up non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja.The visit came as the controversy over Shastri’s remarks continued to grow, with leaders across parties, including the BJP, pushing back against alleged attempts to dictate Bengal’s food habits.

Today is a very big day in our Sanatan culture, a major worship (Mahapuja). Whether it is Kalighat here or Tarapith there, it is happening simultaneously," Adhikari said."State-level worship is being held in Tarapith. Tributes paid to 9/11 victims at Republican midterm convention in Dallas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:37:12 UTC
17:37:12 KST

US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance are scheduled to visit the sites of the 11 September 2001 attacks on Friday, with Trump expected to deliver a speech at the Pentagon.
Emergency responders and military personnel paid tribute those killed in the 11 September 2001 attacks during the Republican Party's midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday.
The usually jovial crowd fell silent as an honour guard performed a solemn bell salute to remember the victims and mark the occasion, the eve of the 25th anniversary of the attacks.
The event saw thousands of people gather at the American Airlines Center to pledge their support for GOP candidates running in the crucial upcoming midterm elections, which will determine the makeup of Congress for the final two years of US President Donald Trump's term.
Trump and Vice President JD Vance are scheduled to visit the sites of the 2001 attacks on Friday, with Trump expected to deliver a speech at the Pentagon.
The National September 11 Memorial & Museum is also planning an event at the 9/11 Memorial plaza in Manhattan, where the families of victims will come together for a ceremony to read aloud the names of the 2,983 people killed in the September 11 attacks and the February 26, 1993, bombing of the World Trade Center.
The museum announced that it would also introduce a seventh moment of silence to honour those who have lost their lives due to health effects from 9/11. It has typically observed six periods of silence to mark major moments of the attacks - when each of the towers were struck, when each fell, and the times of the attacks at the Pentagon as well as the crash of United Airlines Flight 93 in Pennsylvania.
It comes after Trump earlier this week posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom - the US' highest civilian honour - to Welles Crowther, a 24-year-old equities trader and volunteer firefighter from New York who died while rescuing people trapped in the World Trade Center's South Tower.
"Today, in honor of his incredible bravery and all of the other countless unknown acts of heroism that day, it is my privilege to award the very special, the highest honor that we give, highest civilian honor, the Presidential Medal of Freedom. We want to award that to Welles and Welles' family," Trump said while announcing the award.
In New York, thousands of illuminated drones also recreated the Twin Towers in a poignant memorial on Wednesday as part of the anniversary events.
The artwork, titled "2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor," included 2,977 drones, representing each of the lives lost on 9/11.
Writing on X, US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy called it a "breathtaking tribute" that "stands as a solemn reminder of America’s resilience and the extraordinary courage of the heroes and first responders who gave everything."
"To the victims, their families, and all who served: We will never forget," he added.
'Love and solidarity'
In a post on X, Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, also commemorated those who lost their lives in the attacks, which she said had "changed the course of history."
"The attacks on the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and in Pennsylvania shattered lives and fundamentally altered world affairs," she wrote.
"A quarter-century on, Europe remains fully committed to strong ties with the United States," she added.
London Mayor Sadiq Khan also expressed the city's solidarity with New York, writing on social media: "25 years on, London stands with New York, with love and solidarity."
9/11
On 11 September 2001, 19 members of the al-Qaeda terrorist network hijacked four commercial airliners, flying two into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers in New York City and a third into the Pentagon in Virginia. A fourth plane crashed into a field in rural Pennsylvania after passengers fought back against hijackers.

Houthis seize vital Red Sea island for full Bab el-Mandeb control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
08:37:00 UTC
17:37:00 KST

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels took full control of the Bab el-Mandeb Friday when they captured a Red Sea island located in the middle of the vital shipping lane, a local government official and eyewitnesses said.
"Boats carrying armed Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island after government forces withdrew from it yesterday," the official said, referring to an island also known as Perim that divides the strait into lanes.
"The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab el-Mandeb area and Mayyun Island, which is located in the middle of the strait," he added, speaking to Agence France-Presse (AFP) on condition of anonymity.
An eyewitness said gunmen were "deploying along the Bab el-Mandeb shore and are driving around in military vehicles."
Earlier, two sources from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government said its forces had withdrawn from Perim and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, which faces the island.
If the Houthis gain full control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, it could give their backer Iran a critical advantage in the war with the U.S., reducing supplies through a second major transit corridor and sending oil prices surging.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea route since the Iran conflict effectively closed Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil used to flow.
In a further potentially significant development for Riyadh, satellite imagery showed smoke Thursday in the vicinity of Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, which has become a vital means for the kingdom to divert its crude exports from Hormuz.
There was no confirmation from Saudi Arabia of any incident in the area. The Saudi government media office and state oil giant Aramco did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the smoke visible in the imagery verified by Reuters.
Aramco has used the East-West pipeline to ramp up crude flows from Saudi Arabia's eastern coast to the Red Sea to its west after U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iran began six months ago, prompting Tehran to effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi crude supply fell 2.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on the month in August to 6 million bpd, the lowest level in more than three decades, the International Energy Agency said Friday, partly due to the targeting of ships transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait by groups linked to Yemen's Houthis.
Global oil prices were on track to end the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since mid-May, though they were slightly lower Friday after the Financial Times reported that foreign ministers in the Middle East were trying to work out a temporary deal to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Reuters could not immediately verify that report.
Yemeni government forces, meanwhile, indicated they would try to retake areas captured by the Houthi rebels in their lightning offensive this week along the Red Sea coastline.
They announced they would deploy weapons and aircraft to eliminate any movement of the Houthis in strategic areas, including the road leading to the coastal city of Mokha, which the group captured on Thursday along with the Red Sea islands of Hanish.
Military spokesman Colonel Majed al-Nazili called on civilians to avoid using the route between the city of Taiz and Mokha and steer clear of equipment belonging to the Houthis, mountain fighters who withstood years of Saudi airstrikes during Yemen's civil war.
Fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government forces has intensified in recent days, with the Iran-aligned group shifting its focus to control over Yemen's long coastline instead of just the north and the country's most populous areas.
Reuters reported on Thursday that the dramatic Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Tehran's war with the U.S., according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources.
Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close U.S. ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.
While Iran describes the Houthis as an ally, it publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are "not a proxy."
Saudi Arabia has been bombing Houthi targets in Yemen but not the strategic areas the group has seized this week.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called U.S. President Donald Trump twice Thursday and urged him to launch strikes against the Houthis, Axios reported, citing two U.S. officials.
Trump rejected the request and U.S. officials said the administration does not intend to take direct military action against the Houthis at this time, the report said.
According to Axios, the U.S. is increasingly concerned about the rapidly escalating conflict in Yemen and is stepping up support for Saudi Arabia while seeking to avoid direct military involvement.
Gulf foreign ministers plan to meet their Iranian counterpart in a push by Oman and Iran to secure buy-in for a temporary deal to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reported Friday.
The gathering is scheduled to be held Monday in the Omani coastal city of Salalah, the report said, citing two people briefed on the matter.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
